JOHN MEDINA is a developmental molecular biologist and research consultant. He is an affiliate professor of bioengineering at the University of Washington School of Medicine. He was the founding director of two brain research institutes: the Brain Center for Applied Learning Research, at Seattle Pacific University, and the Talaris Research Institute, a nonprofit organization originally focused on how infants encode and process information. Medina lives in Seattle, Washington, with his wife and two boys.
约翰·梅迪纳是一位发育分子生物学家和研究顾问。他是华盛顿大学医学院生物工程系的兼职教授。他曾担任两家脑科学研究所的创始主任：西雅图太平洋大学应用学习研究中心和塔拉里斯研究所（一家非营利组织，最初专注于研究婴儿如何编码和处理信息）。梅迪纳与妻子和两个儿子居住在华盛顿州西雅图市。

Introduction
介绍
GO AHEAD AND MULTIPLY the number 8,388,628 x 2 in your head. Can you do it in a few seconds? There is a young man who can double that number 24 times in the space of a few seconds. He gets it right every time. There is a boy who can tell you the precise time of day at any moment, even in his sleep. There is a girl who can correctly determine the exact dimensions of an object 20 feet away. There is a child who at age 6 drew such vivid and complex pictures, some people ranked her version of a galloping horse over one drawn by da Vinci. Yet none of these children have an IQ greater than 70.
请试着在脑子里计算一下 8,388,628 乘以 2。你能在几秒钟内算出来吗？有个年轻人能在几秒钟内把这个数字翻倍 24 次，而且每次都算对。有个男孩能告诉你任何时刻的准确时间，即使在睡梦中也能做到。有个女孩能准确测量 20 英尺外物体的尺寸。有个孩子 6 岁时就能画出如此生动复杂的图画，以至于有人认为她画的奔马比达·芬奇的作品还要出色。然而，这些孩子的智商都没有超过 70。
The brain is an amazing thing.
大脑真是个神奇的东西。
Your brain may not be nearly so odd, but it is no less extraordinary. Easily the most sophisticated information-transfer system on Earth, your brain is fully capable of taking the little black squiggles in this book and deriving meaning from them. To accomplish this miracle, your brain sends jolts of electricity crackling through hundreds of miles of wires composed of brain cells so small that thousands of them could fit into the period at the end of this sentence. You accomplish all of this in less time than it takes you to blink. Indeed, you have just done it. What’s equally incredible, given our intimate association with it, is this: Most of us have no idea how our brain works.
你的大脑或许没那么奇特，但它同样非凡。作为地球上最精密的讯息传递系统，你的大脑完全能够理解这本书里那些黑色的小符号，并从中解读出意义。为了完成这一奇迹，你的大脑会发出电流，沿着数百英里的神经通路传递信息。这些神经通路由无数微小的脑细胞组成，成千上万个脑细胞加起来才能塞进这句话末尾的句号里。而这一切，你完成得比眨眼还快。事实上，你刚刚就做到了。考虑到我们与大脑的密切联系，同样令人难以置信的是：我们大多数人根本不了解自己的大脑是如何运作的。
12 Brain Rules
12条大脑规则
My goal is to introduce you to 12 things we know about how the brain works. I call these Brain Rules. For each rule, I present the science, introduce you to the researchers behind it, and then offer ideas for how the rule might apply to our daily lives, especially at work and school. The brain is complex, and I am taking only slivers of information from each subject—not comprehensive but, I hope, accessible. Here is a sampling of the ideas you’ll encounter:
我的目标是向你介绍我们目前所知的关于大脑运作的12条规则。我称之为“大脑规则”。对于每一条规则，我都会阐述其背后的科学原理，介绍研究者，并提出一些关于这些规则如何应用于我们日常生活，尤其是在工作和学习中的想法。大脑非常复杂，我只选取每个主题的一小部分信息——并非面面俱到，但我希望这些信息易于理解。以下是你将接触到的一些观点示例：
•We are not used to sitting at a desk for eight hours a day. From an evolutionary perspective, our brains developed while we walked or ran as many as 12 miles a day. The brain still craves this experience. That’s why exercise boosts brain power (Brain Rule #2) in sedentary populations like our own. Exercisers outperform couch potatoes in long-term memory, reasoning, attention, and problem-solving tasks.
我们不习惯每天坐在办公桌前八个小时。从进化角度来看，我们的大脑是在每天步行或跑步多达12英里（约19公里）的情况下发育的。大脑仍然渴望这种体验。这就是为什么运动能够提升像我们这样久坐人群的脑力（大脑法则之二）。在长期记忆、推理、注意力以及解决问题的能力方面，运动者都优于久坐不动的人。
•As you no doubt have noticed if you’ve ever sat through a typical PowerPoint presentation, people don’t pay attention to boring things (Brain Rule #6). You’ve got seconds to grab someone’s attention and only 10 minutes to keep it. At 9 minutes and 59 seconds, you must do something to regain attention and restart the clock—something emotional and relevant. Also, the brain needs a break. That’s why I use stories in this book to make many of my points.
•如果你曾经完整地看过一场典型的PPT演示，你肯定已经注意到，人们对枯燥乏味的内容毫无兴趣（大脑法则#6）。你只有几秒钟的时间来抓住别人的注意力，却只有10分钟的时间来保持他们的注意力。在9分59秒的时候，你必须做些事情来重新吸引他们的注意力，重新开始计时——一些能引起共鸣且与他们相关的内容。此外，大脑也需要休息。这就是为什么我在这本书中运用故事来阐述我的许多观点。
•Ever feel tired about three o’clock in the afternoon? That’s because your brain really wants to take a nap. You might be more productive if you did. In one study, a 26-minute nap improved NASA pilots’ performance by 34 percent. And whether you get enough rest at night affects your mental agility the next day. Sleep well, think well (Brain Rule #3) .
•下午三点左右感到疲倦吗？那是因为你的大脑真的想打个盹儿。如果你睡个午觉，效率可能会更高。一项研究表明，NASA飞行员午睡26分钟后，表现提高了34%。而且，你晚上是否睡够觉也会影响你第二天的思维敏捷度。睡得好，思维好（大脑法则#3）。
•We’ll meet a man who can remember everything he reads after seeing the words just once. Most of us do more forgetting than remembering, of course, and that’s why we must repeat to remember (Brain Rule #7). When you understand the brain’s rules for memory, you’ll see why I want to destroy the notion of homework.
我们会遇到一位只看一遍就能记住所有内容的人。当然，我们大多数人遗忘远多于记住，所以我们必须重复才能记住（大脑法则#7）。当你理解了大脑的记忆法则，你就会明白我为什么想要废除家庭作业的概念。
•We’ll find out why the terrible twos only look like active rebellion but actually are a child’s powerful urge to explore. Babies may not have a lot of knowledge about the world, but they know a whole lot about how to get it. We are powerful and natural explorers (Brain Rule #12). This never leaves us, despite the artificial environments we’ve built for ourselves.
我们将探究为什么“可怕的两岁”看起来像是叛逆，实际上却是孩子强烈的探索欲望。婴儿或许对世界知之甚少，但他们却非常清楚如何获取信息。我们天生就是强大的探索者（大脑法则第12条）。即便我们为自己构建了人为的环境，这种探索精神也从未消失。
The grump factor
暴躁因素
I am a nice guy, but I am a grumpy scientist. For a study to appear in this book, it has to pass what some of my clients call MGF: the Medina Grump Factor. That means the supporting research for each of my points must first be published in a peer-reviewed journal and then successfully replicated. Many of the studies have been replicated dozens of times. (To stay as reader-friendly as possible, extensive references are not in this book but can be found at www.brainrules.net/references .)
我人很好，但作为一名科学家，我脾气有点古怪。本书收录的研究必须通过我一些客户所谓的“麦地那脾气因子”（MGF）。这意味着，我提出的每个观点所依据的研究必须首先发表在同行评审期刊上，然后才能被成功重复验证。许多研究已经被重复验证了数十次。（为了尽可能方便读者，本书未列出详尽的参考文献，但您可以在www.brainrules.net/references上找到。）
No prescriptions
无需处方
There’s a great deal we don’t know about the brain. I am a developmental molecular biologist specializing in psychiatric disorders. I have been a private consultant for most of my professional life, working on countless research projects beyond the lab bench. Over and over in my career, I have seen what a distance there is between a gene (one’s DNA instructions) and a behavior (how a person actually acts). It’s very hard to say with certainty that a specific behavior is caused by a specific gene, or that changing X behavior will produce Y result. Occasionally, I would run across articles and books that made startling claims based on “recent advances” in brain science about how we should teach people and do business. The Mozart Effect comes to mind: the popular idea that listening to classical music makes students better at math. Or the notion that analytical people are “left brain” people and creative people are “right brain” people, and each must be managed accordingly. Sometimes I would panic, wondering if the authors were reading some literature totally off my radar screen. I speak several dialects of brain science, and I knew nothing from those worlds capable of dictating best practices for education and business. In truth, if we ever fully understood how the human brain knew how to pick up a glass of water, it would represent a major achievement. There was no need for me to panic. Brain research still cannot without equivocation tell us how to become better teachers, parents, business leaders, or students. In addition to the ideas you’ll find within each chapter, I end each chapter a few more potential ways to apply the research in our daily lives. But these are not prescriptions. They are hypotheses. If you try them, you will be doing your own little research project to see whether they work for you.
我们对大脑的了解还非常有限。我是一名发育分子生物学家，专攻精神疾病。我的职业生涯大部分时间都在担任私人顾问，参与了无数实验室之外的研究项目。在我的职业生涯中，我一次又一次地看到基因（DNA指令）和行为（一个人的实际行为方式）之间存在着巨大的鸿沟。我们很难确定某种特定行为是由某个特定基因引起的，或者改变某种行为就会产生某种结果。有时，我会看到一些文章和书籍，它们基于脑科学的“最新进展”提出了一些惊人的论断，声称我们应该如何教育他人以及如何开展业务。“莫扎特效应”就是一个例子：这种流行的观点认为，听古典音乐可以提高学生的数学成绩。或者，有人认为分析型人才属于“左脑型”，而创造型人才属于“右脑型”，应该分别进行相应的管理。有时我会感到恐慌，怀疑作者是不是读了一些我完全不了解的文献。我精通脑科学的几个分支，但我从未听说过这些领域有任何理论能够指导教育和商业的最佳实践。事实上，如果我们真的能够完全理解人脑是如何拿起一杯水的，那将是一项重大成就。我完全不必惊慌。脑科学研究至今仍无法明确地告诉我们如何成为更好的教师、父母、商业领袖或学生。除了每章中的观点之外，我还会在每章结尾提出一些将研究成果应用于日常生活的潜在方法。但这些并非既定方案，而是假设。如果你尝试这些方法，就相当于在进行一项小型研究，看看它们是否对你有效。
Back to the jungle
回到丛林
What we know about the brain comes from biologists who study brain tissues, experimental psychologists who study behavior, cognitive neuroscientists who study how the first relates to the second, and evolutionary biologists. Though we know precious little about how the brain works, our evolutionary history tells us this: The brain appears to be designed to (1) solve problems (2) related to surviving (3) in an unstable outdoor environment, and (4) to do so in nearly constant motion. I call this the brain’s performance envelope.
我们对大脑的了解主要来自研究脑组织的生物学家、研究行为的实验心理学家、研究二者关系的认知神经科学家以及进化生物学家。尽管我们对大脑的运作机制知之甚少，但进化史告诉我们：大脑似乎被设计成能够（1）解决与生存相关的问题；（2）在不稳定的户外环境中；（3）并且几乎在持续运动中完成这些任务。我称之为大脑的性能极限。
Each subject in this book—exercise, sleep, stress, wiring, attention, memory, sensory integration, vision, music, gender, and exploration—relates to this performance envelope. We were in motion, getting lots of exercise. Environmental instability led to the extremely flexible way our brains are wired, allowing us to solve problems through exploration. To survive in the great outdoors, we needed to learn from our mistakes. That meant paying attention to certain things at the expense of others, and it meant creating memories in a particular way. Though we have been stuffing them into classrooms and cubicles for decades, our brains actually were built to survive in jungles and grasslands. We have not outgrown this.
本书中的每个主题——运动、睡眠、压力、神经连接、注意力、记忆、感觉统合、视觉、音乐、性别和探索——都与这种表现模式息息相关。我们曾经处于运动状态，进行大量的锻炼。环境的不稳定性造就了我们大脑极其灵活的连接方式，使我们能够通过探索解决问题。为了在广袤的户外生存，我们需要从错误中学习。这意味着我们需要关注某些事物而忽略其他事物，也意味着我们需要以特定的方式创造记忆。尽管几十年来，我们的大脑一直被塞进教室和格子间，但实际上，我们的大脑原本是为了在丛林和草原中生存而构建的。我们并没有超越这种生存本能。
Because we don’t fully understand how our brains work, we do dumb things. We try to talk on our cell phones and drive at the same time, even though it is literally impossible for our brains to multitask when it comes to paying attention. We have created high-stress office environments, even though a stressed brain is significantly less productive than a non-stressed brain. Our schools are designed so that most real learning has to occur at home. Taken together, what do the studies in this book show? Mostly this: If you wanted to create an education environment that was directly opposed to what the brain was good at doing, you probably would design something like a classroom. If you wanted to create a business environment that was directly opposed to what the brain was good at doing, you probably would design something like a cubicle. And if you wanted to change things, you might have to tear down both and start over.
因为我们对大脑的运作方式了解不足，所以我们才会做出愚蠢的事情。我们试图一边开车一边打电话，尽管我们的大脑在注意力集中方面根本无法同时处理多项任务。我们创造了高压的办公环境，尽管压力下的大脑效率远低于压力下的大脑。我们的学校设计使得大部分真正的学习都必须在家里进行。那么，本书中的研究综合起来表明了什么呢？主要结论是：如果你想创造一个与大脑擅长的运作方式截然相反的教育环境，你可能会设计出类似教室的模式。如果你想创造一个与大脑擅长的运作方式截然相反的商业环境，你可能会设计出类似隔间的工作空间。而如果你想改变现状，你可能不得不推倒重来。
Blame it on the fact that brain scientists rarely have a conversation with teachers and business professionals, education majors and accountants, superintendents and CEOs. Unless you have the Journal of Neuroscience sitting on your coffee table, you’re out of the loop.
这要归咎于脑科学家很少与教师、商业人士、教育专业学生、会计师、校长和首席执行官交流。除非你的咖啡桌上放着《神经科学杂志》，否则你根本跟不上时代。
This book is meant to get you into the loop.
这本书旨在让你了解情况。
Survival: Why your brain is so amazing
生存之道：为什么你的大脑如此神奇
Brain Rule #1: The human brain evolved, too
大脑法则第一条：人类大脑也是进化而来的。
When he was 4, my son Noah picked up a stick in our backyard and showed it to me. “Nice stick you have there, young fellow,” I said. He replied earnestly, “That’s not a stick. That’s a sword! Stick ’em up!” I raised my hands to the air. We both laughed. As I went back into the house, I realized my son had just displayed virtually every unique thinking ability a human possesses—one that took several million years to manufacture. And he did so in less than two seconds. Heavy stuff for a 4-year-old. Other animals have powerful cognitive abilities, too, and yet there is something qualitatively different about the way humans think. How and why did our brains evolve this way?
儿子诺亚四岁那年，在后院捡起一根树枝给我看。“你这树枝不错啊，小家伙，”我说。他认真地回答：“这不是树枝，这是剑！举起来！”我举起双手。我们俩都笑了。回到屋里后，我意识到儿子刚刚展现了人类几乎所有独特的思维能力——这些能力历经数百万年才进化而来。而他只用了不到两秒钟就做到了。这对一个四岁的孩子来说，确实很了不起。其他动物也拥有强大的认知能力，但人类的思维方式却有着本质的不同。我们的大脑是如何进化成这样的？又为何如此？
A survival strategy
生存策略
It all comes down to sex. Our bodies latched on to any genetic adaptation that helped us survive long enough to pass our genes on to the next generation. There’s no bigger rule in biology than evolution through natural selection, and the brain is a biological tissue. So it too follows the rule of natural selection.
这一切都与性有关。我们的身体会保留任何有助于我们生存并把基因传递给下一代的遗传适应性。生物学中最重要的法则莫过于自然选择导致的进化，而大脑也是一种生物组织，因此它也遵循自然选择的规律。
There are two ways to beat the cruelty of a harsh environment: You can become stronger or you can become smarter. We did the latter. It seems most improbable that such a physically weak species could take over the planet not by adding muscles to our skeletons but by adding neurons to our brains. But we did, and scientists have expended a great deal of effort trying to figure out how. I want to explore four major concepts that not only set the stage for all of the Brain Rules, but also explain how we came to conquer the world.
面对严酷环境的残酷，有两种方法可以战胜它：要么变得更强壮，要么变得更聪明。我们选择了后者。一个体格如此弱小的物种，竟然能够征服地球，而征服地球的方式并非增强骨骼肌肉，而是增加大脑神经元，这听起来似乎难以置信。但我们做到了，科学家们也为此投入了大量精力，试图揭开其中的奥秘。我想探讨四个核心概念，它们不仅为所有“大脑法则”奠定了基础，也解释了我们是如何征服世界的。
We can make things up
我们可以编造故事
One trait really does separate us from the gorillas: the ability to use symbolic reasoning. When we see a five-sided geometric shape, we’re not stuck perceiving it as a pentagon. We can just as easily perceive the US military headquarters. Or a Chrysler minivan. Our brains can behold a symbolic object as real by itself and yet, simultaneously, also representing something else. That’s what my son was doing when he brandished his stick sword. Researcher Judy DeLoache calls it Dual Representational Theory. Stated formally, it describes our ability to attribute characteristics and meanings to things that don’t actually possess them. Stated informally, we can make things up that aren’t there. We are human because we can fantasize.
确实有一项特质将我们与大猩猩区分开来：那就是运用符号推理的能力。当我们看到一个五边形几何图形时，我们并不会局限于将其视为五边形。我们同样可以将其视为美国军事总部，或者一辆克莱斯勒小型货车。我们的大脑能够将一个符号对象视为真实存在，同时又将其视为其他事物的象征。我儿子挥舞着他的棍剑时，正是如此。研究员朱迪·德洛奇称之为双重表征理论。正式地说，它描述了我们能够将某些特征和意义赋予那些实际上并不具备这些特征和意义的事物。通俗地说，我们可以虚构出并不存在的事物。我们之所以是人类，正是因为我们拥有想象力。
We are so good at dual representation, we combine symbols to derive layers of meaning. It gives us the capacity for language, and for writing down that language. It gives us the capacity to reason mathematically. It gives us the capacity for art. Combinations of circles and squares become geometry and Cubist paintings. Combinations of dots and squiggles become music and poetry. There is an unbroken intellectual line between symbolic reasoning and the ability to create culture. And no other creature is capable of doing it.
我们如此擅长双重表征，以至于能够组合符号来推导出多层次的意义。这赋予了我们语言的能力，以及书写语言的能力。这赋予了我们数学推理的能力。这赋予了我们艺术的能力。圆形和正方形的组合构成了几何图形和立体主义绘画。点和曲线的组合构成了音乐和诗歌。符号推理和创造文化的能力之间存在着一条清晰的逻辑纽带。而其他任何生物都无法做到这一点。
The all-important human trait of symbolic reasoning helped our species not only survive but thrive. Our evolutionary ancestors didn’t have to keep falling into the same quicksand pit if they could tell others about it; even better if they learned to put up warning signs. With words, with language, we could extract a great deal of knowledge about our living situation without always having to experience its harsh lessons directly. It makes sense that once our species evolved to have symbolic reasoning, we kept it. So what was it about our environment that would give a survival advantage to those who could reason symbolically?
符号推理这一至关重要的人类特质不仅帮助我们物种生存下来，而且促进了它们的繁荣发展。如果我们的进化祖先能够将危险告知他人，他们就不必反复陷入同一个流沙陷阱；如果他们还能设置警示标志，那就更好了。借助语言，我们可以获取大量关于生存环境的信息，而无需总是亲身经历其残酷的教训。因此，一旦我们物种进化出符号推理能力，我们就保留了它，这也就不足为奇了。那么，究竟是什么样的环境因素，使得那些能够进行符号推理的人拥有生存优势呢？
We adapted to variation itself
我们适应了变化本身。
Most of what we know about the intellectual progress of our species is based on evidence of toolmaking. That’s not necessarily the most accurate indicator, but it’s the best we’ve got. For the first few million years, the record is not very impressive: We mostly just grabbed rocks and smashed them into things. Scientists, perhaps trying to salvage some of our dignity, called these stones “hand axes.” A million years later, we still grabbed “hand axes,” but we began to smash them into other rocks, making them more pointed. Now we had sharper rocks. It wasn’t much, but it was enough to begin untethering ourselves from a sole reliance on our East African womb, and indeed any other ecological niche. Then things started to get interesting. We created fire and started cooking our food. Eventually, we migrated out of Africa in successive waves, our direct Homo sapiens ancestors making the journey as little as 100,000 years ago. Then, 40,000 years ago, something almost unbelievable happened. Our ancestors suddenly took up painting and sculpture, creating fine art and jewelry. This change was both abrupt and profound. Thirty-seven thousand years later, we were making pyramids. Five thousand years after that, rocket fuel.
我们对人类智力发展的了解大多基于工具制造的证据。这未必是最精确的指标，但却是我们所能掌握的最佳证据。最初几百万年，我们的记录并不令人印象深刻：我们基本上只是抓起石头，把它们砸成各种东西。科学家们或许是为了挽回一些颜面，把这些石头称为“手斧”。一百万年后，我们仍然抓着“手斧”，但我们开始用它们敲击其他石头，使它们变得更加尖锐。现在我们有了更锋利的石头。虽然进步不大，但这足以让我们开始摆脱对东非母体，乃至任何其他生态位的依赖。之后，事情开始变得有趣起来。我们学会了用火，开始烹饪食物。最终，我们分批迁徙出非洲，我们的智人直系祖先早在10万年前就完成了这段旅程。然后，在4万年前，一件几乎难以置信的事情发生了。我们的祖先突然开始从事绘画和雕塑，创作出精美的艺术品和珠宝。这种转变既突然又意义深远。三万七千年后，我们建造了金字塔。又过了五千年，我们研制出了火箭燃料。
Many scientists think our growth spurt can be explained by the onset of dual-representation ability. And many think our dual-representation ability—along with physical changes that precipitated it—can be explained by a nasty change in the weather.
许多科学家认为，我们的生长突增可以用双重表征能力的出现来解释。而许多人则认为，我们的双重表征能力——以及引发这种能力的生理变化——可以用恶劣的天气变化来解释。
Most of human prehistory occurred in junglelike climates: steamy, humid, and in dire need of air-conditioning. This was comfortably predictable. Then the climate changed. Ice cores taken from Greenland show that the climate staggers from being unbearably hot to being sadistically cold. As little as 100,000 years ago, you could be born in a nearly arctic environment but then, mere decades later, be taking off your loincloth to catch the golden rays of the grassland sun. Such instability was bound to have a powerful effect on any creature forced to endure it. Most could not. The rules for survival were changing, and a new class of creatures would start to fill the vacuum created as more and more of their roommates died out.
人类史前时期的大部分时间都生活在类似丛林的气候中：闷热潮湿，亟需空调。这种气候舒适宜人，也在意料之中。然而，气候随后发生了变化。从格陵兰岛采集的冰芯显示，气候在酷热难耐和严寒之间剧烈波动。仅仅10万年前，你可能出生在近乎北极的环境中，但仅仅几十年后，你却可能脱下腰布，沐浴在草原的金色阳光下。这种气候的不稳定性必然会对任何被迫忍受的生物产生巨大的影响。大多数生物都无法适应。生存法则正在改变，随着越来越多的同类灭绝，一种新的生物开始填补由此产生的真空。
The change was enough to shake us out of our comfortable trees, but it wasn’t violent enough to kill us when we landed. Landing was only the beginning of the hard work, however. Faced with grasslands rather than trees, we were rudely introduced to the idea of “flat.” We quickly discovered that our new digs were already occupied. The locals had co-opted the food sources, and most of them were stronger and faster than we were. It is disconcerting to think that we started our evolutionary journey on an unfamiliar horizontal plane with the words “Eat me, I’m prey” taped to our evolutionary butts.
这种变化足以让我们从舒适的树上摔下来，但落地时却不足以致命。然而，着陆仅仅是艰苦征程的开始。面对的是草原而非树林，我们被粗暴地告知了“平坦”的概念。我们很快发现，我们的新家早已被占据。当地居民已经占领了食物来源，而且它们中的大多数都比我们更强壮、更敏捷。想到我们进化之旅的起点竟然是在一片陌生的水平面上，屁股上仿佛贴着“吃我吧，我是猎物”的字样，真是令人不安。
You might suspect that the odds against our survival were great. You would be right. The founding population of our direct ancestors is not thought to have been much larger than 2,000 individuals; some think the group was as small as a few hundred. How, then, did we go from such a wobbly, fragile minority population to a staggering tide of humanity seven billion strong and growing?
你或许会觉得我们生存下来的几率微乎其微。你的想法是对的。据信，我们直系祖先的创始人口不超过2000人；有些人甚至认为只有几百人。那么，我们是如何从这样一个摇摇欲坠、脆弱的少数群体，发展成为如今拥有70亿人口且仍在不断增长的庞大人类群体的呢？
There is only one way, according to Richard Potts, director of the Human Origins Program at the Smithsonian’s National Museum of Natural History. We gave up on stability. We began not to care about consistency within a given habitat, because consistency wasn’t an option. We adapted to variation itself. Those unable to rapidly solve new problems or learn from mistakes didn’t survive long enough to pass on their genes. The net effect of this evolution was that rather than becoming stronger, we became smarter. It was a brilliant strategy. We went on to conquer other ecological niches in Africa. Then we took over the world.
史密森尼国家自然历史博物馆人类起源项目主任理查德·波茨认为，只有一条路可走。我们放弃了稳定。我们开始不再在意特定栖息地内的一致性，因为一致性已不再可行。我们适应了变化本身。那些无法迅速解决新问题或从错误中吸取教训的人，无法生存到足以将基因传递下去。这种进化的最终结果是，我们并没有变得更强壮，而是变得更聪明。这是一个绝妙的策略。我们继续征服了非洲的其他生态位。然后，我们统治了世界。
Potts’s theory predicts some fairly simple things about human learning. It predicts interactions between two powerful features of the brain: a database in which to store a fund of knowledge, and the ability to improvise off that database. One allows us to know when we’ve made mistakes. The other allows us to learn from them. Both give us the ability to add new information under rapidly changing conditions. And both are relevant to the way we design classrooms and cubicles. We’ll uncover more about this database in the Memory chapter.
波茨的理论对人类学习做出了一些相当简单的预测。它预测了大脑两个强大功能之间的相互作用：一个是存储知识库的数据库，另一个是基于该数据库进行即兴发挥的能力。前者使我们能够知道自己何时犯了错误，后者使我们能够从错误中学习。两者都赋予我们在快速变化的环境中添加新信息的能力。而且，两者都与我们设计教室和隔间的方式息息相关。我们将在“记忆”章节中更深入地探讨这个数据库。
Bigger and bigger brains
越来越大的大脑
Adapting to variation provides a context for symbolic reasoning, but it hardly explains our unique ability to invent calculus and write romance novels. After all, many animals create a database of knowledge, and many of them make tools, which they use creatively. Still, it is not as if chimpanzees write symphonies badly and we write them well. Chimps can’t write them at all, and we can write ones that make people spend their life savings on subscriptions to the New York Philharmonic. There must have been something else in our evolutionary history that gave rise to unique human thinking.
适应变化为符号推理提供了背景，但这很难解释我们发明微积分和创作言情小说的独特能力。毕竟，许多动物都会建立知识库，许多动物还会制造工具并进行创造性使用。然而，这并不意味着黑猩猩创作的交响乐很糟糕，而我们创作得很好。黑猩猩根本无法创作交响乐，而我们却能创作出让人们倾尽毕生积蓄订阅纽约爱乐乐团的交响乐。在我们的进化史中，必然存在其他因素，造就了人类独特的思维方式。
One of the random genetic mutations that gave us an adaptive advantage involved walking upright on two legs. Because the trees were gone or going, we needed to travel increasingly long distances between food sources. Walking on two legs instead of four both freed up our hands and used fewer calories. It was energy-efficient. Our ancestral bodies used the energy surplus not to pump up our muscles but to pump up our minds.
赋予我们适应性优势的随机基因突变之一，便是让我们能够直立行走。由于树木消失或正在减少，我们需要在食物来源之间跋涉越来越远的距离。用两条腿行走而不是四条腿，既解放了我们的双手，又减少了卡路里的消耗。这是一种高效的能量利用方式。我们的祖先并没有将多余的能量用于增强肌肉，而是用于提升大脑功能。
This led to the masterpiece of evolution, the region that distinguishes humans from all other creatures. It is a specialized area of the frontal lobe, just behind the forehead, called the prefrontal cortex. What does the prefrontal cortex do? We got our first hints from a man named Phineas Gage, who suffered the most famous occupational injury in the history of brain science.
这造就了进化史上最伟大的杰作——人类区别于其他所有生物的区域。它是额叶的一个特殊区域，位于前额后方，被称为前额皮质。前额皮质的功能是什么？我们最初的线索来自一位名叫菲尼亚斯·盖奇的人，他遭受了脑科学史上最著名的职业伤害。
Gage was a popular foreman of a railroad construction crew. He was funny, clever, hardworking, and responsible, the kind of guy any father would be proud to call “son-in-law.” On September 13, 1848, he set an explosives charge in the hole of a rock using a tamping iron, a three-foot rod about an inch in diameter. The charge blew the rod into Gage’s head. It entered just under the eye and destroyed most of his prefrontal cortex. Miraculously, Gage survived. But he became tactless, impulsive, and profane. He left his family and wandered aimlessly from job to job. His friends said he was no longer Gage.
盖奇是铁路施工队里一位很受欢迎的工头。他风趣幽默、聪明能干、勤奋负责，是那种任何父亲都会引以为傲的“女婿”。1848年9月13日，他用一根三英尺长、直径约一英寸的捣棒，在岩石的孔洞里放置了一枚炸药。炸药爆炸后，捣棒飞进了盖奇的头部。它从眼下进入，摧毁了他大部分的前额叶皮层。奇迹般地，盖奇活了下来。但他变得粗鲁无礼、冲动易怒、满口脏话。他离开了家人，漫无目的地四处漂泊，辗转于各个工作之间。他的朋友们说，他已经不再是以前的盖奇了。
When damage occurs to a specific brain region, we know that any observed behavioral abnormality must in some way be linked to that region’s function. I describe several such cases throughout the book for this reason. Gage’s case was the first real evidence that the prefrontal cortex governs several uniquely human cognitive talents, called “executive functions”: solving problems, maintaining attention, and inhibiting emotional impulses. In short, this region controls many of the behaviors that separate us from other animals (and from teenagers).
当大脑特定区域受损时，我们知道任何观察到的行为异常都必然与该区域的功能存在某种关联。因此，我在书中描述了几个这样的案例。盖奇的案例是第一个确凿的证据，表明前额叶皮层控制着几种人类特有的认知能力，即所谓的“执行功能”：解决问题、保持注意力以及抑制情绪冲动。简而言之，这个区域控制着许多将我们与其他动物（以及青少年）区分开来的行为。
Three brains in one
三脑合一
The prefrontal cortex, however, is only the newest addition to the brain. Three brains are tucked inside your head, and parts of their structure took millions of years to design. Your most ancient neural structure is the brain stem, or “lizard brain.” This rather insulting label reflects the fact that the brain stem functions the same way in you as in a Gila monster. The brain stem controls most of your body’s housekeeping chores: breathing, heart rate, sleeping, waking. Lively as Las Vegas, these neurons are always active, keeping your brain buzzing along whether you’re napping or wide awake.
然而，前额叶皮层只是大脑中最新的一部分。你的头部内藏着三个大脑，它们的结构部分历经数百万年才得以形成。你最古老的神经结构是脑干，也就是所谓的“蜥蜴脑”。这个略带侮辱性的称呼反映了这样一个事实：你的脑干和吉拉毒蜥的脑干功能几乎相同。脑干控制着你身体的大部分日常运作：呼吸、心率、睡眠和觉醒。这些神经元如同拉斯维加斯般活跃，时刻保持运转，无论你是小憩还是清醒，它们都让你的大脑高速运转。
Sitting atop your brain stem is your “mammalian brain.” It appears in you the same way it does in many mammals, such as house cats, which is how it got its name. It has more to do with your animal survival than with your human potential. Most of its functions involve what some researchers call the “four Fs”: fighting, feeding, fleeing, and … reproductive behavior. Several parts of the mammalian brain play a large role in the Brain Rules.
位于脑干顶部的是你的“哺乳动物脑”。它在你体内的形态与许多哺乳动物（例如家猫）体内的形态相同，这也是它得名的原因。它与你的动物生存关系更大，而非与你的人类潜能关系更大。它的大部分功能都与一些研究人员所说的“四F”有关：战斗、觅食、逃跑和……繁殖行为。哺乳动物脑的几个部分在大脑规则中发挥着重要作用。
The amygdala allows you to feel rage. Or fear. Or pleasure. Or memories of past experiences of rage, fear, or pleasure. The amygdala is responsible for both the creation of emotions and the memories they generate. We’ll explore the powerful effects of emotions, and how to harness them, in the Attention chapter.
杏仁核让你感受到愤怒、恐惧、愉悦，以及过去愤怒、恐惧或愉悦的记忆。杏仁核既负责情绪的产生，也负责情绪所生成的记忆。在“注意力”这一章中，我们将探讨情绪的强大影响，以及如何驾驭它们。
The hippocampus converts your short-term memories into longer-term forms. The Memory chapter covers the surprising way that happens, and the key to remembering.
海马体负责将你的短期记忆转化为长期记忆。记忆章节将详细介绍这一过程的奇妙之处，以及记忆的关键所在。
The thalamus is one of the most active, well-connected parts of the brain—a control tower for the senses. Sitting squarely in the center of your brain, it processes and routes signals sent from nearly every corner of your sensory universe. We’ll return to this bizarre, complex process in the Sensory Integration chapter .
丘脑是大脑中最活跃、连接最紧密的区域之一，堪称感觉的控制中心。它位于大脑正中央，负责处理和传递来自几乎所有感觉器官的信号。我们将在“感觉统合”章节中详细探讨这一奇特而复杂的过程。
Folded atop all of this is your “human brain,” a layer called the cortex. Unfolded, this layer would be about the size of a baby blanket, with a thickness ranging from that of blotting paper to that of heavy-duty cardboard. It is in deep electrical communication with the interior. Neurons spark to life, then suddenly blink off, then fire again. Complex circuits of electrical information crackle in coordinated, repeated patterns, racing to communicate their information along large neural highways that branch suddenly into thousands of exits. As we’ll see in the Wiring chapter, these branches are different in every single one of us. Each region of the cortex is highly specialized, with sections for speech, for vision, for memory.
在这一切之上，折叠着你的“人脑”，也就是大脑皮层。展开后，这一层大约只有婴儿毯那么大，厚度从吸墨纸到厚纸板不等。它与内部组织进行着深入的电信号交流。神经元会突然活跃起来，然后又突然熄灭，接着再次活跃起来。复杂的电信号回路以协调的、重复的模式噼啪作响，沿着庞大的神经通路争分夺秒地传递信息，这些通路会突然分支成成千上万个出口。正如我们将在“神经连接”章节中看到的那样，每个人的这些分支都不尽相同。大脑皮层的每个区域都高度专业化，有的负责语言，有的负责视觉，有的负责记忆。
You wouldn’t know all this just by looking at the brain. The cortex looks homogenous, somewhat like the shell of a walnut, which fooled anatomists for hundreds of years. Then World War I happened. It was the first major conflict where medical advances allowed large numbers of combatants to survive shrapnel injuries. Some of these injuries penetrated only to the periphery of the brain, destroying tiny regions of the cortex while leaving everything else intact. Enough soldiers were hurt that scientists could study in detail the injuries and the truly strange behaviors that resulted. Eventually, scientists were able to make a complete structure–function map of the brain. They were able to see that the brain had, over eons, become three.
单凭观察大脑，你无法了解这一切。大脑皮层看起来是均匀的，有点像核桃壳，这曾让解剖学家们困惑了数百年。后来，第一次世界大战爆发了。这是医学进步使得大量士兵得以在弹片伤中幸存的第一次重大冲突。有些弹片伤仅穿透到大脑边缘，破坏了大脑皮层的一小部分区域，而其他部分则完好无损。受伤的士兵数量之多，使得科学家能够详细研究这些损伤以及由此产生的种种奇异行为。最终，科学家们绘制出了大脑完整的结构-功能图谱。他们发现，经过亿万年的演化，大脑已经变成了三个部分。
Scientists found that as our brains evolved, our heads did, too: They were getting bigger all the time. But the pelvis—and birth canal—can be only so wide, which is bonkers if you are giving birth to children with larger and larger heads. A lot of mothers and babies died on the way to reaching an anatomical compromise. Human pregnancies are still remarkably risky without modern medical intervention. The solution? Give birth while the baby’s head is small enough to fit through the birth canal. The problem? You create childhood. Most mammals reach adulthood within months. Our long childhood gave the brain time to finish its developmental programs outside the womb. It also created a creature vulnerable to predators for years and not reproductively fit for more than a decade. That’s an eternity when you live in the great outdoors, as we did for eons.
科学家发现，随着大脑的进化，我们的头部也在不断增大。但骨盆——以及产道——的宽度是有限的，如果婴儿的头部越来越大，这简直是灾难性的。许多母亲和婴儿在达到某种解剖学上的妥协过程中丧生。如果没有现代医疗干预，人类妊娠仍然极其危险。解决方案是什么？在婴儿头部足够小，能够通过产道时分娩。问题在于？你创造了一个漫长的童年。大多数哺乳动物在几个月内就能成年。我们漫长的童年让大脑有时间在子宫外完成其发育程序。这也造就了一种在数年内容易受到捕食者攻击，且在十多年内不具备繁殖能力的生物。对于像我们这样在广袤的户外生活了亿万年的人类来说，这简直是永恒。
But the trade-off was worth it. A child was fully capable of learning just about anything and, at least for the first few years, not good for doing much else. This created the concept not only of learner but, for adults, of teacher. Of course, it was no use having babies who took years to grow if the adults were eaten before they could finish their thoughtful parenting. We weaklings needed to out-compete the big boys on their home turf, leaving our new home safer for sex and babies. We decided on a strange strategy. We decided to try to get along with each other.
但这样的权衡是值得的。孩子完全有能力学习几乎任何东西，而且至少在最初几年里，他们除了学习之外，几乎什么也做不了。这不仅创造了“学习者”的概念，也为成年人创造了“教师”的概念。当然，如果成年人在完成他们精心养育孩子的任务之前就被吃掉了，那么生下需要几年才能长大的婴儿就毫无意义了。我们这些弱者需要在强者的地盘上胜过他们，从而让我们的新家园更适合性爱和生育。我们决定采取一种奇怪的策略：我们决定尝试彼此和睦相处。
We cooperated: You scratch my back …
我们合作：你帮我挠背……
Trying to fight off a woolly mammoth? Alone, and the fight might look like Bambi vs. Godzilla. Two or three of you together—coordinating behavior and establishing the concept of “teamwork”—and you present a formidable challenge. You can figure out how to compel the mammoth to tumble over a cliff, for one. There is ample evidence that this is exactly what we did.
想独自对抗一头猛犸象？那场面可能就像小鹿斑比大战哥斯拉。但如果你们两三个人一起行动——协调行动，建立“团队合作”的概念——就能构成强大的威胁。比如说，你们就能想办法让猛犸象滚下悬崖。有大量证据表明，我们就是这么做的。
This changes the rules of the game. We learned to cooperate, which means creating a shared goal that takes into account our allies’ interests as well as our own. In order to understand our allies’ interests, we must be able to understand others’ motivations, including their reward and punishment systems. We need to know where their “itch” is. To do this, we constantly make predictions about other people’s mental states. Say we hear news about a couple: The husband died, and then the wife died. Our minds start working to infer the mental state of the wife: The husband died, and then the wife died of grief.
这改变了游戏规则。我们学会了合作，这意味着要制定一个既考虑自身利益又兼顾盟友利益的共同目标。为了理解盟友的利益，我们必须能够理解他人的动机，包括他们的奖惩机制。我们需要知道他们的“痛点”在哪里。为此，我们会不断地预测他人的心理状态。假设我们听到一对夫妇的消息：丈夫去世了，然后妻子也去世了。我们的大脑开始运转，推断妻子的心理状态：丈夫去世了，然后妻子因悲伤过度而死。
We create a view, however brief, into the psychological interior of the wife. We have an impression of her mental state, perhaps even knowledge about her relationship with her husband. These inferences are the signature characteristic of something called Theory of Mind. We activate it all the time. We try to see our entire world in terms of motivations, ascribing motivations to our pets and even to inanimate objects. The skill is useful for selecting a mate, for navigating the day-to-day issues surrounding living together, for parenting. Theory of Mind is something humans have like no other creature. It is as close to mind reading as we are likely to get.
我们得以窥见妻子的内心世界，哪怕只是短暂的一瞥。我们对她的精神状态有所感知，甚至可能了解她与丈夫的关系。这些推断正是“心智理论”的典型特征。我们无时无刻不在运用它。我们试图用动机来理解整个世界，甚至会给宠物和无生命物体赋予动机。这种能力在择偶、处理共同生活中的日常琐事以及育儿方面都非常有用。心智理论是人类独有的，它几乎可以算得上是人类所能达到的最接近读心术的能力。
This ability to peer inside somebody’s mental life and make predictions takes a tremendous amount of intelligence and, not surprisingly, brain activity. Knowing where to find fruit in the jungle is cognitive child’s play compared with predicting and manipulating other people within a group setting. Many researchers believe a direct line exists between the acquisition of this skill and our intellectual dominance of the planet.
这种洞察他人内心世界并做出预测的能力需要极高的智力，而且不出所料，也需要大量的脑力活动。与在群体环境中预测和操控他人相比，在丛林中寻找水果简直是小儿科。许多研究者认为，这种技能的习得与我们在这个星球上的智力主导地位之间存在着直接联系。
When we try to predict another person’s mental state, we have physically very little to go on. Signs do not appear above a person’s head, flashing in bold letters his or her motivations. We are forced to detect something that is not physically obvious at all, such as fear, shame, greed, or loyalty. This talent is so automatic, we hardly know when we do it. We began doing it in every domain. Remember dual representation: the stick and the thing that the stick represents? Our intellectual prowess, from language to mathematics to art, may have come from the powerful need to predict our neighbor’s psychological interiors. As I said, your brain is amazing.
当我们试图预测他人的心理状态时，我们几乎无法从任何物理层面进行判断。不会有人头顶冒出醒目的标志，用粗体字标明他们的动机。我们只能去察觉一些完全不明显的心理状态，比如恐惧、羞耻、贪婪或忠诚。这种能力如此自动化，以至于我们几乎意识不到自己在做什么。我们开始在各个领域运用这种能力。还记得双重表征吗？棍子和棍子所代表的事物？从语言到数学再到艺术，我们卓越的智力或许都源于预测他人内心世界的强烈需求。正如我所说，你的大脑非常神奇。
Why did I want to spend time walking you through the brain’s survival strategies? Because they aren’t just part of our species’ ancient history. They give us real insight into how humans acquire knowledge. We improvise off a database, thinking symbolically about our world. We are predisposed to social cooperation, which requires constantly reading other people. Along with the performance envelope, these concepts determine at the most fundamental level how our brains work.
我为什么要花时间向你们讲解大脑的生存策略呢？因为它们不仅仅是我们物种远古历史的一部分。它们让我们真正深入了解人类如何获取知识。我们基于数据库进行即兴发挥，以象征性的方式思考我们的世界。我们天生倾向于社会合作，而这需要我们不断地解读他人。这些概念，连同表现范围，从根本上决定了我们大脑的运作方式。
Now that you’ve gotten the gist of things, let’s dive into the details.
既然你已经了解了大致情况，那么让我们深入了解细节吧。
Brain Rule # 1
大脑法则#1
The human brain evolved, too.
人类大脑也随之进化。
• The brain appears to be designed to (1) solve problems (2) related to surviving (3) in an unstable outdoor environment, and (4) to do so in nearly constant motion.
•大脑似乎被设计成（1）解决与（2）在不稳定的户外环境中生存相关的问题，（3）并且（4）在几乎持续不断的运动中完成这些问题。
• We started with a “lizard brain” to keep us breathing, then added a brain like a cat’s, and then topped those with the thin layer known as the cortex—the third, and powerful, “human” brain.
•我们最初依靠“蜥蜴脑”来维持呼吸，然后添加了类似猫的大脑，最后在上面加上了被称为大脑皮层的薄层——第三个，也是强大的“人类”大脑。
• We adapted to change itself, after we were forced from the trees to the savannah when climate swings disrupted our food supply.
•气候变化扰乱了我们的食物供应，迫使我们从树林搬到稀树草原，我们也因此适应了变化本身。
• Going from four legs to two to walk on the savannah freed up energy to develop a complex brain.
•从四条腿变成两条腿在稀树草原上行走，释放出的能量促进了复杂大脑的发育。
• Symbolic reasoning is a uniquely human talent. It may have arisen from our need to understand one another’s intentions and motivations. This allowed us to coordinate within a group, which is how we took over the Earth.
符号推理是人类独有的天赋。它可能源于我们理解彼此意图和动机的需求。这使我们能够在群体内部进行协调，而这正是我们征服地球的方式。
# ↩
exercise
锻炼
Brain Rule #2
大脑法则#2
Exercise boosts brain power.
运动能增强脑力。
# ↩
IF THE CAMERAS WEREN ’ T rolling and the media abuzz with live reports, it is possible nobody would have believed the following story:
如果没有摄像机拍摄，没有媒体进行现场报道，可能没有人会相信下面的故事：
A man had been handcuffed, shackled, and thrown into California’s Long Beach Harbor, where he was quickly fastened to a floating cable. The cable had been attached at the other end to 70 boats, bobbing up and down in the harbor, each carrying a single person. Battling strong winds and currents, the man then swam, towing all 70 boats (and passengers) behind him, traveling 1½ miles from Queensway Bridge. The man, Jack LaLanne, was celebrating his birthday.
一名男子被戴上手铐和脚镣，扔进了加州长滩港，随后被迅速绑在一根漂浮的缆绳上。缆绳的另一端连接着70艘在港湾中上下起伏的小船，每艘船上都载着一个人。这名男子顶着强风和水流，游了起来，拖着这70艘船（以及船上的乘客），从皇后大道桥游了1.5英里。这名男子名叫杰克·拉兰，当时正在庆祝他的生日。
He had just turned 70 years old.
他刚满70岁。
Jack LaLanne, born in 1914, has been called the godfather of the American fitness movement. He starred in one of the longest-running exercise programs produced for commercial television. A prolific inventor, LaLanne designed the first leg-extension machines, the first cable-fastened pulleys, and the first weight selectors, all now standard issue in the modern gym. He is credited with inventing an exercise that supposedly bears his name, the Jumping Jack. LaLanne lived to the age of 96. But even these feats are probably not the most interesting aspect of this famed bodybuilder’s story.
杰克·拉兰内（Jack LaLanne）生于1914年，被誉为美国健身运动之父。他曾主持过一档在商业电视上播出时间最长的健身节目。拉兰内是一位多产的发明家，他设计了第一台腿部伸展机、第一台钢索滑轮和第一台重量选择器，这些如今都已成为现代健身房的标配。据说，他发明了一种以他名字命名的健身动作——跳跃杰克（Jumping Jack）。拉兰内享年96岁。但即便如此，这些成就或许也并非这位著名健美运动员故事中最引人入胜的部分。
If you watch him during an interview late in his life, your biggest impression will be not the strength of his muscles but the strength of his mind . LaLanne is mentally alert. His sense of humor is both lightning fast and improvisatory. “I tell people I can’t afford to die. It will wreck my image!” he joked to Larry King. He once railed: “Do you know how many calories are in butter and cheese and ice cream? Would you get your dog up in the morning for a cup of coffee and a donut?” (He claims he hasn’t had dessert since 1929.) He has the energy of an athlete in his 20s, and he is possessed of an impressive intellectual vigor.
如果你在他晚年观看他的采访，你印象最深刻的并非他强健的体魄，而是他敏锐的头脑。拉兰思维敏捷，幽默感迅捷而又即兴发挥。“我常跟人开玩笑说，我可不能死，那会毁了我的形象！”他曾对拉里·金说道。他还曾怒斥道：“你知道黄油、奶酪和冰淇淋有多少卡路里吗？你会为了喝杯咖啡吃个甜甜圈就把你家的狗叫醒吗？”（他声称自己从1929年起就没吃过甜点。）他拥有二十多岁运动员般的活力，以及令人印象深刻的敏锐思维。
So it’s hard not to ask, “Is there a relationship between exercise and mental alertness?” The answer, it turns out, is yes.
因此，人们很难不问：“运动与精神警觉性之间是否存在联系？” 答案是肯定的。
Survival of the fittest
适者生存
Though a great deal of our evolutionary history remains shrouded in controversy, the one fact that every paleoanthropologist on the planet accepts can be summarized in two words:
尽管我们进化史的许多方面仍然充满争议，但地球上每一位古人类学家都认同的一个事实可以用两个词来概括：
We moved .
我们搬家了。
A lot. As soon as our Homo erectus ancestors evolved, about 2 million years ago, they started moving out of town. Our direct ancestors, Homo sapiens, rapidly did the same thing. Because bountiful rainforests began to shrink, collapsing the local food supply, our ancestors were forced to wander an increasingly dry landscape looking for more trees to scamper up and dine on. Instead of moving up, down, and across complex arboreal environments, which required a lot of dexterity, we began walking back and forth across arid savannahs, which required a lot of stamina. Homo sapiens started in Africa and then took a victory lap around the rest of the world. The speed of the migration is uncertain; the number changes as we find new physical evidence of habitation and as we’re better able to isolate and characterize ancient DNA. Anthropologists can say that our ancestors moved fast and they moved far. Males may have walked and run 10 to 20 kilometers a day, says anthropologist Richard Wrangham. The estimate for females is half that. Up to 12 miles: That’s the amount of ground scientists estimate we covered every day . That means our fancy brains developed not while we were lounging around but while we were exercising.
很多。大约两百万年前，我们的直立人祖先出现后不久就开始迁徙。我们的直系祖先智人也迅速地开始了同样的迁徙。由于茂密的热带雨林开始萎缩，当地的食物供应锐减，我们的祖先被迫在日益干旱的土地上四处游荡，寻找更多的树木来攀爬觅食。我们不再像以前那样在复杂的树栖环境中上下穿梭（这需要极高的灵活性），而是开始在干旱的稀树草原上来回行走（这需要极强的耐力）。智人从非洲开始迁徙，然后迅速扩展到世界各地。迁徙的速度尚不确定；随着我们发现新的居住遗迹以及我们能够更好地分离和分析古代DNA，这个数字也在不断变化。人类学家可以肯定地说，我们的祖先迁徙速度很快，而且迁徙的距离也很远。人类学家理查德·兰厄姆表示，男性每天可能步行或跑步10到20公里，而女性的步行或跑步量估计只有男性的一半。据地面科学家估计，我们每天的运动量可达12英里。这意味着我们发达的大脑并非在闲暇时进化而来，而是在运动中发展起来的。
Regardless of its exact speed, our ancestors’ migration is an impressive feat. This was no casual stroll on groomed trails. Early travelers had to contend with fires and floods, insurmountable mountain ranges, foot-rotting jungles, and moisture-sucking deserts. They had no GPS to reassure them, no real tools to speak of. Eventually they made oceangoing boats, without the benefit of wheels or metallurgy, and then traveled up and down the Pacific with only the crudest navigational skills. Our ancestors constantly encountered new food sources, new predators, new physical dangers. Along the way they routinely suffered injuries, experienced strange illnesses, and delivered and nurtured offspring, all without the benefit of textbooks or modern medicine. Given our relative wimpiness in the animal kingdom (we don’t even have enough body hair to survive a mildly chilly night), what these data tell us is that we grew up in top physical shape, or we didn’t grow up at all. These data also tell us the human brain became the most powerful in the world under conditions where motion was a constant presence.
无论确切速度如何，我们祖先的迁徙都是一项令人叹为观止的壮举。这绝非沿着平整的道路轻松漫步。早期的旅行者必须应对火灾和洪水、难以逾越的山脉、令人脚底腐烂的丛林以及吸走水分的沙漠。他们没有GPS导航，也没有任何像样的工具。最终，他们在没有轮子和冶金技术的情况下制造出了远洋船只，然后凭借着极其原始的导航技能，在太平洋上航行。我们的祖先不断遭遇新的食物来源、新的捕食者和新的危险。一路上，他们经常受伤，患上各种怪病，还要生育和养育后代，所有这一切都是在没有教科书或现代医学的情况下完成的。考虑到我们在动物王国中相对弱小的体质（我们甚至没有足够的体毛来抵御微寒的夜晚），这些数据告诉我们，要么我们天生拥有极佳的身体素质，要么我们根本没有长大。这些数据还告诉我们，在运动持续存在的条件下，人类大脑成为了世界上最强大的大脑。
If our unique cognitive skills were forged in the furnace of physical activity, is it possible that physical activity still influences our cognitive skills? Are the cognitive abilities of someone in good physical condition different from those of someone in poor physical condition? And what if someone in poor physical condition were whipped into shape? Those are scientifically testable questions. The answers are directly related to why Jack LaLanne can still crack jokes about eating dessert. In his nineties .
如果我们的独特认知能力是在体育锻炼的熔炉中锻造而成的，那么体育锻炼是否仍然会影响我们的认知能力？身体素质良好的人和身体素质较差的人的认知能力是否存在差异？如果一个身体素质较差的人通过严格的训练变得体能充沛，又会发生什么呢？这些都是可以通过科学方法验证的问题。而这些问题的答案，与杰克·拉兰（Jack LaLanne）为何在九十多岁高龄还能开玩笑地谈论吃甜点有着直接的联系。
Will you age like Jim or like Frank?
你会像吉姆那样老去，还是像弗兰克那样老去？
Scientists discovered the beneficial effects of exercise on the brain by looking at aging populations. Years ago while watching television, I came across a documentary on American nursing homes. It showed people in wheelchairs, many in their mid- to late 80s, lining the halls of a dimly lit facility, just sitting around, seemingly waiting to die. One was named Jim. His eyes seemed vacant, lonely, friendless. He could cry at the drop of a hat but otherwise spent the last years of his life mostly staring off into space. I switched channels. I stumbled upon a very young-looking Mike Wallace. The journalist was interviewing architect Frank Lloyd Wright, in his late 80s. I was about to hear a most riveting conversation.
科学家通过研究老年人群发现了运动对大脑的益处。多年前，我在看电视时偶然看到一部关于美国养老院的纪录片。片中，许多八十多岁的老人坐在轮椅上，沿着昏暗的走廊排成一排，只是静静地坐着，似乎在等待死亡。其中一位名叫吉姆。他的眼神空洞、孤独，没有朋友。他动不动就哭，但除此之外，他生命的最后几年大多时间都茫然地凝视着远方。我换了个频道，偶然看到一位看起来很年轻的记者迈克·华莱士。他正在采访八十多岁的建筑师弗兰克·劳埃德·赖特。我即将听到一场引人入胜的对话。
“When I walk into St. Patrick’s Cathedral … here in New York City, I am enveloped in a feeling of reverence,” said Wallace, tapping his cigarette.
“当我走进纽约市的圣帕特里克大教堂时……我就会感到无比的敬畏，”华莱士一边说着，一边轻敲着他的香烟。
The old man eyed Wallace. “Sure it isn’t an inferiority complex?”
老人打量着华莱士。“你确定这不是自卑情结吗？”
“Just because the building is big and I’m small, you mean?”
“你的意思是，仅仅因为大楼很大而我个子小吗？”
“Yes.”
“是的。”
“I think not.”
“我不这么认为。”
“I hope not.”
“我希望不会。”
“You feel nothing when you go into St. Patrick’s?”
“你走进圣帕特里克教堂时没有任何感觉吗？”
“Regret,” Wright said without a moment’s pause, “because it isn’t the thing that really represents the spirit of independence and the sovereignty of the individual which I feel should be represented in our edifices devoted to culture.”
“遗憾，”赖特毫不犹豫地说，“因为它并没有真正代表独立精神和个人主权，而我认为这些精神和主权应该体现在我们致力于文化的建筑中。”
I was dumbfounded by the dexterity of Wright’s response. In the space of a few moments, one could detect the clarity of his mind, his unshakable vision, his willingness to think outside the box. The rest of the interview was just as compelling, as was the rest of Wright’s life. He completed the designs for the Guggenheim Museum, his last work, in 1957, when he was 90 years old. But I also was dumbfounded by something else. As I contemplated Wright’s answers, I remembered Jim from the nursing home. He was the same age as Wright. In fact, most of the residents were. I was beholding two types of aging. Jim and Frank lived in roughly the same period of time. But one mind had almost completely withered, seemingly battered and broken by the aging process, while the other mind remained as incandescent as a light bulb.
赖特的回答之巧妙令我瞠目结舌。短短片刻，便能感受到他思路清晰、目光坚定、勇于突破常规的思维。接下来的访谈同样引人入胜，赖特的一生也同样精彩。他于1957年完成了古根海姆博物馆的设计，那是他最后的杰作，当时他已90岁高龄。然而，令我震惊的还有另一件事。当我思考赖特的回答时，我想起了养老院里的吉姆。他和赖特同龄。事实上，养老院里的大多数住户都和他年纪相仿。我仿佛看到了两种截然不同的衰老方式。吉姆和弗兰克的人生阶段大致相同。但一个人的思维几乎完全枯萎，似乎已被岁月摧残殆尽，而另一个人的思维却依然像灯泡般明亮闪耀。
What was the difference in the aging process between men like Jim and the famous architect? This question has intrigued the research community for a long time. Attempts to explain these differences led to many important discoveries. I have grouped them as answers to six questions.
吉姆和那位著名建筑师的衰老过程有何不同？这个问题长期以来一直吸引着研究界的关注。为了解释这些差异，人们进行了许多尝试，并取得了许多重要的发现。我将这些发现归纳为六个问题的答案。
1) Is there one factor that predicts how well you will age?
1）是否存在一个因素可以预测你的衰老程度？
When research on aging began, this question was a tough one to answer. Researchers found many variables, stemming from both nature and nurture, that contributed to someone’s ability to age gracefully. That’s why the scientific community was both intrigued and cautious when a group of researchers uncovered a powerful environmental influence. One of the greatest predictors of successful aging, they found, is the presence or absence of a sedentary lifestyle.
衰老研究之初，这个问题很难回答。研究人员发现，影响一个人优雅老去的因素有很多，既有先天因素，也有后天因素。正因如此，当一组研究人员发现环境因素对衰老有着显著影响时，科学界既感到好奇又保持谨慎。他们发现，能否成功老去最重要的预测因素之一，就是是否存在久坐的生活方式。
Put simply, if you are a couch potato, you are more likely to age like Jim, if you make it to your 80s at all. If you have an active lifestyle, you are more likely to age like Frank Lloyd Wright—and much more likely to make it to your 90s. The chief reason for the longer life is that exercise improves cardiovascular fitness, which in turn reduces the risk for diseases such as heart attacks and stroke. But researchers wondered why the people who were aging well also seemed to be more mentally alert. This led to an obvious second question.
简而言之，如果你是个“沙发土豆”，你很可能像吉姆那样老去，甚至可能活不到八十岁。如果你生活方式积极健康，你很可能像弗兰克·劳埃德·赖特那样老去——而且更有可能活到九十岁。长寿的主要原因是运动能改善心血管健康，从而降低心脏病和中风等疾病的风险。但研究人员想知道，为什么那些健康老去的人似乎也更思维敏捷。这就引出了第二个显而易见的问题。
2) Were they more mentally alert?
2）他们的精神状态是否更敏锐？
Just about every mental test possible was tried. No matter how it was measured, the answer was consistently yes: A lifetime of exercise results in a sometimes astonishing elevation in cognitive performance, compared with those who are sedentary. Exercisers outperform couch potatoes in tests that measure long-term memory, reasoning, attention, and problem-solving skill. The same is true of fluid-intelligence tasks, which test the ability to reason quickly, think abstractly, and improvise off previously learned material in order to solve a new problem. Essentially, exercise improves a whole host of abilities prized in the classroom and at work.
几乎所有可能的认知测试都尝试过了。无论采用何种测量方法，答案始终如一：与久坐不动的人相比，终身锻炼能显著提升认知能力，有时甚至令人惊叹。在衡量长期记忆、推理能力、注意力以及问题解决能力的测试中，锻炼者的表现都优于久坐不动的人。在考察快速推理、抽象思维以及运用已有知识解决新问题的能力的流体智力测试中，情况也是如此。总之，锻炼能够提升一系列在课堂和工作中都至关重要的能力。
What about people who aren’t elderly? Here, the number of studies done thins out. But in one case, researchers looked at more than 10,000 British civil servants between the ages of 35 and 55, grading their activity levels as low, medium, or high. Those with low levels of physical activity were more likely to have poor cognitive performance. Fluid intelligence, the type that requires improvisatory problem-solving skills, was particularly hurt by a sedentary lifestyle.
那么，对于非老年人群体呢？这方面的研究相对较少。但有一项研究调查了1万多名年龄在35岁至55岁之间的英国公务员，并将他们的活动水平分为低、中、高三个等级。研究发现，活动水平低的人认知能力较差。尤其是需要即兴解决问题能力的流体智力，更容易受到久坐生活方式的损害。
Not every cognitive ability is improved by exercise, however. Short-term memory, for example, and certain types of reaction times appear to be unrelated to physical activity. And, while nearly everybody shows some improvement, the degree varies quite a bit among individuals. It’s one thing to look at a group of people and note, as early studies did, that those who exercise are also smarter. It’s another thing to prove that exercise is the direct cause of the benefits. A more intrusive set of experiments needed to be done to answer the next question.
然而，并非所有认知能力都能通过运动得到提升。例如，短期记忆和某些类型的反应时间似乎与体育活动无关。而且，虽然几乎每个人都会有所进步，但进步的程度因人而异。早期研究发现，观察一群人并注意到那些经常锻炼的人也更聪明，这是一回事；而要证明运动是这些益处的直接原因，则是另一回事。要回答下一个问题，需要进行一系列更具侵入性的实验。
3) Can you turn Jim into Frank?
3）你能把吉姆变成弗兰克吗？
Like producers of a makeover show, researchers found a group of elderly couch potatoes, measured their brain power, exercised them, and then reexamined their brain power. The researchers consistently found that all kinds of mental abilities began to come back online—after as little as four months of aerobic exercise. A different study looked at school-age children. Children jogged for 30 minutes two or three times a week. After 12 weeks, their cognitive performance had improved significantly compared with prejogging levels. When the exercise program was withdrawn, the scores plummeted back to their preexperiment levels. Scientists had found a direct link. Within limits, it does appear that exercise can turn Jim into Frank, or at least turn Jim into a sharper version of himself.
就像改造节目的制作人一样，研究人员找到了一群老年“沙发土豆”，测量了他们的脑力，让他们进行锻炼，然后再重新评估他们的脑力。研究人员一致发现，各种认知能力在短短四个月的有氧运动后就开始恢复。另一项研究则针对学龄儿童。孩子们每周慢跑两到三次，每次30分钟。12周后，他们的认知能力与运动前相比显著提高。当运动计划停止后，他们的认知能力又迅速回落到实验前的水平。科学家们发现了运动与认知能力之间的直接联系。在一定范围内，运动似乎确实能让吉姆变成弗兰克，或者至少能让吉姆变得更敏锐。
As the effects of exercise on cognition became increasingly clear, scientists asked the question dearest to the couch-potato cohort:
随着运动对认知能力的影响越来越清晰，科学家们提出了一个久坐不动的人们最关心的问题：
4) What type of exercise must you do, and how much?
4）你必须进行哪种类型的运动，运动量是多少？
After years of investigating aging populations, researchers’ answer to the question of how much is not much. If all you do is walk several times a week, your brain will benefit. Even couch potatoes who fidget show increased benefit over those who do not fidget. The body seems to be clamoring to get back to its active Serengeti roots. Any nod toward this evolutionary history, be it ever so small, is met with a cognitive war whoop. In the laboratory, the gold standard appears to be aerobic exercise, 30 minutes at a clip, two or three times a week. Add a strengthening regimen and you get even more cognitive benefit. Individual results vary, of course, and exercising too intensely, to exhaustion, can hurt cognition. One should consult a physician before embarking on an exercise program. The data merely point to the fact that one should embark. Exercise, as millions of years traipsing around the globe tell us, is good for the brain. Just how good took everyone by surprise, as they delved into the next question.
经过多年对老龄化人口的研究，研究人员对“运动量多少才算多”这个问题给出了答案：其实运动量并不多。即使只是每周步行几次，你的大脑也会受益。即使是那些喜欢动来动去的“沙发土豆”，也能比那些不爱动的人获得更大的益处。身体似乎渴望回归其在塞伦盖蒂草原上活跃的本能。任何对这种进化史的致敬，哪怕再微小，都会引发认知能力的显著提升。在实验室中，黄金标准似乎是每周进行两到三次，每次30分钟的有氧运动。如果再加上力量训练，认知能力的提升效果会更佳。当然，个体差异会造成影响，过度运动甚至精疲力竭也会损害认知能力。因此，在开始任何锻炼计划之前，都应该咨询医生。数据仅仅表明，人们应该开始锻炼。正如数百万年来人类在地球上迁徙的经验所表明的那样，运动对大脑有益。然而，运动究竟有多大的益处，却让所有人感到惊讶，因为他们开始深入研究下一个问题。
5) Can exercise treat dementia or depression?
5）运动可以治疗痴呆症或抑郁症吗？
Given the robust effect of exercise on typical cognitive performance, researchers wanted to know if it would have an effect on atypical performance. What about diseases such as age-related dementia and its more thoroughly investigated cousin, Alzheimer’s disease? What about affective (mood) disorders such as depression? Researchers looked at both prevention and intervention. With experiments reproduced all over the world, enrolling thousands of people, often studied for decades, the results are clear. Your lifetime risk for general dementia is literally cut in half if you participate in physical activity. Aerobic exercise seems to be the key. With Alzheimer’s, the effect is even greater: Such exercise reduces your odds of getting the disease by more than 60 percent.
鉴于运动对典型认知能力的显著影响，研究人员想知道它是否也会对非典型认知能力产生影响。例如，与年龄相关的痴呆症及其研究更为深入的近亲——阿尔茨海默病，以及抑郁症等情感障碍，运动对认知能力的影响又如何呢？研究人员同时考察了运动的预防和干预措施。世界各地开展的实验，招募了数千名参与者，并往往持续数十年，结果清晰地表明：如果您参与体育锻炼，患上普通痴呆症的终生风险将降低一半。有氧运动似乎是关键。对于阿尔茨海默病，运动的效果更为显著：它可以将患病几率降低60%以上。
How much exercise? Once again, a little goes a long way. The researchers showed you have to participate in some form of exercise just twice a week to get the benefit. Bump it up to a 20-minute walk each day, and you can cut your risk of having a stroke—one of the leading causes of mental disability in the elderly—by 57 percent.
多少运动才算合适？答案是：少即是多。研究人员发现，每周只需进行两次某种形式的运动就能获益。如果增加到每天步行20分钟，就能将中风风险降低57%——中风是老年人导致认知障碍的主要原因之一。
Dr. Steven Blair, the man most responsible for stimulating this line of inquiry, did not start his career wanting to be a scientist. He wanted to be an athletics coach. Surely he was inspired by his own football coach in high school, Gene Bissell. Bissell once forfeited a winning game. He realized after the game that an official had missed a call, and he insisted that his team be penalized. Young Steven never forgot the incident. But Bissell encouraged Blair to continue his interest in research, and Blair went on to write a seminal paper on fitness and mortality. The study stands as a landmark example of how to do work with rigor and integrity in this field. His analysis inspired other investigators. What about using exercise not only as prevention, they asked, but as intervention, to treat mental disorders such as depression and anxiety? That turned out to be a good line of questioning.
史蒂文·布莱尔博士是这一研究方向的主要推动者，但他最初的职业目标并非成为一名科学家，而是成为一名体育教练。这无疑受到了他高中橄榄球教练吉恩·比塞尔的启发。比塞尔曾因一次判罚失误而放弃一场原本领先的比赛。赛后，他意识到裁判漏判了一次犯规，并坚持要求对自己的球队进行处罚。年轻的史蒂文始终铭记着这件事。但比塞尔鼓励布莱尔继续从事研究，布莱尔最终撰写了一篇关于体能与死亡率的开创性论文。这项研究堪称该领域严谨诚信工作的典范。他的分析启发了其他研究者。他们提出疑问：如果不仅将运动作为预防手段，还能将其作为干预手段，用于治疗抑郁症和焦虑症等精神疾病，又会如何呢？事实证明，这是一个值得深入探讨的问题。
A growing body of work now suggests that physical activity can powerfully affect the course of both diseases. We think it’s because exercise regulates the release of most of the biochemicals associated with maintaining mental health. In one experiment on depression, rigorous exercise was substituted for antidepressant medication. Even when compared to medicated controls, the treatment outcomes were astonishingly successful. For both depression and anxiety, exercise is beneficial immediately and over the long term. It is equally effective for men and women. The longer the person exercises, the greater the effect. Although exercise is not a substitute for psychiatric treatment (which usually involves therapy along with medication), the role of exercise on mood is so pronounced that many psychiatrists prescribe physical activity as well. It is especially helpful in severe cases and for older people.
越来越多的研究表明，体育锻炼能够显著影响抑郁症和焦虑症的病程。我们认为这是因为运动能够调节大多数与维持心理健康相关的生化物质的释放。在一项针对抑郁症的实验中，研究人员用高强度运动代替了抗抑郁药物。即使与服用药物的对照组相比，运动组的治疗效果也令人惊叹。对于抑郁症和焦虑症，运动都能带来即时和长期的益处，并且对男性和女性同样有效。运动时间越长，效果越显著。虽然运动不能替代精神科治疗（通常包括药物治疗和心理治疗），但运动对情绪的影响如此显著，以至于许多精神科医生也会建议患者进行体育锻炼。运动对重症患者和老年人尤其有益。
In asking what else exercise can do, researchers looked beyond our oldest members to our youngest.
为了探究运动还能带来哪些其他益处，研究人员将目光从最年长的成员转向了最年轻的成员。
6) Does exercise help kids do better in school?
6）运动能帮助孩子在学校取得更好的成绩吗？
The number of studies in children is downright microscopic. Still, the data point in a familiar direction. Physically fit children identify visual stimuli much faster than sedentary ones. They appear to concentrate better. Brain-activation studies show that children and adolescents who are fit allocate more cognitive resources to a task and do so for longer periods of time. “Kids pay better attention to their subjects when they’ve been active,” Dr. Antronette Yancey said in an interview with NPR. “Kids are less likely to be disruptive in terms of their classroom behavior when they’re active. Kids feel better about themselves, have higher self-esteem, less depression, less anxiety. All of those things can impair academic performance and attentiveness.”
针对儿童的研究数量少得可怜。尽管如此，数据仍然指向一个熟悉的方向：身体健康的儿童比久坐不动的儿童更快地识别视觉刺激，而且他们的注意力似乎也更集中。脑激活研究表明，身体健康的儿童和青少年会将更多的认知资源分配给一项任务，并且持续时间更长。安特罗内特·扬西博士在接受美国国家公共电台（NPR）采访时表示：“孩子们在积极活动后，会更专注于学习内容。他们在课堂上更不容易扰乱课堂秩序。孩子们会感觉更好，拥有更高的自尊心，更少抑郁，更少焦虑。所有这些都会影响他们的学习成绩和注意力。”
Of course, many ingredients make up academic performance. Finding out what those components are—and then which are most important for improving performance—is difficult. But these preliminary findings hint that exercise may be one key ingredient.
当然，学业成绩受多种因素影响。要找出这些因素是什么，以及哪些因素对提高成绩最为重要，并非易事。但这些初步研究结果表明，运动可能是其中一个关键因素。
An exercise in road building
道路建设练习
Why exercise works so well in the brain, at a molecular level, can be illustrated by competitive food eaters—or, less charitably, professional pigs. The crest of the International Federation of Competitive Eating proudly displays the motto In Voro Veritas—literally, “In Gorging, Truth.” Like any sporting organization, competitive food eaters have their heroes. The reigning gluttony god is Takeru “Tsunami” Kobayashi. He is the recipient of many eating awards, including the vegetarian dumpling competition (83 dumplings downed in eight minutes), the roasted pork bun competition (100 in 12 minutes), and the hamburger competition (97 in eight minutes). Kobayashi also is a world champion hot-dog eater. One of his few losses was to a 1,089-pound Kodiak bear. In a 2003 Fox-televised special called Man vs. Beast, the mighty Kobayashi consumed only 31 bunless dogs compared with the ursine’s 50, all in about 2½ minutes. The Tsunami would not accept defeat. In 2012, Kobayashi ate 60 bunless dogs in that amount of time. But my point isn’t about speed.
运动为何能在分子层面如此有效地作用于大脑，我们可以用竞技吃货——或者更不客气地说，职业大胃王——的例子来解释。国际竞技吃货联合会的会徽上赫然印着“In Voro Veritas”的格言，字面意思是“在暴食中，真理永存”。和任何体育组织一样，竞技吃货界也有自己的英雄。当之无愧的吃货之神是“海啸”小林尊。他曾获得众多吃货奖项，包括素饺子大赛（8分钟内吃下83个饺子）、烤猪肉包大赛（12分钟内吃下100个）和汉堡大赛（8分钟内吃下97个）。小林尊还是世界热狗冠军。他为数不多的败绩之一是输给了一头重达1089磅的科迪亚克棕熊。在2003年福克斯电视台播出的一档名为《人兽大战》的特别节目中，体格健壮的小林可梦伟在短短两分半钟内只吃掉了31个无面包热狗，而熊海啸则吃了50个。海啸不甘示弱，誓要取胜。2012年，小林可梦伟在同样的时间内吃掉了60个无面包热狗。但我的重点并非速度。
Like the Tsunami’s, the brain’s appetite for energy is enormous. The brain gobbles up 20 percent of the body’s energy, even though it’s only about 2 percent of the body’s weight. When the brain is fully working, it uses more energy per unit of tissue weight than a fully exercising quadricep. In fact, the human brain cannot simultaneously activate more than 2 percent of its neurons at any one time. More than this, and the brain’s energy supply becomes so quickly exhausted that you will faint.
就像海啸一样，大脑对能量的需求也极其巨大。大脑消耗了人体20%的能量，尽管它的重量只占人体的2%左右。当大脑全力运转时，其单位组织重量消耗的能量比充分运动的股四头肌还要多。事实上，人脑在任何时候都无法同时激活超过2%的神经元。超过这个比例，大脑的能量供应就会迅速耗尽，导致昏厥。
That energy supply is glucose, a type of sugar that is one of the body’s favorite resources. After all of those hot dogs slide down the Tsunami’s throat, his stomach’s acid and his wormy intestines tear the food apart (not getting much help from the teeth, in his case) and reconfigure it into glucose. Glucose and other metabolic products are absorbed into the bloodstream via the small intestines. The nutrients travel to all parts of the body, where they are deposited into cells, which make up the body’s various tissues. The cells seize the sweet stuff like sharks in a feeding frenzy. Cellular chemicals greedily tear apart the molecular structure of glucose to extract its sugary energy.
这种能量来源是葡萄糖，一种人体最喜爱的糖类之一。当海啸吞下那么多热狗后，胃酸和肠道蠕虫会将食物分解（就它而言，牙齿几乎帮不上什么忙），并将其重新转化为葡萄糖。葡萄糖和其他代谢产物通过小肠被吸收到血液中。这些营养物质输送到身体的各个部位，并被细胞吸收，最终形成身体的各种组织。细胞像鲨鱼疯狂捕食一样，争相获取这些甜食。细胞内的化学物质贪婪地破坏葡萄糖的分子结构，从中提取糖分能量。
This energy extraction is so violent that atoms are literally ripped asunder in the process. As in any manufacturing process, such fierce activity generates a fair amount of toxic waste. In the case of food, this waste consists of a nasty pile of excess electrons shredded from the atoms in the glucose molecules. Left alone, these electrons slam into other molecules within the cell, transforming them into some of the most toxic substances known to humankind. They are called free radicals. If not quickly corralled, they will wreck havoc on the innards of a cell and, cumulatively, on the rest of the body. These electrons are fully capable, for example, of causing mutations in your DNA.
这种能量提取过程极其剧烈，原子在这个过程中会被彻底撕裂。如同任何制造过程一样，如此剧烈的活动会产生大量的有毒废物。就食物而言，这些废物是由葡萄糖分子中原子脱离原子而产生的大量过剩电子组成。如果不加以控制，这些电子会撞击细胞内的其他分子，将其转化为人类已知最具毒性的物质之一。它们被称为自由基。如果不及时清除，它们会对细胞内部造成严重破坏，并最终损害身体的其他部分。例如，这些电子完全有能力导致DNA突变。
The reason you don’t die of electron overdose is that the atmosphere is full of breathable oxygen. The main function of oxygen is to act like an efficient electron-absorbing sponge. At the same time the blood is delivering glucose to your tissues, it is also carrying these oxygen sponges. Any excess electrons are absorbed by the oxygen and, after a bit of molecular alchemy, are transformed into equally hazardous—but now fully transportable—carbon dioxide. The blood is carried back to your lungs, where the carbon dioxide leaves the blood and you exhale it. So whether you are a competitive eater or a typical one, the oxygen-rich air you inhale keeps the food you eat from killing you. How important is oxygen? The three requirements for human life are food, drink, and fresh air. But their effects on survival have very different timelines. You can live for 30 days or so without food, and you can go for a week or so without drinking water. Your brain, however, is so active that it cannot go without oxygen for more than five minutes without risking serious and permanent damage. When the blood can’t deliver enough oxygen sponges, toxic electrons overaccumulate.
你之所以不会死于电子过量，是因为大气中充满了可供呼吸的氧气。氧气的主要功能就像一块高效的电子吸收海绵。血液在向组织输送葡萄糖的同时，也携带着这些“氧气海绵”。任何多余的电子都会被氧气吸收，经过一番分子转化后，转化为同样有害——但现在完全可以运输——的二氧化碳。血液被输送回肺部，二氧化碳从血液中排出，然后被你呼出。所以，无论你是大胃王还是普通人，你吸入的富氧空气都能防止你摄入的食物危及你的生命。氧气究竟有多重要？人类生存的三大要素是食物、饮水和新鲜空气。但它们对生存的影响持续时间却截然不同。你可以大约30天不进食，也可以大约一周不喝水。然而，你的大脑活动非常活跃，如果超过五分钟没有氧气，就会面临严重且永久性的损伤。当血液无法输送足够的氧气海绵时，有毒电子就会过度积累。
Getting energy into tissues and getting toxic electrons out are essentially matters of access. That’s why blood—acting as both waitstaff and hazmat team—has to be everywhere inside you. Any tissue without enough blood supply is going to starve to death, your brain included. More access to blood is better. And even in a healthy brain, the blood’s delivery system can be improved.
将能量输送到组织并将有害电子排出体外，本质上取决于能否获得足够的血液供应。这就是为什么血液——既是服务员又是危险品处理小组——必须遍布你体内的各个部位。任何血液供应不足的组织都会因缺氧而死亡，大脑也不例外。血液供应越充足越好。即使是健康的大脑，其血液输送系统也仍有改进的空间。
That’s where exercise comes in .
这就需要锻炼了。
It reminds me of a seemingly mundane little insight that literally changed the history of the world. John Loudon McAdam, a Scottish engineer living in England in the early 1800s, noticed the difficulty people had trying to move goods and supplies over hole-filled, often muddy, frequently impassable dirt roads. He had the splendid idea of raising the level of the road using layers of rock and gravel. This immediately made the roads less muddy and more stable. As county after county adopted his process, now called macadamization, people instantly got more dependable access to one another’s goods and services. Offshoots from the main roads sprang up. Pretty soon entire countrysides had access to far-flung points using stable arteries of transportation. Trade grew. People got richer. By changing the way things moved, McAdam changed the way we lived.
这让我想起一个看似平凡的小小发现，它却彻底改变了世界历史。19世纪初，苏格兰工程师约翰·劳登·麦克亚当（John Loudon McAdam）居住在英国。他注意到，人们在坑洼不平、泥泞不堪、经常无法通行的土路上运输货物和物资十分困难。他灵机一动，想出了一个绝妙的主意：用碎石和砾石层层铺砌，抬高路面。这立刻改善了道路的泥泞状况，使其更加稳固。随着一个又一个郡县效仿他的方法（如今被称为碎石路面），人们之间的货物和服务往来变得更加便捷可靠。主干道两侧也延伸出许多支路。很快，整个乡村地区都通过稳定的交通动脉与偏远地区连接起来。贸易蓬勃发展，人们的生活水平也随之提高。麦克亚当通过改变货物的运输方式，改变了我们的生活方式。
What does this have to do with exercise? McAdam’s central notion wasn’t to improve goods and services, but to improve access to goods and services. You can do the same for your brain by increasing the roads in your body, namely your blood vessels, through exercise. Exercise does not provide the oxygen and the food. It provides your body greater access to the oxygen and the food.
这和运动有什么关系呢？麦克亚当斯的核心理念并非改善商品和服务，而是改善人们获取商品和服务的途径。你也可以通过运动来改善大脑的“道路”，也就是血管，从而达到同样的效果。运动本身并不提供氧气和食物，而是让身体更容易获得氧气和食物。
How this works is easy to understand. When you exercise, you increase blood flow across the tissues of your body. Blood flow improves because exercise stimulates the blood vessels to create a powerful, flow-regulating molecule called nitric oxide. As the flow improves, the body makes new blood vessels, which penetrate deeper and deeper into the tissues of the body. This allows more access to the bloodstream’s goods and services, which include food distribution and waste disposal. The more you exercise, the more tissues you can feed and the more toxic waste you can remove. This happens all over the body. That’s why exercise improves the performance of most human functions. You stabilize existing transportation structures and add new ones, just like McAdam’s roads. All of a sudden, you are becoming healthier .
其原理很容易理解。运动时，身体组织的血液流动会增加。血液流动改善的原因是运动刺激血管产生一种强大的、调节血流的分子——一氧化氮。随着血流的改善，身体会生成新的血管，这些血管会越来越深入地渗透到身体组织中。这使得血液能够更好地输送营养物质和服务，包括食物的输送和废物的清除。运动越多，能够滋养的组织就越多，能够清除的毒素也越多。这种情况发生在全身各处。这就是为什么运动能够改善大多数人体机能的原因。就像麦克亚当斯修建道路一样，运动能够稳定现有的交通运输系统，并增加新的系统。不知不觉中，你的身体就变得更健康了。
The same happens in the human brain. Imaging studies have shown that exercise increases blood volume in a region of the brain called the dentate gyrus. That’s a big deal. The dentate gyrus is a vital constituent of the hippocampus, a region deeply involved in memory formation. This blood-flow increase, likely the result of new capillaries, allows more brain cells greater access to the blood’s waitstaff and hazmat team.
同样的情况也会发生在人脑中。影像学研究表明，运动可以增加大脑齿状回区域的血容量。这意义重大。齿状回是海马体的重要组成部分，而海马体与记忆的形成密切相关。这种血流量的增加，很可能是由于新生毛细血管的生成，使得更多的脑细胞能够更好地获得血液供应。
Another brain-specific effect of exercise is becoming clear. Early studies indicate that exercise also aids in the development of healthy tissue by stimulating one of the brain’s most powerful growth factors, BDNF. That stands for brain-derived neurotrophic factor. “I call it Miracle-Gro, brain fertilizer,” says Harvard psychiatrist John Ratey. “It keeps [existing] neurons young and healthy, and makes them more ready to connect with one another. It also encourages neurogenesis—the creation of new cells.” The cells most sensitive to this are in the hippocampus, inside the very regions deeply involved in human cognition. Exercise increases the level of usable BDNF inside those cells. Most researchers believe this uptick also buffers against the negative molecular effects of stress, which in turn may improve memory formation. We’ll have more to say about this interaction in the Stress chapter.
运动对大脑的另一项特定作用正逐渐显现。早期研究表明，运动还能刺激大脑中最强大的生长因子之一——脑源性神经营养因子（BDNF），从而促进健康组织的生长。哈佛大学精神病学家约翰·雷蒂（John Ratey）称其为“大脑肥料”，并表示：“我称它为‘神奇肥料’。它能保持神经元的年轻健康，并增强它们之间的连接能力。它还能促进神经发生——即新细胞的生成。”对这种作用最敏感的细胞位于海马体中，而海马体正是人类认知功能的核心区域。运动可以提高这些细胞内可利用的BDNF水平。大多数研究人员认为，这种提升还能缓冲压力带来的负面分子效应，进而可能改善记忆的形成。我们将在“压力”章节中详细探讨这种相互作用。
Redefining normal
重新定义正常
All of the evidence points in one direction: Physical activity is cognitive candy. Civilization, while giving us such seemingly forward advances as modern medicine and spatulas, also has had a nasty side effect. It gives us more opportunities to sit on our butts. Whether learning or working, we gradually quit exercising the way our ancestors did. Recall that our evolutionary ancestors were used to walking up to 12 miles per day. This means that our brains were supported for most of our evolutionary history by Olympic-caliber bodies. We were not sitting in a classroom for eight hours at a stretch. We were not sitting in a cubicle for eight hours at a stretch. If we sat around the Serengeti for eight hours—heck, for eight minutes —we were usually somebody’s lunch. We haven’t had millions of years to adapt to our sedentary lifestyle. That lifestyle has hurt both our physical and mental health. There is no question we are living in an epidemic of fatness, a point I will not belabor here. The benefits of exercise seem nearly endless because its impact is systemwide, affecting most physiological systems. Exercise makes your muscles and bones stronger, improving your strength and balance. It helps regulate your appetite, reduces your risk for more than a dozen types of cancer, improves the immune system, changes your blood lipid profile, and buffers against the toxic effects of stress (see the Stress chapter). By enriching your cardiovascular system, exercise decreases your risk for heart disease, stroke, and diabetes. When combined with the intellectual benefits exercise appears to offer, we have in our hands as close to a magic bullet for improving human health as exists in modern medicine. So I am convinced that integrating exercise into those eight hours at work or school will only make us normal .
所有证据都指向同一个方向：体育锻炼是认知的良药。文明在给我们带来现代医学和锅铲等看似进步的事物的同时，也带来了一个令人不快的副作用：它让我们有更多机会久坐不动。无论是学习还是工作，我们都逐渐放弃了像祖先那样锻炼身体。想想看，我们的祖先每天要走12英里（约19公里）。这意味着在进化史的大部分时间里，我们的大脑都由奥运级别的体魄支撑。我们不会连续八小时坐在教室里，也不会连续八小时坐在格子间里。如果我们在塞伦盖蒂草原上坐八小时——哪怕只是八分钟——通常都会成为别人的午餐。我们没有数百万年的时间来适应久坐的生活方式。这种生活方式损害了我们的身心健康。毫无疑问，我们正生活在肥胖的流行之中，这一点我在此不再赘述。运动的好处似乎无穷无尽，因为它对身体系统全面，影响着大多数生理系统。运动能增强肌肉和骨骼，提高力量和平衡能力。它有助于调节食欲，降低患十几种癌症的风险，增强免疫系统，改善血脂，并抵御压力带来的负面影响（参见“压力”章节）。运动还能增强心血管系统功能，降低患心脏病、中风和糖尿病的风险。运动带来的诸多益处，再加上它本身似乎也能提升智力，使其成为现代医学中改善人类健康的“灵丹妙药”。因此，我坚信，将运动融入到每天八小时的工作或学习生活中，只会让我们拥有更健康的生活。
All we have to do is move.
我们只需要搬家。
More ideas
更多想法
I can think of a few simple ways to harness the effects of exercise in the practical worlds of education and business.
我想到了一些简单的方法，可以在教育和商业的实际领域中利用运动的效果。
Recess twice a day
每天休息两次
Because of the increased reliance on test scores for school survival, many districts across the nation are getting rid of physical education and recess. Given the powerful cognitive effects of physical activity, this makes no sense. Dr. Yancey described a real-world test: “They took time away from academic subjects for physical education … and found that, across the board, [adding exercise] did not hurt the kids’ performance on the academic tests. [When] trained teachers provided the physical education, the children actually did better on language, reading, and the basic battery of tests.”
由于学校越来越依赖考试成绩来维持学业，全国许多学区都在取消体育课和课间休息。考虑到体育活动对认知能力的显著提升，这种做法毫无道理。扬西博士描述了一项真实的实验：“他们从学术科目中抽出时间进行体育锻炼……结果发现，总体而言，（增加运动）并没有影响孩子们在学术考试中的表现。（当）由受过专业训练的教师进行体育教学时，孩子们在语言、阅读和基础测试中的表现实际上更好。”
Cutting off physical exercise—the very activity most likely to promote cognitive performance—to do better on a test score is like trying to gain weight by starving yourself. A smarter approach would be to insert more, not less, exercise into the daily curriculum. They might even reintroduce the notion of school uniforms. Of what would the new apparel consist? Simply gym clothes, worn all day long. If your children’s school isn’t on board, consider how you could help your kids get 20 to 30 minutes each morning for aerobic exercise; and 20 to 30 minutes each afternoon for strengthening exercises. Most studies show a benefit from exercising only two or three times a week.
为了提高考试成绩而减少体育锻炼——体育锻炼恰恰是最有可能提升认知能力的活动——就好比节食减肥一样。更明智的做法是在日常课程中增加而非减少运动量。他们甚至可以考虑重新引入校服制度。新的校服会是什么样的呢？其实就是运动服，全天穿着。如果孩子的学校不支持这项措施，您可以考虑如何帮助孩子每天早上进行20到30分钟的有氧运动，下午进行20到30分钟的力量训练。大多数研究表明，每周只需锻炼两到三次就能获益。
You could apply the same idea at work, taking morning and afternoon breaks for exercise. Conduct meetings while you walk, whether in the office or outside. You just might see a boost in problem solving and creativity.
你也可以把这个方法运用到工作中，利用上午和下午的休息时间进行锻炼。无论是在办公室还是户外，都可以边走边开会。你或许会发现，这能显著提升解决问题的能力和创造力。
Treadmills and bikes in classrooms and cubicles
教室和隔间里的跑步机和自行车
Remember the experiment showing that when children aerobically exercised, their brains worked better, and when the exercise stopped, the cognitive gain soon plummeted? These results suggested to the researchers that one’s level of fitness is not as important as a steady increase in oxygen to the brain. Otherwise, the improved mental sharpness would not have fallen off so rapidly. So they did another experiment. They administered supplemental oxygen to young healthy adults, and they found a cognitive improvement similar to that of exercise. This suggests an interesting idea to try in a classroom. (Don’t worry, it doesn’t involve oxygen doping.)
还记得那个实验吗？实验表明，儿童进行有氧运动后，大脑功能会得到提升；而一旦停止运动，认知能力的提升就会迅速下降。这些结果让研究人员意识到，一个人的体能水平并不像大脑氧气供应的持续增加那么重要。否则，思维敏捷度的提升就不会下降得如此之快。于是，他们又做了一个实验。他们给年轻的健康成年人补充氧气，发现他们的认知能力也得到了与运动类似的提升。这启发我们思考如何在课堂上尝试这种方法。（别担心，这跟吸氧无关。）
What if, during a lesson, the children were not sitting at desks but walking on treadmills or riding stationary bikes? Students might study English while peddling comfortably on a bike that accommodates a desk. Workers could easily do the same, composing email while walking on a treadmill at one to two miles per hour. This idea would harness the advantage of increasing the oxygen supply and at the same time harvest all the other advantages of regular exercise.
如果上课时，孩子们不是坐在课桌前，而是在跑步机上行走或骑固定自行车呢？学生们可以一边舒适地骑着配有课桌的自行车学习英语。上班族也可以轻松做到这一点，一边以每小时一到两英里的速度在跑步机上行走，一边撰写电子邮件。这种做法既能增加氧气供应，又能同时获得规律运动的其他益处。
The idea of integrating exercise into the workday or school day may sound foreign, but it’s not difficult. I put a treadmill in my own office, and I now take regular breaks filled not with coffee but with exercise. I constructed a small structure upon which my laptop fits so that I can write while I walk. At first, it was difficult to adapt to such a strange hybrid activity. It took a whopping 15 minutes to become fully functional typing on my laptop while walking 1.8 miles per hour.
将锻炼融入工作或学习日的想法听起来或许有些陌生，但其实并不难。我在自己的办公室里放了一台跑步机，现在我经常利用休息时间锻炼，而不是喝咖啡。我还搭建了一个可以放笔记本电脑的小支架，这样我就可以边走边写。一开始，适应这种奇特的混合活动确实有点困难。我花了整整15分钟才完全掌握了边走边用笔记本电脑打字的技巧，而且速度还能达到每小时1.8英里。
Office workers can sometimes choose their own desk setups, integrating exercise on an individual basis. But businesses have compelling reasons to incorporate such radical ideas into company policy as well. Business leaders already know that if employees exercised regularly, it would reduce health-care costs. There’s no question that halving someone’s lifetime risk of a debilitating stroke or Alzheimer’s disease is a wonderfully humanitarian thing to do. But exercise also could boost the collective brain power of an organization. Fit employees are more capable than sedentary employees of mobilizing their God-given IQs. For companies whose competitiveness rests on creative intellectual horsepower, such mobilization could mean a strategic advantage. In the laboratory, regular exercise improves problem-solving abilities, fluid intelligence, and even memory—sometimes dramatically so. It’s worth finding out whether the same is true in business settings, too.
办公室员工有时可以自行选择办公桌布置，并根据个人情况安排锻炼。但企业也有充分的理由将这种创新理念纳入公司政策。企业领导者早已意识到，如果员工定期锻炼，就能降低医疗保健成本。毫无疑问，将一个人一生中罹患中风或阿尔茨海默病的风险降低一半，是一件极具人道主义意义的事情。但锻炼还能提升整个组织的集体脑力。与久坐不动的员工相比，身体健康的员工更能充分发挥其与生俱来的智商。对于那些以创造性智力为竞争优势的公司而言，这种能力的提升可能意味着战略优势。在实验室中，规律的锻炼可以提高解决问题的能力、流体智力，甚至记忆力——有时效果显著。值得探究的是，这种现象是否也适用于商业环境。
Brain Rule #2
大脑法则#2
Exercise boosts brain power.
运动能增强脑力。
• Our brains were built for walking—12 miles a day!
•我们的大脑天生适合步行——每天走 12 英里！
• To improve your thinking skills, move .
•想要提高思维能力，就动起来。
• Exercise gets blood to your brain, bringing it glucose for energy and oxygen to soak up the toxic electrons that are left over. It also stimulates the protein that keeps neurons connecting.
•运动能促进血液流向大脑，为其提供能量所需的葡萄糖和氧气，以清除剩余的有害电子。它还能刺激维持神经元连接的蛋白质的生成。
• Aerobic exercise just twice a week halves your risk of general dementia. It cuts your risk of alzheimer’s by 60 percent.
•每周只需进行两次有氧运动，就能将患普通痴呆症的风险降低一半，并将患阿尔茨海默病的风险降低60%。
Get illustrations, audio, video, and more at www.brainrules.net
访问 www.brainrules.net 获取插图、音频、视频等更多内容。
# ↩
sleep
睡觉
Brain Rule #3
大脑法则#3
Sleep well, think well.
睡好觉，才能头脑清醒。
# ↩
IT’S NOT THE MOST comfortable way to raise funds for a major American charity. In 1959, New York disk jockey Peter Tripp decided that he would stay awake for 200 straight hours. He got into a glass booth in the most visible place possible in New York—Times Square—and rigged up the radio so that he could broadcast his show. He even allowed scientists (and, wisely, medical professionals) to observe and measure his behavior as he descended into sleeplessness. One of those scientists was famed sleep researcher William Dement. For the first 72 hours, everything seemed fine with Tripp. He gave his normal three-hour show with humor and professional aplomb. Then things changed. Tripp became rude and offensive to the people around him. Hallucinations set in. The researchers testing his cognitive skills halfway through found he could no longer complete certain mental skill tests. At the 120-hour mark—five days in—Tripp showed real signs of mental impairment, which would only worsen with time. Dement described Tripp’s behavior toward the end of the adventure: “The disk jockey developed an acute paranoid psychosis during the nighttime hours, accompanied at times by auditory hallucination. He believed that unknown adversaries were attempting to slip drugs into his food and beverages in order to put him to sleep.” At the 200-hour mark—more than eight days—Tripp was done.
