Presumably, he went to bed and stayed there for a long time.
这可不是为美国大型慈善机构筹款的最轻松的方式。1959年，纽约电台DJ彼得·特里普决定连续200小时不睡觉。他躲进纽约最显眼的地方——时代广场——的一个玻璃隔间里，架设好收音机，以便播出他的节目。他甚至允许科学家（以及明智的医学专家）观察和测量他逐渐失眠时的行为。其中一位科学家是著名的睡眠研究专家威廉·德门特。在最初的72小时里，特里普一切正常。他像往常一样，以幽默和专业的风度完成了三个小时的节目。但之后情况发生了变化。特里普开始对周围的人粗鲁无礼，并出现了幻觉。研究人员在挑战进行到一半时测试了他的认知能力，发现他已经无法完成某些心理测试。到了120小时——也就是五天后——特里普出现了明显的精神障碍迹象，而且随着时间的推移，情况只会越来越糟。德门特这样描述特里普在冒险后期的行为：“这位唱片骑师在夜间出现了严重的妄想性精神病症状，有时还伴有幻听。他认为有不明身份的敌人试图在他的食物和饮料中下药，让他昏睡过去。” 历经200个小时——超过八天——特里普终于崩溃了。想必他上床睡觉，并且很久都没再动弹。
Some unfortunate souls don’t have the luxury of experimenting with sleep deprivation. They become suddenly and permanently incapable of ever going to sleep again. Only about 20 families in the world suffer from Fatal Familial Insomnia, making it one of the rarest human genetic disorders that exists. That rarity is a blessing, because the disease follows a course straight through mental-health hell. In middle to late adulthood, the person begins to experience fevers, tremors, and profuse sweating. As the insomnia becomes permanent, these symptoms are accompanied by increasingly uncontrollable muscular jerks and tics. The person soon experiences crushing feelings of depression and anxiety. He or she becomes psychotic. Finally, mercifully, the patient slips into a coma and dies.
有些不幸的人没有机会尝试睡眠剥夺。他们会突然永久失眠。全世界只有大约20个家庭患有致命性家族性失眠症，使其成为最罕见的人类遗传疾病之一。这种罕见性反而是一种幸运，因为这种疾病会直接导致精神崩溃。在中年或晚年，患者开始出现发烧、颤抖和大量出汗的症状。随着失眠症的持续，这些症状会伴随越来越无法控制的肌肉抽搐和痉挛。患者很快就会感到极度抑郁和焦虑。他们最终会精神错乱。最终，幸运的是，患者会陷入昏迷并死亡。
So we know bad things happen when we don’t sleep. The puzzle is that, from an evolutionary standpoint, bad things also could happen when we do sleep. Because the body goes into a human version of micro-hibernation, sleep makes us exquisitely vulnerable to predators. Indeed, deliberately going off to dreamland unprotected in the middle of a bunch of hostile hunters (such as leopards, our evolutionary roommates in eastern Africa) seems like a plan dreamed up by our worst enemies. There must be something terribly important we need to accomplish during sleep if we are willing to take such risks in order to get it. Exactly what is it that is so darned important?
所以我们知道，不睡觉会带来不好的事情。但令人费解的是，从进化论的角度来看，睡觉也会带来不好的事情。因为睡眠会让身体进入一种类似人类的“微型冬眠”状态，使我们极易受到捕食者的攻击。事实上，在一群充满敌意的猎手（比如我们在东非的进化室友——豹子）的包围下，故意毫无防备地进入梦乡，这听起来像是我们最可怕的敌人精心策划的阴谋。如果我们愿意冒如此大的风险去完成某件事，那么这件事必然极其重要。究竟是什么事如此重要呢？
To begin to understand why we spend a walloping one-third of our time on this planet sleeping, let’s peer in on what the brain is doing while we sleep .
为了了解为什么我们一生中有三分之一的时间都在睡觉，让我们来看看大脑在睡眠时都在做什么。
You call this rest?
你管这叫休息？
If you ever get a chance to listen in on someone’s brain while its owner is slumbering, you’ll have to get over your disbelief. The brain does not appear to be asleep at all. Rather, it is almost unbelievably active during “rest,” with legions of neurons crackling electrical commands to one another in constantly shifting, extremely active patterns. In fact, the only time you can observe a real resting period for the brain—where the amount of energy consumed is less than during a similar awake period—is during the phase called non-REM sleep. But that takes up only about 20 percent of the total sleep cycle. This is why researchers early on began to disabuse themselves of the notion that the reason we rest is so that we can rest. When we are asleep, the brain is not resting at all. Even so, most people report that sleep is powerfully restorative, and they point to the fact that if they don’t get enough sleep, they don’t think as well the next day. That is measurably true, as we shall see shortly. And so we find ourselves in a quandary: Given the amount of energy the brain is using, it seems impossible that you could receive anything approaching mental rest and restoration during sleep.
如果你有机会旁听一个人睡梦中的大脑活动，你一定会难以置信。大脑看起来根本不像在睡觉。相反，即使在“休息”状态下，它也异常活跃，无数神经元以不断变化的、极其活跃的模式相互传递电信号。事实上，只有在非快速眼动睡眠阶段，大脑才能真正进入休息状态——此时能量消耗低于类似的清醒状态。但这只占整个睡眠周期的20%左右。正因如此，研究人员很早就开始摒弃“我们休息是为了休息”这种观念。当我们睡着时，大脑根本没有休息。即便如此，大多数人仍然认为睡眠具有强大的恢复作用，他们指出，如果睡眠不足，第二天思维就会变得迟钝。这一点在测量上是成立的，我们稍后会看到。因此，我们陷入了困境：考虑到大脑消耗的能量，似乎不可能在睡眠期间获得任何接近精神休息和恢复的东西。
Two scientists made substantial early contributions to our understanding of what the brain is doing while we sleep. Dement, who studied sleepless Peter Tripp, is a white-haired man with a broad smile who at this writing is in his late 80s. He says pithy things about our slumbering habits, such as “Dreaming permits each and every one of us to be quietly and safely insane every night of our lives.” Dement’s mentor, a gifted researcher named Nathaniel Kleitman, gave him many of his initial insights. If Dement can be considered the father of sleep research, Kleitman certainly could qualify as its grandfather. An intense Russian man with bushy eyebrows, Kleitman may be best noted for his willingness to experiment not only on himself but also on his children. When it appeared that a colleague of his had discovered rapid eye movement (REM) sleep, Kleitman promptly volunteered his daughter for experimentation, and she just as promptly confirmed the finding. He also persuaded a colleague to live with him underground to see what would happen to their sleep cycles without the influence of light and social cues. Here are some of the things Dement and Kleitman discovered about sleep.
两位科学家对我们理解睡眠时大脑的活动做出了早期重大贡献。德门特研究了失眠症患者彼得·特里普，他是一位白发苍苍、笑容可掬的老人，撰写本文时已年近九旬。他对我们的睡眠习惯有着精辟的见解，例如“做梦让我们每个人每晚都能在平静而安全的状态下体验疯狂”。德门特的导师，一位才华横溢的研究员纳撒尼尔·克莱特曼，给予了他许多最初的启发。如果说德门特是睡眠研究之父，那么克莱特曼无疑可以称得上是睡眠研究的祖父。克莱特曼是一位性格坚毅的俄罗斯人，浓眉大眼，他最令人称道的或许是他不仅愿意在自己身上做实验，也愿意在自己的孩子身上做实验。当他的一位同事似乎发现了快速眼动睡眠（REM睡眠）时，克莱特曼立即自愿让自己的女儿进行实验，而她也很快证实了这一发现。他还说服一位同事和他一起住在地下，观察在没有光线和社交线索影响的情况下，他们的睡眠周期会发生什么变化。以下是德门特和克莱特曼关于睡眠的一些发现。
Sleep is a battle
睡眠是一场战斗
Like soldiers on a battlefield, we have two powerful and opposing drives locked in vicious, biological combat. The armies, each made of legions of brain cells and biochemicals, have very different agendas. Though localized in the head, the theater of operations for these armies engulfs every corner of the body. The war they are waging has some interesting rules. First, these forces are engaged not just during the night, while we sleep, but also during the day, while we are awake. Second, they are doomed to a combat schedule in which each army sequentially wins one battle, then promptly loses the next battle, then quickly wins the next and so on, cycling through this win/loss column every day and every night. Third, neither army ever claims final victory. This incessant engagement is referred to as the “opponent process” model. It results in the waking and sleeping modes all humans cycle through every day (and night) of our lives.
如同战场上的士兵，我们体内两种强大且对立的驱动力正进行着激烈的生物性斗争。这两支军队，各自由大量的脑细胞和生化物质组成，有着截然不同的目标。虽然它们主要集中在大脑，但它们的作战范围却遍及身体的每一个角落。这场战争遵循着一些有趣的规则。首先，这些力量不仅在我们睡眠的夜晚交战，也在我们清醒的白天持续作战。其次，它们注定要遵循一种循环往复的战斗模式：每支军队都会依次赢得一场战斗，然后迅速输掉下一场，接着又迅速赢得下一场，如此往复，日夜不停地循环着胜负。第三，任何一方都无法宣称最终的胜利。这种持续不断的交战被称为“对立过程”模型。它导致了我们每个人每天（包括夜晚）都会经历的清醒和睡眠模式的循环。
One army is composed of neurons, hormones, and various other chemicals that do everything in their power to keep you awake. This army is called the circadian arousal system (often simply called “process C”). If this army had its way, you would stay up all the time. It is opposed by an equally powerful army, also made of brain cells, hormones, and various chemicals. These combatants do everything in their power to put you to sleep. They are termed the homeostatic sleep drive (“process S”). If this army had its way, you would go to sleep and never wake up. These drives define for us both the amount of sleep we need and the amount of sleep we get. Stated formally, process S maintains the duration and intensity of sleep, while process C determines the tendency and timing of the need to go to sleep .
一支由神经元、激素和其他各种化学物质组成的“军队”竭尽全力让你保持清醒。这支“军队”被称为昼夜节律觉醒系统（通常简称为“过程C”）。如果这支“军队”得逞，你将永远保持清醒。与之对抗的是另一支同样强大的“军队”，它也由脑细胞、激素和各种化学物质组成。这支“军队”竭尽全力让你入睡。它们被称为稳态睡眠驱动（“过程S”）。如果这支“军队”得逞，你将一睡不醒。这些驱动力决定了我们需要的睡眠量和实际获得的睡眠量。具体来说，过程S维持睡眠的持续时间和强度，而过程C决定了入睡的倾向和时间。
It is a paradoxical war. The longer one army controls the field, for example, the more likely it is to lose the battle. It’s almost as if each army becomes exhausted from having its way and eventually waves a temporary white flag. Indeed, the longer you are awake (the victorious process C doing victory laps around your head), the greater the probability becomes that the circadian arousal system will cede the field to its opponent. You then go to sleep. For most people, this act of capitulation comes after about 16 hours of active consciousness. This will occur, Kleitman found, even if you are living in a cave.
这是一场充满悖论的战争。例如，一方军队控制战场的时间越长，就越有可能输掉战斗。这几乎就像双方军队都因占据上风而精疲力竭，最终不得不暂时举起白旗。事实上，你清醒的时间越长（胜利的过程C在你脑海里欢呼雀跃），昼夜节律唤醒系统就越有可能将战场拱手让给对手。然后你就睡着了。对大多数人来说，这种投降行为发生在大约16小时的清醒状态之后。克莱特曼发现，即使你住在山洞里，这种情况也会发生。
Conversely, the longer you are asleep (the triumphant process S now doing the heady victory laps), the greater the probability becomes that the homeostatic sleep drive will similarly cede the field to its opponent, which is, of course, the drive to keep you awake. The result of this surrender is that you wake up. For most people, the length of time prior to capitulation is about half of its opponent’s, about eight hours of blissful sleep. And this also will occur even if you are living in a cave.
反之，你睡得越久（此时，负责维持体内平衡的睡眠驱动力正得意洋洋地庆祝胜利），就越有可能让位于它的对手——也就是让你保持清醒的驱动力。这种让步的结果就是你醒来。对大多数人来说，从睡眠到让步所需的时间大约只有对手的一半，也就是大约八个小时的酣睡。即使你住在山洞里，这种情况也会发生。
Such dynamic tension is a normal—even critical—part of our daily lives. In fact, the circadian arousal system and the homeostatic sleep drive are locked in a cycle of victory and surrender so predictable, you can graph it.
这种动态张力是我们日常生活中正常甚至至关重要的组成部分。事实上，昼夜节律唤醒系统和稳态睡眠驱动力之间存在着一种可预测的胜负循环，甚至可以绘制成图表。
In one of Kleitman’s most interesting experiments, he and a colleague spent an entire month living 1,300 feet underground in Mammoth Cave in Kentucky. Free of sunlight and daily schedules, Kleitman could find out whether the routines of wakefulness and sleep cycled themselves automatically through the human body. His experiment provided the first real hint that such an automatic device did exist in our bodies. Indeed, we now know that the body possesses a series of internal clocks, all controlled by discrete regions in the brain, providing a regular rhythmic schedule to our waking and sleeping experiences. This is surprisingly similar to the buzzing of a wristwatch’s internal quartz crystal. An area of the brain called the suprachiasmatic nucleus appears to contain just such a timing device. Of course, we have not been characterizing these pulsing rhythms as a benign wristwatch. We have been characterizing them as a war. One of Kleitman and Dement’s greatest contributions was to show that this nearly automatic rhythm occurs as a result of the continuous conflict between two opposing forces.
在克莱特曼最有趣的实验之一中，他和一位同事在肯塔基州猛犸洞穴地下1300英尺（约400米）处生活了一个月。没有阳光，也没有日常作息的束缚，克莱特曼得以探究人体的觉醒和睡眠周期是否能够自动循环。他的实验首次真正揭示了这种自动机制确实存在于我们体内。事实上，我们现在知道，人体拥有一系列内部时钟，它们都由大脑中不同的区域控制，为我们的觉醒和睡眠体验提供规律的节律。这与手表内部石英晶体的嗡嗡声惊人地相似。大脑中一个名为视交叉上核的区域似乎就包含着这样一个计时装置。当然，我们并没有把这些脉动的节律比作一块无害的手表，而是把它们比作一场战争。克莱特曼和德门特最伟大的贡献之一，就是证明了这种近乎自动的节律是两种对立力量持续冲突的结果。
Are you a lark, owl, or hummingbird?
你是云雀、猫头鹰还是蜂鸟？
Each of us wages this war on a slightly different schedule. The late advice columnist Ann Landers apparently would take her phone off the hook between 1:00 a.m. and 10:00 a.m. Why? This was the time she normally slept. “No one’s going to call me,” she said, “until I’m ready.” The cartoonist Scott Adams, creator of the comic strip Dilbert , never would think of starting his day at 10:00 a.m. “I’m quite tuned into my rhythms,” he told the authors of The Body Clock Guide to Better Health . “I never try to do any creating past noon. … I do the strip from 6:00 to 7:00 a.m.” Here we have two creative and well-accomplished professionals, one who starts working just as the other’s workday is finished.
我们每个人都以略微不同的时间表来应对这场“战争”。已故的专栏作家安·兰德斯（Ann Landers）似乎会在凌晨1点到上午10点之间把电话线拔掉。为什么呢？因为这段时间是她睡觉的时间。“在我准备好之前，没人会给我打电话，”她说。漫画家斯科特·亚当斯（Scott Adams），《呆伯特》（Dilbert）的创作者，也从不会在上午10点开始一天的工作。“我非常了解自己的生物钟，”他告诉《身体时钟健康指南》（The Body Clock Guide to Better Health）的作者，“我从不在中午之后进行任何创作……我早上6点到7点画漫画。” 这里我们看到两位才华横溢、成就斐然的专业人士，一位开始工作的时间恰好是另一位下班的时间。
About one in 10 of us is like Dilbert ’s Adams. The scientific literature calls such people larks (more palatable than the proper term, “early chronotype”). In general, larks report being most alert around noon and feel most productive at work a few hours before they eat lunch. They don’t need an alarm clock, because they invariably get up before the alarm rings—often before 6:00 a.m. Larks cheerfully report their favorite mealtime as breakfast and generally consume much less coffee than non-larks. Getting increasingly drowsy in the early evening, most larks go to bed (or want to go to bed) around 9:00 p.m.
大约十分之一的人就像迪尔伯特漫画里的亚当斯一样。科学文献称这类人为“百灵鸟型”（比更准确的术语“早起型”更易接受）。一般来说，“百灵鸟型”的人表示他们在中午前后最清醒，并在午餐前几个小时感觉工作效率最高。他们不需要闹钟，因为他们总是会在闹钟响起之前起床——通常在早上6点之前。百灵鸟型的人乐于分享他们最喜欢的用餐时间是早餐，而且他们通常比非百灵鸟型的人喝的咖啡少得多。傍晚时分，他们会越来越困，大多数百灵鸟型的人会在晚上9点左右上床睡觉（或者想要上床睡觉）。
Larks are incomprehensible to the one in 10 humans who lie at the other extreme of the sleep spectrum: “late chronotypes,” or owls. In general, owls report being most alert around 6:00 p.m., experiencing their most productive work times in the late evening. They rarely want to go to bed before 3:00 a.m. Owls invariably need an alarm clock to get them up in the morning, with extreme owls requiring multiple alarms to ensure arousal. Indeed, if owls had their druthers, most would not wake up much before 10:00 a.m. Not surprisingly, late chronotypes report their favorite mealtime as dinner, and they would drink gallons of coffee all day long to prop themselves up at work if given the opportunity. If it sounds to you as though owls do not sleep as well as larks in American society, you are right on the money. Indeed, late chronotypes usually accumulate a massive “sleep debt” as they go through life.
对于那些睡眠时间处于另一个极端——“晚睡型”或“猫头鹰型”——的人来说，百灵鸟式的作息简直难以理解。一般来说，猫头鹰型的人在下午6点左右最为清醒，工作效率最高的时候也是深夜。他们很少在凌晨3点之前睡觉。猫头鹰型的人早上起床总是需要闹钟，而极度晚睡型的人甚至需要多个闹钟才能确保醒来。事实上，如果猫头鹰型的人可以自由选择，他们中的大多数人会在上午10点之前醒来。不出所料，晚睡型的人最喜欢的用餐时间是晚餐，如果可以的话，他们会整天喝大量的咖啡来提神醒脑。如果你觉得在美国社会，猫头鹰型的人睡眠不如百灵鸟型的人好，那么你的感觉完全正确。事实上，晚睡晚起的人一生中通常会积累大量的“睡眠债”。
Whether lark or owl, researchers think these patterns are detectable in early childhood and burned into genes that govern our sleep/wake cycle. At least one study shows that if Mom or Dad is a lark, half of their kids will be, too. Larks and owls, though, cover only about 20 percent of the population. The rest of us are called hummingbirds. True to the idea of a continuum, some hummingbirds are more owlish, some are more larkish, and some are in between.
无论是百灵鸟还是猫头鹰，研究人员认为这些作息模式在幼儿时期就能被检测到，并深深地烙印在控制我们睡眠/觉醒周期的基因中。至少有一项研究表明，如果父母一方是百灵鸟型，那么他们的孩子中有一半也会是。然而，百灵鸟型和猫头鹰型只占人口的20%左右。其余的人则被称为蜂鸟型。正如连续谱的概念一样，有些蜂鸟更像猫头鹰，有些更像百灵鸟，还有一些则介于两者之间。
Nappin’ in the free world
在自由世界打盹
It must have taken some getting used to, if you were a staffer in the socially conservative early 1960s. Lyndon Baines Johnson, 36th president of the United States and leader of the free world, routinely closed the door to his office in the midafternoon and put on his pajamas. He then proceeded to take a 30-minute nap. Rising refreshed, he would then resume his role as commander in chief. Such presidential behavior might seem downright weird. But if you asked a sleep researcher like Dement, his response might surprise you: It was LBJ who was acting normally. The rest of us, who refuse to bring our pajamas to work, are the abnormal ones.
如果你是上世纪六十年代初社会保守主义盛行时期的一名幕僚，想必需要一段时间才能适应。美国第36任总统、自由世界的领袖林登·贝恩斯·约翰逊经常在下午关上办公室的门，换上睡衣，然后小睡30分钟。醒来后精神焕发，他便会继续履行三军统帅的职责。这种总统行为或许看起来十分怪异。但如果你问问像德门特这样的睡眠研究专家，他的回答可能会让你大吃一惊：约翰逊的行为才是正常的，而我们这些拒绝穿着睡衣上班的人才是不正常的。
LBJ was responding to something experienced by nearly everyone on the planet. It goes by many names—the midday yawn, the post-lunch dip, the afternoon “sleepies.” We’ll call it the nap zone, a period of time in the midafternoon when we experience transient sleepiness. It can be nearly impossible to get anything done during this time, and if you attempt to push through, which is what most of us do, you can spend much of your afternoon fighting a gnawing tiredness. It’s a fight because the brain really wants to take a nap and doesn’t care what its owner is doing. The concept of “siesta,” institutionalized in many other cultures, may have come as an explicit reaction to the nap zone.
约翰逊总统的讲话回应了几乎地球上每个人都经历过的现象。这种现象有很多叫法——午睡打哈欠、午后犯困、下午犯困等等。我们姑且称之为“午睡期”，指的是下午中段我们感到短暂困倦的那段时间。在这段时间里，几乎什么都做不了，如果你试图硬撑过去（而我们大多数人都是这么做的），那么你整个下午的大部分时间都会用来对抗这种难以忍受的困倦感。之所以说是“对抗”，是因为大脑真的想打个盹，它才不管主人在做什么。“午睡”的概念在许多其他文化中已经制度化，它或许正是对这种午睡期的一种直接回应。
At first, scientists didn’t believe the nap zone existed except as an artifact of sleep deprivation. That has changed. We now know that some people feel it more intensely than others. We know it is not related to a big lunch (although a big lunch, especially one loaded with carbs, can greatly increase its intensity). We also know that when you chart the process S curve and process C curve, you can see that they flatline in the same place—in the afternoon. The biochemical battle reaches a climactic stalemate. An equal tension now exists between the two drives, which extracts a great deal of energy to maintain. Some researchers, though not all, think this equanimity in tension drives the need to nap. Some think that a long sleep at night and a short midday nap represent default human sleep behavior, that it is part of our evolutionary history.
起初，科学家们认为午睡区的存在仅仅是睡眠不足造成的假象。但现在情况发生了改变。我们现在知道，有些人比其他人更能感受到午睡的强烈程度。我们知道它与午餐吃得太多无关（尽管午餐吃得太多，尤其是富含碳水化合物的午餐，会显著增强午睡的强度）。我们还知道，当你绘制S曲线和C曲线时，你会发现它们在同一位置——下午——趋于平缓。生化作用的博弈达到了一个僵局。两种驱动力之间达到了一种平衡的张力，需要消耗大量的能量来维持。一些研究人员（但并非所有研究人员）认为，这种张力的平衡正是午睡需求的驱动因素。有些人认为，夜间长时间睡眠和午间短暂小睡代表了人类默认的睡眠行为，这是我们进化史的一部分。
Regardless of the cause, the nap zone matters, because our brains don’t work as well during it. If you are a public speaker, you already know it is darn near fatal to give a talk in the midafternoon. The nap zone also is literally fatal: More traffic accidents occur during it than at any other time of the day.
无论原因是什么，午睡时段都至关重要，因为我们的大脑在午睡时段运转不佳。如果你是公众演讲者，你肯定知道在下午进行演讲几乎是致命的。午睡时段也确实会造成交通事故：这段时间发生的交通事故比一天中任何其他时间都多。
If you embrace the need to nap rather than pushing through, as LBJ found, your brain will work better afterward. One NASA study showed that a 26-minute nap reduced a flight crew’s lapses in awareness by 34 percent, compared to a control group who didn’t nap. Nappers also saw a 16 percent improvement in reaction times. And their performance stayed consistent throughout the day rather than dropping off at the end of a flight or at night. (The flight crew was given a 40-minute break, it took about six minutes for people to fall asleep, and the average nap lasted 26 minutes.) Another study showed that a 45-minute nap produces a similar boost in cognitive performance, a boost lasting more than six hours. Also, napping for 30 minutes before pulling an all-nighter keeps your mind sharper in the wee hours.
如果你像约翰逊总统那样，接受小憩的需求而不是强撑着工作，你的大脑在小憩后会运转得更好。美国宇航局的一项研究表明，与没有小憩的对照组相比，26分钟的小憩能将机组人员的注意力不集中情况减少34%。小憩者的反应速度也提高了16%。而且，他们的表现一整天都保持稳定，不会像其他机组人员那样在飞行结束时或夜间出现下滑。（机组人员有40分钟的休息时间，大约6分钟后入睡，平均小憩时间为26分钟。）另一项研究表明，45分钟的小憩也能带来类似的认知能力提升，而且这种提升效果可以持续超过6个小时。此外，在熬夜前小憩30分钟也能让你在凌晨时分保持头脑清醒。
What happens if we don’t get enough sleep
如果我们睡眠不足会怎么样？
Given our understanding of how and when we sleep, you might expect that scientists would have an answer to the question of how much sleep we need. Indeed, they do. The answer is: We don’t know. You did not read that wrong. After all of these centuries of experience with sleep, we still don’t know how much of the stuff people actually need. Generalizations don’t work. When you dig into the data on humans, what you find is not remarkable uniformity but remarkable individuality. To make matters worse, sleep schedules are unbelievably dynamic. They change with age. They change with gender. They change depending upon whether or not you are pregnant, and whether or not you are going through puberty. One must take into account so many variables that it almost feels as though we’ve asked the wrong question.
鉴于我们对睡眠方式和时间的了解，你可能会认为科学家们应该能够回答“我们需要多少睡眠”这个问题。的确，他们确实有答案。但答案是：我们不知道。你没看错。经过几个世纪对睡眠的研究，我们仍然不知道人们究竟需要多少睡眠。概括是行不通的。当你深入研究人类数据时，你会发现的不是惊人的一致性，而是惊人的个体差异。更糟糕的是，睡眠规律极其动态。它会随着年龄而变化，随着性别而变化，也会根据你是否怀孕、是否处于青春期而变化。我们必须考虑如此多的变量，以至于我们似乎一开始就问错了问题。
So let’s invert the query. How much sleep don’t you need? In other words, what are the numbers that disrupt normal function?
那么，让我们反过来问：你到底不需要多少睡眠？换句话说，哪些睡眠量会扰乱正常的生理机能？
Sleep loss = brain drain
睡眠不足会导致脑力流失。
One study showed that a highly successful student can be set up for a precipitous academic fall just by getting less than seven hours of sleep a night. Take an A student used to scoring in the top 10 percent of virtually anything she does. If she gets just under seven hours of sleep on weekdays, and about 40 minutes more on weekends, her scores will begin to match the scores of the bottom 9 percent of individuals who are getting enough sleep. Cumulative losses during the week add up to cumulative deficits during the weekend—and, if not paid for, that sleep debt will be carried into the next week .
一项研究表明，即使是成绩优异的学生，如果每晚睡眠时间少于7小时，也可能导致学业成绩急剧下滑。假设一位成绩优异的学生，几乎在所有方面都能名列前10%。如果她工作日睡眠时间不足7小时，周末睡眠时间仅增加约40分钟，那么她的成绩就会与睡眠充足的9%人群的成绩持平。工作日睡眠不足的累积会导致周末睡眠不足的加剧——如果不及时补觉，这种睡眠债就会延续到下周。
Another study followed soldiers responsible for operating complex military hardware. One night’s loss of sleep resulted in about a 30 percent loss in overall cognitive skill, with a subsequent drop in performance. Bump that to two nights of sleep loss, and the loss in cognitive skill doubles to 60 percent.
另一项研究追踪了负责操作复杂军事装备的士兵。结果发现，一晚睡眠不足会导致他们的整体认知能力下降约30%，进而导致工作表现下滑。如果睡眠不足持续两晚，认知能力的下降幅度则会翻倍，达到60%。
Other studies showed that when sleep was restricted to six hours or less per night for just five nights, cognitive performance matched that of a person suffering from 48 hours of continual sleep deprivation.
其他研究表明，如果连续五晚每晚睡眠时间限制在六小时或更少，认知能力就会达到连续 48 小时睡眠不足者的水平。
What do these data tell us? That some people need at least seven hours of sleep a night. And that some people need at least six hours of sleep a night. On the other hand, you may have heard of people who seem to need only four or five hours of sleep. They are referred to as suffering from “healthy insomnia.” Essentially, it comes down to whatever amount of sleep is right for you. When robbed of that, bad things really do happen to your brain.
这些数据告诉我们什么？有些人每晚至少需要七个小时的睡眠，而有些人每晚至少需要六个小时的睡眠。另一方面，你可能听说过有些人似乎只需要四五个小时的睡眠，他们被称为患有“健康失眠”。归根结底，睡眠时间的长短取决于什么对你来说是合适的。睡眠不足会对大脑造成损害。
Sleep loss takes a toll on the body, too—on functions that do not at first blush seem associated with sleep. When people become sleep deprived, for example, their body’s ability to utilize the food they are consuming falls by about one-third. The ability to make insulin and to extract energy from the brain’s favorite source, glucose, begins to fail miserably. At the same time, you find a marked need to have more of it, because the body’s stress hormone levels begin to rise in an increasingly deregulated fashion. If you keep up the behavior, you appear to accelerate parts of the aging process. For example, if healthy 30-year-olds are sleep deprived for six days (averaging, in this study, about four hours of sleep per night), parts of their body chemistry soon revert to that of a 60-year-old. And if they are allowed to recover, it will take them almost a week to get back to their 30-year-old systems.
睡眠不足也会对身体造成损害——甚至会影响一些乍看之下似乎与睡眠无关的功能。例如，当人们睡眠不足时，身体对所摄入食物的利用能力会下降约三分之一。胰岛素的生成能力以及从大脑最常用的能量来源——葡萄糖中提取能量的能力都会严重下降。与此同时，你会明显感到需要摄入更多能量，因为体内的压力激素水平开始以一种越来越失调的方式升高。如果长期如此，似乎会加速某些衰老过程。例如，如果健康的30岁年轻人连续六天睡眠不足（在本研究中，平均每晚睡眠时间约为4小时），他们身体的部分化学成分很快就会恢复到60岁老年人的状态。即使允许他们恢复，也需要近一周的时间才能恢复到30岁时的状态。
Taken together, these studies show that sleep loss cripples thinking in just about every way you can measure thinking. Sleep loss hurts attention, executive function, working memory, mood, quantitative skills, logical reasoning ability, general math knowledge. Eventually, sleep loss affects manual dexterity, including fine motor control, and even gross motor movements, such as the ability to walk on a treadmill.
综合这些研究表明，睡眠不足几乎会从各个方面损害思维能力。睡眠不足会损害注意力、执行功能、工作记忆、情绪、定量技能、逻辑推理能力和一般数学知识。最终，睡眠不足还会影响手部灵巧性，包括精细动作控制，甚至会影响粗大动作，例如在跑步机上行走的能力。
So what can a good night’s sleep do for us?
那么，睡个好觉对我们有什么好处呢？
Sleep on it: benefits of a solid night’s rest
好好睡一觉：充足睡眠的好处
Dimitri Ivanovich Mendeleyev was your archetypal brilliant-but-mad-looking scientist. Hairy and opinionated, Mendeleyev possessed the lurking countenance of a Rasputin, the haunting eyes of Peter the Great, and the moral flexibility of both. He once threatened to commit suicide if a young lady didn’t marry him. She consented, which was quite illegal, because unbeknownst to the poor girl, Mendeleyev was already married. This trespass kept him out of the Russian Academy of Sciences for some time, which in hindsight may have been a bit rash, as Mendeleyev single-handedly systematized the entire science of chemistry. His Periodic Table of the Elements—a way of organizing every atom that had so far been discovered—was so prescient, it allowed room for all of the elements yet to be found and even predicted some of their properties.
德米特里·伊万诺维奇·门捷列夫是那种典型的才华横溢却又外表古怪的科学家。他毛发旺盛，固执己见，长着一张拉斯普京般阴险的面孔，一双彼得大帝般摄人心魄的眼睛，以及两者兼具的道德灵活性。他曾威胁一位年轻女子，如果她不嫁给他，他就自杀。女子答应了，这在当时是违法的，因为可怜的姑娘并不知道门捷列夫已经结婚了。这一“罪行”使他一度被逐出俄罗斯科学院，现在看来，这或许有些草率，因为门捷列夫凭借一己之力系统化了整个化学领域。他设计的元素周期表——一种将当时已发现的所有原子排列起来的方法——极具前瞻性，不仅为所有尚未发现的元素预留了位置，甚至还预测了它们的一些性质。
But what’s most extraordinary is this: Mendeleyev says he came up with the idea in his sleep. Contemplating the nature of the universe while playing solitaire one evening, he nodded off. When he awoke, he knew how all of the atoms in the universe were organized, and he promptly created his famous table. Interestingly, he organized the atoms in repeating groups of seven, just the way you play solitaire.
但最令人惊奇的是：门捷列夫说他是在睡梦中想到这个主意的。一天晚上，他一边玩纸牌游戏一边思考宇宙的本质，不知不觉就睡着了。醒来后，他已经知道宇宙中所有原子是如何排列的，并立即创建了他著名的原子序数表。有趣的是，他把原子排列成七个一组的重复单元，就像玩纸牌游戏一样。
Mendeleyev is hardly the only scientist who has reported feelings of inspiration after having slept. Is there something to the notion of “Let’s sleep on it”? Mountains of data say there is. A healthy night’s sleep can indeed boost learning significantly. Sleep scientists debate how we should define learning, and what exactly is improvement. But there are many examples of the phenomenon. One study stands out in particular.
门捷列夫并非唯一一位在睡眠后获得灵感的科学家。“睡一觉再思考”的说法真的有道理吗？大量数据表明确实如此。充足的睡眠确实能显著提升学习能力。睡眠科学家们仍在争论我们应该如何定义学习，以及究竟什么才算进步。但这种现象的例证不胜枚举。其中一项研究尤为引人注目。
Students were given a series of math problems and prepped with a method to solve them. The students weren’t told there was also an easier “shortcut” way to solve the problems, potentially discoverable while doing the exercise. The question was: Is there any way to jump-start, even speed up, the insight into the shortcut? The answer was yes, if you allow them to sleep on it. If you let 12 hours pass after the initial training and ask the students to do more problems, about 20 percent will have discovered the shortcut. But, if in that 12 hours you also allow eight or so hours of regular sleep, that figure triples to about 60 percent. No matter how many times the experiment is run, the sleep group consistently outperforms the non-sleep group about three to one.
学生们被布置了一系列数学题，并事先学习了一种解题方法。他们并不知道还有一种更简单的“捷径”解题方法，这种方法可能会在练习过程中被发现。问题是：有没有办法快速甚至加速学生发现这种捷径？答案是肯定的，只要让他们睡一觉。如果在最初的训练之后等待12个小时，再让学生做更多的题，大约20%的学生会发现捷径。但是，如果在这12个小时里，你还允许他们睡大约8个小时，那么发现捷径的学生比例会翻三倍，达到60%左右。无论实验重复多少次，睡眠组的表现始终比非睡眠组高出大约三倍。
Sleep also has been shown to enhance tasks that involve visual texture discrimination (the ability to pick out an object from an ocean of similar-looking objects), motor adaptations (improving movement skills), and motor sequence learning. The type of learning that appears to be most sensitive to sleep improvement is that which involves learning a procedure. Simply disrupt the night’s sleep at specific stages and retest in the morning, and you eliminate any overnight learning improvement. Clearly, for specific types of intellectual skill, sleep can be a great friend to learning.
睡眠已被证实能够增强视觉纹理辨别能力（即从大量相似物体中识别目标物体的能力）、运动适应能力（即运动技能的提升）以及运动序列学习能力。其中，对睡眠改善最为敏感的学习类型似乎是程序性学习。只需在睡眠的特定阶段打断睡眠，并在第二天早上重新测试，就能消除任何一夜之间学习能力的提升。显然，对于某些类型的智力技能而言，睡眠是学习的得力助手。
Why we sleep
我们为什么睡觉
Consider the following true story of a successfully married, incredibly detail-oriented accountant. Even though dead asleep, he regularly gives financial reports to his wife all night long. Many of these reports come from the day’s activities. (Incidentally, if his wife wakes him up—which is often, because his financial broadcasts are loud—the accountant becomes amorous and wants to have sex.) Are we all organizing our previous experiences while we sleep? Could this not only explain all of the other data we have been discussing, but also provide the reason why we sleep?
请看下面这个真实的故事：一位婚姻美满、极其注重细节的会计师。即使睡梦中，他也会整夜向妻子汇报财务状况。这些汇报大多源于他白天的各项工作。（顺便一提，如果妻子把他吵醒——这种情况经常发生，因为他汇报财务状况的声音很大——这位会计师就会变得情欲高涨，想要亲热。）我们是否都在睡梦中整理过往的经历呢？这不仅能解释我们之前讨论的种种现象，还能解释我们为什么会睡觉吗？
To answer these questions, we turn to a group of researchers who left a bunch of wires stuck inside a rat’s brain—electrodes placed near individual neurons. The rat had just learned to negotiate a maze when it decided to take a nap. The wires were attached to a recording device, which happened to still be on. The device allows scientists to eavesdrop on the brain while it is talking to itself, something like an NSA phone tap. Even in a tiny rat’s brain, it is not unusual these days to listen in on the chattering of up to 500 neurons at once as they process information. So what are they all saying?
为了解答这些问题，我们不妨看看一组研究人员的做法。他们将一堆电线——电极——留在老鼠的大脑里，这些电极就放置在单个神经元附近。这只老鼠刚刚学会走迷宫，就决定打个盹儿。电线连接着一个录音设备，而这个设备恰好还开着。这个设备可以让科学家们监听大脑内部的对话，有点像美国国家安全局的电话监听。如今，即使是在一只小小的老鼠的大脑里，同时监听多达500个神经元处理信息时的“聊天”也并不罕见。那么，它们到底在说什么呢？
If you listen in while the rat is acquiring new information, like learning to navigate a maze, you soon will detect something extraordinary. A very discrete “maze-specific” pattern of electrical stimulation begins to emerge. Working something like the old Morse code, a series of neurons begin to crackle in a specifically timed sequence while the mouse is learning. Afterward, the rat will always fire off that same pattern whenever it travels through the maze. It appears to be an electrical representation of the rat’s new maze-navigating thought patterns (at least, as many as 500 electrodes can detect).
如果你在老鼠学习新信息（例如学习如何穿过迷宫）时进行监听，很快就会发现一些非同寻常的现象。一种非常独特的“迷宫特异性”电刺激模式开始显现。类似于古老的摩尔斯电码，当老鼠学习时，一系列神经元会按照特定的时间顺序发出噼啪声。之后，每当老鼠穿过迷宫时，它都会发出相同的电信号。这似乎是老鼠新的迷宫导航思维模式的电信号表征（至少，500个电极可以检测到这种模式）。
When the rat goes to sleep, its brain begins to replay the maze-pattern sequence . Reminiscent of our accountant, the animal’s brain repeats what it learned that day. Always executing the pattern in a specific stage of sleep, the rat repeats it over and over again—and much faster than during the day. The rate is so furious, the sequence is replayed thousands of times. If a mean graduate student decides to wake up the rat during this stage, called slow-wave sleep, something equally extraordinary is observed. The rat has trouble remembering the maze the next day. Quite literally, the rat seems to be consolidating the day’s learning the night after that learning occurred, and an interruption of that sleep disrupts the learning cycle.
当老鼠入睡时，它的大脑会开始重现迷宫图案的序列。就像我们的会计师一样，老鼠的大脑会重复当天学到的东西。在特定的睡眠阶段，老鼠总是重复执行这个图案，而且速度比白天快得多。这种重复速度如此之快，以至于该序列会被重现数千次。如果一个刻薄的研究生决定在这个被称为慢波睡眠的阶段唤醒老鼠，就会观察到同样奇特的现象：第二天老鼠很难记住迷宫。确切地说，老鼠似乎在学习后的第二天晚上巩固了当天的学习内容，而睡眠的中断会扰乱这个学习周期。
This naturally caused researchers to ask whether the same was true for humans. The answer? Not only do we do such processing, but we do it in a more complex fashion. Like the rat, humans appear to replay certain learning experiences at night, during the slow-wave phase. Unlike the rat, more emotionally charged memories appear to replay at a different stage in the sleep cycle.
这自然而然地促使研究人员探究人类是否也存在同样的现象。答案是：我们不仅会进行此类信息处理，而且处理方式更为复杂。与老鼠一样，人类似乎也会在夜间慢波睡眠阶段重现某些学习经历。但与老鼠不同的是，情绪更为强烈的记忆似乎会在睡眠周期的不同阶段重现。
These findings represent a bombshell of an idea: Some kind of offline processing is occurring at night. Is it possible that the reason we need to sleep is simply to shut off the exterior world for a while, allowing us to divert more attention to our cognitive interiors? Is it possible that the reason we need to sleep is so that we can learn?
这些发现揭示了一个惊人的观点：某种离线处理过程在夜间也在进行。我们睡眠的原因是否仅仅是为了暂时隔绝外部世界，从而让我们能够将更多注意力集中在内在的认知活动上？我们睡眠的原因是否是为了学习？
It sounds compelling, but of course the real world of research is much messier. Some findings appear to complicate, if not fully contradict, the idea of offline processing. For example, brain-damaged individuals who lack the ability to sleep in the slow-wave phase nonetheless have normal, even improved, memory. So do individuals whose REM sleep is suppressed by antidepressant medications. Exactly how to reconcile these data with the previous findings is a subject of intense scientific debate. Newer findings in mice suggest that the brain uses the time to clean house, sweeping away the toxic molecules that are a byproduct of the brain doing its thinking. With more time and more research, we’ll gain a greater understanding of what the brain is doing as we sleep—and why.
这听起来很有说服力，但现实研究当然要复杂得多。一些研究结果似乎使离线处理的概念变得复杂，甚至完全否定了这一概念。例如，脑损伤患者即使无法进入慢波睡眠阶段，记忆力也正常，甚至有所提高。服用抗抑郁药物抑制快速眼动睡眠的患者也同样如此。如何将这些数据与之前的研究结果调和起来，是目前科学界激烈争论的话题。小鼠的最新研究表明，大脑会利用睡眠时间进行“清理”，清除大脑思考过程中产生的有毒分子。随着时间的推移和研究的深入，我们将更清楚地了解大脑在睡眠期间的活动及其原因。
For now, a consistent concept emerges: Sleep is intimately involved in learning. It is observable with large amounts of sleep; it is observable with small amounts of sleep; it is observable all the time. It is time we did a better job of observing its importance in our lives.
目前来看，一个普遍的观点是：睡眠与学习密切相关。无论睡眠时间长短，睡眠对学习都有影响；睡眠不足时，睡眠对学习同样重要；无论何时，睡眠对学习都至关重要。我们应该更加重视睡眠在我们生活中的重要性。
More ideas
更多想法
If businesses and schools took sleep seriously, what would a modern office building look like? A modern school? These are not idle questions. The effects of sleep deprivation are thought to cost US businesses more than $100 billion a year .
如果企业和学校都重视睡眠，现代办公楼会是什么样子？现代学校又会是什么样子？这些问题并非空穴来风。据估计，睡眠不足每年给美国企业造成的损失超过1000亿美元。
Match schedules to chronotypes
将日程安排与生物钟类型相匹配
Behavioral tests can easily discriminate larks from owls from hummingbirds. Given advances in genetic research, in the future you may need only a blood test to characterize your process C and process S graphs. That means you can determine the hours when you are likely to experience productivity peaks. Twenty percent of the workforce is already at suboptimal productivity in the current nine-to-five model. So here’s an obvious idea: Set your schedule—whether college class schedule or work schedule—to match your chronotype.
行为测试可以轻松区分百灵鸟、猫头鹰和蜂鸟。随着基因研究的进步，未来你可能只需要一次血液检测就能了解你的C过程和S过程图。这意味着你可以确定自己最有可能达到生产力高峰的时间段。在目前的朝九晚五模式下，已有20%的员工生产力低于最佳水平。因此，一个显而易见的建议是：根据你的生物钟类型来安排你的日程——无论是大学课程表还是工作时间表。
Businesses could create several work schedules, based on the chronotypes of the employees. They might gain more productivity and a greater quality of life for those unfortunate people who otherwise are doomed to carry a permanent sleep debt. A business of the future takes sleep schedules seriously.
企业可以根据员工的生物钟类型制定多种工作时间表。这或许能提高生产力，并改善那些不幸长期睡眠不足的人的生活质量。未来的企业会认真对待员工的睡眠时间表。
We could do the same in education. Teachers are just as likely to be late chronotypes as their students. Why not put them together? You might increase the competencies of both the teacher and the students. Freed of the nagging consequences of their sleep debts, each might be more fully capable of mobilizing his or her God-given IQ.
我们也可以把这种方法运用到教育领域。教师和学生一样，都有可能属于晚睡晚起型。为什么不让他们一起学习呢？这样或许能提高教师和学生的学习能力。摆脱了睡眠不足的困扰，他们或许都能更充分地发挥自身与生俱来的智商。
Variable schedules also would take advantage of the fact that sleep needs change throughout a person’s life. For example, data suggest that students temporarily shift to more of an owl chronotype as they transit through their teenage years. This has led some school districts to start their high-school classes after 9:00 a.m. This may make some sense. Sleep hormones (such as the protein melatonin) are at their maximum levels in the teenage brain. The natural tendency of these kids is to sleep more, especially in the morning. As we age, we tend to get less sleep, and some evidence suggests we need less sleep, too. An employee who starts out with her greatest productivity in one schedule may, as the years go by, keep a similar high level of output simply by switching to a different schedule .
灵活的作息时间表还能利用睡眠需求随年龄变化这一事实。例如，数据显示，学生在青少年时期会暂时转变为更偏向“夜猫子”的作息类型。这导致一些学区将高中课程的开始时间推迟到上午9点以后。这或许有一定道理。青少年大脑中的睡眠激素（例如褪黑激素）水平达到峰值。这些孩子自然倾向于睡得更多，尤其是在早上。随着年龄的增长，我们的睡眠时间往往会减少，一些证据表明，我们所需的睡眠时间也会减少。一位员工如果最初在某种作息时间表下工作效率最高，那么随着时间的推移，她只需调整作息时间表，就能保持类似的高效率。
Respect the nap zone
尊重午睡区
Don’t schedule meetings or classes during the time when the process C and process S curves are flatlined. Don’t give high-demand presentations or take critical exams anywhere near the collision of these two curves. Can you actually get a nap? That’s often easier said than done. College students can perhaps get back to their dorm rooms. Stay-at-home parents might be able to sleep when baby does. Some employees sneak out to their cars.
不要在流程 C 曲线和流程 S 曲线趋于平缓的时间段安排会议或课程。不要在两条曲线交汇处附近进行高强度演讲或参加关键考试。你真的能睡个午觉吗？这通常说起来容易做起来难。大学生或许可以回宿舍休息。全职父母或许可以在孩子睡觉的时候也睡一会儿。有些员工会偷偷溜到车里去。
Even better would be if schools and businesses deliberately planned downshifts during the nap zone. Naps would be accorded the same deference that businesses reluctantly treat lunch, or even potty breaks: a necessary nod to an employee’s biological needs. Companies could create a designated space for employees to take one half-hour nap each workday. The advantage would be straightforward. People hired for their intellectual strength would be allowed to keep that strength in tip-top shape. “What other management strategy will improve people’s performance 34 percent in just 26 minutes?” said Mark Rosekind, the NASA scientist who conducted that eye-opening research on naps and pilot performance.
如果学校和企业能特意安排午睡时段，那就更好了。午睡应该像企业勉强对待午餐甚至上厕所休息一样受到重视：这是对员工生理需求的必要尊重。公司可以设立专门区域，供员工每天午睡半小时。这样做的好处显而易见：那些因智力而被聘用的人，能够保持最佳状态。“还有什么管理策略能在短短26分钟内将员工的工作效率提高34%呢？”美国宇航局科学家马克·罗斯金德说道，他曾进行过一项关于午睡与飞行员表现的突破性研究。
Sleep on it
好好想想
Given the data about a good night’s rest, organizations might tackle their most intractable problems by having the entire “solving team” go on a mini-retreat. Once arrived, employees would be presented with the problem and asked to think about solutions. But they would not start coming to conclusions, or even begin sharing ideas with each other, before they had slept about eight hours. When they awoke, would the same increase in problem-solving rates available in the lab also be available to that team? It’s worth finding out.
鉴于睡眠质量对解决问题至关重要，企业或许可以尝试让整个“问题解决团队”进行一次小型静修，以此来解决最棘手的问题。抵达静修地点后，员工们会被告知问题并被要求思考解决方案。但在他们睡足八小时之前，他们不会开始得出结论，甚至不会开始彼此分享想法。当他们醒来时，实验室中观察到的问题解决率提升是否也能同样适用于这个团队呢？这值得探究。
Brain Rule # 3
大脑法则#3
Sleep well, think well.
睡好觉，才能头脑清醒。
• The brain is in a constant state of tension between cells and chemicals that try to put you to sleep and cells and chemicals that try to keep you awake.
•大脑处于一种持续的紧张状态，一方面有细胞和化学物质试图让你入睡，另一方面又有细胞和化学物质试图让你保持清醒。
• The neurons of your brain show vigorous rhythmical activity when you’re asleep—perhaps replaying what you learned that day.
•当你睡觉时，你大脑中的神经元会表现出活跃的节律性活动——也许是在重现你当天所学到的东西。
• People vary in how much sleep they need and when they prefer to get it, but the biological drive for an afternoon nap is universal.
•每个人的睡眠需求量和睡眠时间都不一样，但午睡的生物本能是普遍存在的。
• Loss of sleep hurts attention, executive function, working memory, mood, quantitative skills, logical reasoning, and even motor dexterity.
•睡眠不足会损害注意力、执行功能、工作记忆、情绪、定量技能、逻辑推理能力，甚至运动灵活性。
# ↩
stress
压力
Brain Rule #4
大脑法则#4
Stressed brains don’t learn the same way.
压力过大的大脑学习方式与正常大脑不同。
# ↩
IT IS, BY ANY measure, a thoroughly rotten experiment. Here is this beautiful German shepherd, lying in one corner of a metal box, whimpering. He is receiving painful electric shocks, stimuli that should leave him howling in pain. Oddly enough, the dog could easily get out. The other side of the box is perfectly insulated from shocks, and only a low barrier separates the two sides. Though the dog could jump over to safety when the whim strikes him, the whim doesn’t strike him. He just lies down in the corner of the electric side, whimpering with each jarring jolt. He must be physically removed by the experimenter to be relieved of the experience.
无论从哪个角度来看，这都是一场彻头彻尾的糟糕实验。瞧，这只漂亮的德国牧羊犬躺在金属箱的一角，呜咽着。它正遭受着痛苦的电击，这种刺激本应让它痛得嚎叫。奇怪的是，这只狗明明可以轻易逃脱。箱子的另一侧完全绝缘，两边之间只隔着一道低矮的屏障。虽然这只狗可以在实验开始时跳到安全的地方，但实验并没有让它得逞。它只是躺在带电一侧的角落里，随着每一次剧烈的电击呜咽。实验人员必须把它抱走，才能让它摆脱这种痛苦。
What has happened to that dog?
那只狗怎么了？
A few days before entering the box, the animal was strapped to a restraining harness rigged with electric wires, inescapably receiving the same painful shock day and night. And at first he didn’t just stand there taking it, he reacted . He howled in pain. He urinated. He strained mightily against his harness in an increasingly desperate attempt to link some behavior of his with the cessation of the pain. But it was no use. As the hours and even days ticked by, his resistance eventually subsided. Why? The dog began to receive a very clear message: The pain was not going to stop; the shocks were going to be forever. There was no way out. Even after the dog had been released from the harness and placed into the metal box with the escape route, he could no longer understand his options. Learning had been shut down.
在进入箱子前几天，这只动物被绑在装有电线的束缚带上，日夜不停地遭受着同样的痛苦电击。起初，它并非只是默默忍受，而是有所反应。它痛苦地嚎叫，随地小便，拼命挣扎，试图将自己的某些行为与痛苦的停止联系起来。但这毫无用处。随着时间的流逝，甚至几天过去，它的抵抗最终消退了。为什么？这只狗开始接收到一个非常明确的信息：痛苦不会停止，电击将永无止境。它无路可逃。即使后来它被解开了束缚带，放进了有逃生通道的金属箱子里，它也无法理解自己的选择。它的学习能力已经停止了。
Those of you familiar with psychology already know I am describing a famous set of experiments begun in the late 1960s by legendary psychologist Martin Seligman. He coined the term “learned helplessness” to describe both the perception of inescapability and its associated cognitive collapse. Many animals behave in a similar fashion when punishment is unavoidable, and that includes humans. Inmates in concentration camps routinely experienced these symptoms in response to their horrid conditions. Some camps gave it the name Gammel , derived from the colloquial German word Gammeln , which literally means “rotting.” Perhaps not surprisingly, Seligman spent the rest of his career studying how humans respond to optimism.
熟悉心理学的朋友应该知道，我接下来要介绍的是传奇心理学家马丁·塞利格曼（Martin Seligman）在20世纪60年代末期开展的一系列著名实验。他创造了“习得性无助”（learned helplessness）一词，用来描述人们对无法逃避的处境的感知以及由此导致的认知崩溃。许多动物在无法避免惩罚时都会表现出类似的行为，人类也不例外。集中营里的囚犯经常会因为恶劣的生存环境而出现这些症状。有些集中营甚至将这种现象称为“Gammel”，这个词源于德语口语“Gammeln”，字面意思是“腐烂”。或许并不令人意外，塞利格曼在余下的职业生涯中，一直致力于研究人类如何应对乐观情绪。
What is so awful about severe, chronic stress that it can cause behavioral changes as devastating as learned helplessness? Why is learning so radically altered? We’ll begin with a definition of stress, talk about biological responses, and then move to the relationship between stress and learning. Along the way, we will talk about marriage and parenting, about the workplace, and about the first and only time I ever heard my mother, a fourth-grade teacher, swear. It was her first real encounter with learned helplessness.
严重且慢性的压力究竟有何可怕之处，竟能导致习得性无助这样具有毁灭性的行为改变？学习能力为何会发生如此剧烈的变化？我们将首先定义压力，探讨其生理反应，然后深入分析压力与学习之间的关系。在此过程中，我们还会谈到婚姻与育儿、职场，以及我第一次也是唯一一次听到我母亲——一位小学四年级老师——说脏话的经历。那是她第一次真正体验到习得性无助。
What is stress? It depends
什么是压力？这取决于很多因素。
Not all stress is the same. Certain types of stress really hurt learning, but some types of stress boost learning. Second, it’s difficult to detect when someone is experiencing stress. Some people love skydiving for recreation; it’s others’ worst nightmare. Is jumping out of an airplane inherently stressful? The answer is no, and that highlights the subjective nature of stress.
并非所有压力都一样。某些类型的压力会严重阻碍学习，而另一些类型的压力则能促进学习。其次，很难察觉一个人是否正在承受压力。有些人喜欢跳伞作为休闲活动，而对另一些人来说，跳伞却是噩梦。从飞机上跳下来本身就是一种压力吗？答案是否定的，这也凸显了压力的主观性。
The body alone isn’t of much help in providing a definition, either. There is no unique grouping of physiological responses capable of telling a scientist whether you are experiencing stress. That’s because many of the mechanisms that cause you to shrink in horror from a predator are the same mechanisms used when you are having sex—or even while you are consuming your Thanksgiving dinner. To your body, saber-toothed tigers and orgasms and turkey gravy look remarkably similar. An aroused physiological state is characteristic of both stress and pleasure.
单凭身体反应也难以对压力做出明确定义。并没有一组独特的生理反应能够告诉科学家你是否正经历压力。这是因为，许多让你因捕食者而惊恐缩缩的机制，与你在性爱时——甚至在你享用感恩节大餐时——所使用的机制相同。对你的身体而言，剑齿虎、性高潮和火鸡肉汁看起来非常相似。兴奋的生理状态既是压力的特征，也是愉悦的特征。
So what’s a scientist to do? A few years ago, gifted researchers Jeansok Kim and David Diamond came up with a three-part definition that covers many of the bases. In their view, if all three are happening simultaneously, a person is stressed.
那么科学家该怎么办呢？几年前，两位才华横溢的研究人员金珍淑（Jeansok Kim）和大卫·戴蒙德（David Diamond）提出了一个涵盖诸多方面的三部分定义。在他们看来，如果这三者同时出现，那么这个人就处于压力状态。
A measurable physiological response: There must be an aroused physiological response to the stress, and it must be measurable by an outside party. I saw this the first time my then 18-month-old son encountered a carrot on his plate at dinner. He promptly went ballistic: He screamed and cried and peed in his diaper. His aroused physiological state was immediately measurable by his dad, and probably by anyone else within a half mile of our kitchen table.
可测量的生理反应：必须有对压力的生理反应，而且这种反应必须能够被外部人员测量到。我第一次亲眼目睹这一点，是在我当时18个月大的儿子在晚餐时看到盘子里的胡萝卜时。他立刻就崩溃了：尖叫、哭闹，还尿湿了尿布。他这种激动的生理状态，他爸爸立刻就能测量到，而且方圆半英里内的任何人可能都能测量到。
A desire to avoid the situation: The stressor must be perceived as aversive—something that, given the choice, you’d rather not experience. It was obvious where my son stood on the matter. Within seconds, he snatched the carrot off his plate and threw it on the floor. Then he deftly got down off his chair and tried to stomp on the predatory vegetable.
想要逃避这种情况：压力源必须被视为令人厌恶的——如果可以选择，你宁愿不去经历它。我儿子对这件事的态度很明显。几秒钟之内，他就从盘子里抓起胡萝卜扔到地上。然后他灵巧地从椅子上跳下来，试图踩扁这根“凶猛”的蔬菜。
A loss of control: The person must not feel in control of the stressor. Like a volume knob on some emotional radio, the more the loss of control, the more severe the stress is perceived to be. This element of control and its closely related twin, predictability, lie at the heart of learned helplessness. My son reacted as strongly as he did in part because he knew I wanted him to eat the carrot, and he was used to doing what I told him to do. Control was the issue. Despite my picking up the carrot, washing it, then rubbing my tummy while enthusiastically saying “yum, yum,” he was having none of it. Or, more important, he wanted to have none of it, and he thought I was going to make him have all of it. Feeling out of control over the carrot equaled out-of-control behavior.
失控感：这个人必须感觉无法掌控压力源。就像调节情绪收音机的音量旋钮一样，失控感越强，感受到的压力就越严重。这种控制感及其密切相关的可预测性，正是习得性无助的核心所在。我儿子之所以反应如此强烈，部分原因是他知道我想让他吃胡萝卜，而且他习惯了听我的话。问题出在控制感上。尽管我拿起胡萝卜，洗干净，然后一边揉着肚子一边兴奋地说“好吃好吃”，他却一点也不吃。或者更确切地说，他根本不想吃，却认为我会强迫他吃完。对胡萝卜失去控制感，就导致了失控的行为。
When you find this trinity of components working together, you have the type of stress easily measurable in a laboratory setting. When I talk about stress, I am usually referring to situations like these.
当这三个因素共同作用时，就会产生一种在实验室环境下易于测量的应力。我所说的应力，通常指的就是这种情况。
We’re built for stress that lasts only seconds
我们天生就能应对短暂的压力。
You can feel your body responding to stress: Your pulse races, your blood pressure rises, and you feel a massive release of energy. That’s the famous hormone adrenaline at work. This fight-or-flight response is spurred into action by your brain’s hypothalamus, that pea-size organ sitting almost in the middle of your head. When your sensory systems detect stress, the hypothalamus signals your adrenal glands to dump buckets of adrenaline into your bloodstream. There’s a less famous hormone at work, too—also released by the adrenals, and just as powerful as adrenalin. It’s called cortisol. It’s the second wave of our defensive reaction to stressors. In small doses, it wipes out most unpleasant aspects of stress, returning us to normalcy.
你能感觉到身体对压力的反应：脉搏加快，血压升高，感觉能量瞬间释放。这就是著名的肾上腺素在起作用。这种“战斗或逃跑”反应是由大脑的下丘脑触发的，下丘脑是位于头部中央附近、豌豆大小的器官。当你的感觉系统检测到压力时，下丘脑会发出信号，促使肾上腺向血液中释放大量的肾上腺素。还有一种不太为人所知的激素也在发挥作用——它同样由肾上腺释放，而且效力与肾上腺素不相上下。这种激素叫做皮质醇。它是我们应对压力的第二波防御反应。少量皮质醇可以消除压力带来的大部分不适感，使我们恢复正常状态。
Why do our bodies need to go through all this trouble? The answer is very simple. Without a flexible, immediately available, highly regulated stress response, we would die. Remember, the brain is the world’s most sophisticated survival organ. All of its many complexities are built toward a mildly erotic, singularly selfish goal: to live long enough to thrust our genes on to the next generation. Our reactions to stress help us manage the threats that could keep us from procreating.
我们的身体为什么需要经历这一切？答案很简单。如果没有灵活、即时可用且高度调节的应激反应，我们就会死亡。记住，大脑是世界上最复杂的生存器官。它所有复杂的结构都服务于一个略带情欲色彩、却又极其自私的目标：活得足够长，将我们的基因传递给下一代。我们对压力的反应帮助我们应对那些可能阻碍我们繁衍后代的威胁。
And what kinds of survival threats did we experience in our evolutionary toddlerhood? Predators would make the top 10 list. So would physical injury. In modern times, a broken leg means a trip to the doctor. In our distant past, a broken leg often meant a death sentence. The day’s weather would have been a concern, the day’s offering of food another. A lot of very immediate needs rise to the surface. Most of the survival issues we faced in our first few million years did not take long to settle. The saber-toothed tiger either ate us or we ran away from it—or a lucky few might stab it, but the whole thing was usually over in moments. Consequently, our stress responses were shaped to solve problems that lasted not for years, but for seconds. They were primarily designed to get our muscles moving us as quickly as possible out of harm’s way.
那么，在我们进化的幼年时期，我们经历了哪些生存威胁呢？捕食者肯定位列前十。身体伤害也同样如此。在现代，腿骨折意味着去看医生。但在遥远的过去，腿骨折往往意味着死刑。当天的天气状况令人担忧，食物供应情况也同样重要。许多迫在眉睫的需求会浮出水面。在最初的几百万年里，我们面临的大多数生存问题都很快就能得到解决。剑齿虎要么吃掉我们，要么我们逃离它——或者少数幸运儿或许能刺伤它，但整个过程通常都转瞬即逝。因此，我们的应激反应是为了解决那些持续数年而非数年的问题而形成的。它们的主要目的是让我们的肌肉尽快将我们带离危险。
These days, our stresses are measured not in moments with mountain lions, but in hours, days, and sometimes months with hectic workplaces, screaming toddlers, and money problems. Our system isn’t built for that. And when moderate amounts of stress hormones build up to large amounts, or hang around too long, they become quite harmful. That’s how an exquisitely tuned system can become deregulated enough to affect a report card or a performance review—or a dog in a metal crate.
如今，我们的压力不再以遭遇美洲狮的惊险瞬间来衡量，而是以小时、天，甚至有时是数月来衡量，包括忙碌的工作环境、哭闹的幼儿和经济问题。我们的身体系统并非为应对这种情况而设计的。当适量的压力激素积累到很高的水平，或持续时间过长时，就会造成相当大的危害。这就是为什么一个原本精密运转的系统会失调到足以影响成绩单、绩效考核，甚至影响一只被关在金属笼子里的狗的原因。
Cardiovascular system
心血管系统
Stress affects both our bodies and our brains, in both good and bad ways. Acute stress can boost cardiovascular performance—the probable source of those urban legends about grandmothers lifting one end of a car to rescue their grandchildren stuck under the wheels. Over the long term, however, too much adrenaline produces scarring on the insides of your blood vessels. These scars become magnets for molecules to accumulate, creating lumps called plaques. These can grow large enough to block the blood vessels. If it happens in the blood vessels of your heart, you get a heart attack; in your brain, you get a stroke. Not surprisingly, people who experience chronic stress have an elevated risk of heart attacks and strokes.
压力会对我们的身体和大脑产生影响，既有积极的一面，也有消极的一面。急性压力可以增强心血管功能——这或许就是那些关于祖母抬起汽车一端救出被困车轮下的孙辈的都市传说的由来。然而，长期来看，过多的肾上腺素会在血管内壁形成疤痕。这些疤痕会吸引分子聚集，形成称为斑块的肿块。这些斑块会不断增大，最终阻塞血管。如果发生在心脏血管，就会引发心脏病；如果发生在脑血管，就会引发中风。因此，长期承受压力的人患心脏病和中风的风险更高，这并不令人意外。
Immune system
免疫系统
Stress also affects our immune response. At first, the stress response helps equip your white blood cells, sending them off to fight on your body’s most vulnerable fronts, such as the skin. Acute stress can even make you respond better to a flu shot. But chronic stress reverses these effects, decreasing your number of heroic white-blood-cell soldiers, stripping them of their weapons, even killing them outright. Over the long term, stress ravages parts of the immune system involved in producing antibodies. Together, these can cripple your ability to fight infection. Chronic stress also can coax your immune system to fire indiscriminately, even at targets that aren’t shooting back—like your own body. Not surprisingly, people who experience chronic stress are sick more often. A lot more often. One study showed that stressed individuals were three times more likely to suffer from the common cold, especially if the stress was social in nature and lasted more than a month. They also are more likely to suffer from autoimmune disorders, such as asthma and diabetes.
压力也会影响我们的免疫反应。起初，压力反应有助于增强白细胞的防御能力，将它们派往身体最脆弱的部位，例如皮肤。急性压力甚至可以提高流感疫苗的接种效果。但慢性压力会逆转这些效果，减少体内英勇的白细胞数量，剥夺它们的防御能力，甚至直接杀死它们。长期来看，压力会破坏免疫系统中负责产生抗体的部分。这些因素共同作用，会削弱人体抵抗感染的能力。慢性压力还会诱使免疫系统不加选择地攻击目标，甚至攻击那些没有反击的目标——例如人体自身。毫不奇怪，长期承受慢性压力的人更容易生病，而且频率高得多。一项研究表明，压力大的人患普通感冒的几率是其他人的三倍，尤其是当压力来自社交方面且持续超过一个月时。他们也更容易患上自身免疫性疾病，例如哮喘和糖尿病。
To show how sensitive the immune system can be to stress, you need look no further than an experiment done at UCLA. Trained actors practiced Method acting, in which if a scene calls for you to be scared, you think of something frightening, then recite your lines while plumbing those memories. On one day, the actors performed using only happy memories. On another day, they performed using only sad memories. The researchers took blood samples, continually assessing their immune systems. On the “happy days,” the actors had healthy immune systems. Their immune cells were plentiful, happy, readily available for work. On the “sad days,” the actors showed something unexpected: a marked decrease in immune responsiveness. Their immune cells were not plentiful, not as robust, not as available to protect against infection.
要了解免疫系统对压力的敏感性，只需看看加州大学洛杉矶分校的一项实验即可。训练有素的演员们练习方法演技，即如果某个场景需要他们表现出恐惧，他们会想象一些可怕的事情，然后在回忆这些记忆的同时背诵台词。有一天，演员们只用快乐的记忆进行表演；另一天，他们只用悲伤的记忆进行表演。研究人员采集了他们的血液样本，持续评估他们的免疫系统。在“快乐的日子”里，演员们的免疫系统非常健康。他们的免疫细胞数量充足、状态良好，随时准备发挥作用。而在“悲伤的日子”里，演员们却表现出意想不到的情况：免疫反应显著下降。他们的免疫细胞数量减少、活力下降，无法有效地抵御感染。
Memory and problem solving
记忆力和问题解决能力
Stress affects memory. The hippocampus, that fortress of human memory, is studded with cortisol receptors like cloves in a ham. This makes it very responsive to stress signals. If the stress is not too severe, your brain performs better when it is stressed than when it is not stressed. You can solve problems more effectively and you are more likely to retain information. There’s an evolutionary reason for this. Our survival on the savannah depended upon remembering what was life-threatening and what was not. Ancestors who could commit those experiences to memory the fastest (and recall them accurately with equal speed) were more apt to survive than those who couldn’t. Indeed, research shows that memories of stressful experiences are formed almost instantaneously in the human brain, and they can be recalled very quickly during times of crises.
压力会影响记忆。海马体，这个人类记忆的堡垒，像火腿上的丁香一样布满了皮质醇受体。这使得它对压力信号非常敏感。如果压力不太严重，大脑在压力下的表现甚至比非压力状态下更好。你能更有效地解决问题，也更容易记住信息。这背后有进化论的解释。我们在稀树草原上的生存取决于记住哪些是危及生命的，哪些不是。那些能够最快地将这些经历记入记忆（并且能够同样快速准确地回忆起来）的祖先，比那些做不到这一点的人更容易生存下来。事实上，研究表明，压力经历的记忆几乎瞬间就能在人脑中形成，并且在危机时刻能够迅速被回忆起来。
If the stress is too severe or too prolonged, however, stress begins to harm learning. Stressed people don’t do math very well. They don’t process language very efficiently. They have poorer memories, both short and long forms. Stressed people do not generalize or adapt old pieces of information to new scenarios as well as non-stressed individuals. They can’t concentrate. In almost every way it can be tested, chronic stress hurts our ability to learn. One study showed that adults with high levels of stress performed 50 percent worse than adults with low levels of stress on tests of declarative memory (things you can declare) and executive function (the type of thinking that involves problem solving and self control). Those, of course, are the skills needed to excel in school, at work, and in relationships.
然而，如果压力过大或持续时间过长，就会开始损害学习能力。压力过大的人数学成绩不佳，语言处理效率低下，记忆力（包括短期记忆和长期记忆）也较差。与压力较小的人相比，压力过大的人更难将旧信息概括或应用于新的情境，也难以集中注意力。几乎所有可以测试的方面都表明，慢性压力会损害我们的学习能力。一项研究表明，压力水平高的成年人在陈述性记忆（可以陈述的事物）和执行功能（涉及问题解决和自我控制的思维方式）测试中的表现比压力水平低的成年人差50%。而这些技能，恰恰是我们在学校、工作和人际关系中取得成功所必需的。
I remember a story by a flight instructor I knew well. He told me about the best student he ever had, and a powerful lesson he learned about what it meant to teach her. The student excelled in ground school. She aced the simulations, aced her courses. In the skies, she showed natural skill, improvising even in rapidly changing weather conditions. One day in the air, the instructor saw her doing something naïve. He was having a bad day and he yelled at her. He pushed her hands away from the airplane’s equivalent of a steering wheel. He pointed angrily at an instrument. Dumbfounded, the student tried to correct herself, but in the stress of the moment, she made more errors, said she couldn’t think, and then buried her head in her hands and started to cry. The teacher took control of the aircraft and landed it. For a long time, the student would not get back into the same cockpit. The incident hurt not only the teacher’s professional relationship with the student but the student’s ability to learn. It also crushed the instructor. If he had been able to predict how the student would react to his threatening behavior, he never would have acted that way. Relationships matter when attempting to teach human beings—whether you’re a parent, teacher, boss, or peer. Here we are talking about the highly intellectual venture of flying an aircraft. But its success is fully dependent upon feelings.
我记得一位我认识的飞行教员讲过一个故事。他跟我讲了他教过的最优秀的学生，以及他从教这个学生身上学到的一个深刻教训。这个学生地面理论课成绩优异，模拟飞行和课程都轻松过关。在空中，她展现出与生俱来的天赋，即使在瞬息万变的天气条件下也能随机应变。有一天，在空中，教员看到她做了一件很幼稚的事情。那天他心情不好，冲她大吼。他把她的手从飞机方向盘上推开，愤怒地指着仪表。学生不知所措，试图纠正自己的错误，但在当时的紧张情绪下，她犯了更多错误，说自己脑子一片空白，然后双手捂脸哭了起来。教员接管了飞机，安全着陆。很长一段时间，这个学生都不敢再坐进驾驶舱。这件事不仅损害了教员和学生之间的专业关系，也影响了学生的学习能力。这件事也深深地打击了教员。如果他能预料到学生会如何回应他的威胁行为，他绝不会那样做。在教导他人时，人际关系至关重要——无论你是家长、老师、老板还是同事。我们现在讨论的是驾驶飞机这项高度依赖智力的活动，但它的成功却完全取决于情感。
The villain: cortisol
罪魁祸首：皮质醇
The biology behind this assault on our intelligences can be described as a tale of two molecules: one a villain, the other a hero. The villain is the aforementioned cortisol, part of a motley crew of stress hormones going by the name glucocorticoids. These hormones are secreted by the adrenal glands, which lie like a roof on top of your kidneys. The adrenal glands are so exquisitely responsive to neural signals, they appear to have once been a part of your brain that somehow fell off and landed in your mid-abdomen.
这种对我们智力的攻击背后的生物学机制，可以用两个分子的故事来概括：一个是反派，另一个是英雄。反派就是前面提到的皮质醇，它是糖皮质激素这一复杂压力激素家族的成员之一。这些激素由肾上腺分泌，肾上腺就像屋顶一样覆盖在肾脏上方。肾上腺对神经信号极其敏感，它们似乎曾经是大脑的一部分，不知何故脱落下来，落在了腹部中央。
Stress hormones can do some truly nasty things to your brain if boatloads of the stuff are given free access to your central nervous system. And that’s what is going on when you experience chronic stress. Stress hormones seem to have a particular liking for cells in the hippocampus, which is a problem because the hippocampus is deeply involved in many aspects of human learning. Stress hormones can make cells in the hippocampus more vulnerable to other stresses. Stress hormones can disconnect neural networks, the webbing of brain cells that store your most precious memories. For example, a bodyguard was in the car with Princess Diana on the night of her death. To this day, he cannot remember the events several hours before or after the car crash. Amnesia is a typical response to catastrophic stress. Its lighter cousin, forgetfulness, is quite common when the stress is less severe but more pervasive.
如果大量的压力激素畅通无阻地进入中枢神经系统，它们会对大脑造成极其严重的损害。而这正是慢性压力下的状况。压力激素似乎特别偏爱海马体中的细胞，这很成问题，因为海马体与人类学习的许多方面都密切相关。压力激素会使海马体中的细胞更容易受到其他压力的影响。压力激素还会破坏神经网络——也就是储存你最珍贵记忆的脑细胞网络。例如，戴安娜王妃去世当晚，她的一位保镖与她同乘一辆车。直到今天，他仍然记不起车祸前后几个小时发生的事情。失忆是应对灾难性压力的典型反应。而当压力不那么严重但影响范围更广时，则很容易出现失忆的轻微表现——健忘。
Stress hormones also can stop the hippocampus from giving birth to brand-new baby neurons. Under extreme conditions, stress hormones can even kill hippocampal cells. Quite literally, severe stress can cause brain damage in the very tissues most likely to help you succeed in life.
压力激素还会阻止海马体产生新的神经元。在极端情况下，压力激素甚至会杀死海马体细胞。毫不夸张地说，严重的压力会损伤大脑中那些最有可能帮助你获得成功的组织。
One of the most insidious effects of prolonged stress is that it pushes people into depression. I don’t mean the “blues” people can experience as a normal part of daily living. Nor do I mean the grief resulting from tragic circumstance, such as the death of a relative. I am talking about the kind of depression that causes as many as 800,000 people a year to attempt suicide. It is a disease every bit as organic as diabetes, and often deadlier. Chronic exposure to stress can lead you to depression’s doorstep, then push you through. Depression is a deregulation of thought processes, including memory, language, quantitative reasoning, fluid intelligence, and spatial perception. The list is long and familiar. But one of its hallmarks may not be as familiar, unless you are in depression. Many people who feel depressed also feel there is no way out of their depression. They feel that life’s shocks are permanent and things will never get better. Even though there is a way out—treatment is often very successful—they have no perception of it. The situation feels so helpless that they don’t seek treatment. Yet they can no more argue their way out of a depression than they could argue their way out of a heart attack. Clearly, stress hurts learning. Most important, however, stress hurts people .
长期压力最阴险的后果之一就是会让人陷入抑郁。我指的不是日常生活中常见的“情绪低落”，也不是因亲人去世等悲剧事件而产生的悲伤。我指的是那种每年导致多达80万人试图自杀的抑郁症。它和糖尿病一样，都是由生理因素引起的，而且往往更致命。长期处于压力之下，会将你推向抑郁的边缘，然后彻底击垮你。抑郁症会导致思维过程失调，包括记忆力、语言能力、定量推理能力、流体智力和空间感知能力。这些症状不胜枚举，而且大家都很熟悉。但除非你正经历抑郁症，否则你可能并不了解它的一个显著特征：许多抑郁症患者感觉自己无路可走。他们觉得生活中的打击是永久性的，一切都不会好转。尽管其实是有出路的——治疗通常非常有效——但他们却对此毫无察觉。他们感到如此无助，以至于不愿寻求治疗。然而，他们无法通过争辩摆脱抑郁症，就像他们无法通过争辩摆脱心脏病发作一样。显然，压力会阻碍学习。但最重要的是，压力会伤害人。
The hero: BDNF
英雄：BDNF
The brain seems to be aware of all this and has supplied our story not only with a villain but also with a hero. We met this champion in the Exercise chapter. It’s brain-derived neurotrophic factor. BDNF is the premier member of a powerful group of proteins called neurotrophins. BDNF in the hippocampus acts like a peacekeeping force, keeping neurons alive and growing in the presence of hostile action. As long as there is enough BDNF around, stress hormones cannot do their damage.
大脑似乎对这一切了如指掌，并为我们的故事不仅塑造了一个反派，也塑造了一个英雄。我们在“运动”章节中就认识了这位英雄——脑源性神经营养因子（BDNF）。BDNF是神经营养因子这一强大蛋白质家族中的佼佼者。海马体中的BDNF就像一支维和部队，在有害作用下维持神经元的存活和生长。只要体内有足够的BDNF，压力激素就无法造成损害。
How, then, does the system break down? The problem begins when too many stress hormones hang around in the brain too long, a situation you find in chronic stress, especially learned helplessness. As wonderful as the BDNF forces are, it is possible to overwhelm them if they are assaulted with a sufficiently strong (and sufficiently lengthy) glucocorticoid siege. Like a fortress overrun by invaders, enough stress hormones will eventually overwhelm the brain’s natural defenses and wreak their havoc. In sufficient quantities, stress hormones are fully capable of turning off the gene that makes BDNF in hippocampal cells, causing long-lasting damage. You read that right: Not only can they overwhelm our natural defenses, but they can actually turn them off .
那么，这个系统是如何崩溃的呢？问题始于过多的压力激素在大脑中停留过久，这种情况常见于慢性压力，尤其是习得性无助。尽管脑源性神经营养因子（BDNF）的作用非常强大，但如果受到足够强烈（且持续时间足够长）的糖皮质激素攻击，它们也可能不堪重负。就像堡垒被入侵者攻破一样，足够的压力激素最终会突破大脑的自然防御，造成严重破坏。当压力激素达到一定浓度时，它们完全能够关闭海马细胞中产生BDNF的基因，造成持久性损伤。你没看错：它们不仅能突破我们的自然防御，还能将其关闭。
A genetic buffer
遗传缓冲
Out-of-control stress is bad news for the brains of most people. But of course “most” doesn’t mean “all.” Like oddly placed candles in a dark room, some people illuminate corners of human behavior with unexpected clarity. They illustrate the complexity of environmental and genetic factors.
失控的压力对大多数人的大脑来说都是坏消息。当然，“大多数人”并不意味着“所有人”。就像黑暗房间里摆放位置奇特的蜡烛一样，有些人能以意想不到的清晰度照亮人类行为的某些角落。他们展现了环境和遗传因素的复杂性。
Jill was born into an inner-city home. Her father began having sex with Jill and her sister during their preschool years. Her mother was institutionalized twice because of what used to be termed “nervous breakdowns.” When Jill was 7 years old, her agitated dad called a family meeting in the living room. In front of the whole clan, he put a handgun to his head, said, “You drove me to this,” and then blew his brains out. The mother’s mental condition continued to deteriorate, and she revolved in and out of mental hospitals for years. When Mom was home, she would beat Jill. Beginning in her early teens, Jill was forced to work outside the home to help make ends meet. As Jill got older, we would have expected to see deep psychiatric scars, severe emotional damage, drugs, maybe even a pregnancy or two. Instead, Jill developed into a charming and quite popular young woman at school. She became a talented singer, an honor student, and president of her high-school class. By every measure, she was emotionally well-adjusted and seemingly unscathed by the awful circumstances of her childhood.
吉尔出生在一个贫民窟家庭。她的父亲在她和妹妹上幼儿园时就开始与她们发生性关系。她的母亲曾两次因所谓的“精神崩溃”而被送进精神病院。吉尔7岁那年，情绪激动的父亲在客厅里召集了一次家庭会议。在全家人面前，他用手枪抵住自己的头，说道：“是你们把我逼到这个地步的。”然后饮弹自尽。母亲的精神状况持续恶化，多年来她频繁出入精神病院。母亲在家时，经常殴打吉尔。从十几岁起，吉尔就被迫外出打工补贴家用。随着吉尔长大，我们原本以为她会留下严重的心理创伤、情感创伤、吸毒，甚至可能怀孕一两次。然而，吉尔却成长为一个魅力四射、在学校里很受欢迎的年轻女性。她成为了一名才华横溢的歌手、一名优等生，并担任了高中班长。无论从哪个角度来看，她的情绪都适应良好，似乎并没有受到童年可怕经历的影响。
Her story, published in a leading psychiatric journal, illustrates the unevenness of the human response to stress. Psychiatrists long have observed that some people are more tolerant of stress than others. Molecular geneticists are beginning to shed light on the reasons. Some people’s genetic complement naturally buffers them against the effects of stress, even the chronic type. Scientists have isolated some of these genes. In the future, we may be able to tell stress-tolerant from stress-sensitive individuals with a simple blood test, looking for the presence of these genes.
她的故事发表在一家顶尖精神病学期刊上，揭示了人类对压力反应的不均衡性。精神科医生长期以来观察到，有些人比其他人更能耐受压力。分子遗传学家正开始揭示其中的原因。有些人的基因组合天然具有缓冲作用，使他们能够抵御压力的影响，即使是慢性压力也不例外。科学家们已经分离出其中一些基因。未来，我们或许能够通过简单的血液检测，检测这些基因的存在，从而区分出压力耐受型和压力敏感型个体。
We each have our own tipping point
我们每个人都有自己的临界点。
How can we explain the various ways humans respond to stress—both the typical cases and the exceptions? The answer is that stress is neutral. Aversive stimuli are neither beneficial nor bad. Whether stress becomes damaging depends on the severity of the stress, how long you are exposed to the stress, and on your body’s ability to handle stress. There’s a tipping point where stress becomes toxic. Scientist Bruce McEwen calls it the allostatic load. Allo is from a Greek word meaning variable; stasis means a condition of balance. McEwen’s idea is that we have systems that keep us stable by constantly changing themselves. The stress system, with all of its intricacies, is one of those. The brain coordinates body-wide changes—from hormonal to behavioral changes—in response to the approach and retreat of potential threats.
我们该如何解释人类应对压力的各种方式——包括典型案例和例外情况？答案是：压力本身是中性的。厌恶性刺激既非有益也非有害。压力是否会造成损害取决于压力的严重程度、持续时间以及身体应对压力的能力。压力存在一个临界点，超过这个临界点就会产生毒性。科学家布鲁斯·麦克尤恩称之为“异质性负荷”。“异质性负荷”一词源于希腊语，意为“可变的”；“异质性负荷”意为“平衡状态”。麦克尤恩的观点是，我们体内存在一些系统，通过不断自我调节来维持我们的稳定。压力系统及其所有复杂机制正是其中之一。大脑会协调全身范围内的变化——从激素水平到行为模式——以应对潜在威胁的接近和撤退。
Stress at home shows up at school
家庭压力会影响到学校生活。
I know the allostatic load as the first time, and only time, I ever heard my mother swear. As you may recall, my mother was a fourth-grade teacher. I was upstairs in my room, unbeknownst to my mother, who was upstairs in her room grading papers. She was grading one of her favorite students, a sweet, brown-haired wisp of a girl I will call Kelly. Kelly was every teacher’s dream kid: smart, socially poised, blessed with a wealth of friends. Kelly had done very well in the first half of the school year. The second half of the school year was another story, however. My mother sensed something was very wrong the moment Kelly walked into class after Christmas break. Her eyes were mostly downcast, and within a week she had gotten into her first fight. In another week, she got her first C on an exam, which would prove to be the high point, as her grades for the rest of the year fluttered between Ds and Fs. She was sent to the principal’s office numerous times, and my mother, exasperated, decided to find out what caused this meltdown. She learned that Kelly’s parents had decided to get a divorce over Christmas and that the family conflicts, from which the parents valiantly had insulated Kelly, had begun spilling out into the open. As things unraveled at home, things also unraveled at school. And on that snowy day, when my mother gave Kelly her third straight D in spelling, my mother also swore: “Damn it!” she said, nearly under her breath. I froze as she shouted, “THE ABILITY OF KELLY TO DO WELL IN MY CLASS HAS NOTHING TO DO WITH MY CLASS!”
我知道“异质性负荷”指的是我第一次，也是唯一一次听到母亲说脏话。你可能还记得，我母亲是一位四年级老师。当时我在楼上的房间里，母亲浑然不知，她正在楼上批改作业。她正在批改她最喜欢的学生之一的作业，一个甜美可人、棕色头发的小女孩，我姑且叫她凯莉吧。凯莉是每个老师梦寐以求的学生：聪明伶俐，社交能力强，朋友众多。凯莉在上半学年表现非常出色。然而，下半学年却截然不同。圣诞假期后，凯莉走进教室的那一刻，母亲就察觉到情况不对劲。她总是低着头，不到一周就和人打了起来。又过了一周，她第一次考试得了C，而这竟然成了她成绩的巅峰，因为接下来的整个学年，她的成绩都在D和F之间徘徊。她被送到校长办公室好几次，我母亲实在忍无可忍，决定弄清楚她情绪崩溃的原因。她得知凯莉的父母在圣诞节期间决定离婚，而父母一直竭力保护凯莉免受其影响的家庭矛盾，如今开始公之于众。家里的事情一团糟，学校里的事情也跟着乱了套。在那个下雪天，我母亲连续第三次给凯莉的拼写打了D，她也忍不住爆了粗口：“该死！”她几乎是低声咒骂道。我愣住了，因为她大声喊道：“凯莉在我班上的表现好不好跟我班的教学水平一点关系都没有！”
She was describing the relationship between home life and school life, a link that has frustrated teachers for a long time. One of the greatest predictors of performance in school turns out to be the emotional stability of the home.
她描述的是家庭生活和学校生活之间的关系，这种联系长期以来一直困扰着教师们。事实证明，家庭的情感稳定性是预测学生在校表现的最重要因素之一。
I have firsthand experience with the effects of stress on grades. I was a senior in high school when my mother was diagnosed with the disease that would eventually kill her. She had come home late from a doctor’s visit and was attempting to fix the family dinner. But when I found her, she was just staring at the kitchen wall. She haltingly related the terminal nature of her medical condition and then, as if that weren’t enough, unloaded another bombshell. My dad, who knew of Mom’s condition, was not handling the news very well and had decided to file for divorce. I felt as if I had just been punched in the stomach. For a few seconds I could not move. School the next day, and for the next 13 weeks, was a disaster. I don’t remember much of the lectures. I only remember staring at my textbooks, thinking that this amazing woman had taught me to read and love such books, that we used to have a happy family, and that all of this was coming to an end. What she must have been feeling, much worse than I could ever fathom, she never related. Not knowing how to react, my friends soon withdrew from me even as I withdrew from them. I lost the ability to concentrate, my mind continually wandering back to childhood. My academic effort became a train wreck. I got the only D I would ever get in my school career, and I couldn’t have cared less.
我亲身经历过压力对成绩的影响。我读高三那年，母亲被确诊患上了最终夺走她生命的疾病。那天她去看医生回来很晚，正准备做晚饭。我找到她时，她只是呆呆地望着厨房的墙壁。她断断续续地告诉我病情是绝症，然后，仿佛这还不够，她又抛出了一个重磅炸弹。我的父亲知道母亲的病情，但他无法接受这个消息，决定提出离婚。我感觉就像被人狠狠地打了一拳，胃里像被重重地击了一拳。有那么几秒钟，我动弹不得。第二天，以及接下来的13周，学校生活简直是一场灾难。我几乎不记得课堂上讲了什么。我只记得自己盯着课本，想着这位了不起的女人教会了我阅读，教会了我热爱书籍，我们曾经拥有一个幸福的家庭，而这一切即将结束。她当时的感受一定比我所能想象的要痛苦得多，但她从未告诉我。不知所措，朋友们很快疏远了我，我也渐渐疏远了他们。我失去了集中注意力的能力，思绪总是飘回到童年。我的学业一团糟。我拿到了学生生涯中唯一一个D，但我却毫不在意。
Even after all these years, it is still tough to write about that time in my life. But it effectively illustrates Brain Rule #4: Stressed brains do not learn the same way as non-stressed brains.
即使过了这么多年，回忆起那段日子仍然很艰难。但这确实印证了大脑法则第四条：压力下的大脑学习方式与非压力下的大脑截然不同。
My grief at least had an end point. In an emotionally unstable home, the stress seems never-ending. Consider the all-too-common case of children witnessing their parents fighting. The simple fact is that kids find unresolved marital conflict deeply disturbing. They cover their ears, stand motionless with clenched fists, cry, scowl, ask to leave, beg parents to stop. Study after study has shown that children—some as young as 6 months—react to adult arguments physiologically, such as with a faster heart rate and higher blood pressure. Kids of all ages who watch parents constantly fight have more stress hormones in their urine. They have more difficulty regulating their emotions, soothing themselves, and focusing their attention on others. They are powerless to stop the conflict, and the loss of control is emotionally crippling. As you know, perception of control is a powerful influence on the perception of stress. They are experiencing allostatic load.
我的悲伤至少有尽头。但在情绪不稳定的家庭里，压力似乎永无止境。想想那些目睹父母争吵的常见例子吧。事实很简单，孩子们会觉得未解决的婚姻冲突令人极度不安。他们会捂住耳朵，紧握双拳一动不动地站着，哭泣，皱眉，要求离开，恳求父母停止争吵。一项又一项的研究表明，儿童——有些甚至只有6个月大——会对成人的争吵做出生理反应，例如心跳加快和血压升高。所有年龄段的孩子，如果目睹父母不断争吵，尿液中的压力激素水平都会更高。他们更难调节自己的情绪，安抚自己，也更难将注意力集中在他人身上。他们无力阻止冲突，而这种失控感会让他们情绪崩溃。正如你所知，控制感对压力感知有着强大的影响。他们正在经历异质性负荷。
Given that stress can powerfully affect learning, one might predict that children living in high-anxiety households would not perform as well academically as kids living in more nurturing households. That is exactly what studies show. Marital stress at home can negatively affect academic performance in almost every way measurable, and at nearly any age. Initial studies focused on grade-point averages over time, revealing striking disparities in achievement between kids whose parents are going through a divorce and control groups. Even when a couple stays together, children living in emotionally unstable homes get lower grades and do worse on standardized tests of math and reading. Careful subsequent investigations showed that it was the presence of overt conflict, not divorce, that predicted grade failure.
鉴于压力会对学习产生显著影响，人们可能会预测，生活在高焦虑家庭中的儿童在学业上的表现不如生活在更温馨家庭中的儿童。研究结果也证实了这一点。家庭中的婚姻压力几乎会对所有可衡量的学业表现产生负面影响，而且这种影响几乎发生在任何年龄段。最初的研究侧重于学生的平均绩点随时间的变化，结果显示，父母正在经历离婚的儿童与对照组儿童的学业成绩存在显著差异。即使夫妻双方没有离婚，生活在情绪不稳定的家庭中的儿童成绩也更低，在数学和阅读标准化测试中的表现也更差。后续的深入研究表明，导致学业失败的并非离婚本身，而是家庭中存在的公开冲突。
The stronger the degree of conflict, the greater the effect on performance. When teachers are asked to rate children’s intelligence and aptitude, children from homes with conflict score lower. Such children are three times more likely to be expelled from school or to become pregnant as teenagers, and five times more likely to live in poverty. As social activist Barbara Whitehead put it, writing for the Atlantic Monthly: “Teachers find many children emotionally distracted, so upset and preoccupied by the explosive drama of their own family lives that they are unable to concentrate on such mundane matters as multiplication tables.”
冲突程度越强，对孩子表现的影响就越大。当老师们被要求评估孩子的智力和能力时，来自冲突家庭的孩子得分更低。这些孩子被学校开除或青少年时期怀孕的可能性是其他孩子的三倍，生活在贫困中的可能性是其他孩子的五倍。正如社会活动家芭芭拉·怀特黑德在《大西洋月刊》上撰文指出：“老师们发现很多孩子情绪低落，他们被家庭生活中的冲突和矛盾所困扰，以至于无法集中精力学习乘法表这类简单的知识。”
Physical health deteriorates; truancy and absenteeism increase. The absenteeism may occur because stress is depleting the immune system, which increases the risk of infection. Though the evidence is not as conclusive, a growing body of data suggests that children living in hostile environments are at greater risk for certain psychiatric disorders, such as depression and anxiety disorders. As children grow up, they can bring the effects of childhood stress into their own relationships and work lives.
身体健康状况恶化；旷课和缺勤率上升。缺勤可能是由于压力削弱了免疫系统，从而增加了感染风险。虽然证据尚不确凿，但越来越多的数据表明，生活在恶劣环境中的儿童更容易患上某些精神疾病，例如抑郁症和焦虑症。随着儿童长大，他们可能会将童年时期的压力影响到自己的人际关系和工作生活中。
Stress at work: too expensive to ignore
工作压力：代价太高，不容忽视。
Lisa Nowak was a lethal combat pilot, decorated electronics warfare specialist, pretty, smart. The government spent millions of dollars training her to be an astronaut. She also was a mother with three kids on the verge of divorcing her husband one month before her biggest professional assignment: mission control specialist for a shuttle mission. Talk about built-up stress. She put some weapons in her automobile, grabbed a disguise, and even packed a bunch of adult diapers so that she didn’t have to stop to use a bathroom. She then drove virtually nonstop from Houston to Orlando, allegedly to kidnap her target, a woman she thought was a threat to a fellow astronaut to whom she had taken a fancy. Instead of serving as the lead for one of America’s most technically challenging jobs, this highly skilled engineer sat awaiting trial on attempted kidnapping and battery. Nowak later pled guilty to lesser charges and retired with a “less than honorable” discharge. She will never fly again, which makes this sad story nearly heartbreaking. It also makes the money spent on her training a colossal waste. But those few million dollars are minuscule compared with the cost of stress on the workplace as a whole.
丽莎·诺瓦克曾是一名身手不凡的战斗机飞行员，一位功勋卓著的电子战专家，漂亮又聪明。政府花费数百万美元训练她成为一名宇航员。然而，就在她最重要的职业任务——航天飞机任务的控制中心专家——执行前一个月，她还是三个孩子的母亲，正处于与丈夫离婚的边缘。这无疑给她带来了巨大的压力。她在车里放了一些武器，准备了伪装，甚至还带了一堆成人尿布，这样就不用停车上厕所了。然后，她几乎不停地从休斯顿开车到奥兰多，据称是为了绑架她的目标——一个她认为对她心仪的宇航员同事构成威胁的女人。这位技艺精湛的工程师本应领导美国最具技术挑战性的工作之一，却不得不等待因企图绑架和殴打罪名受审。诺瓦克后来承认了较轻的指控，并以“非荣誉退伍”的方式结束了她的职业生涯。她再也无法飞行了，这让她的悲惨故事令人心碎。这也让政府在她身上花费的巨额训练资金显得格外浪费。但与压力给整个工作场所造成的损失相比，这几百万美元简直微不足道。
The American Stress Institute estimates that American businesses lose $300 billion every year because of work-related stress. Sources of that loss include health-related costs, worker compensation bills, employee turnover, and absenteeism. That last item is a big deal. About one million people stay home from work every day because of stress (about 40% of all absences occur because of tension felt at work!). The Bureau of Labor Statistics found the average amount of time off due to stress was 20 days. That’s costly. One day’s absence costs the company about two times what the worker would make in that day. If the prolonged stress leads to depression, organizations are dealing with a direct assault on their intellectual capital. Depression hobbles fluid intelligence, problem-solving abilities (including quantitative reasoning), and memory formation. In a knowledge-based economy where intellectual dexterity is often the key to survival, that’s bad news. Yet executives often give stress the shortest shrift.
美国压力研究所估计，美国企业每年因工作压力损失高达3000亿美元。这些损失包括医疗保健成本、工伤赔偿、员工流动和缺勤。其中，缺勤问题尤为严重。每天约有100万人因压力而请假（约40%的缺勤是由于工作中的紧张情绪造成的！）。美国劳工统计局的数据显示，员工因压力而请假的平均天数为20天。这代价不菲。员工一天的缺勤给公司造成的损失大约是该员工当天收入的两倍。如果长期压力导致抑郁，企业将面临智力资本的直接冲击。抑郁会削弱流体智力、问题解决能力（包括定量推理能力）和记忆形成能力。在知识经济时代，智力敏捷往往是生存的关键，这无疑是个坏消息。然而，企业高管往往对压力问题轻描淡写。
What makes a workplace stressful
什么因素会导致工作场所压力？
Three things matter in determining whether your workplace is stressful or productive: the type of stress you experience, the balance between stimulation and boredom in your job, and the condition of your home life.
决定你的工作场所是充满压力还是富有成效，有三件事很重要：你所经历的压力类型、工作中刺激与无聊之间的平衡，以及你的家庭生活状况。
The perfect storm of occupational stress appears to be a combination of two factors: (1) a great deal is expected of you, and (2) you have no control over whether you will perform well. This sounds like a formula for learned helplessness. On the positive side, restoration of control can return groups to productivity.
