Some companies are using a stress-reduction program involving increasingly popular mindfulness training. Mindfulness is a form of controlled meditation in which you learn to become aware of your environment without judging and learn to enjoy the moment, among other practices. A few companies tested the programs to see whether they work. They do. About 36 percent of the employees in an insurance company who enrolled in mindfulness training noticed a marked reduction in stress after taking the program. About 30 percent noticed an improvement in sleep. It has also been found to be effective against depression.
职业压力的完美风暴似乎是由两个因素共同造成的：(1) 别人对你寄予厚望，(2) 你无法掌控自己的表现。这听起来像是习得性无助的诱因。但从积极的一面来看，恢复控制感能够帮助团队重回高效工作状态。一些公司正在采用一种减压方案，其中包含日益流行的正念训练。正念是一种有控制的冥想形式，它教会人们在不加评判的情况下觉察周围环境，并学会享受当下，以及其他一些练习。一些公司测试了这些方案的效果，结果证明确实有效。一家保险公司的员工中，约有36%的人在参加正念训练后明显感到压力减轻，约有30%的人睡眠质量有所改善。此外，正念训练也被证实对抑郁症有效。
Control isn’t the only factor in productivity. Employees on an assembly line, doing the same tired thing day after day, certainly can feel in control of their work processes. But the brain-numbing tedium can become a source of stress. What spices things up? Studies show that a certain amount of uncertainty can be good for productivity, especially for bright, motivated employees. What they need is a balance between controllability and uncontrollability. Slight feelings of uncertainty may cause them to deploy unique problem-solving strategies.
控制并非生产力的唯一因素。流水线上的员工日复一日地重复着同样的枯燥工作，他们当然可以对自己的工作流程感到掌控自如。但这种令人麻木的单调乏味会成为压力的来源。那么，什么才能让工作更有趣呢？研究表明，一定程度的不确定性有利于提高生产力，尤其对于那些聪明上进的员工而言。他们需要的是在可控性和不可控性之间找到平衡。轻微的不确定感可能会促使他们运用独特的解决问题的策略。
The third characteristic, if you are a manager, is none of your business. I am talking about workers’ family lives. There’s no such thing as a firewall between personal issues and work productivity. We don’t have two brains that we can swap out depending upon whether we are in our office or in our living room. Stress in the workplace affects family life, causing more stress in the family. Stress in the family causes more stress at work, which in turn gets brought home again. It’s a downward spiral, and researchers call it “work-family conflict.” If you are a worker, you may have the most wonderful feelings about autonomy at work, and you may have tremendous problem-solving opportunities with your colleagues. But if your home life is a wreck, you can still suffer the negative effects of stress, and so can your employer.
如果你是管理者，那么第三个特点与你无关。我指的是员工的家庭生活。个人问题和工作效率之间并不存在防火墙。我们没有两个大脑，可以根据身处办公室还是在家而互换。工作场所的压力会影响家庭生活，进而导致家庭压力增加。家庭压力又会加剧工作压力，最终再次将压力带回家。这是一个恶性循环，研究人员称之为“工作-家庭冲突”。如果你是一名员工，你或许对工作中的自主性感到无比欣喜，或许与同事们有很多解决问题的机会。但如果你的家庭生活一团糟，你仍然会受到压力带来的负面影响，你的雇主也会受到影响。
Whether we look at school performance or job performance, we keep running into the profound influence of the emotional stability of the home. Is there anything we can do about something so fundamentally personal, given that its influence can be so terribly public? The answer, surprisingly, may be yes.
无论考察学业成绩还是工作表现，我们都会发现家庭情感稳定性有着深远的影响。鉴于这种影响可能如此公开，我们对于如此私密的事情又能做些什么呢？答案或许出乎意料：是的。
Marriage intervention
婚姻干预
Famed marriage researcher John Gottman can predict the future of a relationship within three minutes of interacting with a couple. His ability to accurately forecast marital success or failure is close to 90 percent. His track record is confirmed by peer-reviewed publications. He may very well hold the future of the American education and business sectors in his hands .
著名婚姻研究专家约翰·戈特曼只需与一对夫妇互动三分钟，就能预测他们关系的未来走向。他对婚姻成败的预测准确率接近90%。他的研究成果已得到同行评审期刊的证实。他很可能掌握着美国教育和商业的未来。
How is he so successful? After years of careful observation, Gottman isolated specific marital behaviors—both positive and negative—that hold most of the predictive power. But this research was ultimately unsatisfying to a man like Gottman, akin to telling people they have a life-threatening illness but not being able to cure them. And so the next step in his research was to find a cure. Gottman devised a marriage intervention strategy based on improving the behaviors proven to predict marital success and eliminating the ones proven to predict failure. Even in its most modest forms, his intervention drops divorce rates by nearly 50 percent. What do his interventions actually do? They show couples how to decrease both the frequency and severity of their hostile interactions. This return to civility has many positive side effects besides marital reconstruction, especially if the couples have kids. And the couples often do have kids.
他为何如此成功？经过多年的细致观察，戈特曼提炼出一些特定的婚姻行为——包括积极的和消极的——这些行为具有极强的预测能力。但对于像戈特曼这样的人来说，这项研究最终仍无法让他满意，就像告诉别人他们患有危及生命的疾病却无法治愈一样。因此，他研究的下一步是找到治愈方法。戈特曼设计了一种婚姻干预策略，旨在改善那些已被证明能预测婚姻成功的行为，并消除那些已被证明会导致婚姻失败的行为。即使是最温和的干预措施，也能使离婚率降低近50%。他的干预措施究竟有何作用？它教会夫妻如何减少敌对互动的频率和严重程度。这种回归文明的模式除了有助于婚姻重建之外，还有许多积极的副作用，尤其是在夫妻育有子女的情况下。而这些夫妻往往都有孩子。
Gottman’s marriage research invariably put him in touch with couples who were starting families. When the baby arrived, Gottman noticed that the couple’s hostile interactions skyrocketed. Causes ranged from chronic sleep deprivation to the increased demands of a helpless new family member (little ones typically require that an adult satisfy some demand of theirs about three times a minute). By the time the baby was 1 year old, marital satisfaction had plummeted 70 percent. At the one-year mark, the risk for maternal depression had risen from 25 percent to a whopping 62 percent. The couples’ risk for divorce increased, which meant American babies often were born into a turbulent emotional world.
戈特曼的婚姻研究总是让他接触到即将组建家庭的夫妇。当孩子出生后，戈特曼注意到夫妻间的冲突急剧升级。原因多种多样，从长期睡眠不足到照顾无助的新家庭成员带来的各种需求（小孩子通常每分钟都要大人满足他们的需求约三次）。到孩子一岁时，夫妻的婚姻满意度骤降了70%。在孩子一岁时，母亲患抑郁症的风险从25%飙升至惊人的62%。夫妻离婚的风险也随之增加，这意味着美国婴儿往往出生在一个充满情感动荡的环境中。
That single observation gave Gottman and fellow researcher Alyson Shapiro an idea. What if he deployed his proven marital intervention strategies to married couples while the wife was pregnant? Before the hostility floodgates opened up? Before the depression rates went through the roof? Based on his years of research, he already knew the marriage would improve. The big question concerned the kids. What would an emotionally stable home environment do to the baby’s developing nervous system? Gottman decided to find out.
正是这一观察让戈特曼和他的同事艾莉森·夏皮罗萌生了一个想法。如果他在妻子怀孕期间，也就是在夫妻间敌意爆发之前，运用他行之有效的婚姻干预策略，会怎么样呢？在抑郁症发病率飙升之前呢？基于他多年的研究，他已经知道婚姻状况会得到改善。但最大的问题在于孩子。一个情绪稳定的家庭环境会对婴儿正在发育的神经系统产生怎样的影响？戈特曼决定一探究竟。
The research investigation, deployed over several years, was called Bringing Baby Home. It consisted of exposing expectant couples to the marital interventions whether their marriages were in trouble or not, and then assessing the development of the child. Gottman and Shapiro uncovered a gold mine of information. They found that babies raised in the intervention households didn’t look anything like the babies raised in the controls. Their nervous systems didn’t develop the same way. Their behaviors weren’t in the same emotional universe. Children in the intervention groups didn’t cry as much. They had stronger attention-shifting behaviors. They responded to external stressors in remarkably stable ways. Physiologically, the intervention babies showed all the cardinal signs of healthy emotional regulation, while the controls showed all the signs of unhealthy, disorganized nervous systems. The differences were remarkable and revealed something hopeful and filled with common sense. By stabilizing the parents, Gottman and Shapiro were able to change not only the marriage but the child. I think Gottman’s findings can change the world.
这项历时数年的研究调查名为“带宝宝回家”（Bringing Baby Home）。研究内容包括让即将为人父母的夫妇接受婚姻干预，无论他们的婚姻是否出现问题，然后评估孩子的发育情况。戈特曼和夏皮罗从中挖掘出了大量有价值的信息。他们发现，在干预组家庭中长大的婴儿与对照组家庭中长大的婴儿截然不同。他们的神经系统发育方式不同，行为模式也截然不同。干预组的孩子哭闹较少，注意力转移能力更强，对外部压力的反应也异常稳定。生理方面，干预组婴儿表现出所有健康情绪调节的关键特征，而对照组婴儿则表现出所有不健康、紊乱的神经系统特征。这些差异令人瞩目，揭示了一些充满希望且符合常理的道理。通过稳定父母的婚姻，戈特曼和夏皮罗不仅改变了婚姻，也改变了孩子。我认为戈特曼的研究成果能够改变世界。
More ideas
更多想法
What people do in their private life is their own business, of course. Unfortunately, what people do in their private life often affects the public. Consider the criminal history of a fellow who had recently moved from Texas to Washington. He absolutely hated his new home and decided to leave. Stealing the car of a neighbor (for the second time that month), he drove several miles to the airport and ditched the car. He then found a way to fool both the security officials and the gate managers and hopped a free ride back to Texas. He accomplished this feat a few months shy of his 10th birthday. Not surprisingly, this boy comes from a troubled home. And he is hardly alone. If something doesn’t change the course of their lives, the private issue of raising such children soon will become a very public problem.
当然，人们的私生活是他们自己的事。不幸的是，人们的私生活往往会影响到公众。想想一个刚从德克萨斯搬到华盛顿的年轻人的犯罪记录吧。他极其厌恶新家，决定离开。他偷了邻居的车（这已经是当月第二次了），开了好几英里到机场，然后把车扔了。接着，他设法骗过了安保人员和登机口管理员，搭便车回到了德克萨斯。他完成这一切时，离他十岁生日还有几个月。不出所料，这个男孩来自一个问题家庭。而且他绝非个例。如果他们的生活轨迹得不到改变，那么抚养这类孩子的私人问题很快就会演变成一个公共问题。
How can we capture this chapter’s Brain Rule—stressed brains learn differently from non-stressed brains—and change the way we educate, parent, and do business? I have thought a lot about that.
我们如何才能抓住本章提出的“大脑法则”——压力下的大脑与非压力下的大脑学习方式不同——并改变我们的教育、育儿和经商方式？我一直在思考这个问题。
Teach parents first
先教导家长
The current education system starts in first grade, typically around age 6. The curriculum is a little writing, a little reading, a little math. The teacher is often a complete stranger. And something important is missing. The stability of the home is completely ignored, even though it is one of the greatest predictors of future success at school. What if we took the home influence seriously?
目前的教育体系从一年级开始，通常孩子六岁左右。课程内容包括少量写作、少量阅读和少量数学。老师往往是完全陌生的人。而且，一些重要的东西缺失了。家庭的稳定性被完全忽视，尽管它是预测孩子未来学业成功与否的最重要因素之一。如果我们认真对待家庭的影响，结果会怎样呢？
My idea envisions an educational system where the first students are not the children but the parents. The curriculum? How to create a stable home life, using Gottman’s powerful baby-nervous-system-changing protocols. The intervention could even start in a maternity ward, offered by a hospital (like a Lamaze class, which takes just about as much time). This would be a unique partnership between the health system and the education system. And it makes education, from the beginning of a child’s life, a family affair.
我的设想是建立一种教育体系，其中第一批学生不是孩子，而是他们的父母。课程内容是什么？是运用戈特曼强效的婴儿神经系统调节方案，营造稳定的家庭生活。干预甚至可以从医院的产房开始（类似于拉玛泽分娩法课程，耗时相近）。这将是医疗系统和教育系统之间一种独特的合作模式。它让教育从孩子生命之初就成为家庭的一份子。
A week after birth, parents and tots would engage in a curriculum designed around the amazing cognitive abilities of infants, from language acquisition to the powerful need for luxurious amounts of active playtime. Parents would learn things like how to talk with their babies and what types of objects help children learn about the physical world. (This is not a call to implement products in the strange industry that seeks to turn babies into Einsteins in the first year of life. Most of those products have not been tested, and some have been shown to be harmful to learning. My idea envisions a mature, rigorously tested pedagogy that does not yet exist—one more reason for educators and brain scientists to work together.) Along with this, parents would take an occasional series of marital refresher courses, just to ensure the stability of the home. Can you imagine what a child might look like academically after years of thriving in an emotionally stable environment? The child flourishes in this fantasy.
宝宝出生一周后，父母和宝宝将参与一套围绕婴儿惊人认知能力设计的课程，涵盖从语言习得到对充足活跃玩耍时间的强烈需求等各个方面。父母将学习如何与宝宝交流，以及哪些类型的物品有助于孩子了解物理世界。（这并非提倡推广那些试图在宝宝出生第一年就把他们培养成爱因斯坦的奇特产品。大多数此类产品未经测试，有些甚至已被证明对学习有害。我的想法是设想一种成熟且经过严格测试的教育方法，而这种方法目前尚不存在——这也是教育工作者和脑科学家携手合作的又一理由。）与此同时，父母还会定期参加一些婚姻辅导课程，以确保家庭的稳定。你能想象一个孩子在多年情感稳定的环境中茁壮成长后，在学业上会取得怎样的成就吗？在这种理想化的环境中，孩子会如鱼得水。
At the very least, couples (struggling or not) can seek out Gottman’s research-based marriage intervention. They are readily available to individuals.
至少，夫妻（无论婚姻是否出现问题）都可以寻求戈特曼基于研究的婚姻干预方法。这些方法很容易获得。
Free family counseling and child care
免费家庭咨询和儿童保育
Historically, people have done their best work—sometimes world-changing work—in their first few years after joining the workforce. In the field of economics, most Nobel Prize–winning research is done in the first 10 years of the recipient’s career. Albert Einstein published most of his creative ideas at the ripe old age of 26. It’s no wonder that companies want to recruit young intellectual talent.
从历史上看，人们往往在进入职场后的最初几年里做出最杰出的贡献——有时甚至是改变世界的贡献。在经济学领域，大多数诺贝尔奖获奖研究都是在获奖者职业生涯的前十年内完成的。阿尔伯特·爱因斯坦的大部分创造性思想都是在他26岁时发表的。难怪企业都想招揽年轻的智力人才。
The problem in today’s economy is that people typically are starting a family at the very time they are also supposed to be doing their best work. They are trying to be productive at some of the most stressful times of their lives. What if companies took this unhappy collision of life events seriously? They could offer Gottman’s intervention as a benefit for every newly married, or newly pregnant, employee. It might reverse the negative flow of family stress that normally enters the workplace at this time in a person’s life, enhance productivity, and perhaps even generate grateful, loyal employees.
当今经济面临的问题是，人们往往在组建家庭的同时，也应该在工作中发挥出最佳水平。他们试图在人生中最艰难的时期保持高效。如果企业认真对待这种不幸的人生阶段冲突，情况又会如何呢？他们可以将戈特曼干预法作为一项福利，提供给每一位新婚或新怀孕的员工。这或许能够扭转家庭压力在这个人生阶段通常会对职场造成的负面影响，提高生产力，甚至可能培养出心怀感激、忠诚的员工。
Businesses also risk losing their best and brightest at this time, a decision especially hard on women. What if talented people didn’t have to choose between career and family? Businesses could offer on-site child care and flexible work schedules simply to retain employees at the very time they are most likely to be valuable. As this affects women the most, businesses immediately would achieve more gender balance. My guess is that such an offering would so affect productivity that the costs of providing child care are offset by the gains. Not only might businesses create more stable employees in the current generation, they might be raising far healthier children for work in the next.
此时，企业也面临着失去最优秀人才的风险，这对女性来说尤其艰难。如果优秀人才不必在事业和家庭之间做出选择呢？企业可以提供公司内部托儿服务和灵活的工作时间，从而在员工最有价值的时候留住他们。由于这种情况对女性的影响最大，企业可以立即实现更好的性别平衡。我猜测，这样的举措将显著提高生产力，其带来的收益足以抵消提供托儿服务的成本。企业不仅能为当代培养更多稳定的员工，还能为下一代培养更健康的子女。
Power to the people
权力归于人民
Plenty of books discuss how to manage stress, and the good ones all say the key is to get control back into your life. For individuals, that may mean leaving a stressful job or an abusive relationship.
很多书都探讨过如何应对压力，而好的书籍都指出，关键在于重新掌控自己的生活。对个人而言，这可能意味着离开一份压力巨大的工作或一段充满虐待的关系。
Companies could detect work-related problems by developing a questionnaire based on Jeansok Kim and David Diamond’s three-pronged definition of stress, to assess whether an employee feels powerless. The next step would be to change the situation.
公司可以根据Jeansok Kim和David Diamond提出的压力三要素定义，设计一份问卷来检测与工作相关的问题，评估员工是否感到无力。下一步就是改变现状。
It’s no coincidence that stress researchers, education scientists, and business professionals come to similar conclusions about the effects of toxic stress on people. We have known most of the salient points since Marty Seligman stopped shocking those dogs in the mid-1970s. It is time we made productive use of that horrible line of research.
压力研究者、教育科学家和商业人士对毒性压力对人类的影响得出相似的结论，这绝非巧合。自从马蒂·塞利格曼在20世纪70年代中期停止电击狗以来，我们已经了解了其中的大部分要点。现在是时候有效地利用这项可怕的研究成果了。
Exercise
锻炼
Even if you’re not experiencing the kind of out-of-control stress we’ve been discussing, you can minimize the stress in your daily life. Aerobic exercise, several times a week for 30 minutes each, is an excellent way to shore up your BDNF peacekeeping forces.
即使你没有经历我们讨论过的那种失控的压力，你也可以在日常生活中尽量减少压力。每周进行几次，每次30分钟的有氧运动，是增强脑源性神经营养因子（BDNF）水平的绝佳方法。
Brain Rule # 4
大脑法则#4
Stressed brains don’t learn the same way.
压力过大的大脑学习方式与正常大脑不同。
• Your body’s defense system—the release of adrenaline and cortisol—is built for an immediate response to a serious but passing danger, such as a saber-toothed tiger. Chronic stress, such as hostility at home, dangerously deregulates a system built only to deal with short-term responses.
•人体的防御系统——肾上腺素和皮质醇的释放——是为了应对短暂但严重的危险（例如剑齿虎）而建立的。而慢性压力，例如家庭中的敌意，会危险地扰乱这个原本只用于应对短期威胁的系统。
• Under chronic stress, adrenaline creates scars in your blood vessels that can cause a heart attack or stroke, and cortisol damages the cells of the hippocampus, crippling your ability to learn and remember.
•长期处于压力之下，肾上腺素会在血管中形成疤痕，可能导致心脏病发作或中风；皮质醇会损害海马体的细胞，削弱学习和记忆能力。
• individually, the worst kind of stress is the feeling that you have no control over the problem—you are helpless.
•就个人而言，最糟糕的压力是感觉自己对问题没有控制权——你感到无助。
• Emotional stress has huge impacts across society, on children’s ability to learn in school and on employees’ productivity at work.
•情绪压力对整个社会都有巨大的影响，包括影响儿童在学校的学习能力和员工在工作中的生产力。

wiring
接线
Brain Rule #5
大脑法则#5
Every brain is wired differently.
每个人的大脑构造都不同。
# ↩
MICHAEL JORDAN ’ S ATHLETIC FAILURES are puzzling, don’t you think? In 1994, one of the best basketball players in the world—ESPN’s greatest athlete of the 20th century—decided to quit the game and take up baseball instead. It was an attempt to fulfill a childhood dream. Jordan failed miserably. He played only one full season, during which he posted a .202 batting average and committed 11 errors in the outfield: the league’s worst. Jordan’s performance was so poor, he couldn’t even qualify for a triple-A farm team. Though it seems preposterous that anyone with his physical ability could fail at any athletic activity he put his mind to, here was proof that one could. That same year, another athletic legend, Ken Griffey Jr., was burning up the baseball diamond. Like Jordan, Griffey Jr. played in the outfield but, unlike Jordan, he was known for catches so spectacular he seemed to float in the air. Float in the air ? Wasn’t that the space Jordan was accustomed to inhabiting? But the sacred atmosphere of the baseball park refused to budge for Jordan, and he soon went back to what his brains and muscles did better than anyone else’s, creating a legendary sequel to an already stunning basketball career. Griffey, then playing for the red-hot Seattle Mariners, went on to bat .300 for seven years in the 1990s and, in that same decade, slug out 382 home runs. He is still sixth on the all-time home-runs list.
迈克尔·乔丹在运动方面的失败令人费解，不是吗？1994年，这位世界顶级篮球运动员——ESPN评选的20世纪最伟大运动员——决定放弃篮球，转战棒球。这是为了实现他儿时的梦想。然而，乔丹却惨败。他只打了一个完整的赛季，打击率仅为.202，外野失误更是高达11次，是联盟最差的。乔丹的表现如此糟糕，甚至连3A级球队的资格都没拿到。虽然拥有他这样天赋的人在任何一项运动中都失败似乎匪夷所思，但乔丹的例子证明了这种可能性确实存在。同年，另一位体育传奇人物小肯·格里菲在棒球场上大放异彩。和乔丹一样，格里菲也打外野，但与乔丹不同的是，他以精彩绝伦的接球而闻名，仿佛在空中漂浮一般。漂浮在空中？那不正是乔丹习以为常的舞台吗？但棒球场的神圣氛围始终无法撼动乔丹，他很快便回归到他最擅长的领域——棒球，在那里，他创造了辉煌篮球生涯的又一传奇续篇。当时效力于炙手可热的西雅图水手队的格里菲，在20世纪90年代连续七年保持.300的打击率，并在那十年间轰出382支本垒打。他至今仍位列历史本垒打榜第六位。
What made the talents of these two athletes so specialized? What was going on with the way their brains communicated better with certain muscles than others? It has to do with how their brains were wired. To understand what that means, we will take a guided tour through the brain to watch what happens as it is learning. We will discuss the enormous role of one’s experience in how one’s brain develops—including the fact that identical twins having an identical experience will not emerge with identical brains. And we will discover that we each have a Jennifer Aniston neuron. I am not kidding.
是什么造就了这两位运动员如此独特的才能？他们的大脑为何能更好地控制某些肌肉？这与他们的大脑构造息息相关。为了理解这一点，我们将跟随导览，深入了解大脑的学习过程。我们将探讨个人经历对大脑发育的巨大影响——包括同卵双胞胎即使拥有完全相同的经历，最终也不会拥有完全相同的大脑。而且，我们还会发现，我们每个人都拥有一个“詹妮弗·安妮斯顿神经元”。我可不是在开玩笑。
Learning rewires your brain
学习会重塑你的大脑
When you learn something, the wiring in your brain changes. Eric Kandel is the scientist mostly responsible for showing that acquiring even simple pieces of information physically alters the structure of our neurons. Taken broadly, these physical changes result in the functional organization and reorganization of the brain. This is astonishing. The brain is constantly learning things, so the brain is constantly rewiring itself.
当你学习新事物时，大脑中的神经连接会发生改变。埃里克·坎德尔是证明即使是获取简单的信息也会从物理层面改变我们神经元结构的科学家，他的贡献功不可没。从广义上讲，这些物理变化会导致大脑功能性的组织和重组。这令人惊叹。大脑不断学习，因此也在不断地自我重塑。
Kandel first discovered this fact not by looking at humans but by looking at sea slugs. He soon found, somewhat insultingly, that human nerves learn things in the same way slug nerves learn things. And so do lots of animals in between slugs and humans. Kandel shared a Nobel Prize in 2000 for his work in part because it described the thought processes of virtually every creature with the means to think.
坎德尔最初发现这一事实并非通过研究人类，而是通过研究海蛞蝓。他很快发现，尽管这多少有些令他感到不快，但人类的神经学习方式与海蛞蝓的神经学习方式并无二致。介于海蛞蝓和人类之间的许多动物也同样如此。坎德尔因其研究成果于2000年荣获诺贝尔奖，部分原因在于他的研究描述了几乎所有具有思考能力的生物的思维过程。
What are these physical alterations? As neurons learn, they swell, sway, and split. They break connections in one spot, glide over to a nearby region, and form connections with their new neighbors. Many others stay put, simply strengthening their electrical connections with each other, increasing the efficiency of information transfer. Indeed, at this very moment inside your brain, bits of neurons are moving around like reptiles: slithering to new spots, getting fat at one end or creating split ends. All so that you can remember a few things about Eric Kandel and sea slugs.
这些物理变化是什么呢？神经元在学习过程中会膨胀、摇摆和分裂。它们会断开一个位置的连接，滑到附近的区域，并与新的邻居建立连接。许多其他神经元则保持原位，只是加强彼此之间的电连接，从而提高信息传递的效率。事实上，就在此刻，你的大脑中，一些神经元碎片正像爬行动物一样四处移动：滑向新的位置，一端膨胀或分叉。这一切都是为了让你记住一些关于埃里克·坎德尔和海蛞蝓的事情。
This line of scientific inquiry started long before Kandel. In the 18th century, the Italian scientist Vincenzo Malacarne did a surprisingly modern series of biological experiments. He trained a group of birds to do complex tricks, then killed them and dissected their brains. He found that his trained birds had more extensive folding patterns in specific regions of their brains than his untrained birds. Fifty years later, Charles Darwin noted similar differences between the brains of wild animals and their domestic counterparts. The brains of wild animals were 15 to 30 percent larger than those of their tame, domestic counterparts. It appeared that the cold, hard world forced the wild animals into a constant learning mode. Those experiences wired their brains much differently.
这种科学探索早在坎德尔之前就开始了。18世纪，意大利科学家文森佐·马拉卡内进行了一系列颇具现代感的生物学实验。他训练一群鸟表演复杂的技巧，然后杀死它们并解剖了它们的大脑。他发现，受过训练的鸟大脑特定区域的褶皱模式比未经训练的鸟更为复杂。50年后，查尔斯·达尔文也注意到野生动物和家养动物大脑之间存在类似的差异。野生动物的大脑比驯养的家养动物大15%到30%。看来，严酷的自然环境迫使野生动物不断学习。这些经历使它们的大脑结构与人类截然不同。
It is the same with humans. This can be observed in places ranging from New Orleans’s Zydeco beer halls to the staid palaces of the New York Philharmonic—both the natural habitat of violin players. In violin players’ brains, the neural regions that control their left hands, where complex, fine motor movement is required on the strings, look as if they’ve been gorging on a high-fat diet. These regions are enlarged, swollen, and crisscrossed with complex associations. By contrast, the areas controlling the right hand, which draws the bow, look positively anorexic, with much less complexity.
人类也是如此。从新奥尔良的柴迪科啤酒馆到纽约爱乐乐团庄严肃穆的殿堂——这些都是小提琴演奏者的天然栖息地——都能观察到这种现象。在小提琴演奏者的大脑中，控制左手（需要精细复杂的拨弦动作）的神经区域，看起来就像是摄入了大量高脂肪食物。这些区域肿胀、扩张，并且交错纵横，连接着复杂的神经通路。相比之下，控制右手（负责拉弓）的区域则显得异常瘦弱，结构远没有那么复杂。
The brain acts like a muscle: The more activity you do, the larger and more complex it can become. Whether that equates to more intelligence is another issue, but one fact is indisputable: What you do in life physically changes what your brain looks like. You can wire and rewire your brain with the simple choice of which musical instrument—or professional sport—you play .
大脑就像肌肉一样：活动越多，它就会变得越大越复杂。这是否等同于更高的智力是另一个问题，但有一点毋庸置疑：你的生活方式会从生理上改变大脑的结构。你甚至可以通过选择演奏哪种乐器——或者从事哪种职业运动——来改变和重塑你的大脑。
Where wiring starts: the humble cell
电路的起点：不起眼的细胞
You have heard since grade school that living things are made of cells, and for the most part, that’s true. There isn’t much that complex biological creatures can do that doesn’t involve cells. You may have little gratitude for cells’ generous contribution to your existence, but the cells make up for your indifference by ensuring that you can’t control them. For the most part, they purr and hum behind the scenes, content to supervise virtually everything you will ever experience, much of which lies outside your awareness. Some cells are so unassuming, they find their normal function only after they can’t function. The surface of your skin, for example—all nine pounds of it—literally is deceased. This allows the rest of your cells to support your daily life free of wind, rain, and spilled nacho cheese at a baseball game. It is accurate to say that nearly every inch of your outer physical presentation to the world is dead.
你从小学就听说过，生物是由细胞构成的，而且在大多数情况下，这话没错。复杂的生物体能活动几乎都离不开细胞。你或许对细胞为你的生命所做出的慷慨贡献缺乏感激之情，但细胞也用实际行动弥补了你的冷漠，确保你无法控制它们。大多数时候，它们在幕后默默运转，尽职尽责地监督着你几乎所有的经历，其中很多都发生在你的意识之外。有些细胞如此低调，以至于只有在失去功能之后，它们才会发现自己的正常功能。例如，你皮肤的表面——足足有九磅重——实际上已经死亡。这使得你身体的其他细胞能够支撑你的日常生活，让你免受风吹雨打，甚至在棒球比赛中被洒出的玉米片奶酪的侵扰。可以说，你展现给世人的外在身体几乎每一寸都已死亡。
Of the cells that are alive, most look just like fried eggs. The white of the egg we call the cytoplasm; the center yolk is the nucleus. The nucleus contains that master blueprint molecule, DNA. DNA possesses genes, small snippets of biological instructions, that guide everything from how tall you become to how you respond to stress. A lot of genetic material fits inside that yolk-like nucleus. Nearly six feet of the stuff are crammed into a space that is measured in microns. A micron is 1/25,000th of an inch, which means putting DNA into your nucleus is like taking 30 miles of ribbon and stuffing it into an eggshell.
在所有活细胞中，大多数看起来就像煎蛋。蛋清部分我们称之为细胞质；中间的蛋黄部分是细胞核。细胞核内含有主蓝图分子——DNA。DNA包含基因，也就是一小段生物指令，它指导着从身高到压力反应等一切生理过程。大量的遗传物质被塞进了这个类似蛋黄的细胞核里。近六英尺长的遗传物质被压缩到一个以微米为单位的空间里。一微米等于1/25,000英寸，这意味着把DNA塞进你的细胞核就像把30英里长的丝带塞进一个蛋壳里一样。
One of the most unexpected findings of recent years is that DNA, or deoxyribonucleic acid, is not randomly jammed into the nucleus. Rather, DNA is folded into the nucleus in a complex and tightly regulated manner. The reason for this molecular origami: cellular career options. Fold the DNA one way and the cell will become a contributing member of your liver. Fold it another way and the cell will become part of your busy bloodstream. Fold it a third way and you get the all-important nerve cell—and the ability to read this sentence.
近年来最出人意料的发现之一是，DNA（脱氧核糖核酸）并非随意地塞进细胞核。相反，DNA以一种复杂且受到严格调控的方式折叠并进入细胞核。这种分子折纸的原理在于：决定细胞的“职业选择”。DNA以一种方式折叠，细胞就会成为肝脏的组成部分；以另一种方式折叠，细胞就会成为血液循环系统的一部分；以第三种方式折叠，就形成了至关重要的神经细胞——以及阅读这句话的能力。
What does a nerve cell look like? Like an uprooted tree: a large mass of roots on one end, connected to a small mass of branches on the other. The root mass in a nerve cell is called the cell body, and within it lies the nucleus. The tips of the roots are called dendrites. The thin, connecting trunk is called an axon, and the smaller mass of branches is called the axon terminal.
神经细胞长什么样？就像一棵被连根拔起的树：一端是一大团根，另一端连接着一小团枝条。神经细胞的根状结构称为细胞体，细胞核位于细胞体内部。根的末端称为树突。连接细胞体和树突的细长部分称为轴突，而较小的枝条则称为轴突末梢。
Nerve cells—also called neurons—help to mediate something as sophisticated as human learning. To understand how, I would like to take you on a guided tour of a neuron, borrowing from a science-fiction movie I saw as a child. It was called Fantastic Voyage , written by Harry Kleiner and popularized afterward in a book by the legendary Isaac Asimov. In the movie, four people are shrunk to microscopic size, and they board a tiny submarine to explore the internal workings of the human body. We are going to do the same. We’ll roam around inside a typical neuron and the watery world in which it is anchored. Let’s steer over to the hippocampus, the structure in the center of the brain where short-term knowledge is converted to longer-term knowledge.
神经细胞——也叫神经元——帮助人类进行着像学习这样复杂的过程。为了理解其中的原理，我想带大家参观一下神经元，灵感来自我小时候看过的一部科幻电影。这部电影叫《神奇旅程》，由哈里·克莱纳编剧，后来被传奇作家艾萨克·阿西莫夫改编成小说，广为人知。电影里，四个人被缩小到微观尺寸，然后登上了一艘微型潜艇，探索人体内部的运作机制。我们今天也要这样做。我们将漫游在一个典型的神经元内部，以及它所处的“水世界”。让我们先来看看海马体，它是大脑中心的一个结构，负责将短期知识转化为长期知识。
When our little ship enters the hippocampus, our eyes adjust to the darkness and we peer out the windows. It looks as if we’ve entered an ancient, underwater forest. Everywhere there are submerged jumbles of branches, limbs, and trunks. Suddenly we see flashes of light in the darkness: sparks of electric current run up and down the trunks. The forest is electrified! We are going to have to be careful. Occasionally, large clouds of chemicals erupt from one end of the tree trunks, after electricity has convulsed through them.
当我们的小船进入海马体时，我们的眼睛适应了黑暗，向窗外望去。眼前的景象仿佛是一片古老的水下森林。到处都是浸没在水下的树枝、树干和树桩。突然，黑暗中闪过一道道光芒：电流火花在树干间窜动。这片森林带电了！我们必须小心。偶尔，电流穿过树干后，会从树干的一端喷涌出大量的化学物质。
These are not trees. These are neurons, with some odd structural distinctions. Sliding alongside one of the trunks, for example, we realize that the “bark” seems surprisingly slick, like grease. That’s because it is grease. In the balmy interior of the human body, the exterior of the neuron, the phospholipid bilayer, is the consistency of Mazola oil. The neuron’s interior structure is what gives it its shape, much as the human skeleton gives the body its shape. When we plunge into the interior of the cell, one of the first things we will see is this skeleton. So let’s plunge.
这些不是树，而是神经元，它们有一些奇特的结构特征。例如，当我们沿着其中一个“树干”滑动时，会发现它的“树皮”出奇地光滑，像油脂一样。那是因为它的确是油脂。在人体温暖舒适的内部环境中，神经元的外部结构——磷脂双分子层——的稠度就像玉米油一样。神经元的内部结构赋予了它形状，就像人体的骨骼赋予了身体形状一样。当我们深入细胞内部时，首先看到的就是这个骨骼。那么，让我们开始探索吧。
It’s instantly, insufferably overcrowded, even hostile, in here. Everywhere we have to navigate through a dangerous scaffolding of spiky, coral-like protein formations: the neural skeleton. Though these dense formations give the neuron its three-dimensional shape, many of the skeletal parts are in constant motion—which means we have to do a lot of dodging. Millions of molecules still slam against our ship, however, and every few seconds we are jolted by electrical discharges. We don’t want to stay long.
这里瞬间变得拥挤不堪，甚至令人难以忍受，甚至充满敌意。我们处处都要在由尖刺状、珊瑚状蛋白质构成的危险支架——神经骨架——间穿行。虽然这些密集的结构赋予了神经元三维形状，但许多骨架部分都在不断运动——这意味着我们必须不停地躲避。然而，数百万个分子仍然撞击着我们的“飞船”，每隔几秒钟，我们就会受到电击的冲击。我们不想久留。
We escape from one end of the neuron. Instead of perilously winding through sharp thickets of proteins, we now find ourselves free-floating in a calm, seemingly bottomless watery canyon. In the distance, we can see another neuron looming ahead. We are in the space between two neurons, called a synaptic cleft, and the first thing we notice is that we are not alone. We appear to be swimming with large schools of tiny molecules. They are streaming out of the neuron we just visited and thrashing helter-skelter toward the one we are facing. In a few seconds, they reverse themselves, swimming back to the neuron we just left. It instantly gobbles them up. These schools of molecules are called neurotransmitters, and they function like tiny couriers. Neurons use these molecules to communicate information across the synaptic cleft. The cell that releases them is called the presynaptic neuron, and the cell that receives them is called the postsynaptic neuron.
我们从神经元的一端逃脱出来。我们不再需要小心翼翼地穿过锋利的蛋白质丛林，而是自由地漂浮在一个平静、仿佛深不见底的水谷中。远处，我们可以看到另一个神经元隐约可见。我们身处两个神经元之间的空间，称为突触间隙，首先注意到的是我们并非孤身一人。我们似乎正与大量的微小分子一起游动。它们从我们刚刚访问过的神经元中涌出，杂乱无章地朝着我们面前的神经元游去。几秒钟后，它们又折返回去，游回我们刚刚离开的神经元。它瞬间将它们吞噬。这些分子群被称为神经递质，它们就像微小的信使。神经元利用这些分子在突触间隙中传递信息。释放神经递质的细胞称为突触前神经元，接收神经递质的细胞称为突触后神经元。
Neurons release these chemicals into the synapse usually in response to being electrically stimulated. The neuron that receives these chemicals then reacts negatively or positively. In something like a cellular temper tantrum, the neuron can turn itself off to the rest of the neuroelectric world—a process termed inhibition. Or the neuron can become electrically stimulated, allowing a signal to be transferred: “I got stimulated and I am passing on the good news to you.” The neurotransmitters then return to the cell of origin, a process appropriately termed reuptake. When that cell gobbles them up, the system is reset and ready for another signal.
神经元通常在受到电刺激时，会将这些化学物质释放到突触中。接收到这些化学物质的神经元随后会做出抑制或正向反应。就像细胞发脾气一样，神经元可能会关闭自身与周围神经电信号的联系——这个过程被称为抑制。或者，神经元也可能受到电刺激，从而传递信号：“我受到了刺激，现在把好消息传递给你。” 之后，神经递质会返回到其来源细胞，这个过程被称为再摄取。当该细胞重新吸收这些神经递质后，系统就被重置，准备接收下一个信号。
As we gaze at this underwater hippocampal forest, we notice several disturbing developments. Some of these branches appear to be swaying, snakelike. Occasionally, the end of one neuron swells up, greatly increasing in diameter. The terminal ends of other neurons split down the middle like forked tongues, creating two connection points where there was only one. Electricity crackles through these moving neurons at a blinding 250 miles per hour, some quite near us, with clouds of neurotransmitters filling the synaptic spaces as the electric current passes by.
当我们凝视着这片水下海马森林时，我们注意到了一些令人不安的现象。有些分支似乎在摇摆，如同蛇一般。偶尔，某个神经元的末端会膨胀，直径显著增大。另一些神经元的末端则像分叉的舌头一样从中间裂开，原本只有一个连接点的地方变成了两个。电流以惊人的速度（每小时250英里）在这些移动的神经元中噼啪作响，有些甚至离我们很近，电流流过时，神经递质如云般涌入突触间隙。
What we should do now is take off our shoes and bow low in our submarine, for we are on Neural Holy Ground. We are observing the process of the human brain learning .
我们现在应该做的，是脱掉鞋子，在潜艇里深深鞠躬，因为我们来到了神经圣地。我们正在观察人类大脑的学习过程。
As we slowly spin our ship 360 degrees, we notice how complicated this forest is. Take the two neurons between which we are floating. We are between just two connection points, two dendrites. If you can imagine two trees being uprooted by giant hands, turned 90 degrees so that the roots face each other, and then moved close enough to almost touch, you can visualize the real world of two neurons interacting in the brain. And that’s just the simplest case. Usually, thousands of neurons are jammed up against one another, all occupying a single small parcel of real estate in the brain. The branches form connections with one another in a nearly incomprehensible mass of confusion. Ten thousand points of connection is typical.
当我们缓缓旋转飞船360度时，我们会注意到这片森林有多么复杂。就拿我们漂浮在两个神经元之间的情况来说吧。我们仅仅处于两个连接点——两个树突之间。你可以想象两棵树被巨手连根拔起，旋转90度，让树根彼此相对，然后靠近到几乎要接触，这样你就能想象出大脑中两个神经元相互作用的真实场景。而这仅仅是最简单的情况。通常情况下，成千上万个神经元紧密排列，占据着大脑中一小块区域。这些分支相互连接，形成近乎难以理解的复杂网络。通常情况下，连接点的数量会达到一万个。
Frenetic growth and frantic pruning
疯狂生长和疯狂修剪
How do we get so many neurons? Infants provide a front-row seat to one of the most remarkable construction projects on Earth. The human brain, only partially constructed at birth, won’t be fully assembled for years. The biggest construction programs aren’t finished until you are in your early 20s, with fine-tuning well into your 40s. When babies are born, their brains have about the same number of connections as adults have. That doesn’t last long. By the time children are 3 years old, the connections in specific regions of their brains have doubled or even tripled. That doesn’t last long, either. The brain soon takes thousands of tiny pruning shears and trims back a lot of this hard work. By the time children are 8 or so, they’re back to their adult numbers. And if kids never went through puberty, that would be the end of the story. In fact, it is only the middle of the story. At puberty, the whole process begins again, but with different regions in the brain. Once again, you see frenetic neural outgrowth and furious pruning back. It isn’t until parents begin thinking about college financial aid that children’s brains begin to settle into their adult forms. From a connectivity point of view, there is a great deal of activity in the terrible twos and then, during the terrible teens, a great deal more.
我们是如何拥有如此多的神经元的呢？婴儿为我们提供了一个绝佳的视角，见证地球上最奇妙的“建造工程”之一。人脑在出生时只是部分发育，需要数年时间才能完全成型。最大的“建造工程”要到二十岁出头才能完成，而精细的调整则会持续到四十多岁。婴儿出生时，他们的大脑拥有与成人大致相同的连接数量。但这并不会持续太久。到了三岁左右，他们大脑特定区域的连接数量会翻倍甚至三倍。但这也不会持续太久。大脑很快就会像无数把微型修枝剪一样，修剪掉许多“辛勤”的成果。到了八岁左右，他们的连接数量就会恢复到成人的水平。如果孩子们从未经历过青春期，故事就到此结束了。但实际上，这仅仅是故事的中段。青春期到来时，整个过程会再次开始，但这次涉及的是大脑的不同区域。你会再次看到神经系统疯狂生长和快速修剪的过程。直到父母开始考虑大学助学金的问题，孩子的大脑才开始逐渐稳定下来，最终发育成成人的形态。从神经连接的角度来看，两岁左右的“可怕时期”神经活动非常活跃，而到了青少年时期，活跃程度则更高。
Because this happens to every person at about the same time, it might seem like cellular soldiers are obeying growth commands in lockstep formation. But nothing approaching military precision is observed in the messy world of brain development. And it is at this imprecise point that brain development meets Brain Rule: Every brain is wired differently. Even a cursory inspection of the data reveals remarkable variation in growth patterns from one person to the next. Whether examining toddlers or teenagers, different regions in different children develop at different rates. There is a remarkable degree of diversity in the specific areas that grow and prune, and with what enthusiasm they do so.
由于每个人大脑发育的时间大致相同，细胞似乎像士兵一样整齐划一地执行生长指令。然而，在复杂多变的大脑发育过程中，根本不存在任何军事般的精确性。正是在这种不确定性中，大脑发育与“大脑法则”不谋而合：每个人的大脑构造都各不相同。即使是对数据进行粗略的分析，也能发现个体间大脑发育模式的显著差异。无论是幼儿还是青少年，不同儿童大脑的不同区域发育速度都存在差异。大脑中哪些区域会生长和修剪，以及生长和修剪的强度，都存在着显著的个体差异。
I’m reminded of this whenever I see the class pictures from my wife’s journey through the American school system. My wife went to school with virtually the same people for her entire K–12 experience (and actually remained friends with most of them). Comparing the kids to each other back then, I always shake my head in disbelief. In the first-grade picture, the kids are all about the same age, but they don’t look it. Some kids are short. Some are tall. Some look like mature little athletes. Some look as if they just got out of diapers. The girls almost always appear older than the boys. It’s even worse in the junior-high pictures. Some of the boys look as if they haven’t developed much since third grade. Others are clearly beginning to sprout whiskers. Some of the girls, flat-chested, look a lot like boys. Others look developed enough to make babies. And if we could look inside these kids’ heads, we would see that their brains are just as unevenly developed as their bodies. Let’s find out why.
每当我看到妻子在美国求学时期的班级合影，都会想起这件事。妻子从幼儿园到高中，几乎都是和同一群人一起上学（而且实际上和他们中的大多数人都保持着朋友关系）。每次看到这些孩子小时候的样子，我都难以置信地摇头。一年级的照片里，孩子们年龄相仿，但看起来却截然不同。有的孩子矮，有的孩子高，有的孩子像成熟的小运动员，有的孩子看起来却像刚换尿布一样。女孩几乎总是比男孩看起来更成熟。初中时的情况更糟。有些男孩看起来好像从三年级开始就没怎么发育，而有些男孩却明显开始长胡子了。有些女孩胸部平坦，看起来很像男孩，而有些女孩看起来发育得像能生孩子一样。如果我们能窥探这些孩子的内心，就会发现他们的大脑发育和身体发育一样不均衡。让我们一起来探究一下原因。
The Jennifer Aniston neuron
詹妮弗·安妮斯顿神经元
Some of the neural connections you’re born with have preset functions: they control basic housekeeping functions like breathing, heartbeat, your ability to know where your foot is even if you can’t see it, and so on. Researchers call this “experience independent” wiring. The brain also holds off connecting neurons, waiting for external experience to direct it. “Experience expectant” wiring is related to areas such as visual acuity and perhaps language acquisition. And, finally, we have “experience dependent” wiring. It may best be explained by the following scene, which would be right at home in a grade B movie.
你与生俱来的一些神经连接具有预设功能：它们控制着呼吸、心跳等基本生理功能，甚至在你看不见脚的情况下也能感知脚的位置等等。研究人员称之为“经验独立型”连接。大脑还会延迟连接神经元，等待外部经验的引导。“经验预期型”连接与视觉敏锐度以及语言习得等领域相关。最后，我们还有“经验依赖型”连接。以下场景或许能更好地解释这种连接，它放在一部低成本电影里也毫不违和。
A man is lying on a surgical table, electrodes implanted in his brain to create a kind of GPS pinpointing electrical activity in the brain. The man needs to have some of his neural tissue removed—resected, in surgical parlance—because of life-threatening epilepsy, and the depth electrodes will help surgeons determine where the seizures are starting. The man is conscious. Suddenly, a researcher whips out a photo of Jennifer Aniston and shows it to the patient. A neuron in the man’s head fires. The researcher lets out a war whoop.
一名男子躺在手术台上，大脑中植入了电极，这些电极如同GPS定位系统，用于精确定位大脑的电活动。由于患有危及生命的癫痫，这名男子需要切除部分神经组织——用外科术语来说是“切除术”——而这些深部电极将帮助外科医生确定癫痫发作的起始位置。男子意识清醒。突然，一名研究人员拿出詹妮弗·安妮斯顿的照片给病人看。男子大脑中的一个神经元瞬间放电。研究人员发出了一声欢呼。
This experiment really happened. The neuron in question responded to seven photographs of actress Jennifer Aniston, while it practically ignored the 80 other images of everything else, including famous and nonfamous people. Lead scientist Quian Quiroga said, “The first time we saw a neuron firing to seven different pictures of Jennifer Aniston—and nothing else—we literally jumped out of our chairs.” There is a neuron lurking in your head that is stimulated only when Jennifer Aniston is in the room.
这个实验是真实发生的。实验中，一个神经元对七张女演员詹妮弗·安妮斯顿的照片有反应，而对其他80张照片（包括名人和普通人的照片）几乎完全无动于衷。首席科学家奎安·奎罗加说：“我们第一次看到一个神经元只对七张詹妮弗·安妮斯顿的照片有反应——而对其他任何照片都没有反应——我们简直惊呆了。” 你的大脑里可能就潜藏着这样一个神经元，只有当詹妮弗·安妮斯顿出现在房间里时，它才会被激活。
A Jennifer Aniston neuron ? How could this be? Surely nothing in our evolutionary history suggests that Jennifer Aniston is a permanent denizen of our brain wiring. (Aniston wasn’t even born until 1969, and there are regions in our brain whose designs are millions of years old). To make matters worse, the researchers also found a Halle Berry–specific neuron, a cell in a patient’s brain that wouldn’t respond to pictures of Aniston or anything else. Just Berry. A patient also had a neuron specific to Bill Clinton. It no doubt was helpful to have a sense of humor while doing this kind of brain research.
詹妮弗·安妮斯顿的神经元？这怎么可能？我们的进化史中肯定没有任何迹象表明詹妮弗·安妮斯顿会永久存在于我们的大脑回路中。（安妮斯顿1969年才出生，而我们大脑中有些区域的构造已经有数百万年的历史了。）更糟糕的是，研究人员还发现了一个哈莉·贝瑞专属神经元，这个神经元存在于一位患者的大脑中，它对安妮斯顿的照片或其他任何事物都没有反应，只对贝瑞的照片有反应。另一位患者还发现了一个比尔·克林顿专属神经元。毫无疑问，在进行这类脑科学研究时，保持幽默感是有帮助的。
Welcome to the world of experience-dependent brain wiring, where a great deal of the brain is hardwired not to be hardwired. Like a beautiful, rigorously trained ballerina, we are hardwired to be flexible. We can immediately divide the world’s brains into those who know of Jennifer Aniston or Halle Berry or Bill Clinton and those who don’t. The brains of those who do are wired differently from those who don’t. This seemingly ridiculous observation underlies a much larger concept. Our brains are so sensitive to external inputs that their physical wiring depends upon the culture in which they find themselves.
欢迎来到经验依赖型大脑连接的世界，在这个世界里，大脑的很大一部分天生就不是为了适应环境而存在的。就像一位美丽而训练有素的芭蕾舞演员一样，我们天生就具有灵活性。我们可以立即将世界上的人的大脑分为两类：一类是认识詹妮弗·安妮斯顿、哈莉·贝瑞或比尔·克林顿的人，另一类是不认识他们的人。认识他们的人的大脑连接方式与不认识他们的人的大脑连接方式截然不同。这个看似荒谬的观察背后隐藏着一个更为宏大的概念。我们的大脑对外部输入如此敏感，以至于其物理连接方式取决于我们所处的文化环境。
Even identical twins do not have identical brain wiring. Consider this thought experiment: Suppose two adult male twins rent the Halle Berry movie Catwoman , and we in our nifty little submarine are viewing their brains while they watch. Even though the twins are in the same room, sitting on the same couch, the twins see the movie from slightly different angles. We find that their brains are encoding visual memories of the video differently, in part because it is impossible to observe the video from the same spot. Seconds into the movie, they are already wiring themselves differently. One of the twins earlier in the day read a magazine story about panned action movies, a picture of Berry figuring prominently on the cover. While watching the video, this twin’s brain is simultaneously accessing memories of the magazine story. We observe that his brain is busy comparing and contrasting comments from the text with the movie and is assessing whether he agrees with them. The other twin has not seen this magazine, so his brain isn’t doing this. Even though the difference may seem subtle, the two brains are creating different memories of the same movie.
即使是同卵双胞胎，他们的大脑结构也不完全相同。不妨考虑以下这个思想实验：假设一对成年男性双胞胎租借了哈莉·贝瑞主演的电影《猫女》，而我们则通过我们精巧的“潜水艇”观察他们观看时的大脑活动。尽管双胞胎身处同一房间，坐在同一张沙发上，但他们观看电影的角度略有不同。我们发现，他们的大脑对视频的视觉记忆编码方式也不同，部分原因是他们不可能从完全相同的位置观看视频。电影开始几秒钟后，他们的大脑结构就已经出现了差异。其中一位双胞胎当天早些时候读过一篇关于被批评的动作电影的杂志文章，贝瑞的照片赫然出现在封面上。在观看电影时，这位双胞胎的大脑同时也在提取关于这篇杂志文章的记忆。我们观察到，他的大脑忙于将文章中的评论与电影进行比较和对比，并评估他是否同意这些评论。另一位双胞胎没有看过这本杂志，所以他的大脑没有进行这些操作。尽管这种差异看似细微，但两个大脑对同一部电影却产生了不同的记忆。
That’s the power of the Brain Rule. Learning results in physical changes in the brain, and these changes are unique to each individual. Not even identical twins having identical experiences possess brains that wire themselves exactly the same way. Given this, can we know anything about the organ? Well, yes. The brain has billions of cells whose collective electrical efforts work in a similar fashion. Every human comes equipped with a hippocampus, a pituitary gland, and the most sophisticated thinking store of electrochemistry on the planet: a cortex. These tissues function the same way in every brain. How then can we explain the individuality? Consider a highway.
这就是大脑法则的力量。学习会导致大脑发生物理变化，而这些变化对每个人来说都是独一无二的。即使是经历完全相同的同卵双胞胎，他们的大脑连接方式也并非完全一致。既然如此，我们还能了解大脑吗？答案是肯定的。大脑由数十亿个细胞组成，它们的集体电活动以相似的方式运作。每个人都拥有海马体、垂体以及地球上最复杂的电化学思维储存库：大脑皮层。这些组织在每个大脑中的功能都相同。那么，我们该如何解释个体差异呢？不妨想象一下高速公路。
For each brain, a different road map
每个大脑都有不同的路线图
The United States has one of the most extensive and complex ground transportation systems in the world. There are lots of variations on the idea of “road,” from interstate freeways, turnpikes, and state highways to residential streets, one-lane alleys, and dirt roads. Pathways in the human brain are similarly diverse. We have the neural equivalents of large interstate freeways, turnpikes, and state highways. These big trunks are the same from one person to the next, functioning in yours about the same way they function in mine. So a great deal of the structure and function of the brain is predictable. This may be the ultimate result of the double-humped growth and pruning program we talked of previously. That’s the experience-independent wiring .
美国拥有世界上最庞大、最复杂的地面交通系统之一。从州际高速公路、收费公路和州级公路到居民区街道、单行道和土路，“道路”的概念有很多种。人脑中的通路也同样多种多样。我们大脑中存在着与大型州际高速公路、收费公路和州级公路相对应的神经通路。这些“主干线”在每个人身上都是一样的，在你我大脑中的运作方式也大致相同。因此，大脑的结构和功能在很大程度上是可以预测的。这或许是我们之前提到的双峰生长和修剪机制的最终结果。这就是独立于经验的神经回路。
It’s when you get to the smaller routes—the brain’s equivalent of residential streets, one-laners and dirt roads—that individual patterns begin to show up. In no two people are they identical. That’s the experience-dependent wiring. Every brain has a lot of these smaller paths, which is why the very small amounts to a big deal. It’s why, for example, human intellect is so multifaceted. Psychologist Howard Gardner believes we have at least seven categories of intelligence: verbal/linguistic, musical/rhythmic, logical/mathematical, spatial, bodily/kinesthetic, interpersonal, and intrapersonal. It’s a much broader idea of intelligence than the standard IQ test implies.
当你深入到那些较小的路径——大脑中相当于居民区街道、单行道和土路的路径——个体模式就开始显现。每个人的这些模式都不尽相同。这就是经验依赖性神经回路。每个人的大脑都拥有许多这样的较小路径，因此，即使是微小的因素也能产生巨大的影响。例如，正因如此，人类的智力才如此多元化。心理学家霍华德·加德纳认为，我们至少拥有七种智力：语言/语言能力、音乐/节奏能力、逻辑/数学能力、空间能力、身体/动觉能力、人际能力和内省能力。这比标准的智商测试所揭示的智力概念要广泛得多。
We can grasp the magnitude of each brain’s differences by watching a skilled neurosurgeon at work. George Ojemann has a shock of white hair, piercing eyes, and the quiet authority of someone who for decades has watched people live and die in the operating room. He is one of the great neurosurgeons of our time, and he is an expert at a technique called electrical stimulation mapping.
我们可以通过观察一位技艺精湛的神经外科医生进行手术来了解每个人大脑差异之大。乔治·奥杰曼一头银发，目光锐利，举手投足间散发着一种沉稳的权威感，仿佛他几十年来一直在手术室里见证着人们的生死。他是我们这个时代最伟大的神经外科医生之一，也是电刺激映射技术的专家。
Ojemann is hovering over the exposed brain of a man with severe epilepsy. The man’s name is Neil. Ojemann is there to remove some of Neil’s misbehaving brain cells. Before Ojemann takes anything out, however, he has to make a map. To do this, he needs to talk to Neil during surgery, so Neil is fully conscious. Fortunately, the brain has no pain receptors. Ojemann wields a thin silver wire, which sends out small, unobtrusive electrical shocks to anything it touches. If it brushed against your hand, you would feel only a slight tingling sensation. Ojemann gently touches one end of the wire to an area of his patient’s brain. In the book Conversations with Neil’s Brain , he describes what happens next:
奥杰曼正俯身观察一位患有严重癫痫的男子的裸露大脑。这名男子名叫尼尔。奥杰曼此行的目的是切除尼尔大脑中一些异常活跃的脑细胞。然而，在进行任何操作之前，奥杰曼必须先绘制一张脑图。为此，他需要在手术过程中与尼尔交谈，以确保尼尔完全清醒。幸运的是，大脑没有痛觉感受器。奥杰曼挥舞着一根细银线，这根银线会向接触到的物体发出微弱而不易察觉的电击。如果它擦过你的手，你只会感到轻微的刺痛感。奥杰曼轻轻地将银线的一端接触到病人大脑的某个区域。在《与尼尔的大脑对话》一书中，他描述了接下来发生的事情：
“Feel anything?”
“有什么感觉吗？”
“Hey! Someone touched my hand,” Neil volunteers. Neither the anesthesiologist nor I had come anywhere close to Neil’s hand.
“嘿！有人碰了我的手！”尼尔主动说道。麻醉师和我都没有靠近过尼尔的手。
“Which hand?” asks George .
“哪只手？”乔治问。
“My right one, sort of like someone brushed the back side of it. It’s still tingling a little.” The right hand reports to the left side of the brain, and George evidently has located the hand area of [the] somatosensory cortex with the stimulator.
“我的右手，感觉就像有人轻轻拂过它的背面。现在还有点麻麻的。”右手由大脑左侧控制，而乔治显然已经用刺激器找到了体感皮层的手部区域。
Ojemann marks the area by putting a small sterile piece of paper on it. He touches another spot. Neil says he feels something near his right cheek. Another tiny piece of paper. This call and response goes on for hours. Like a neural cartographer, Ojemann is mapping the various functions of his patient’s brain, with special attention paid to the areas close to the epileptic tissue.
奥杰曼用一小张无菌纸片标记出患处。他又触摸了另一个点。尼尔说他感觉右脸颊附近有东西。又是一张小纸片。这种一问一答持续了几个小时。奥杰曼就像一位神经地图绘制师，正在绘制他病人大脑的各种功能图，尤其关注癫痫组织附近的区域。
These are tests of the patient’s motor skills. For reasons not well understood, however, epileptic tissues are often disturbingly adjacent to areas critical for language. So Ojemann also pays close attention to the regions involved in language processing, where words and sentences and grammatical concepts are stored. If the patient is bilingual, he will map critical language areas for both Spanish and English. He applies a paper dot marked S to the regions where Spanish exists, and he applies a small E where English is stored. Ojemann does this painstaking work with every single patient who undergoes this type of surgery. Why? The answer is a stunner. He has to map each individual’s critical function areas because he doesn’t know where they are.
这些是对患者运动技能的测试。然而，由于一些尚不完全清楚的原因，癫痫病灶通常与语言关键区域惊人地相邻。因此，奥杰曼医生也密切关注语言处理相关的区域，也就是存储单词、句子和语法概念的区域。如果患者会说两种语言，他会分别绘制西班牙语和英语的关键语言区域。他会在存储西班牙语的区域贴上一个标有“S”的纸点，在存储英语的区域贴上一个小的“E”。奥杰曼医生对每一位接受此类手术的患者都进行这项细致的工作。为什么？答案令人震惊。他必须绘制每个人的关键功能区域，因为他并不知道这些区域的具体位置。
Ojemann can’t predict the function of very precise areas in advance of the surgery because no two brains are wired identically. Not in terms of structure. Not in terms of function. For example, from nouns to verbs to aspects of grammar, we each store language in different areas, recruiting different regions for different components. Bilingual people don’t even store their Spanish and their English in similar places.
奥杰曼无法在手术前精确预测大脑特定区域的功能，因为每个人的大脑构造都不尽相同。无论是结构还是功能，都存在差异。例如，从名词到动词再到语法知识，我们每个人将语言信息存储在不同的区域，不同的信息成分会调用不同的脑区。即使是双语者，他们存储西班牙语和英语信息的区域也各不相同。
This individuality has fascinated Ojemann for years. He once combined the brain maps for 117 patients he had operated on over the years. Only in one region did he find a spot where most people had a critical language area, and “most” means 79 percent of the patients.
这种个体差异多年来一直令奥杰曼着迷。他曾将多年来接受手术的117名患者的脑图谱进行整合。结果发现，只有在一个区域内，大多数人的大脑都存在一个关键的语言区域，而“大多数人”指的是79%的患者。
Data from electrical stimulation mapping give the most dramatic illustration of the brain’s individuality. But Ojemann also wanted to know how stable these differences were during life, and if any of those differences predicted intellectual competence. He found interesting answers to both questions. First, the brain’s road maps are established very early in life, and they remain stable throughout. Even if a decade or two had passed between surgeries, the brain region recruited to host a critical language area remained the same. Second, Ojemann found that structural differences were associated with performance on a language test (given before surgery). If patients performed poorly on the test, the wiring pattern of their critical language area tended to be widely distributed. It was tightly focused in patients who performed well on the test. Lower scores on the test also predicted that a patient’s critical language area had taken up residence in the superior temporal gyrus, as opposed to another brain region. Again, experience had wired each brain differently, with real-world consequences.
电刺激映射的数据最能生动地展现大脑的个体差异。但奥杰曼还想知道这些差异在人的一生中有多稳定，以及这些差异是否能预测智力水平。他找到了这两个问题的有趣答案。首先，大脑的“路线图”在生命早期就已形成，并且终生保持稳定。即使两次手术之间间隔十年或二十年，大脑中负责关键语言区域的部位也保持不变。其次，奥杰曼发现结构差异与术前语言测试的成绩相关。如果患者测试成绩差，其关键语言区域的连接模式往往分布广泛；而测试成绩好的患者，其关键语言区域的连接模式则高度集中。较低的测试分数也预示着患者的关键语言区域位于颞上回，而非其他脑区。再次证明，经验以不同的方式塑造了每个人的大脑，并产生了现实世界的影响。
More ideas
更多想法
Does it make any sense that most schools expect every child to learn like every other? For example, we expect that kids should be able to read by age 6. Yet students of the same age show a great deal of intellectual variability. Studies show that about 10 percent of students do not have brains sufficiently wired to read at that age. And does it make any sense that most businesses strive to treat each employee the same, especially in a global economy replete with various cultural experiences? As you can guess, I don’t think so. Here are a few ideas for aligning our schools and businesses with the way the brain works .
大多数学校都期望每个孩子学习的方式都一样，这合理吗？例如，我们期望孩子在6岁时就能阅读。然而，同龄学生的智力水平却存在很大差异。研究表明，大约10%的学生大脑发育尚未达到阅读所需的水平。同样，在全球化经济中，文化差异如此之大，大多数企业却力求平等对待每一位员工，这合理吗？正如你所料，我认为并不合理。以下是一些建议，旨在使我们的学校和企业更好地适应大脑的运作方式。
Smaller class size
班级规模较小
All else being equal, it has been known for many years that smaller, more intimate schools create better learning environments than megaplex houses of learning. Smaller is better because a teacher can deeply understand the individual needs of only so many students. If you are a parent, you can look for (and lobby for) schools with smaller classes or a more favorable teacher-student ratio. A college student might consider attending a smaller school. A manager looking to train employees should do it in smaller groups.
在其他条件相同的情况下，多年来人们已经认识到，规模较小、氛围更亲密的学校比大型综合学校更能营造良好的学习环境。规模小的优势在于，教师能够更深入地了解每个学生的个性化需求。如果您是家长，您可以寻找（并争取）班级规模较小或师生比例更合理的学校。大学生也可以考虑就读规模较小的学校。管理者在培训员工时，也应该采用小班授课的方式。
Theory of Mind testing
心智理论测试
As you may recall from the Introduction, Theory of Mind is about as close to mind reading as humans get. It is the ability to understand the interior motivations of someone else and the ability to construct a predictable “theory of how their mind works.” Nearly all of us can do it, but some of us are better at it than others.
正如你在引言中可能已经了解到的，心智理论是人类所能达到的最接近读心术的能力。它指的是理解他人内在动机并构建可预测的“其思维运作方式理论”的能力。几乎所有人都能做到这一点，但有些人比其他人更擅长。
Theory of Mind skills give teachers critical knowledge about their students, a heightened sensitivity for when they are confused, when they are fully engaged, and when they have truly learned what is being taught. I have come to believe that people with advanced Theory of Mind skills possess the single most important ingredient for effectively communicating information. If I’m right, it’s possible that the best teachers possess advanced Theory of Mind skills and the worst teachers don’t.
心智理论技能使教师能够深入了解学生，敏锐地感知学生何时感到困惑、何时全神贯注，以及何时真正掌握了所学内容。我逐渐相信，拥有高级心智理论技能的人掌握了有效沟通信息的最重要要素。如果我的观点正确，那么最优秀的教师可能拥有高级心智理论技能，而最差的教师则可能不具备。
In the future, Theory of Mind tests should be as standard as IQ tests. Schools and other organizations could use the tests to reveal the better teachers. Companies could include Theory of Mind tests as they screen for leaders. People considering careers as teachers or managers could take the tests to help them decide whether they’re a good fit for the role .
未来，心智理论测试应该像智商测试一样成为标准测试。学校和其他机构可以利用这些测试来选拔优秀的教师。公司可以在筛选领导人才时加入心智理论测试。考虑从事教师或管理工作的人员也可以参加这些测试，以帮助他们判断自己是否适合该职位。
Customized classrooms and workplaces
定制化教室和工作场所
As an instructor teaches a class, students inevitably will experience learning gaps. Left untreated, these gaps cause students to fall further behind. Developers of educational apps are using software to determine where a student’s competencies lie and then adaptively tailor exercises for the student in order to fill in any gaps. The effect is greatest when the software is integrated into a school program. In a large classroom, teacher alone or software alone is not as effective. I would like to see more research on this—as would parents and teachers anxious about the infiltration of tablets into classrooms. Studies should include typical and optimized student-teacher ratios.
教师授课过程中，学生难免会遇到学习上的不足。如果不加以弥补，这些不足会导致学生进一步落后。教育应用程序的开发者利用软件来判断学生的现有能力，并根据学生的实际情况调整练习内容，以弥补知识上的差距。当软件融入学校课程体系时，效果最为显著。在大班教学中，仅靠教师或软件的辅助效果并不理想。我希望看到更多相关的研究——家长和教师也同样希望看到更多此类研究，因为他们担心平板电脑会逐渐渗透到课堂中。研究应涵盖典型的师生比例和优化后的师生比例。
Parents could embrace the apps and pay close attention to the effect on their kids. Parents could look for a school adopting the trend of a flipped classroom, where students review the lecture at home before class. Class time is instead spent on homework, and teachers give individualized help as needed. Parents who are financially able might choose schools organized around the idea that children learn different things at different speeds, such as Montessori schools. Students can supplement school classes with free online courses, which allow them to view and review material at their own pace, such as those available through Khan Academy.
家长可以尝试使用这些应用程序，并密切关注它们对孩子的影响。家长可以寻找采用翻转课堂模式的学校，在这种模式下，学生可以在课前在家预习课程内容。课堂时间则用于完成作业，老师会根据需要提供个性化辅导。经济条件允许的家长可以选择一些以儿童学习速度差异为理念的学校，例如蒙特梭利学校。学生还可以利用免费的在线课程来补充课堂学习，例如可汗学院提供的课程，这些课程允许他们按照自己的节奏观看和复习学习材料。
As for employees working at organizations who treat all people the same way, it will be up to you to push for the things you value: the balance of vacation time versus pay, a flexible schedule, the way your role within the company works. If you’re a manager, make a list of the cognitive strengths of your team. Some of your employees may be great at memorizing things. Others may be better at quantitative tasks. Some have good people skills. Some don’t. Assigning work projects based on an employee’s strengths may be critical to your group’s productivity. You may discover you had a Michael Jordan on your team but couldn’t see it because you were only asking him to play baseball.
对于那些在人人平等的组织中工作的员工来说，你需要主动争取你所重视的东西：比如假期与薪酬的平衡、灵活的工作时间安排，以及你在公司中的角色定位。如果你是管理者，不妨列出团队成员的认知优势。有些员工可能记忆力超群，有些则更擅长定量分析，有些拥有良好的人际交往能力，有些则不然。根据员工的优势分配工作任务，对团队的效率至关重要。你可能会发现，你的团队里就有一个迈克尔·乔丹，只是你之前只让他打棒球，而没有发现他的潜力。
Brain Rule # 5
大脑法则#5
Every brain is wired differently.
每个人的大脑构造都不同。
• What you do and learn in life physically changes what your brain looks like—it literally rewires it.
•你在生活中所做和所学的一切都会从物理上改变你的大脑形态——它会从根本上重塑你的大脑。
• The various regions of the brain develop at different rates in different people.
•不同人的大脑各个区域发育速度不同。
• Neurons go through a growth spurt and pruning project during the terrible twos and teen years.
•神经元在可怕的两岁和青少年时期会经历快速生长和修剪过程。
• No two people’s brains store the same information in the same way in the same place.
•每个人的大脑都不会以相同的方式在相同的位置存储相同的信息。
• We have a great number of ways of being intelligent, many of which don’t show up on IQ tests.
•我们有很多种展现智慧的方式，其中很多都无法通过智商测试体现出来。
# ↩
attention
注意力
Brain Rule #6
大脑法则#6
We don’t pay attention to boring things.
我们不关注无聊的事情。
# ↩
IT WAS ABOUT THREE o’clock in the morning when I was startled into sudden consciousness by a small spotlight sweeping across the walls of our living room. In the moonlight, I could see the six-foot frame of a young man in a trench coat, clutching a flashlight and examining the contents of our house. His other hand held something metallic, glinting in the silvery light. As my sleepy brain was immediately and violently aroused, it struck me that my home was about to be robbed by someone younger than me, bigger than me, and in possession of a firearm. Heart pounding, knees shaking, I turned on the lights, went to stand guard outside my children’s room, called the police, and prayed. Miraculously, a police car was in the vicinity and came within a minute of my phone call. This all happened so quickly that my would-be assailant left his getaway car in our driveway, engine still running. He was quickly apprehended.
凌晨三点左右，一束小光束扫过客厅的墙壁，把我从睡梦中惊醒。月光下，我看到一个身高六英尺的年轻男子，穿着风衣，手里拿着手电筒，正在查看家里的东西。他的另一只手拿着什么金属物件，在银色的灯光下闪闪发光。我昏昏欲睡的大脑瞬间清醒过来，意识到有人要闯入我家行窃，而且这个人比我年轻，比我高大，还持有枪支。我心跳加速，双腿发抖，赶紧打开灯，走到孩子们的房间外守卫，打电话报警，然后默默祈祷。奇迹般地，附近就有一辆警车，在我打电话后不到一分钟就赶到了。这一切发生得太快了，那个企图抢劫的人甚至还没来得及发动引擎，就把车停在了我们家的车道上。他很快就被抓住了。
That experience lasted only 45 seconds, but aspects of it are indelibly impressed in my memory, from the outline of the young man’s coat to the shape of his firearm. My brain fully aroused, I will never forget the experience as long as I live.
那次经历虽然只有短短45秒，但其中的一些细节却深深地烙印在我的记忆中，从年轻人的外套轮廓到他手中的枪的形状，都历历在目。我的大脑瞬间被唤醒，我这辈子都不会忘记那次经历。
The more attention the brain pays to a given stimulus, the more elaborately the information will be encoded—that is, learned—and retained. That has implications for employees, parents, and students. Whether you are an eager preschooler or a bored-out-of-your-mind undergrad, better attention always equals better learning. A multitude of studies, both old and new, show that paying attention improves retention of reading material, increases accuracy, and boosts clarity in writing, math, science, and every academic category that has ever been tested.
大脑对特定刺激的关注度越高，信息的编码（即学习）和记忆就越精细。这对员工、家长和学生都至关重要。无论你是求知欲旺盛的学龄前儿童，还是百无聊赖的大学生，注意力越集中，学习效果就越好。大量新旧研究表明，集中注意力能够提高阅读材料的记忆力，提升准确性，并增强写作、数学、科学以及所有其他学科领域的理解能力。
So I ask this question in every college course I teach: “Given a class of medium interest, not too boring and not too exciting, when do you start glancing at the clock, wondering when the class will be over?” There is always some nervous shuffling, a few smiles, then a lot of silence.
所以我会在我教的每一门大学课程中问这个问题：“如果一门课趣味性中等，既不太无聊也不太精彩，你什么时候会开始看表，想着什么时候下课？” 总会有人紧张地挪动脚步，偶尔露出些许微笑，然后便是长时间的沉默。
Eventually someone blurts out, “Ten minutes, Dr. Medina.”
最后有人脱口而出：“还有十分钟，梅迪纳医生。”
“Why 10 minutes?” I inquire.
“为什么是十分钟？”我问道。
“That’s when I start to lose attention. That’s when I begin to wonder when this torment will be over.” The comments are always said in frustration. A college lecture is still about 50 minutes long.
“那时候我就开始注意力不集中了。那时候我就开始想，这种折磨什么时候才能结束。” 这些话总是带着沮丧的语气说出来的。大学讲座通常还是要讲50分钟左右。
Studies confirm my informal inquiry. Noted educator Wilbert McKeachie says in his book Teaching Tips that “typically, attention increases from the beginning of the lecture to 10 minutes into the lecture and decreases after that point.” He’s right. Before the first quarter hour is over in a typical presentation, people usually have checked out. If keeping someone’s interest in a lecture were a business, it would have an 80 percent failure rate. What happens in the brain at the 10-minute mark to cause such trouble? Nobody knows. The brain seems to be making choices according to some stubborn timing pattern, undoubtedly influenced by both culture and gene. This fact suggests a teaching and business imperative: Find a way to get and hold somebody’s attention for 10 minutes, then do it again .
研究证实了我的非正式调查。著名教育家威尔伯特·麦基奇（Wilbert McKeachie）在他的著作《教学技巧》（Teaching Tips）中写道：“通常情况下，听众的注意力会在讲座开始后的前十分钟逐渐集中，之后便开始下降。”他的说法没错。在典型的讲座中，不到一个十五分钟，听众通常就已经走神了。如果把如何吸引听众的注意力算作一项生意，那么它的失败率将高达80%。究竟是什么原因导致听众在讲座进行到十分钟时注意力分散？没有人知道答案。大脑似乎遵循着某种根深蒂固的时间模式，而这种模式无疑受到文化和基因的双重影响。这一事实揭示了一个教学和商业的必然要求：找到一种方法，能够吸引并保持听众十分钟的注意力，然后再次重复这个过程。
But how? To answer that question, we will need to explore some complex pieces of neurological real estate. We are about to investigate the remarkable world of human attention—including what’s going on in our brains when we turn our attention to something, the importance of emotions to attention, and the myth of multitasking.
但究竟该如何实现呢？要回答这个问题，我们需要探索一些复杂的神经系统层面。我们将深入探究人类注意力的奇妙世界——包括当我们把注意力集中到某件事上时，大脑中发生了什么；情绪对注意力的重要性；以及多任务处理的迷思。
Can I have your attention, please?
请各位注意！
While you are reading this paragraph, millions of sensory neurons in your brain are firing simultaneously, all carrying messages, each attempting to grab your attention. Only a few will succeed in breaking through to your awareness, and the rest will be ignored either in part or in full. It is easy for you to alter this balance, effortlessly granting airplay to one of the many messages you were previously ignoring. (While still reading this sentence, can you feel where your elbows are right now?) The messages that do grab your attention are connected to memory, interest, and awareness.
当你阅读这段文字时，你大脑中数百万个感觉神经元同时活跃，它们都在传递信息，试图吸引你的注意力。只有少数信息能够成功进入你的意识，其余的则会被部分或完全忽略。你很容易就能改变这种平衡，毫不费力地让之前被你忽略的众多信息中的一条进入你的视野。（读这句话的时候，你能感觉到你的手肘现在的位置吗？）那些真正吸引你注意力的信息与记忆、兴趣和意识息息相关。
Memory
记忆
What you pay attention to is often profoundly influenced by memory. In everyday life, you use your previous experiences to predict where you should pay attention.
你的注意力往往深受记忆的影响。在日常生活中，你会利用过去的经验来预测应该关注什么。
Different environments create different expectations. This was profoundly illustrated by the scientist Jared Diamond in his book Guns, Germs, and Steel. He describes an adventure traipsing through the New Guinea jungle with native New Guineans. He relates that these natives tend to perform poorly at tasks Westerners have been trained to do since childhood. But they are hardly stupid. They can detect the most subtle changes in the jungle, good for following the trail of a predator or for finding their way back home. They know which insects to leave alone, know where food exists, and can erect and tear down shelters with ease. Diamond, who had never spent time in such places, has no ability to pay attention to these things. Were he to be tested on such tasks, he also would perform poorly.
不同的环境造就不同的期望。科学家贾雷德·戴蒙德在他的著作《枪炮、病菌与钢铁》中对此进行了深刻的阐述。他描述了自己与新几内亚土著居民一起穿越新几内亚丛林的冒险经历。他指出，这些土著居民在西方人从小就接受训练的任务上往往表现不佳。但他们绝非愚笨。他们能够察觉丛林中最细微的变化，这有助于追踪捕食者的踪迹或找到回家的路。他们知道哪些昆虫不该碰，知道哪里有食物，还能轻松地搭建和拆除庇护所。从未在这样的地方生活过的戴蒙德，自然无法注意到这些细节。如果让他接受同样的测试，他的表现也会很糟糕。
Different cultures create different expectations as well. For example, Science magazine notes that “Asians pay more attention to context and to the relationships between focal (foreground) objects and background in their descriptions of visual scenes, whereas Americans mention the focal items with greater frequency.” Such differences can affect how an audience perceives a given business presentation or class lecture.
不同的文化也会带来不同的期望。例如，《科学》杂志指出，“亚洲人在描述视觉场景时更注重语境以及焦点（前景）物体与背景之间的关系，而美国人则更频繁地提及焦点物体本身。” 这些差异会影响听众对特定商务演示或课堂讲座的理解。
Interest
兴趣
If you have an interest in a subject or a person, or something is important to you, you tend to pay more attention to things related to that subject or person. That’s why, if you get a certain breed of dog or buy a certain model of car, you suddenly start noticing the same dog or car everywhere you go. Your brain continuously scans the sensory horizon, constantly assessing events for their potential interest or importance. It gives the more important events extra attention.
如果你对某个事物或人物感兴趣，或者某件事对你很重要，你往往会更加关注与此相关的事物。这就是为什么，如果你养了某种特定品种的狗或买了某种特定型号的汽车，你会突然发现无论走到哪里都能看到同样的狗或同样的车。你的大脑会持续扫描感官范围，不断评估事件的潜在趣味性或重要性，并给予更重要的事件额外的关注。
Can the reverse occur, with attention creating interest? Marketing professionals think so. They have known for years that novel stimuli—the unusual, unpredictable, or distinctive—are powerful ways to harness attention in the service of creating interest. One example is a print ad for Sauza Conmemorativo tequila. It shows a single picture of an old, dirty, bearded man, donning a brimmed hat and smiling broadly, revealing a single tooth. Printed above the mouth is: “This man only has one cavity.” A larger sentence below says: “Life is harsh. Your tequila shouldn’t be.” Flying in the face of most tequila marketing strategies, which consist of scantily clad 20-somethings dancing at a party, the ad is effective at using attention to create interest .
反过来，注意力能否激发兴趣？营销专家认为可以。多年来，他们深知新颖刺激——不寻常的、不可预测的或独特的——是吸引注意力、激发兴趣的有效手段。例如，Sauza Conmemorativo 龙舌兰酒的一则平面广告。广告画面是一位上了年纪、满身污垢、留着胡须的男士，他戴着宽边帽，咧嘴大笑，露出一颗牙齿。嘴巴上方印着：“这位男士只有一颗蛀牙。”下方则是一句更大的句子：“生活不易，但你的龙舌兰酒不应该如此。”这则广告与大多数龙舌兰酒的营销策略截然不同——后者通常以衣着暴露的二十多岁年轻人派对跳舞的画面为卖点——它有效地利用注意力激发了人们的兴趣。
Awareness
意识
Of course, we must be aware of something for it to grab our attention. A strange illustration of this comes from neurologist Oliver Sacks. He describes a wonderful older woman in his care: intelligent, articulate, and gifted with a sense of humor. She suffered a massive stroke in the back region of her brain that left her with a most unusual deficit: She could no longer pay attention to anything that was to her left. She could pick up objects only in the right half of her visual field. She could put lipstick only on the right half of her face. She ate only from the right half of her plate. This caused her to complain to the hospital nursing staff that her portions were too small! Only when the plate was turned and the food entered her right visual field could she pay any attention to it and have her fill.
当然，我们必须先意识到某件事的存在，它才会吸引我们的注意力。神经学家奥利弗·萨克斯举了一个奇特的例子来说明这一点。他描述了一位他照料过的很棒的老妇人：聪明、口齿伶俐、极富幽默感。她大脑后部突发严重中风，导致她出现了一种非常罕见的缺陷：她无法再关注左侧的事物。她只能拿起视野右侧的物体。她只能在右半边脸上涂口红。她只能吃盘子右侧的食物。这导致她向医院的护士抱怨说她的饭量太少了！只有当盘子被翻转，食物进入她的右侧视野时，她才能注意到食物并吃饱。
How could this be? The brain can be divided roughly into two hemispheres of unequal function, and patients can get strokes in either. The hemispheres contain separate “spotlights” for visual attention. The left hemisphere’s spotlight is small, capable of paying attention only to items on the right side of the visual field. The right hemisphere, however, has a global spotlight. According to Marsel Mesulam of Northwestern University, who made these discoveries, getting a stroke on your left side is much less catastrophic because your right side can pitch in under duress to aid vision.
这怎么可能呢？大脑大致可以分为功能不等的两个半球，患者任何一个半球都可能发生中风。这两个半球各自拥有独立的视觉注意力“聚光灯”。左半球的“聚光灯”范围较小，只能关注视野右侧的物体。而右半球则拥有全局性的“聚光灯”。据西北大学的马塞尔·梅苏拉姆（Marsel Mesulam）介绍，左半球中风的后果远没有右半球严重，因为在紧急情况下，右半球可以辅助视觉功能。
Of course, sight is only one stimulus to which the brain is capable of paying attention. Just let a bad smell into the room for a moment, make a loud noise, touch someone’s arm, or taste an unexpectedly bitter bite of food, and people easily will shift attention. We also pay close attention to our psychological interiors, mulling over internal events and feelings again and again with complete focus, with no obvious external sensory stimulation.
当然，视觉只是大脑能够关注的刺激之一。哪怕只是让难闻的气味短暂地进入房间，发出巨大的噪音，触碰别人的手臂，或者尝到一口意想不到的苦味食物，人们的注意力都会轻易转移。我们也会密切关注自己的内心世界，一遍又一遍地全神贯注地思考内部的事件和感受，即使没有明显的外部感官刺激。
You can imagine how tough it is to research such an ephemeral concept. For one thing, we don’t know the neural location of consciousness, loosely defined as that part of the mind where awareness resides. The best data suggest that several systems are scattered throughout the brain.
你可以想象研究这样一个转瞬即逝的概念有多么困难。首先，我们并不清楚意识在大脑中的具体位置，意识可以粗略地定义为意识所在的那个脑区。目前最好的数据表明，大脑中存在多个意识系统。
How the brain pays attention
大脑如何集中注意力
What’s going on in our heads when we turn our attention to something? Thirty years ago, a scientist by the name of Michael Posner derived a theory that remains popular today. Posner started his research career in physics, joining the Boeing Aircraft Company soon out of college. His first major research contribution was to figure out how to make jet-engine noise less annoying to passengers riding in commercial airplanes. You can thank your relatively quiet airborne ride, even if the screaming turbine is only a few feet from your eardrums, in part on Posner’s first research efforts. His work on planes eventually led him to wonder how the brain processes information of any kind. This led him to a doctorate in research and to a powerful idea that’s sometimes jokingly referred to as the Trinity Model. Posner hypothesized that we pay attention to things using three separable but fully integrated networks of neural circuitry in the brain. I’ll use a simple story to illustrate his model.
当我们把注意力集中在某件事上时，我们的大脑里究竟在想些什么？三十年前，一位名叫迈克尔·波斯纳的科学家提出了一个至今仍然广为流传的理论。波斯纳大学毕业后不久便加入了波音飞机公司，开始了他在物理学领域的研究生涯。他的第一个重大研究贡献是找到了降低商用飞机喷气式发动机噪音的方法，从而减轻了乘客的不适感。即使轰鸣的涡轮发动机离你的耳膜只有几英尺远，你现在相对安静的飞行体验也部分归功于波斯纳早期的研究成果。他对飞机的研究最终让他开始思考大脑是如何处理各种信息的。这促使他攻读了博士学位，并提出了一个有时被戏称为“三位一体模型”的强大理论。波斯纳假设，我们利用大脑中三个独立但又完全整合的神经回路网络来关注事物。我将用一个简单的故事来阐释他的模型。
One pleasant Saturday morning, my wife and I were sitting on our outdoor deck, watching a robin drink from our birdbath, when all of a sudden we heard a loud “swoosh” above our heads. Looking up, we caught the shadow of a red-tailed hawk, dropping like a thunderbolt from its perch in a nearby tree, grabbing the helpless robin by the throat. As the raptor swooped by us, not three feet away, blood from the robin splattered on our table. What started as a leisurely repast ended as a violent reminder of the savagery of the real world. We were stunned into silence.
一个阳光明媚的周六早晨，我和妻子坐在户外露台上，看着一只知更鸟在鸟浴盆里喝水。突然，我们听到头顶传来一声响亮的“嗖”的一声。抬头一看，只见一只红尾鹰的影子像闪电般从附近树上的栖木上俯冲而下，一口咬住了那只无助的知更鸟的喉咙。猛禽从我们身边掠过，距离不到三英尺，知更鸟的鲜血溅到了我们的桌子上。原本悠闲的用餐时光，却变成了残酷现实的暴力提醒。我们震惊得说不出话来。
In Posner’s model, the brain’s first system functions much like the two-part job of a museum security officer: surveillance and alert. He called it the Alerting or Arousal Network. It monitors the sensory environment for any unusual activities. This is the general level of attention our brains are paying to our world, a condition termed “intrinsic alertness.” My wife and I were using this network as we sipped our coffee, watching the robin. If the system detects something unusual, such as the hawk’s swoosh, it can sound an alarm heard brain-wide. That’s when intrinsic alertness transforms into specific attention, called phasic alertness.
在波斯纳的模型中，大脑的第一系统功能很像博物馆保安的双重职责：监视和警觉。他称之为警觉或唤醒网络。它监控感官环境，寻找任何异常活动。这是我们大脑对周围世界投入的一般注意力，这种状态被称为“内在警觉”。我和妻子一边啜饮咖啡，一边观察知更鸟，当时我们就在使用这个网络。如果系统检测到异常情况，例如老鹰的掠过，它就会发出全脑都能听到的警报。这时，内在警觉就会转化为特定的注意力，称为阶段性警觉。
After the alarm sounds, we orient ourselves to the attending stimulus, activating the second network: the Orienting Network. We may turn our heads toward the stimulus, perk up our ears, perhaps move toward (or away) from something. It’s why both my wife and I immediately lifted our heads away from the robin, attending to the growing shadow of the hawk. The purpose is to gain more information about the stimulus, allowing the brain to decide what to do.
警报响起后，我们会将注意力集中到刺激物上，激活第二个神经网络：定向网络。我们可能会转头看向刺激物，竖起耳朵，或者朝着（或远离）某个东西移动。这就是为什么我和妻子立刻将头从知更鸟身上移开，转而关注鹰的影子越来越大的原因。这样做的目的是为了获取更多关于刺激物的信息，以便大脑决定下一步该怎么做。
The third system, the Executive Network, controls what action we take next. Actions may include setting priorities, planning on the fly, controlling impulses, weighing the consequences of our actions, or shifting attention. For my wife and me, it was stunned silence, until one of us moved to clean off the blood.
第三个系统，执行网络，控制着我们下一步的行动。这些行动可能包括设定优先级、临时计划、控制冲动、权衡行动后果或转移注意力。我和妻子当时都震惊得说不出话来，直到我们其中一人动身去清理血迹。
So we have the ability to detect a new stimulus, the ability to turn toward it, and the ability to decide what to do based on its nature. Posner’s model offered testable predictions about brain function and attention, leading to neurological discoveries that would fill volumes. Hundreds of behavioral characteristics have since been discovered as well. We’ll focus on four that have considerable practical potential: emotions, meaning, multitasking, and timing.
因此，我们能够感知新的刺激，能够转向它，并能够根据其性质决定采取何种行动。波斯纳的模型对大脑功能和注意力提出了可验证的预测，由此引发了神经学领域的诸多发现，这些发现足以写成厚厚的书籍。此后，人们又发现了数百种行为特征。我们将重点关注其中四种具有巨大实际应用潜力的特征：情绪、意义、多任务处理和时间感知。
Emotions get our attention
情绪会引起我们的注意
As the television advertisement opens, we see two men talking in a car. They are having a mildly heated discussion about one of them overusing the word “like” in conversation. As the argument continues, we notice out the passenger window another car barreling toward the men. It smashes into them. There are screams, sounds of shattering glass, quick-cut shots showing the men bouncing in the car, twisted metal. The final shot shows the men standing, in disbelief, outside their wrecked Volkswagen Passat. In a twist on a well-known expletive, these words flash on the screen: “Safe Happens.” The spot ends with a picture of another Passat, this one intact and complete with its five-star side-crash safety rating. It is a memorable, even disturbing, 30-second spot.
电视广告开场，我们看到两个男人在车里交谈。他们正就其中一人过度使用“like”这个词而进行着略显激烈的争论。争论持续进行，我们透过副驾驶的车窗看到另一辆车疾驰而来，猛烈撞击。尖叫声、玻璃破碎声、快速剪辑的镜头展现了车内两人被撞得弹跳的画面以及扭曲变形的金属。最后一个镜头是两个男人难以置信地站在他们损毁的大众帕萨特车外。屏幕上闪现出一句改编自一句著名脏话的文字：“安全无虞”。广告结尾，画面定格在另一辆完好无损的帕萨特上，这辆车还保留着五星级侧面碰撞安全评级。这是一则令人印象深刻，甚至有些令人不安的30秒广告。
That’s because it’s charged with emotion. Emotionally charged events are better remembered—for longer, and with more accuracy—than neutral events. While this idea may seem intuitively obvious, it’s frustrating to demonstrate scientifically because the research community is still debating exactly what an emotion is. What we can say for sure is that when your brain detects an emotionally charged event, your amygdala (a part of your brain that helps create and maintain emotions) releases the chemical dopamine into your system. Dopamine greatly aids memory and information processing. You can think of it like a Post-it note that reads “Remember this!” Getting one’s brain to put a chemical Post-it note on a given piece of information means that information is going to be more robustly processed. It is what every teacher, parent, and ad executive wants.
这是因为情绪被赋予了意义。与中性事件相比，带有情绪色彩的事件更容易被记住——记忆更持久，也更准确。虽然这个观点看似显而易见，但要用科学方法证明却并非易事，因为研究界仍在争论情绪究竟是什么。我们可以肯定的是，当大脑检测到带有情绪色彩的事件时，杏仁核（大脑中负责产生和维持情绪的部分）会释放多巴胺这种化学物质。多巴胺极大地促进了记忆和信息处理。你可以把它想象成一张写着“记住这个！”的便签。让大脑在某个信息上贴上这种化学物质便签，意味着该信息将被更有效地处理。这正是每位教师、家长和广告主管都梦寐以求的。
Certain events have an emotional charge only for specific people. For example, my brain pays a great deal of attention if someone is banging pots and pans. When my mother got angry (which was rare), she went to the kitchen, washing LOUDLY any dishes she discovered in the sink. And if there were pots and pans, she deliberately would crash them together as she put them away. This noise served to announce to the entire household (if not the city block) her displeasure at something. To this day, whenever I hear loudly clanging pots and pans, I experience an emotional stimulus—a fleeting sense of “You’re in trouble now!” My wife, whose mother never displayed anger in this fashion, does not associate anything emotional with the noise of pots and pans. It’s a John-specific stimulus .
某些事件只会对特定的人产生特定的情感反应。例如，如果有人敲打锅碗瓢盆，我的大脑会格外关注。我母亲生气的时候（这种情况很少），她会冲进厨房，大声地清洗水槽里找到的所有碗碟。如果水槽里有锅碗瓢盆，她会在收拾的时候故意把它们撞在一起。这种噪音仿佛在向全家人（甚至整个街区）宣告她对某件事的不满。直到今天，每当我听到锅碗瓢盆的叮当声，我都会感到一种情绪上的刺激——一种转瞬即逝的“你这下闯祸了！”的感觉。我的妻子，她的母亲从未以这种方式表达过愤怒，所以她不会把锅碗瓢盆的叮当声与任何情绪联系起来。这是一种只有约翰才能感受到的刺激。
But certain emotionally charged events are universal, capable of capturing the attention of all of us. Such stimuli come directly from our evolutionary heritage, so they hold the greatest potential for use in teaching and business. They are strictly related to survival concerns. Regardless of who you are, the brain pays a great deal of attention to several questions:
但某些能引发强烈情绪的事件是普遍存在的，能够吸引我们所有人的注意力。这类刺激直接源于我们的进化本能，因此在教学和商业领域具有最大的应用潜力。它们与生存息息相关。无论你是谁，大脑都会高度关注以下几个问题：
“Can I eat it? Will it eat me?”
“我可以吃它吗？它会吃我吗？”
“Can I mate with it? Will it mate with me?”
“我可以和它交配吗？它会和我交配吗？”
“Have I seen it before?”
“我以前见过吗？”
Any of our ancestors who didn’t remember threatening experiences thoroughly or acquire food adequately would not live long enough to pass on his or her genes. So the human brain has many dedicated systems exquisitely tuned to the perception of threat (that’s why the robbery story grabbed your attention); to reproductive opportunity (sex sells); and to patterns (we constantly assess our environment for similarities, and we tend to remember things if we think we have seen them before).
我们的祖先如果不能彻底记住威胁性的经历或无法获得充足的食物，就无法活到足以将基因传递下去的年纪。因此，人类大脑拥有许多专门的系统，这些系统极其精细地适应于感知威胁（这就是为什么抢劫的故事会吸引你的注意力）；适应于繁殖机会（性能够吸引眼球）；以及适应于模式（我们会不断评估周围环境的相似之处，如果我们认为以前见过某些东西，就往往会记住它们）。
One of the best TV spots ever made employed all three of those elements in an ever-increasing spiral. Steve Hayden produced the commercial, introducing the Apple computer in 1984. It won every major advertising award that year and set a standard for Super Bowl ads. The commercial opens onto a bluish auditorium filled with robot-like men all dressed alike.
