Actually, I saw eight people die. The son of a career Air Force official, I was very used to seeing military airplanes in the sky. But I looked up one afternoon to see a cargo plane do something I had never seen before or since. It was falling from the sky, locked in a dead man’s spiral. It hit the ground less than a thousand feet from where I stood, and I felt both the shock wave and the heat of the explosion. There are two things I could have done with this information. I could have kept it to myself, or I could have told the world. I chose the latter. After immediately rushing home to tell my parents, I called some of my friends. We met for sodas and began talking about what had just happened. The sounds of the engine cutting out. Our surprise. Our fear. As horrible as the accident was, we talked about it so much in the next week that the subject got tiresome. One of my teachers actually forbade us from bringing it up during class time, threatening to make T-shirts saying, “You’ve done enough talking.”
事实上，我亲眼目睹了八条人命。我父亲是空军的一名资深军官，所以我对天空中的军用飞机早已习以为常。但一天下午，我抬头看到一架货机做出了我前所未见、后也再未见过的景象：它从空中坠落，陷入了死亡螺旋。它坠落的地点离我不到一千英尺，我真切地感受到了冲击波和爆炸的灼热。当时我有两种选择：要么将此事藏在心底，要么公之于众。我选择了后者。我立刻赶回家告诉父母，然后给几个朋友打了电话。我们聚在一起喝汽水，开始谈论刚才发生的一切。引擎熄火的声音。我们的震惊。我们的恐惧。尽管事故惨烈，但在接下来的一个星期里，我们反复谈论此事，以至于我们都感到厌烦了。我的一位老师甚至禁止我们在课堂上谈论此事，还威胁说要印制T恤，上面写着：“你们说得够多了。”
Why do I still remember the details of this story? Because of my eagerness to yap about the experience. The gabfest after the accident forced a consistent reexposure to the basic facts, followed by a detailed elaboration of our impressions. This is called elaborative rehearsal, and it’s the type of repetition most effective for the most robust retrieval. A great deal of research shows that thinking or talking about an event immediately after it has occurred enhances memory for that event, even when accounting for differences in type of memory. This is one of the reasons why it is so critical to have a witness recall information as soon as is humanely possible after a crime.
为什么我至今仍记得这件事的细节？因为我急于讲述这段经历。事故发生后的喋喋不休迫使我反复回忆基本事实，随后又详细阐述了我们的感受。这被称为精细复述，也是最有效的记忆提取方式。大量研究表明，即使考虑到记忆类型的差异，在事件发生后立即思考或谈论该事件也能增强对该事件的记忆。这也是为什么让目击者在犯罪发生后尽快回忆信息至关重要的原因之一。
The timing of the repetitions is a key component. This was demonstrated by German researcher Hermann Ebbinghaus more than 100 years ago. He showed that repeated exposure to information in spaced intervals provides the most powerful way to fix memory into the brain .
重复的时机至关重要。德国研究员赫尔曼·艾宾浩斯早在100多年前就证明了这一点。他指出，以一定的间隔重复接触信息是巩固大脑记忆的最有效方法。
Repetitions must be spaced out, not crammed in
重复次数必须间隔安排，而不是密集进行。
Much like concrete, memory takes an almost ridiculous amount of time to settle into its permanent form. While it is hardening, it is maddeningly subject to amendment. As we discussed, new information can reshape or wear away previously existing memory traces. Such interference is likely to occur when we encounter an overdose of information without breaks, much like what happens in most conferences and classrooms. But this interference doesn’t occur if the information is built up slowly, repeated in deliberately spaced cycles. Repetition cycles add information to our knowledge base, rather than disturbing the resident tenants.
就像混凝土一样，记忆需要相当长的时间才能最终定型。在定型过程中，它却又令人抓狂地容易被修改。正如我们之前讨论的，新的信息会重塑或抹去先前存在的记忆痕迹。当我们不间断地接收大量信息时，这种干扰就很容易发生，就像大多数会议和课堂上的情况一样。但如果信息是缓慢积累的，以刻意间隔的循环方式重复出现，就不会出现这种干扰。重复循环会为我们的知识库添加信息，而不是干扰已有的知识。
If scientists want to know whether you are retrieving a vivid memory, they don’t have to ask you. They can simply look in their fMRI machine and see whether your left inferior prefrontal cortex is active. Scientist Anthony Wagner used this fact to study two groups of students given a list of words to memorize. The first group was shown the words via mass repetition, reminiscent of students cramming for an exam. The second group was shown the words in spaced intervals over a longer period of time. The second group recalled the list of words with much more accuracy, with more activity in the cortex showing up on the fMRI (that’s “functional magnetic resonance imaging) machine. Based on these results, Harvard psychology professor Dan Schacter wrote: “[I]f you want to study for a test you will be taking in a week’s time, and are able to go through the material 10 times, it is better to space out the 10 repetitions during the week than to squeeze them all together.”
如果科学家想知道你是否能清晰地回忆起某个记忆，他们无需询问你。他们只需通过功能磁共振成像（fMRI）仪观察你左侧下前额叶皮层的活跃程度即可。科学家安东尼·瓦格纳利用这一原理，研究了两组学生，并给他们布置了一项单词记忆任务。第一组学生通过大量重复的方式学习单词，类似于考前突击。第二组学生则在更长的时间内，以间隔的方式学习单词。结果显示，第二组学生对单词的记忆准确率更高，fMRI（即“功能磁共振成像”）仪也显示出他们大脑皮层活动更为活跃。基于这些结果，哈佛大学心理学教授丹·沙克特写道：“如果你想为一周后的考试做准备，并且能够复习10遍，那么最好将这10遍复习分散在一周内进行，而不是集中进行。”
Scientists aren’t yet sure which time intervals supply all the magic. But taken together, the relationship between repetition and memory is clear. Deliberately re-expose yourself to information if you want to retrieve it later. Deliberately re-expose yourself to information more elaborately if you want to remember more of the details. Deliberately reexpose yourself to the information more elaborately and in fixed, spaced intervals if you want the retrieval to be as vivid as possible.
科学家们目前还不确定哪些时间间隔发挥了所有神奇的作用。但总的来说，重复与记忆之间的关系是清晰的。如果你想在以后回忆起某个信息，就应该有意识地重新接触它。如果你想记住更多细节，就应该有意识地更详细地重新接触它。如果你想让回忆尽可能生动，就应该有意识地以固定的时间间隔，更详细地重新接触它。
Memory consolidation goes fast, then slow
记忆巩固过程先快后慢。
I was dating somebody else when I first met Kari—and so was she. But I did not forget Kari. She is a physically beautiful, talented, Emmy-nominated composer, and one of the nicest people I have ever met. When we both became “available” six months later, I immediately asked her out. We had a great time, and I began thinking about her more and more. Turns out she was feeling the same. Soon we were seeing each other regularly. After two months, it got so that every time we met, my heart would pound, my stomach would flip-flop, and I’d get sweaty palms. Eventually I didn’t even have to see her to raise my pulse. Just a picture would do, or a whiff of her perfume, or … just music ! Even a fleeting thought was enough to send me into hours of rapture. I knew I was falling in love.
我第一次见到卡莉的时候，我们俩都有男朋友。但我并没有忘记卡莉。她是一位外表美丽、才华横溢、获得艾美奖提名的作曲家，也是我见过最善良的人之一。六个月后，当我们都恢复单身时，我立刻约她出去。我们相处得很愉快，我对她的思念也与日俱增。结果发现她也有同样的感觉。很快，我们就开始频繁见面。两个月后，每次见面，我的心都会怦怦直跳，胃里翻江倒海，手心也会冒汗。最终，我甚至不需要见到她就能心跳加速。一张照片，一缕她的香水味，或者……仅仅是她的音乐！哪怕只是一闪而过的念头，也足以让我沉浸在幸福的海洋中数小时。我知道，我恋爱了。
What was happening to effect such change? With increased exposure to this wonderful woman, I became increasingly sensitive to her presence, needing increasingly smaller “input” cues (perfume, for heaven’s sake?) to elicit increasingly stronger “output” responses. The effect has been long-lasting, with a tenure of more than three decades. Leaving the whys of the heart to poets and psychiatrists, the idea that increasingly limited exposures can result in increasingly stronger responses lies at the heart of how neurons learn things. Only it’s not called romance; it’s called long-term potentiation. LTP shows us how timed repetition works at the level of the neuron.
究竟是什么导致了这种变化？随着与这位美好女性接触的增多，我对她的存在变得越来越敏感，只需要越来越少的“输入”线索（天哪，竟然是香水味！）就能引发越来越强烈的“输出”反应。这种效应持续了三十多年。至于爱情的缘由，就留给诗人或精神科医生去探究吧。但这种“越来越少的接触就能引发越来越强烈的反应”的现象，正是神经元学习的核心。只不过，这不叫浪漫，而是叫长时程增强（LTP）。LTP 向我们展示了定时重复在神经元层面是如何运作的。
Fast consolidation
快速整合
To describe LTP, we need to leave the world of behavior and drop down to the more intimate world of cell and molecule. Let’s return to our tiny submarine in the hippocampus, where we were floating between two connected neurons. I will call the presynaptic neuron the “teacher” and the postsynaptic neuron the “student.” The goal of the teacher neuron is to pass on information, electrical in nature, to the student cell. The teacher neuron, after receiving some stimulus, cracks off an electrical signal to its student. For a short period of time, the student becomes stimulated and fires excitedly in response. The synaptic interaction between the two is said to be temporarily “strengthened.” This phenomenon is termed early LTP.
要描述长时程增强（LTP），我们需要暂时离开行为层面，深入到细胞和分子层面。让我们回到海马体中那艘小小的潜艇，它正漂浮在两个相连的神经元之间。我将突触前神经元称为“老师”，突触后神经元称为“学生”。老师神经元的目标是将信息（电信号）传递给学生神经元。老师神经元在接收到刺激后，会向学生神经元发出电信号。在短时间内，学生神经元受到刺激，兴奋地做出反应。这两个神经元之间的突触相互作用被暂时“增强”。这种现象被称为早期长时程增强（early LTP）。
Unfortunately, the excitement lasts only for an hour or two. If the student neuron does not get the same information from the teacher within about 90 minutes, the student neuron’s level of excitement will vanish. The cell will literally reset itself to zero and act as if nothing happened, ready for any other signal that might come its way. But if the information is repeatedly pulsed in discretely timed intervals—the timing for cells in a petri dish is three pulses, with about 10 minutes between each—the relationship between the teacher neuron and the student neuron begins to change. Much like my relationship with Kari after a few dates, increasingly smaller and smaller inputs from the teacher are required to elicit increasingly stronger and stronger outputs from the student. This response is termed late LTP.
可惜的是，这种兴奋状态只能持续一两个小时。如果学生神经元在大约90分钟内没有从老师那里接收到相同的信息，它的兴奋程度就会消失。细胞会彻底重置，仿佛什么都没发生过一样，随时准备接收任何其他信号。但是，如果信息以离散的时间间隔反复脉冲式地传递——培养皿中的细胞通常以三次脉冲的形式传递，每次间隔约10分钟——老师神经元和学生神经元之间的关系就会开始发生变化。就像我和卡莉几次约会后的关系一样，老师需要越来越小的输入才能引发学生越来越强的输出。这种反应被称为晚期长时程增强（LTP）。
When two neurons make it from early LTP to late LTP, you get synaptic consolidation. Scientists also call it fast consolidation, because it happens within minutes or hours. If it happens, that is. Any manipulation—behavioral, pharmacological, or genetic—that interferes with any part of this developing relationship will entirely block memory formation.
当两个神经元从早期长时程增强（LTP）发展到晚期LTP时，就会发生突触巩固。科学家也称之为快速巩固，因为它发生在几分钟或几小时内。当然，前提是它能够成功。任何干扰这种发展中关系的任何环节的操作——无论是行为上的、药理上的还是基因上的——都会完全阻断记忆的形成。
Slow consolidation
缓慢整合
Two neurons alone don’t allow us to form long-term memories. It’s the fact that many neurons connect the hippocampus to the cortex, marrying the two in a chatty relationship. The cortex is that paper-thin layer of surface tissue that’s about the size of a baby blanket when unfurled. The cortex is composed of six discrete layers of neural cells. These cells process signals originating from many parts of the body, including those lassoed by your sense organs. The cortex is connected to the deeper parts of the brain—including the hippocampus—by a hopelessly incomprehensible thicket of neural connections, like a complex root system. Communication between the cortex and hippocampus (lots of synaptic consolidation) is what allows the creation of long-term memories. This system consolidation takes a long time, so scientists call it slow consolidation.
仅仅两个神经元不足以让我们形成长期记忆。正是由于许多神经元将海马体与大脑皮层连接起来，使两者之间形成了一种密切的联系。大脑皮层是一层薄如纸的表面组织，展开后大约只有婴儿毯那么大。它由六层独立的神经细胞组成。这些细胞处理来自身体各个部位的信号，包括感觉器官接收到的信号。大脑皮层通过错综复杂的神经连接与大脑更深层的部分（包括海马体）相连，就像一个复杂的根系。大脑皮层和海马体之间的交流（大量的突触巩固）使得长期记忆的形成成为可能。这种系统巩固需要很长时间，因此科学家称之为慢速巩固。
Remember H.M., the man who couldn’t recognize his own face in the mirror after his hippocampus was surgically removed? H.M. could meet you twice in two hours, with absolutely no recollection of the first meeting. He doesn’t remember ever meeting a researcher who has worked with him for decades. This inability to encode information for long-term storage is called anterograde amnesia. H.M. also had retrograde amnesia, a loss of memory of the past. You could ask H.M. about an event that occurred three years before his surgery. No memory. Seven years before his surgery. No memory. If that’s all you knew about H.M, you might conclude that his hippocampal loss created a complete memory meltdown. But you’d be wrong.
还记得H.M.吗？他做了海马体切除手术后，竟然无法在镜子里认出自己的脸。H.M.可能在两小时内与你见面两次，却完全不记得第一次见面的内容。他甚至不记得见过一位与他共事几十年的研究人员。这种无法将信息编码以进行长期存储的现象被称为顺行性遗忘症。H.M.还患有逆行性遗忘症，即对过去的记忆丧失。你可以问H.M.手术前三年发生的一件事。他记不起来了。七年前发生的一件事？他也记不起来了。如果你对H.M.的了解仅限于此，你可能会认为他的海马体切除导致了彻底的记忆崩溃。但你错了。
If you asked H.M. about the very distant past, say early childhood, he would display a perfectly normal recollection, just as you and I might. He can remember his family, where he lived, details of various events, and so on. This is a conversation with the researcher who studied him for many years:
如果你问H.M.关于非常遥远的过去，比如他的童年早期，他会展现出完全正常的记忆力，就像你我一样。他能记住他的家人、他住的地方、各种事件的细节等等。以下是与一位研究他多年的研究人员的对话：
Researcher: Can you remember any particular event that was special—like a holiday, Christmas, birthday, Easter?
研究员：您还记得什么特别的事件吗？比如节日、圣诞节、生日、复活节？
H.M.: There I have an argument with myself about Christmastime.
H.M.：我当时正在和自己争论圣诞节的事。
Researcher: What about Christmas ?
研究员：那圣诞节呢？
H.M.: Well, ’cause my daddy was from the South, and he didn’t celebrate down there like they do up here—in the North. Like they don’t have the trees or anything like that. And uh, but he came North even though he was born down Louisiana. And I know the name of the town he was born in.
H.M.：嗯，因为我爸爸是南方人，他那边不像北方这边那样庆祝节日。他们那儿没有圣诞树什么的。而且，他虽然出生在路易斯安那州，但后来还是去了北方。我知道他出生的那个小镇叫什么名字。
H.M.’s childhood memory is intact starting about 11 years before his surgery. How is that possible? If the hippocampus is involved in all memory formation, removing the hippocampus should wipe the memory clean. But it doesn’t. The hippocampus is relevant to memory formation for about 11 years after an event is recruited for long-term storage. After that, the memory somehow makes it to another region, one not affected by H.M.’s brain losses. Here’s the interaction between the cortex and hippocampus that allows us to form long-term memories, and the reason H.M. still remembers Christmas:
H.M.的童年记忆在他手术前大约11年就已完好无损。这怎么可能呢？如果海马体参与所有记忆的形成，那么切除海马体应该会抹去所有记忆。但事实并非如此。在事件被纳入长期存储后，海马体在大约11年的时间里仍然与记忆的形成相关。之后，记忆会以某种方式转移到另一个区域，一个不受H.M.脑损伤影响的区域。以下是大脑皮层和海马体之间的相互作用，正是这种相互作用使我们能够形成长期记忆，也是H.M.至今仍记得圣诞节的原因：
1) The cortex receives sensory information and sends it to the hippocampus. They chat about it—a lot. Long after the initial stimulus has faded away, the hippocampus and the relevant cortical neurons are still yapping. As you sleep, the hippocampus is busy feeding signals back to the cortex, replaying a memory over and over again. The importance of sleep to learning is described in the Sleep chapter.
1）大脑皮层接收感觉信息并将其发送到海马体。它们会就这些信息进行大量的交流。即使最初的刺激早已消退，海马体和相关的皮层神经元仍然在不停地传递信息。当你睡觉时，海马体也在忙着将信号反馈给大脑皮层，一遍又一遍地重现记忆。睡眠对学习的重要性将在“睡眠”章节中进行阐述。
2) While the hippocampus and cortex are actively engaged, any memory they mediate is labile and subject to amendment.
2）当海马体和皮层积极参与时，它们介导的任何记忆都是不稳定的，并且容易被修改。
3) After a period of time, the hippocampus will let go, effectively terminating the relationship with the cortex. The cortex is left holding the memory of the event. The hippocampus files for cellular separation only if the memory has become durable and fixed (consolidated) in the cortex. This process is at the heart of system consolidation, and it involves a complex reorganization of the brain regions supporting a particular memory trace.
3）一段时间后，海马体将脱离皮层，从而有效地终止与皮层的联系。皮层则保留了事件的记忆。只有当记忆在皮层中变得持久且固定（巩固）时，海马体才会申请细胞分离。这一过程是系统巩固的核心，它涉及支持特定记忆痕迹的大脑区域的复杂重组。
How long does it take before the hippocampus lets go of its relationship with the cortex? In other words, how long does it take for a piece of information, once recruited for long-term storage, to become completely stable? Hours? Days? Months? The answer surprises nearly everybody who hears it for the first time. It can take years .
海马体需要多久才能完全脱离与大脑皮层的联系？换句话说，一条信息一旦被纳入长期存储，需要多久才能完全稳定下来？几个小时？几天？几个月？答案几乎会让所有第一次听到的人都感到惊讶。这可能需要数年时间。
That’s what the case of H.M., and patients like him, tell us. System consolidation, the process of transforming a short-term memory into a long-term one, can take years to complete. During that time, the memory is not stable.
H.M.的案例以及与他类似的患者就告诉我们这一点。系统巩固，也就是将短期记忆转化为长期记忆的过程，可能需要数年才能完成。在此期间，记忆并不稳定。
As with short-term memories, long-term memories are stored in the same places that initially processed the stimulus. Retrieving a long-term memory 10 years later may simply be an attempt to reconstruct the initial moments of learning, when the memory was only a few milliseconds old!
与短期记忆一样，长期记忆也存储在最初处理刺激的同一区域。10年后提取长期记忆可能仅仅是对最初学习时刻的尝试，那时记忆仅仅存在了几毫秒！
Forgetting
遗忘
We’ve talked about encoding, storage, and retrieval, the first three steps of declarative memory. The last step is forgetting. Forgetting plays a vital role in our ability to function for a deceptively simple reason. Forgetting allows us to prioritize. Anything irrelevant to our survival will take up wasteful cognitive space if we assign it the same priority as events critical to our survival. So we don’t. At least, most of us don’t.
我们已经讨论了编码、存储和提取，这是陈述性记忆的前三个步骤。最后一步是遗忘。遗忘在我们正常运转中扮演着至关重要的角色，原因看似简单。遗忘使我们能够分清轻重缓急。如果我们把与生存无关的事情和生存至关重要的事情赋予相同的优先级，那么这些无关的事情就会占用宝贵的认知空间。所以我们不会这样做。至少，我们大多数人不会。
Solomon Shereshevskii, a Russian journalist born in 1886, seemed to have a virtually unlimited memory. Scientists would give him a list of things to memorize, usually combinations of numbers and letters, and then test his recall. Shereshevskii needed only three or four seconds to “visualize” (his words) each item. Then he could repeat the lists back perfectly, forward or backward—even lists with more than 70 elements. In one experiment, developmental psychologist Alexander Luria exposed Shereshevskii to a complex formula of 30 letters and numbers. After a single recall test, which Shereshevskii accomplished flawlessly, the researcher put the list in a safe-deposit box and waited 15 years . Luria then took out the list, found Shereshevskii, and asked him to repeat the formula. Without hesitation, he reproduced the list on the spot, again without error.
1886年出生的俄罗斯记者所罗门·谢列舍夫斯基似乎拥有近乎无限的记忆力。科学家们会给他一份需要记忆的清单，通常是一些数字和字母的组合，然后测试他的记忆力。谢列舍夫斯基只需要三四秒钟就能“想象”（用他的话说）清单上的每一项。之后，他就能完美地复述清单，无论是正着背还是倒着背——即使是包含70多个元素的清单也不例外。在一项实验中，发展心理学家亚历山大·卢里亚让谢列舍夫斯基接触一个由30个字母和数字组成的复杂公式。在谢列舍夫斯基完美完成一次记忆测试后，研究人员将清单放入保险箱，等待了15年。之后，卢里亚取出清单，找到谢列舍夫斯基，让他复述这个公式。谢列舍夫斯基毫不犹豫地当场复述了清单，同样一字不差。
Shereshevskii’s memory of everything he encountered was so clear, so detailed, so unending , he lost the ability to organize it into meaningful patterns. Like living in a permanent snowstorm, he saw much of his life as blinding flakes of unrelated sensory information. He couldn’t see the “big picture,” meaning he couldn’t focus on the ways two things might be related, look for commonalities, and discover larger patterns. Poems, carrying their typical heavy load of metaphor and simile, were incomprehensible to him. Shereshevskii couldn’t forget, and it affected the way he functioned.
谢列舍夫斯基对所经历的一切记忆如此清晰、如此详尽、如此无穷无尽，以至于他失去了将它们组织成有意义模式的能力。就像生活在永不停歇的暴风雪中，他眼中的人生如同漫天飞舞的雪花，彼此毫无关联。他无法看到“全貌”，也就是说，他无法专注于两件事物之间的关联，无法寻找共同点，也无法发现更大的模式。诗歌中常见的大量隐喻和明喻，对他来说更是难以理解。谢列舍夫斯基无法忘记，这严重影响了他的日常生活。
We have many types of forgetting, categories cleverly enumerated by researcher Dan Schacter in his book The Seven Sins of Memory . Tip-of-the-tongue lapses, absentmindedness, blocking habits, misattribution, biases, suggestibility—the list doesn’t sound good. But they all have one thing in common. They allow us to drop pieces of information in favor of others. In so doing, forgetting helped us to conquer the Earth.
我们有很多种遗忘，研究员丹·沙克特在他的著作《记忆的七宗罪》中巧妙地列举了这些类别：舌尖遗忘、心不在焉、习惯性记忆障碍、错误归因、偏见、易受暗示——这份清单听起来不太妙。但它们都有一个共同点：它们让我们能够舍弃一些信息，而专注于其他信息。正因如此，遗忘帮助我们征服了地球。
More ideas
更多想法
Thinking and talking a lot about information soon after we encounter it (elaborate rehearsal) helps commit it to memory. Allowing time between repetitions is better than cramming. Unfortunately, we can’t say exactly how much talking or exactly how much time produces the best result. You’ll have to experiment.
接触信息后尽快进行大量的思考和讨论（精细复述）有助于记忆。重复练习之间留出时间比临时抱佛脚效果更好。遗憾的是，我们无法确切地说出多少讨论或多少时间才能达到最佳效果。你需要自己尝试。
I have some ideas about how we could systemically apply the concept of repetition in schools and companies .
我有一些想法，可以探讨如何将重复的概念系统地应用于学校和公司。
Teaching in cycles
循环教学
The day of a typical high-school student is segmented into five or six 50-minute periods, consisting of unrelenting, unrepeated streams of information. Here’s my fantasy: In the school of the future, lessons are divided into 25-minute modules, cyclically repeated throughout the day. Subject A is taught for 25 minutes. Ninety minutes later, the 25-minute content of Subject A is repeated, and then a third time. All classes are segmented and interleaved in such a fashion.
普通高中生的一天被分割成五六节课，每节课五十分钟，信息流一气呵成，永无止境。我的设想是：在未来的学校里，课程被分成二十五分钟的模块，在一天中循环往复。比如，先讲授A科目二十五分钟，九十分钟后，再重复一遍A科目的二十五分钟内容，如此往复。所有课程都以这种方式分割和交错进行。
Every third or fourth day would be reserved for quickly reviewing the facts delivered in the previous 72 to 96 hours. Students would inspect their notes, comparing them with what the teacher was saying in the review. This would result in a greater elaboration of the information and an opportunity to confirm facts. Because teachers wouldn’t be able to address as much information, the school year would extend into the summer. Homework would be unnecessary, because students would already be repeating content during the day.
每隔三四天，老师会安排时间快速复习前72到96小时所讲的内容。学生们会检查笔记，并与老师在复习环节的讲解进行比对。这有助于他们更深入地理解信息，并有机会核实事实。由于老师无法讲解那么多内容，学年将会延长至暑假。由于学生白天已经复习了课程内容，因此家庭作业也就没有必要了。
As I said, it’s just a fantasy. Deliberately spaced repetitions have not been tested rigorously in the real world, so there are lots of questions. Do you really need three repetitions per subject per day to see a positive outcome? Do all subjects need such repetition? Would constant repetitions begin to interfere with one another as the day wore on? Do you even need the review sessions? We don’t know.
正如我所说，这只是一种设想。刻意间隔重复训练在现实世界中尚未经过严格测试，因此存在诸多疑问。真的需要每个受试者每天重复三次才能看到积极效果吗？所有受试者都需要这样的重复训练吗？随着时间的推移，频繁的重复训练会不会相互干扰？甚至真的需要复习环节吗？我们不得而知。
Repetition over many years
多年来的重复
Beyond doing well on the year-end test, our education system doesn’t seem to care whether students actually remember what they learned. Given that system consolidation can take years , perhaps critical information should be repeated on a yearly or semiyearly basis.
除了期末考试成绩之外，我们的教育体系似乎并不关心学生是否真正记住了所学内容。鉴于体系整合可能需要数年时间，或许应该每年或每半年复习一次关键知识点。
In my fantasy class, this is exactly what happens. Take math. Repetitions begin with a review of multiplication tables, fractions, and decimals. Starting in the third grade, six-month and yearly review sessions occur through sixth grade. As students’ competency grows, the review content becomes more sophisticated. But the cycles are still in place. I can imagine enormous benefits for every academic subject, especially foreign languages.
在我的理想课堂里，情况正是如此。以数学为例。复习从乘法表、分数和小数开始。从三年级开始，一直到六年级，每半年和每年都会进行一次复习。随着学生能力的提高，复习内容也会变得更加深入。但循环模式始终不变。我想，这种模式对所有学科，尤其是外语学习，都将大有裨益。
For businesses, I would extend the bachelor’s degree into the workplace. You’ve probably heard that many corporations, especially in technical fields, are disappointed by the quality of the American undergraduates they hire. They have to spend money retraining many of their newest employees in basic skills that should have been covered in college.
对于企业而言，我认为应该将学士学位延伸到工作场所。你可能听说过，许多公司，尤其是在技术领域，对他们雇佣的美国本科毕业生的素质感到失望。他们不得不花钱对许多新员工进行再培训，让他们掌握本应在大学期间学习到的基本技能。
I would turn your company into a learning and leadership factory, offering a full range of classes that would review every subject important to a new employee’s job. Research would establish the optimal spacing of the repetition. More experienced employees might even begin attending these refresher courses, inadvertently rubbing shoulders with younger generations. The old guard would be surprised by how much they have forgotten, and how much the experience aids their own job performance.
我会把贵公司打造成一个学习和领导力培训中心，提供全方位的课程，涵盖新员工工作中所有重要的知识点。我们会进行研究，确定最佳的复习间隔。经验丰富的员工甚至可能会开始参加这些进修课程，无意中与年轻一代交流学习。老员工会惊讶地发现自己遗忘了多少知识，以及这些经验对他们自身工作表现的巨大帮助。
I wish I could tell you this all would work. Instead, all I can say is that memory is not fixed at the moment of learning, and repetition provides the fixative.
我真希望我能告诉你这一切都会奏效。然而，我只能说，记忆并非在学习的那一刻就固定下来，而重复才能起到巩固记忆的作用。
Brain Rule # 7
大脑法则#7
Repeat to remember.
反复练习以加深记忆。
• The brain has many types of memory systems. Declarative memory follows four stages of processing: encoding, storing, retrieving, and forgetting.
大脑拥有多种类型的记忆系统。陈述性记忆的处理过程分为四个阶段：编码、存储、提取和遗忘。
• Information coming into your brain is immediately fragmented and sent to different regions of the cortex.
•进入大脑的信息会立即被分解并发送到大脑皮层的不同区域。
• The more elaborately we encode a memory during its initial moments, the stronger it will be.
•我们在记忆的最初时刻对其进行的编码越精细，记忆就会越牢固。
• You can improve your chances of remembering something if you reproduce the environment in which you first put it into your brain.
•如果你重现当初将某件事记入脑海的环境，就能提高你记住它的几率。
• Working memory is a collection of busy work spaces that allows us to temporarily retain newly acquired information. If we don’t repeat the information, it disappears.
工作记忆是一系列繁忙的工作空间，使我们能够暂时保留新近获取的信息。如果我们不重复这些信息，它就会消失。
• Long-term memories are formed in a two-way conversation between the hippocampus and the cortex, until the hippocampus breaks the connection and the memory is fixed in the cortex—which can take years.
•长期记忆是在海马体和大脑皮层之间的双向对话中形成的，直到海马体断开连接，记忆才固定在大脑皮层中——这可能需要数年时间。
• Our brains give us only an approximate view of reality, because they mix new knowledge with past memories and store them together as one.
•我们的大脑只能给我们提供对现实的近似看法，因为它们将新知识与过去的记忆混合在一起，并将它们作为一个整体存储起来。
• The way to make long-term memory more reliable is to incorporate new information gradually and repeat it in timed intervals.
•提高长期记忆可靠性的方法是逐步吸收新信息，并定期重复。
# ↩
sensory integration
感觉统合
Brain Rule #8
大脑法则第8条
Stimulate more of the senses.
刺激更多感官。
# ↩
EVERY TIME TIM SEES the letter E , he also sees the color red. He describes the color change as if suddenly forced to look at the world through red-tinted glasses. When Tim looks away from the letter E , his world returns to normal, until he encounters the letter O . Then the world turns blue. For Tim, reading a book is like living in a disco. For a long time, Tim thought this happened to everyone. When he discovered this happened to no one—at least no one he knew—he began to suspect he was crazy. Neither impression was correct. Tim is suffering—if that’s the right word—from a brain condition called synesthesia. It’s experienced by perhaps one in 2,000 people; some think more.
每次蒂姆看到字母E，他都会同时看到红色。他形容这种颜色变化就像突然被迫戴上一副红色眼镜看世界一样。当蒂姆的视线从字母E移开时，他的世界就恢复正常，直到他看到字母O。这时，世界又变成了蓝色。对蒂姆来说，读书就像置身于迪斯科舞厅。很长一段时间，蒂姆都以为每个人都会这样。当他发现这种情况并非发生在任何人身上——至少在他认识的人当中——他开始怀疑自己是不是疯了。但这两种想法都错了。蒂姆患有——如果用“患有”这个词合适的话——一种叫做联觉的脑部疾病。大约每2000人中就有一人患有这种疾病；有些人认为患病人数更多。
Synesthesia appears to be a short circuiting in the way the brain processes the world’s many senses. But it also provides a strong clue that our sensory processes are wired to work together. In one of the strangest types of synesthesia—there are at least three dozen—people see a word and immediately experience a taste on their tongue. This isn’t the typical mouthwatering response, such as imagining the taste of a candy bar after hearing the word “chocolate.” This is like seeing the word “sky” in a novel and suddenly tasting a sour lemon in your mouth. A clever experiment showed that even when the synesthete could not recall the exact word, he or she would still get the taste from a general description of the word. Even when the brain’s wiring gets confused, the senses still attempt to work together.
联觉似乎是大脑处理外界多种感官信息时的一种短路现象。但它也有力地表明，我们的感官过程原本是相互协作的。在至少三十多种最奇特的联觉类型中，有一种是这样的：人们看到一个词，舌头上立刻就能尝到某种味道。这并非典型的令人垂涎欲滴的反应，比如听到“巧克力”这个词后想象出巧克力棒的味道。这就像在小说中看到“天空”这个词，嘴里突然尝到酸柠檬的味道。一项巧妙的实验表明，即使联觉者无法回忆起确切的词语，他们仍然能够根据对该词的概括性描述来获得相应的味道。即使大脑的神经回路出现混乱，各种感官仍然会尝试协同工作。
Here’s another way we know the brain likes sensory integration. Suppose researchers show you a video of a person saying the surprisingly ugly syllable “ga.” Unbeknownst to you, the scientists have turned off the sound of the original video and dubbed the sound “ba” onto it. When the scientist asks you to listen to the video with your eyes closed, you hear “ba” just fine. But if you open your eyes, your brain suddenly encounters the shape of the lips saying “ga” while your ears are still hearing “ba.” The brain has no idea what to do with this contradiction. So it makes something up. If you are like most people, what you actually will hear when your eyes open is the syllable “da.” This is the brain’s compromise between what you hear and what you see—its need to attempt integration. It’s called the McGurk effect.
我们知道大脑喜欢感觉统合的另一个例子是这样的：假设研究人员给你看一段视频，视频里的人说着一个听起来很别扭的音节“ga”。你不知道的是，科学家们已经把原视频的声音关掉了，换成了“ba”的声音。当科学家让你闭上眼睛听视频时，你当然能清楚地听到“ba”。但如果你睁开眼睛，你的大脑会突然看到嘴唇的形状在说“ga”，而你的耳朵仍然在听“ba”。大脑不知道该如何处理这种矛盾，于是它编造了一个声音。如果你和大多数人一样，睁开眼睛后实际听到的其实是音节“da”。这就是大脑在听觉和视觉之间做出的妥协——它试图进行整合的需要。这被称为麦格克效应。
But you don’t have to be in a laboratory to see it in action. You can just go to a movie. The actors you see speaking to each other on-screen are not really speaking to each other at all. Their voices emanate from speakers cleverly placed around the room: some behind you, some beside you; none centered on the actors’ mouths. Even so, you believe the voices are coming from those mouths. Your eyes observe lips moving in tandem with the words your ears are hearing, and the brain combines the experience to trick you into believing the dialogue comes from the screen. Together, these senses create the perception of someone speaking in front of you, when actually nobody is speaking in front of you.
但你无需身处实验室就能亲眼目睹这种现象。只需去看场电影就明白了。你在银幕上看到的演员们其实并非真的在对话。他们的声音是从巧妙布置在房间各处的扬声器中发出的：有的在你身后，有的在你身旁；没有一个扬声器正对着演员的嘴。即便如此，你仍然会相信这些声音是从他们的嘴里发出来的。你的眼睛会观察到嘴唇随着耳朵听到的词语同步移动，大脑会将这些体验结合起来，让你误以为对话是从屏幕上发出的。所有这些感官共同作用，让你产生有人在你面前说话的错觉，而实际上，你面前根本没有人说话。
The process of sensory integration has such a positive effect on learning that it forms the heart of Brain Rule #8: Stimulate more of the senses at the same time .
感觉统合过程对学习有着如此积极的影响，以至于它构成了大脑法则第 8 条的核心：同时刺激更多感官。
A fire hose of sights and sounds
各种景象和声音如同消防水管般涌来。
An incredible amount of sensory information comes at us in any given moment. Imagine, for example, that you’ve gone out on a Friday night to a dance club in New York. The beat of the music dominates, hypnotic, felt more than heard. Laser lights shoot across the room. Bodies move. The smells of sweat, alcohol, and illegal smoking mix in the atmosphere like a second sound track. In the corner, a jilted lover is crying. You step out for a breath of fresh air. The jilted lover follows you. All of these external physical inputs and internal emotional inputs are presented to your brain in a never-ending fire hose of sensations. Does the example of a dance club seem extreme? It probably holds no more information than what you’d normally experience the next morning on the streets of Manhattan. Faithfully, your brain perceives the screech of the taxis, the smell of the pretzels for sale, the blink of the crosswalk signal, the touch of people brushing past. And your brain integrates them all into one coherent experience.
在任何时刻，我们都会接收到海量的感官信息。例如，想象一下，你周五晚上去了纽约的一家夜店。音乐的节奏强劲有力，令人着迷，与其说是听觉上的享受，不如说是感官上的冲击。激光灯在房间里闪烁。人们舞动着身体。汗水、酒精和非法吸烟的气味混杂在一起，如同第二层背景音乐。角落里，一个失恋的人正在哭泣。你走出去呼吸新鲜空气。那个失恋的人跟了出去。所有这些外部的生理输入和内部的情感输入，如同永不停歇的感官洪流，涌入你的大脑。夜店的例子听起来很极端吗？它可能包含的信息量并不比你第二天早上在曼哈顿街头所经历的更多。你的大脑忠实地感知着出租车的刺耳声、待售椒盐卷饼的香味、人行横道信号灯的闪烁、行人擦肩而过的触感。然后，你的大脑将所有这些信息整合为一个连贯的体验。
You are a wonder. We in brain-science land are only beginning to figure out how you do it.
你真是个奇迹。我们这些研究脑科学的人才刚刚开始弄明白你是怎么做到的。
It’s mysterious: On one hand, your head crackles with the perceptions of the whole world—sight, sound, taste, smell, touch—as energetic as that dance party. On the other hand, the inside of your head is a darkened, silent place, lonely as a cave. The Greeks didn’t think the brain did much of anything. They thought it just sat there like an inert pile of clay. Indeed, it does not generate enough electricity to prick your finger. Aristotle thought the heart held all the action. Pumping out rich, red blood 24 hours a day, the heart, he reasoned, harbored the “vital flame of life.” This fire produced enough heat to give the brain a job description: to act as a cooling device. (He thought the lungs helped out, too.) Perhaps taking a cue from Aristotle, we still use the word “heart” to describe many aspects of mental life. Now we know that one of the brain’s major job descriptions is to handle all of the inputs that our senses pick up and allow us to perceive the world.
这很神秘：一方面，你的大脑充斥着对整个世界的感知——视觉、听觉、味觉、嗅觉、触觉——如同舞会般活力四射。另一方面，你的大脑内部却是一个黑暗、寂静的地方，如同洞穴般孤独。古希腊人认为大脑几乎什么也不做。他们认为它只是像一堆惰性的黏土一样静静地待在那里。的确，它产生的电流甚至不足以刺破你的手指。亚里士多德认为心脏才是所有活动的源泉。心脏日夜不停地泵出富含营养的血液，他认为，心脏蕴藏着“生命之火”。这团火焰产生的热量足以赋予大脑一项职责：作为冷却装置。（他认为肺也起到了辅助作用。）或许是受到了亚里士多德的启发，我们至今仍然用“心脏”一词来描述精神生活的许多方面。现在我们知道，大脑的主要职责之一是处理我们感官接收到的所有信息，使我们能够感知世界。
How we perceive something
我们如何感知事物
During the Revolutionary War, the British—steeped in the traditions of large European land wars—had lots of central planning. The field office gathered information from leaders on the battleground and then issued its commands. The Americans—steeped in the traditions of nothing—used guerrilla tactics: on-the-ground analysis and decision making prior to consultation with a central command. These very different approaches are a good way to describe the two main theories scientists have about how the brain goes from sensing something to perceiving it. Imagine the sound of a single gunshot over a green field during that war.
在独立战争期间，深受欧洲大规模陆战传统影响的英国人实行了严格的中央计划。野战指挥部从前线指挥官那里收集信息，然后下达命令。而秉持“无为而治”传统的美国人则采用游击战术：在与中央指挥部协商之前，先进行实地分析和决策。这两种截然不同的方法恰好可以用来描述科学家关于大脑如何从感知到理解的两大主要理论。想象一下战争期间，一声枪响划破绿野的声音。
In the British model of this experience, our senses function separately, sending their information into the brain’s central command, its sophisticated perception centers. Only in these centers does the brain combine the sensory inputs into a cohesive perception of the environment. The ears hear the rifle and generate a complete auditory report of what just occurred. The eyes see the smoke from the gun arising from the turf and process the information separately, generating a visual report of the event. The nose, smelling gunpowder, does the same thing. They each send their data to central command. There, the inputs are bound together, a cohesive perception is created, and the brain lets the soldier in on what he just experienced.
在英国的这种体验模式中，我们的感官各自独立运作，将信息发送到大脑的中央指挥中心——其精密的感知中枢。只有在这些中枢，大脑才会将感官输入整合起来，形成对环境的完整感知。耳朵听到步枪的声音，并生成对刚刚发生的事情的完整听觉报告。眼睛看到草地上升起的枪声硝烟，并分别处理这些信息，生成对事件的视觉报告。鼻子闻到火药味，也做着同样的事情。它们各自将数据发送到中央指挥中心。在那里，输入的信息被整合在一起，形成一个完整的感知，大脑最终将士兵刚刚经历的一切告知他。
The American model puts things very differently. Here the senses work together from the very beginning, consulting and influencing one another quite early in the process. As the ears and eyes simultaneously pick up gunshot and smoke, the two impressions immediately confer with each other. They perceive that the events are occurring in tandem, without conferencing with any higher authority. The picture of a rifle firing over an open field emerges in the observer’s brain. Perception is not where the integration begins but where the integration culminates.
美国模式则截然不同。在这种模式下，感官从一开始就协同运作，在感知过程的早期阶段就相互影响、相互交流。当耳朵和眼睛同时捕捉到枪声和硝烟时，这两种印象会立即相互印证。它们感知到事件是同步发生的，无需任何更高层级的指令。观察者的脑海中浮现出一幅步枪在开阔地带射击的画面。感知并非整合的起点，而是整合的终点。
Which model is correct? The data are edging in the direction of the second model. There are tantalizing suggestions that the senses do help one another, and in a precisely coordinated fashion. We’ll talk about them in a couple of pages.
哪个模型是正确的？数据似乎更倾向于第二个模型。一些令人振奋的迹象表明，感官之间确实存在相互帮助，而且是以精确协调的方式进行的。我们将在后面的几页中讨论这些迹象。
First sensing and routing, then perceiving
首先是感知和路由，然后是感知。
No matter which model is eventually declared the winner, the underlying processes are the same, and they operate in the same order: sensing, routing, and perceiving. Sensing involves capturing the energies from our environment that are pushing themselves into our orifices and rubbing against our skin. The brain converts this external information into a brain-friendly electrical language. Once the sensory information is encoded, it is routed to appropriate regions of the brain for further processing. As we discussed in the Wiring chapter, the signals for vision, hearing, touch, taste, and smell all have separate, specialized places where this processing occurs. A region called the thalamus—a well-connected, egg-shaped structure in the middle of your “second brain”—supervises most of this shuttling.
无论最终哪个模型胜出，其基本过程都是相同的，并且遵循相同的顺序：感知、路由和知觉。感知是指捕捉来自环境的能量，这些能量会涌入我们的孔窍，摩擦我们的皮肤。大脑会将这些外部信息转换成大脑能够理解的电信号。一旦感觉信息被编码，它就会被路由到大脑的相应区域进行进一步处理。正如我们在“连接”一章中所讨论的，视觉、听觉、触觉、味觉和嗅觉的信号都有各自独立的、专门的区域进行处理。丘脑——位于“第二大脑”中心，是一个连接紧密的卵形结构——负责大部分的信号传递。
The information, dissected into sensory-size pieces and flung widely across the brain, next needs to be reassembled. Specialized areas throughout the brain take over from the thalamus to make this happen. They are not exactly sensory regions, and they are not exactly motor regions, but they are bridges between them. Hence, they are called association cortices. (“Cortices” is the plural of “cortex.”) As sensory signals ascend through higher and higher orders of neural processing, the association cortices kick in.
信息被分解成感觉层面的碎片，并广泛散布在大脑各处，接下来需要重新组装。大脑中一些专门的区域会接替丘脑的功能来完成这项工作。它们既不是纯粹的感觉区域，也不是纯粹的运动区域，而是连接两者的桥梁。因此，它们被称为联合皮层（“皮层”的复数形式为“cortices”）。随着感觉信号不断向上传递，经过越来越高级的神经处理，联合皮层开始发挥作用。
The association cortices employ two types of processors: bottom up and top down. Let’s walk through what they might be doing in your brain as you read the next sentence—a randomly chosen quote attributed to author W. Somerset Maugham .
联合皮层使用两种类型的处理器：自下而上和自上而下。让我们一起来看看，当你阅读下一句话——一句随机选取的、据说是作家W·萨默塞特·毛姆的名言——时，它们在你的大脑中可能在做什么。
The rank and file make a report
普通成员提交了一份报告。
“There are only three rules for writing a novel,” Maugham once said. “Unfortunately, nobody knows what they are.”
毛姆曾说过：“写小说只有三条规则。可惜的是，没人知道这三条规则是什么。”
After your eyes look at that sentence and your thalamus has routed each aspect of the sentence to the appropriate brain regions, “bottom-up” processors go to work. The visual system is a classic bottom-up processor. It has feature detectors that greet the sentence’s visual stimuli. These detectors, working like auditors in an accounting firm, inspect every structural element in each letter of every word in Maugham’s quote. They file a report, a visual conception of letters and words. An upside-down arch becomes the letter U . Two straight lines at right angles become the letter T . Combinations of straight lines and curves become the word “three.” Written information has a lot of visual features in it, and this report takes a great deal of effort and time for the brain to organize. It is one of the reasons that reading is a relatively slow way to put information into the brain.
当你的眼睛注视着那句话，丘脑将句子的各个方面传递到相应的脑区后，“自下而上”的处理器就开始工作了。视觉系统就是一个典型的自下而上处理器。它拥有特征检测器，能够识别句子中的视觉刺激。这些检测器就像会计事务所的审计员一样，仔细检查毛姆引文中每个单词的每个字母的每个结构元素。它们会生成一份报告，一份关于字母和单词的视觉概念。一个倒置的弧线变成了字母U。两条垂直的直线变成了字母T。直线和曲线的组合变成了单词“three”。书面信息包含大量的视觉特征，而大脑需要花费大量的时间和精力来组织这份报告。这也是阅读是一种相对较慢的信息输入方式的原因之一。
Higher-ups interpret the report
高层解读这份报告
Next comes “top-down” processing. This can be likened to a board of directors reading the auditor’s report and then reacting to it. Many comments are made. Sections are analyzed in light of preexisting knowledge. The board in your brain has heard of the word “three” before, for example, and it has been familiar with the concept of rules since you were a toddler. Some board members have even heard of W. Somerset Maugham before, and they recall to your consciousness a movie called Of Human Bondage , which you saw in a film history course . Information is added to the data stream or subtracted from the data stream. In plenty of cases, as we saw in the McGurk effect, the brain resorts to making something up.
接下来是“自上而下”的处理过程。这可以比作董事会阅读审计报告并做出反应。他们会提出许多意见，并根据已有的知识分析报告的各个部分。例如，你大脑中的董事会成员之前就听说过“三”这个词，而且从你蹒跚学步起就熟悉规则的概念。有些董事会成员甚至听说过W·萨默塞特·毛姆，他们会让你想起你在电影史课程中看过的电影《人性的枷锁》。信息会被添加到数据流中，或从数据流中删除。在很多情况下，正如我们在麦格克效应中看到的那样，大脑会编造一些信息。
At this point, the brain generously lets you in on the fact that you are perceiving something .
这时，大脑会慷慨地让你意识到，你正在感知某些事物。
Given that people have unique previous experiences, they bring different interpretations to their top-down analyses. Thus, two people can see the same input and come away with vastly different perceptions. It is a sobering thought. There is no one accurate way to perceive the world.
鉴于每个人都有独特的过往经历，他们会对自上而下的分析做出不同的解读。因此，两个人即使面对相同的信息输入，也可能得出截然不同的结论。这令人深思。看待世界并不存在唯一正确的方式。
Smell is a powerful exception
嗅觉是一个强有力的例外。
Every sensory system must send a signal to the thalamus asking permission to connect to the higher levels of the brain where perception occurs—except for smell. Like an important head of state in a motorcade, nerves carrying information about smell bypass the thalamus and gain immediate access to their higher destinations.
除了嗅觉之外，所有感觉系统都必须向丘脑发送信号，请求允许其连接到大脑中负责感知的更高级区域。就像车队中的重要国家元首一样，传递嗅觉信息的神经绕过丘脑，直接连接到更高级的区域。
Right between the eyes lies a patch of neurons about the size of a large postage stamp. This patch is called the olfactory region. The outer surface of this region, the one closest to the air in the nose, is the olfactory epithelium. When we sniff, odor molecules enter the nose chamber, penetrate a layer of snot, and collide with nerves there. The odor molecules brush against little quill-like protein receptors that stud the neurons in the olfactory epithelium. These neurons begin to fire excitedly, and you are well on your way to smelling something. The rest of the journey occurs in the brain.
在两眼之间，有一片大小与邮票相仿的神经元区域，称为嗅觉区。该区域的外表面，也就是最靠近鼻腔空气的那一部分，是嗅觉上皮。当我们吸气时，气味分子进入鼻腔，穿透一层鼻涕，并与那里的神经发生碰撞。这些气味分子会触碰到嗅觉上皮神经元上排列的细小针状蛋白受体。这些神经元开始兴奋地放电，你便开始闻到气味了。接下来的嗅觉处理则在大脑中进行。
One of the neurons’ destinations is the amygdala. The amygdala supervises not only the formation of emotional experiences but also the memory of emotional experiences. Because smell directly stimulates the amygdala, smell directly stimulates emotions. Smell signals also beeline for a part of your brain deeply involved in decision making. It is almost as if the odor is saying, “My signal is so important, I am going to give you a memorable emotion. What are you going to do about it?”
神经元的其中一个目的地是杏仁核。杏仁核不仅负责情绪体验的形成，还负责情绪体验的记忆。由于气味直接刺激杏仁核，因此气味也直接刺激情绪。气味信号还会直达大脑中与决策密切相关的区域。这就像气味在说：“我的信号如此重要，我将带给你一段难忘的情绪体验。你打算怎么做？”
Smell signals are in such a hurry, our receptor cells for smell aren’t guarded by much of a protective barrier. This is different from most other sensory receptor cells in the human body. Visual receptor neurons in the retina are protected by the cornea, for example. Receptor neurons that allow hearing in our ears are protected by the eardrum. The only things protecting receptor neurons for smell are boogers.
嗅觉信号传递如此迅速，以至于我们嗅觉受体细胞几乎没有任何保护屏障。这与人体内大多数其他感觉受体细胞不同。例如，视网膜中的视觉受体神经元受到角膜的保护；耳朵中负责听觉的受体神经元受到耳膜的保护。而唯一能保护嗅觉受体神经元的，只有鼻涕。
Pairing two senses boosts one
两种感官的结合可以增强一种感官。
We’ve talked about the fact that the brain strives to integrate all of the senses, and we’ve touched on the regions of the brain involved in perceiving those senses. (We haven’t talked about exactly how the brain integrates the senses, because, well, no one knows how that works.) Now let’s look at those tantalizing hints that stimulating multiple senses at the same time increases the capability of the senses.
我们已经讨论过大脑会努力整合所有感官信息，也略微提及了大脑中负责感知这些感官的区域。（我们还没有详细讨论大脑是如何整合感官信息的，因为，嗯，没人知道它是如何运作的。）现在，让我们来看看那些引人入胜的迹象：同时刺激多种感官可以增强感官能力。
In one experiment, people watched a video of someone speaking, but with no sound. At the same time, scientists peered in on the brain using fMRI technology. The fMRI scans showed that the area of the brain responsible for processing the sound, the auditory cortex, was stimulated as if the person actually were hearing sound. If the subject was presented with a person simply “making faces,” the auditory cortex was silent. It had to be a visual input related to sound. Then, visual inputs influence auditory inputs.
在一项实验中，受试者观看了一段无声的视频，视频中有人在说话。与此同时，科学家利用功能磁共振成像（fMRI）技术观察受试者的大脑活动。fMRI扫描结果显示，大脑中负责处理声音的区域——听觉皮层——受到了刺激，就像受试者真的听到了声音一样。如果受试者看到的只是一个人“做鬼脸”，那么听觉皮层则没有反应。这必然是一种与声音相关的视觉输入。视觉输入会影响听觉输入。
In another experiment, researchers showed short flashes of light near the subjects’ hands, which were rigged with a tactile stimulator. Sometimes researchers would stimulate the subjects’ hands while the light flashed, sometimes not. No matter how many times they did this, the visual portion of the brain always lighted up the strongest when the tactile response was paired with it. They could literally get a 30 percent boost in the visual system by introducing touch. This effect is called multimodal reinforcement.
在另一项实验中，研究人员向受试者的手部（手上装有触觉刺激器）展示了短暂的闪光。有时，研究人员会在闪光的同时刺激受试者的手部，有时则不会。无论重复多少次，当触觉刺激与视觉刺激同时出现时，大脑的视觉区域总是最为活跃。他们发现，通过引入触觉刺激，视觉系统的反应强度可以提升30%。这种效应被称为多模态强化。
Multiple senses affect our ability to detect stimuli, too. Most people, for example, have a very hard time seeing a flickering light if the intensity of the light is gradually decreased. Researchers decided to test that threshold by precisely coordinating a short burst of sound with the light flickering off. The presence of sound actually changed the threshold. The subjects found that they could see the light way beyond their normal threshold if sound was part of the experience.
多种感官都会影响我们对刺激的感知能力。例如，大多数人如果看到灯光强度逐渐减弱，就很难察觉到闪烁的灯光。研究人员决定通过将短暂的声音与灯光的熄灭精确同步来测试这一阈值。结果发现，声音的存在确实改变了阈值。受试者发现，如果体验过程中有声音的参与，他们就能看到远超正常阈值的灯光。
Why does the brain have such powerful integrative instincts? The answer seems a bit obvious: The world is multisensory and has been for a very long time. Our East African crib did not unveil its sensory information one sense at a time during our development. Our environment did not possess only visual stimuli, like a silent movie, and then suddenly acquire an audio track a few million years later, and then, later, odors and textures. By the time we came down out of the trees, our evolutionary ancestors were already champions at experiencing a multisensory world. So it makes sense that in a multisensory environment, our muscles react more quickly, our eyes react to visual stimuli more quickly, and our threshold for detecting stimuli improves.
为什么大脑拥有如此强大的整合本能？答案似乎显而易见：世界是多感官的，而且由来已久。我们东非的摇篮并非在我们成长过程中逐一揭示感官信息。我们的环境并非最初只有视觉刺激，如同无声电影一般，几百万年后才突然获得声音，之后又陆续有了气味和触感。当我们离开树栖生活时，我们的进化祖先早已是体验多感官世界的佼佼者。因此，在多感官环境中，我们的肌肉反应更快，眼睛对视觉刺激的反应更迅速，对刺激的感知阈值也更高，这也就不足为奇了。
A multisensory environment enhances learning
多感官环境有助于学习
Knowing that the brain cut its developmental teeth in an overwhelmingly multisensory environment, you might hypothesize that its learning abilities are increasingly optimized the more multisensory the situation is. You might further hypothesize that the opposite is true: Learning is less effective in a unisensory situation. That is exactly what you find.
鉴于大脑是在高度多感官的环境中发育成熟的，你可能会假设，感官刺激越多，大脑的学习能力就越强。你也可能进一步假设，事实恰恰相反：在单一感官的环境中，学习效率会降低。而你的发现恰恰印证了这一点。
Cognitive psychologist Richard Mayer probably has done more than anybody else to explore the link between multimedia exposure and learning. He sports a 10-megawatt smile, and his head looks exactly like an egg (albeit a very clever egg). His experiments are just as smooth: He divides the room into three groups. One group gets information delivered via one sense (say, hearing), another the same information from another sense (say, sight), and the third group the same information delivered as a combination of the first two senses.
认知心理学家理查德·梅耶尔或许是研究多媒体接触与学习之间联系方面贡献最大的人。他笑容灿烂，脑袋长得像个鸡蛋（当然，是个非常聪明的鸡蛋）。他的实验也同样精妙：他将房间分成三组。一组通过一种感官（比如听觉）接收信息，另一组通过另一种感官（比如视觉）接收相同的信息，第三组则通过前两种感官的结合接收相同的信息。
The groups in the multisensory environments always do better than the groups in the unisensory environments. Their recall is more accurate, more detailed, and longer lasting—evident even 20 years later. Problem-solving ability improves, too. In one study, the group given multisensory presentations generated more than 50 percent more creative solutions on a problem-solving test than students who saw unisensory presentations. In another study, the improvement was more than 75 percent! Multisensory presentations are the way to go.
在多感官环境下学习的小组表现总是优于在单感官环境下学习的小组。他们的记忆更准确、更详细、更持久——即使在20年后依然如此。他们的问题解决能力也得到了提升。一项研究表明，接受多感官演示的小组在问题解决测试中提出的创造性解决方案比接受单感官演示的学生多出50%以上。另一项研究显示，这一提升幅度超过了75%！多感官演示才是最佳选择。
Many researchers think multisensory experiences work because they are more elaborate. Do you recall the counterintuitive concept that more elaborate information given at the moment of learning enhances learning? It’s like saying that if you carry two heavy backpacks on a hike instead of one, you will accomplish your journey more quickly. But apparently our brains like heavy lifting. This is the “elaborative” processing that we saw in the Memory chapter. Stated formally, the extra cognitive processing of information helps the brain integrate the new material with prior information.
许多研究者认为多感官体验之所以有效，是因为它们更加精细复杂。你是否还记得那个看似违反直觉的观点：在学习过程中提供更精细的信息反而能促进学习？这就像说，如果你背着两个沉重的背包去徒步旅行，而不是只背一个，你就能更快地完成旅程。但显然，我们的大脑喜欢“负重”。这就是我们在“记忆”章节中看到的“精细加工”。更正式地说，对信息进行额外的认知加工有助于大脑将新信息与已有信息整合起来。
One more example of synesthesia supports this, too. Remember Solomon Shereshevskii’s amazing mental abilities? He accurately reproduced a complex formula 15 years after seeing it once. Shereshevskii had multiple categories of (dis)ability. He felt that some colors were warm or cool, which is common. But he also thought the number one was a proud, well-built man, and that the number six was a man with a swollen foot—which is not common. Some of his imaging was nearly hallucinatory. He related: “One time I went to buy some ice cream … I walked over to the vendor and asked her what kind of ice cream she had. ‘Fruit ice cream,’ she said. But she answered in such a tone that a whole pile of coals, of black cinders, came bursting out of her mouth, and I couldn’t bring myself to buy any ice cream after she had answered that way.”
另一个联觉的例子也印证了这一点。还记得所罗门·谢列舍夫斯基惊人的心智能力吗？他只见过一次一个复杂的公式，15年后却能准确地复述出来。谢列舍夫斯基的联觉能力存在多方面的差异。他能感觉到某些颜色是暖色还是冷色，这很常见。但他还认为数字1是一个骄傲健壮的男人，数字6是一个脚肿的男人——这就不常见了。他的一些想象近乎幻觉。他回忆道：“有一次我去买冰淇淋……我走到摊主面前，问她有什么口味的冰淇淋。‘水果冰淇淋，’她说。但她回答的语气却像是从她嘴里喷出一堆煤炭，一堆黑色的煤渣，在她那样回答之后，我实在没法买冰淇淋了。”
Synesthetes like Shereshevskii almost universally respond to the question “What good does this extra information do?” with an immediate and hearty, “It helps you remember.” Most synesthetes report their odd experiences as highly pleasurable, which may, by virtue of dopamine, aid in memory formation. Indeed, synesthetes often have a photographic memory.
像谢列舍夫斯基这样的联觉者，几乎都会毫不犹豫地回答“这些额外信息有什么用？”这个问题：“它能帮助你记住。”大多数联觉者都表示，他们奇特的体验非常愉悦，而这种愉悦感可能正是由于多巴胺的作用，有助于记忆的形成。事实上，联觉者往往拥有过目不忘的本领。
Smell boosts memory all by itself
嗅觉本身就能增强记忆力。
I once heard a story about a man who washed out of medical school because of his nose. To fully understand his story, you have to know something about the smell of surgery, and you have to have killed somebody. Surgery can assault many of the senses. When you cut somebody’s body, you invariably cut their blood vessels. To keep the blood from interfering with the operation, surgeons use a cauterizing tool, hot as a soldering iron. It’s applied directly to the wound, burning it shut, filling the room with the acrid smell of smoldering flesh. Combat can smell the same way. And the medical student in question was a Vietnam vet with heavy combat experience. He didn’t seem to suffer any aversive effects when he came home. He was accepted into medical school. But then the former soldier started his first surgery rotation. When he smelled the burning flesh from the cauterizer, it brought back to mind the immediate memory of an enemy combatant he had shot in the face, point-blank, an experience he had suppressed for years. The memory literally doubled him over. He resigned from the program the next week.
我曾听过一个故事，讲的是一个男人因为鼻子的问题而被医学院开除。要完全理解他的故事，你必须了解手术室的气味，而且你得有过杀人的经历。手术会刺激你的多种感官。当你切开别人的身体时，你必然会切断他们的血管。为了防止血液干扰手术，外科医生会使用一种像烙铁一样热的止血工具。它直接作用于伤口，烧灼伤口使其闭合，房间里弥漫着刺鼻的烧焦肉味。战斗的气味也与之类似。而这位医学生是一位参加过越战的老兵，拥有丰富的战斗经验。他回国后似乎并没有受到任何不良影响。他被医学院录取了。但是，这位前士兵开始了他的第一次外科轮转。当他闻到止血工具烧焦肉味时，他立刻想起了自己近距离射杀一名敌方战斗人员的场景，那段经历他已经压抑了多年。那段记忆让他痛苦地弯下了腰。他于次周辞去了该项目的职务。
This story illustrates something scientists have known for years: Smell can evoke memory. It’s called the Proust effect. Marcel Proust, the French author of the profoundly moving book Remembrance of Things Past , talked freely 100 years ago about smells and their ability to elicit long-lost memories. Why? Remember, smell neurons gain VIP access to the amygdala.
这个故事印证了科学家们多年来早已知晓的现象：气味可以唤起记忆。这被称为普鲁斯特效应。法国作家马塞尔·普鲁斯特，这位创作了感人至深的《追忆似水年华》的作家，早在100年前就曾畅谈气味及其唤起尘封记忆的能力。为什么呢？要知道，嗅觉神经元能够便捷地进入杏仁核。
Smell has the unique advantage of being able to boost learning directly, without being paired with another sense. That’s because it is an ancient sense, not fully integrated with the rest of the brain’s sensory circuitry but instead closely wired to the emotional learning centers of the brain. In the typical experiment testing the effect of smell on remembering, two groups of people might be assigned to see a movie together and then told to report to the lab for a memory test. The control group takes the test in a plain room. The experimental group takes the test in a room smelling of popcorn. The second group blows away the first group in terms of number of events recalled, accuracy of events recalled, specific details, and so on. In some cases, they can accurately retrieve twice as many memories as the controls.
嗅觉的独特优势在于它能够直接促进学习，而无需与其他感官协同作用。这是因为嗅觉是一种古老的感官，它并未完全融入大脑的其他感觉回路，而是与大脑的情感学习中心紧密相连。在典型的嗅觉对记忆影响的实验中，两组人会被安排一起观看电影，然后前往实验室进行记忆测试。对照组在普通的房间里进行测试，而实验组则在充满爆米花香味的房间里进行测试。结果显示，实验组在回忆事件的数量、回忆事件的准确性、具体细节等方面都远胜于对照组。在某些情况下，他们甚至能够准确回忆起对照组两倍的记忆。
However, this is true for only certain types of memory. Odors appear to do their finest work when subjects are asked to retrieve the emotional details of a memory—as our medical student experienced—or to retrieve autobiographical memories. You get the best results if the smells are congruent. A movie test in which the smell of gasoline is pumped into the experimental room does not yield the same positive results as the smell of popcorn does.
然而，这仅适用于某些类型的记忆。当受试者被要求回忆起某段记忆的情感细节（正如我们这位医学生的经历）或回忆起自传体记忆时，气味似乎能发挥最佳作用。如果气味与记忆内容相符，效果会更好。例如，在电影测试中，如果实验室里弥漫着汽油味，其效果就远不如爆米花味。
Odors are not so good at retrieving declarative memory. Smell boosts declarative scores in only a couple of scenarios. It works if you’re emotionally aroused—usually, that means mildly stressed—before the experiment begins. For some reason, showing a film of young Australian aboriginal males being circumcised is a favorite way to do this. And it works if you’re asleep. Researchers used a version of a delightful card game my sons and I play on a regular basis. We use a deck of cards we purchased at a museum, resplendent with 26 pairs of animals. We turn all of the cards facedown, then start selecting two cards to find matches. It is a test of declarative memory. The one with the most correct pairs wins the game. In the experiment, the control groups played the game normally. But the experimental groups didn’t. They played the game in the presence of rose scent. Then everybody went to bed. The control groups slept unperturbed. Soon after the snoring began in the experimental groups, however, the researchers filled their rooms with the same rose scent. Upon awakening, the subjects were tested on their knowledge of where the matches had been discovered the previous day. The control group answered correctly 86 percent of the time. Those exposed and reexposed to the scent answered correctly 97 percent of the time. Brain imaging experiments showed the direct involvement of the hippocampus, that region of the brain deeply involved in memory. Smell, it appeared, enhanced recall during the offline brain processing that normally occurs during sleep.
气味在提取陈述性记忆方面效果并不理想。气味只有在少数情况下才能提升陈述性记忆得分。如果你在实验开始前情绪激动——通常这意味着轻微的压力——气味才会起作用。不知何故，播放澳大利亚原住民年轻男性接受割礼的影片是激发这种情绪的常用方法。而且，如果你处于睡眠状态，气味也有效。研究人员使用了一种我和儿子们经常玩的趣味纸牌游戏。我们用的是一副在博物馆买的纸牌，上面有26对动物图案。我们把所有牌面朝下，然后开始抽取两张牌来寻找匹配项。这是一种陈述性记忆测试。匹配对最多的人获胜。在实验中，对照组正常进行游戏。但实验组则不同。他们在玫瑰香味的环境中进行游戏。然后所有人都去睡觉了。对照组安然入睡。然而，实验组受试者开始打鼾后不久，研究人员便在他们的房间里弥漫了同样的玫瑰香味。醒来后，受试者被测试对前一天发现火柴地点的记忆。对照组的正确率为86%，而那些接触过玫瑰香味并再次接触过香味的受试者的正确率则高达97%。脑成像实验显示，海马体（大脑中与记忆密切相关的区域）直接参与了这一过程。看来，嗅觉增强了睡眠期间大脑离线处理过程中的记忆力。
Smell aside, there is no question that multiple cues, dished up via different senses, enhance learning. They speed up responses, increase accuracy, improve stimulation detection, and enrich encoding at the moment of learning.
撇开嗅觉不谈，毫无疑问，通过不同感官传递的多种线索能够促进学习。它们可以加快反应速度，提高准确性，改善刺激检测，并在学习过程中丰富信息编码。
More ideas
更多想法
Multimedia presentations
多媒体演示
Over the decades, Mayer has isolated a number of rules for multimedia presentations, linking what we know about working memory with his own empirical findings on how multimedia exposure affects human learning. Here are five of them, as he summarized in his book Multimedia Learning , useful for anyone giving a lecture, teaching a class, or creating a business presentation.
几十年来，梅耶总结了一系列多媒体演示规则，将我们对工作记忆的认知与他自身关于多媒体接触如何影响人类学习的实证研究结果联系起来。以下是他在其著作《多媒体学习》中总结的五条规则，对任何进行讲座、授课或制作商务演示文稿的人都很有帮助。
Multimedia principle: Students learn better from words and pictures than from words alone.
多媒体原理：学生从图文结合的方式学习效果比单纯的文字更好。
Temporal contiguity principle: Students learn better when corresponding words and pictures are presented simultaneously rather than successively.
时间邻近性原则：当相应的文字和图片同时呈现而不是先后呈现时，学生学习效果更好。
Spatial contiguity principle: Students learn better when corresponding words and pictures are presented near to each other rather than far from each other on the page or screen .
空间邻近性原则：当对应的文字和图片在纸上或屏幕上彼此靠近而不是彼此远离时，学生学习效果更好。
Coherence principle: Students learn better when extraneous material is excluded rather than included.
连贯性原则：排除无关内容比包含无关内容更有利于学生学习。
Modality principle: Students learn better from animation and narration than from animation and on-screen text.
模态原则：学生从动画和旁白中学习的效果优于从动画和屏幕文字中学习的效果。
Sensory branding
感官品牌
Author Judith Viorst once said, “Strength is the capacity to break a [chocolate] bar into four pieces … and then to eat just one of the pieces.” No doubt, smell affects motivation. Can it also affect the motivation to buy?
作家朱迪思·维奥斯特曾说过：“真正的力量在于能够把一块巧克力掰成四块……然后只吃掉其中一块。”毫无疑问，气味会影响人的动机。那么，气味是否也会影响购买动机呢？
One company tested the effects of smell on business and found a whopper of a result. Emitting the scent of chocolate from a vending machine, it found, drove chocolate sales up 60 percent. The same company installed a waffle-cone-smell emitter near a location-challenged ice cream shop: It was inside a large hotel and hard to find. Sales soared 50 percent, leading the inventor to coin the term “aroma billboard” to describe the technique.
一家公司测试了气味对商业的影响，结果令人震惊。他们发现，从自动售货机散发巧克力香味，竟使巧克力销量增长了60%。同一家公司还在一家位置偏僻的冰淇淋店附近安装了华夫饼筒香味发射器：这家冰淇淋店位于一家大型酒店内，很难找到。结果，冰淇淋销量飙升了50%，发明者因此创造了“香味广告牌”一词来描述这项技术。
Welcome to the world of sensory branding. Businesses are beginning to pay attention to human sensory responses, with smell as the centerpiece. For example, Starbucks does not allow employees to wear perfume on company time because it interferes with the seductive smell of the coffee they serve and its potential to attract customers.
欢迎来到感官品牌的世界。企业开始关注人类的感官反应，而嗅觉正是其中的核心。例如，星巴克不允许员工在工作时间使用香水，因为这会影响咖啡诱人的香气，从而影响咖啡吸引顾客的潜力。
Evidence for doing so comes from research by Dr. Eric Spangenberg, dean of the business school at Washington State University. Spangenberg knew from prior work that the male nose responds positively to the smell of rose maroc (spicy floral notes), the female nose to vanilla. What if he pumped rose maroc into the air of the men’s section at a clothing store and vanilla into the women’s section? Spangenberg hit pay dirt, generating twice the sales throughout the store. What if he then flipped the smells, introducing the male-preferred odor to the female section and vice versa? Spangenberg hit pay dirt again: Sales went down. “You can’t just use a pleasant scent and expect it to work,” Spangenberg explained in an interview with Fast Company . “It has to be congruent.”
华盛顿州立大学商学院院长埃里克·斯潘根伯格博士的研究为此提供了证据。斯潘根伯格此前的研究表明，男性对摩洛哥玫瑰（一种辛辣的花香调）的气味反应良好，而女性则对香草味更敏感。如果他在一家服装店的男装区喷洒摩洛哥玫瑰的香味，在女装区喷洒香草的香味，结果会怎样呢？斯潘根伯格大获成功，整个商店的销售额翻了一番。如果他反过来，将男性喜欢的香味引入女装区，反之亦然，结果又会怎样呢？斯潘根伯格再次大获成功：销售额下降了。“你不能仅仅使用一种令人愉悦的香味就指望它奏效，”斯潘根伯格在接受《快公司》采访时解释说，“它必须与顾客的需求相符。”
Smell also can be used to differentiate a brand. Enter any Subway fast-food restaurant blindfolded and you’d instantly know where you were. In choosing a scent to represent your brand, one newspaper article advises, consider the aspirations of your potential buyer. Realtors sometimes employ the smell of freshly baked bread or cookies during an open house to remind buyers of the comforts of home, for example. Also match the odor to the “personality” of the object for sale, the article suggests. For potential buyers browsing an SUV dealership, the fresh scent of a forest or the salty odor of a beach might evoke a sense of adventure more so than, say, the scent of vanilla.
气味也可以用来区分品牌。蒙上眼睛走进任何一家赛百味快餐店，你都能立刻知道自己身在何处。一篇报纸文章建议，在选择代表品牌的气味时，要考虑潜在买家的期望。例如，房地产经纪人有时会在开放日使用新鲜出炉的面包或饼干的香味，让买家想起家的舒适。文章还建议，气味要与待售物品的“个性”相匹配。对于正在浏览SUV经销店的潜在买家来说，森林的清新气息或海滩的咸味可能比香草味更能唤起他们的冒险感。
Research shows that the less complex the smell (the fewer interacting ingredients), the more likely it is to drive sales. Simpler smells drive sales 20 percent more than complex smells, or no smells at all.
研究表明，气味越简单（相互作用的成分越少），就越有可能促进销售。简单的气味比复杂的气味或无味更能促进销售，效果高出20%。
Smells at work (not coming from the fridge)
工作场所的异味（并非来自冰箱）
I occasionally teach a molecular biology class for engineers, and I decided to do my own little Proust experiment. (There was nothing rigorous about this little parlor trick; it was simply an informal inquiry.) Every time I taught a section on the enzyme RNA polymerase II, I prepped the room by squirting the perfume Brut on one wall. In an identical class in another building, I taught the same material, but I did not squirt Brut when describing the enzyme. Then I tested everybody, squirting the perfume into both classrooms. Every time I did this experiment, I got the same result. The students who were exposed to the perfume during learning did better on subject matter pertaining to the enzyme—sometimes dramatically better—than those who were not. And that led me to an idea. Many businesses have a need to teach their clients about their products, from how to implement software to how to repair engines. For financial reasons, the classes are often compressed in time and packed with information—90 percent of which is forgotten a day later. (For most declarative subjects, memory degradation starts the first few hours after the teaching is finished.) But what if you pair a smell with each lesson, as in my Brut experiment? Teachers could do this for the class as a whole, or you could do it on your own. You could spritz a bit of the scent near your pillow before you go to sleep, too. Overnight, you could not help but associate the autobiographical experience of the class—complete with the intense transfer of information—with the scent. Back at your company, when you need to apply what you learned, you could review your notes in the presence of the smell you encountered during the learning. See if it improves your performance, even cuts down on errors.
我偶尔会给工程师们上分子生物学课，于是我决定自己做一个小小的普鲁斯特实验。（这个小实验并不严谨，只是个非正式的探究。）每次讲到RNA聚合酶II时，我都会在教室的一面墙上喷洒一些香水，营造一种氛围。在另一栋楼里，我上同样的课，讲的也是同样的内容，但讲解酶的时候我没有喷香水。然后我做了个实验，把香水喷到两个教室里。每次做这个实验，结果都一样。那些在学习过程中接触过香水的学生，在讲解酶相关内容时表现得更好——有时甚至好得多。这让我想到一个问题。很多企业都需要向客户讲解他们的产品，从如何实施软件到如何维修发动机。出于成本考虑，这些课程通常时间很紧，信息量却很大——其中90%的内容第二天就被遗忘了。 （对于大多数陈述性学科，记忆衰退通常在教学结束后的几个小时内就开始了。）但如果像我的Brut实验那样，将一种气味与每节课结合起来呢？教师可以为全班学生这样做，你也可以自己尝试。睡前，你还可以在枕头附近喷洒一些这种气味。一夜之间，你就会不由自主地将课堂上的亲身经历——包括信息密集吸收的过程——与这种气味联系起来。回到公司后，当你需要运用所学知识时，你可以在闻到课堂上闻到的气味的环境下复习笔记。看看这是否能提高你的工作效率，甚至减少错误。
Is this context-dependent learning (remember those deep-sea divers from the Memory chapter) or a true multisensory environment? Either way, it’s a start toward thinking about learning environments that go beyond our usual addiction to images and sounds.
这是情境依赖型学习（还记得“记忆”章节中提到的深海潜水员吗？）还是真正的多感官学习环境？无论如何，这都是我们开始思考超越以往对图像和声音依赖的学习环境的开端。
Brain Rule # 8
大脑法则第8条
Stimulate more of the senses at the same time.
同时刺激多种感官。
• We absorb information about an event through our senses, translate it into electrical signals (some for sight, others from sound, etc.), disperse those signals to separate parts of the brain, then reconstruct what happened, eventually perceiving the event as a whole.
•我们通过感官吸收有关事件的信息，将其转化为电信号（有些来自视觉，有些来自听觉等），将这些信号分散到大脑的不同部分，然后重建所发生的事情，最终将事件感知为一个整体。
• The brain seems to rely partly on past experience in deciding how to combine these signals, so two people can perceive the same event very differently.
•大脑似乎部分依赖于过去的经验来决定如何组合这些信号，因此两个人对同一事件的感知可能截然不同。
• Our senses evolved to work together—vision influencing hearing, for example—which means that we learn best if we stimulate several senses at once.
•我们的感官进化是为了协同工作——例如视觉影响听觉——这意味着如果我们同时刺激多种感官，学习效果会更好。
• Smells have an unusual power to bring back memories, maybe because smell signals bypass the thalamus and head straight to their destinations, which include that supervisor of emotions known as the amygdala .
•气味具有唤起记忆的非凡力量，这可能是因为气味信号绕过了丘脑，直接到达目的地，其中包括负责情绪的杏仁核。
# ↩
vision
想象
Brain Rule #9
大脑法则#9
Vision trumps all other senses.
视觉凌驾于其他所有感官之上。
# ↩
WE DO NOT SEE with our eyes. We see with our brains.
我们并非用眼睛看，而是用大脑看。
The evidence lies with a group of 54 wine aficionados.
证据来自 54 位葡萄酒爱好者。
Stay with me here. To the untrained ear, the vocabularies that wine tasters use to describe wine may seem pretentious, more reminiscent of a psychologist describing a patient. (“Aggressive complexity, with just a subtle hint of shyness” is something I once heard at a wine-tasting soirée to which I was mistakenly invited—and from which, once picked off the floor rolling with laughter, I was hurriedly escorted out the door.)
请听我细细道来。对于不熟悉葡萄酒的人来说，品酒师用来描述葡萄酒的词汇可能显得矫揉造作，更像是心理学家描述病人。（“复杂而富有攻击性，又略带一丝羞涩”——我曾在一次误打误撞受邀参加的品酒会上听到过这样的说法——结果我笑得前仰后合，被人匆匆请出了门。）
These words are taken very seriously by the professionals, however. A specific vocabulary exists for white wines and a specific vocabulary for red wines, and the two are never supposed to cross. Given how individually we each perceive any sense, I have often wondered how objective these tasters actually could be. So, apparently, did a group of brain researchers in Europe. They descended upon ground zero of the wine-tasting world, the University of Bordeaux, and asked: “What if we dropped odorless, tasteless red dye into white wines, then gave it to 54 wine-tasting professionals?” With only visual sense altered, how would the enologists now describe their wine? Would their delicate palates see through the ruse, or would their noses be fooled? The answer is “their noses would be fooled.” When the wine tasters encountered the altered whites, every one of them employed the vocabulary of the reds. The visual inputs overrode their other highly trained senses. Folks in the scientific community had a field day. Professional research papers were published with titles like “The Color of Odors” and “The Nose Smells What the Eye Sees.” That’s about as much frat-boy behavior as prestigious brain journals tolerate, and you can almost see the wicked gleam in the researchers’ eyes. Studies such as these point to the nuts and bolts of Brain Rule #9. Visual processing doesn’t just assist in the perception of our world. It dominates the perception of our world.
然而，专业人士对这些词汇却极其重视。白葡萄酒和红葡萄酒分别有各自的专属词汇，两者之间绝不应混用。鉴于每个人对感官的感知都各不相同，我常常怀疑这些品酒师的客观性究竟如何。显然，欧洲的一群脑科学研究人员也抱有同样的疑问。他们来到葡萄酒品鉴界的圣地——波尔多大学，提出了这样一个问题：“如果我们在白葡萄酒中加入无色无味的红色染料，然后让54位专业的葡萄酒品鉴师品尝，结果会如何？” 仅仅改变视觉感官，这些酿酒师会如何描述他们的葡萄酒？他们灵敏的味蕾能否识破这种伎俩，还是会被他们的鼻子蒙蔽？答案是“他们的鼻子会被蒙蔽”。当品酒师们品尝到这些经过处理的白葡萄酒时，他们每个人都使用了描述红葡萄酒的词汇。视觉信息压倒了他们其他高度训练的感官。科学界对此大为兴奋。一些专业研究论文的标题诸如《气味的颜色》和《鼻子闻到眼睛所见的气味》。这种略显幼稚的学术行为，几乎是权威脑科学期刊所能容忍的极限了，你几乎都能看到研究人员眼中闪烁的狡黠光芒。诸如此类的研究揭示了大脑法则第九条的精髓：视觉处理不仅辅助我们感知世界，它还主导着我们对世界的感知。
Not like a camera
不像相机
Many people think that the brain’s visual system works like a camera, simply collecting and processing the raw visual data provided by our outside world. Seeing seems effortless, 100 percent trustworthy, capable of providing a completely accurate representation of what’s actually out there. Though we are used to thinking about our vision in such reliable terms, nothing in that last sentence is true. The process is extremely complex, seldom provides a completely accurate representation of our world, and is not 100 percent trustworthy. We actually experience our visual environment as a fully analyzed opinion about what the brain thinks is out there.
许多人认为大脑的视觉系统就像一台摄像机，简单地收集和处理来自外部世界的原始视觉数据。视觉似乎毫不费力，百分之百可靠，能够完全准确地呈现我们真实世界的面貌。尽管我们习惯于用如此可靠的方式看待视觉，但这句话其实并不完全正确。视觉过程极其复杂，很少能完全准确地呈现我们所处的世界，也并非百分之百可靠。实际上，我们所体验到的视觉环境，是大脑对外界事物进行全面分析后得出的结果。
It starts with the retina, vying for the title of amateur filmmaker. We used to think the retina acted like a passive antenna in an automated process: First, light (groups of photons, actually) enters our eyes, where it is bent by the cornea, the fluid-filled structure upon which your contacts normally sit. The light travels through the eye to the lens, where it is focused and allowed to strike the retina, a group of neurons in the back of the eye. The collision generates electric signals in these cells, and the signals travel to the back of the brain via the optic nerve for analysis. But, it turns out, the retina isn’t just waving through a series of unaltered electric signals. Instead, specialized nerve cells deep within the retina interpret the patterns of photons, assemble the patterns into a collection of “movies,” and then send these movies for analysis. The retina, it seems, is filled with teams of tiny Martin Scorseses. These movies are called tracks.
一切始于视网膜，它仿佛在争夺“业余电影制作人”的称号。我们过去认为视网膜就像一个被动的天线，参与着一个自动化的过程：首先，光（实际上是光子群）进入我们的眼睛，被角膜（通常隐形眼镜所在的充满液体的结构）折射。光线穿过眼球到达晶状体，在那里聚焦并照射到视网膜上——位于眼球后部的一组神经元。碰撞在这些细胞中产生电信号，这些信号通过视神经传递到大脑后部进行分析。但事实证明，视网膜并非只是简单地传递一系列未经处理的电信号。相反，视网膜深处的特殊神经细胞会解读光子的模式，将这些模式组合成一系列“电影”，然后将这些电影发送出去进行分析。视网膜上似乎充满了无数个微型的马丁·斯科塞斯。这些电影被称为“轨迹”。
Tracks are coherent, though partial, abstractions of specific features of the visual environment. One track appears to transmit a movie you might call Eye Meets Wireframe . It is composed only of outlines, or edges. Another makes a film you might call Eye Meets Motion , processing only the movement of an object (and often in a specific direction). Another makes Eye Meets Shadows . There may be as many as 12 of these tracks operating simultaneously in the retina, sending off interpretations of specific features of the visual field. This new view is quite unexpected. It’s like discovering that the reason your TV gives you feature films is that your cable is infested by a dozen independent filmmakers, hard at work creating the feature while you watch it.
这些“轨迹”是对视觉环境特定特征的连贯但又不完整的抽象。其中一条轨迹似乎在传输一段你可以称之为“眼见线框”的影片，它只由轮廓或边缘构成。另一条轨迹则生成一段你可以称之为“眼见运动”的影片，它只处理物体的运动（通常是特定方向的运动）。还有一条轨迹生成一段“眼见阴影”的影片。视网膜上可能同时存在多达12条这样的轨迹，它们各自对视觉场域特定特征进行解读。这种新观点相当出乎意料。这就像发现你的电视之所以播放故事片，是因为你的有线电视频道里挤满了十几位独立电影制作人，他们在你观看的同时辛勤地制作着这些故事片。
Rivers of visual information
视觉信息的河流
These movies now stream out from the optic nerve, one from each eye, and flood the thalamus, that egg-shaped structure in the middle of our heads that serves as a central distribution center for most of our senses. If these streams of visual information can be likened to a large, flowing river, the thalamus can be likened to the beginning of a delta. Once the information leaves the thalamus, it travels along increasingly divided neural streams. Eventually, thousands of small neural tributaries will be carrying parts of the original information to the back of the brain. (Put your hand on the back of your head. Your palm is now less than a quarter of an inch away from the visual cortex, the area of the brain that is currently allowing you to see these words.) The information drains into a large complex region within the occipital lobe called the visual cortex.
这些影像现在从视神经（每只眼睛各一条）流出，涌入丘脑——位于我们头部中央的卵形结构，它是我们大部分感官信息的中央分配中心。如果把这些视觉信息流比作一条奔流不息的大河，那么丘脑就像是三角洲的源头。信息离开丘脑后，会沿着越来越分支的神经通路传递。最终，成千上万条细小的神经支流会将原始信息的一部分传递到大脑后部。（把手放在后脑勺上。你的手掌现在距离视觉皮层不到四分之一英寸，视觉皮层是大脑中让你看到这些文字的区域。）这些信息最终汇入枕叶内一个被称为视觉皮层的复杂区域。
Once they reach the visual cortex, the various streams flow into specific parcels. There are thousands of lots, and their functions are almost ridiculously specific. Some parcels respond only to diagonal lines, and only to specific diagonal lines (one region responds to a line tilted at 40 degrees, but not to one tilted at 45 degrees). Some process only the color information in a visual signal; others, only edges; others, only motion.
一旦信号到达视觉皮层，各种信息流就会汇入特定的脑区。脑区成千上万，它们的功能几乎精细得令人难以置信。有些脑区只对斜线有反应，而且只对特定的斜线有反应（例如，某个区域对倾斜40度的斜线有反应，但对倾斜45度的斜线没有反应）。有些脑区只处理视觉信号中的颜色信息；有些只处理边缘信息；还有一些只处理运动信息。
This means you can damage the region of the brain in charge of, say, motion, and get an extraordinary deficit. You’d be able to see and identify objects quite clearly, but not tell whether the objects are stationary or moving. This happened to a patient known to scientists as L.M. It’s called cerebral akinetopsia, or motion blindness. L.M. perceives a moving object as a progressive series of still snapshots—like looking at an animator’s drawings one page at a time. This can be quite hazardous. When L.M. crosses the street, for example, she can see a car, but she does not know if it is actually coming at her.
这意味着，如果大脑中负责运动感知的区域受损，就可能导致严重的认知缺陷。患者能够清晰地看到并识别物体，但却无法判断物体是静止的还是运动的。一位名叫L.M.的患者就患有这种疾病。这种疾病被称为脑性运动盲症，或运动性盲。L.M.将运动物体感知为一系列连续的静止画面——就像一页一页地看动画师的画作一样。这种情况非常危险。例如，当L.M.过马路时，她可以看到一辆车，但她无法判断这辆车是否真的会朝她驶来。
L.M.’s experience illustrates just how modular visual processing is. And if that was the end of the visual story, we might perceive our world with the unorganized fury of a Picasso painting—a nightmare of fragmented objects, untethered colors, and strange, unboundaried edges. But that’s not what happens, because of what takes place next. The brain reassembles the scattered information. Individual tributaries start recombining, merging, pooling their information, comparing their findings, and then sending their analysis to higher brain centers. The centers gather these hopelessly intricate calculations from many sources and integrate them at an even more sophisticated level. Higher and higher they go, eventually collapsing into two giant streams of processed information. One of these, called the ventral stream, recognizes what an object is and what color it possesses. The other, termed the dorsal stream, recognizes the location of the object in the visual field and whether it is moving .
L.M.的经历恰恰说明了视觉处理的模块化程度。如果视觉故事到此结束，我们或许会像毕加索的画作那样，以杂乱无章的狂暴视角来感知世界——支离破碎的物体、混乱无序的色彩和怪异无界的边缘，构成一场噩梦。但事实并非如此，因为接下来发生的事情会让我们更清楚地了解世界。大脑会重新组装这些分散的信息。各个信息通路开始重组、融合、汇集信息，比较结果，然后将分析结果发送到更高级的大脑中枢。这些中枢从多个来源收集极其复杂的计算结果，并在更高层次上进行整合。信息不断向上传递，最终汇聚成两大信息流。其中一条被称为腹侧通路，负责识别物体是什么以及它是什么颜色。另一条被称为背侧通路，负责识别物体在视野中的位置以及它是否在移动。
“Association cortices” do the work of integrating the signals. They associate—or, better to say, reassociate—the balkanized electrical signals. Then you see something. So the process of vision is not as simple as a camera taking a picture. The process is more complex and more convoluted than anyone could have imagined. There is no real scientific agreement about why this disassembly and reassembly strategy occurs.
“联合皮层”负责整合这些信号。它们将原本分散的电信号关联起来——或者更准确地说，是重新关联起来。然后你就能看到东西了。所以，视觉过程并非像相机拍照那么简单。它比任何人想象的都要复杂得多。至于这种拆解和重组策略背后的原因，科学界目前还没有真正的共识。
Complex as visual processing is, things are about to get worse.
视觉处理已经很复杂了，但情况即将变得更糟。
You’re hallucinating right now
你现在出现幻觉了。
You might inquire whether I had too much to drink if I told you right now that you were actively hallucinating. But it’s true. At this very moment, while reading this text, you are perceiving parts of this page that do not exist. Which means you, my friend, are hallucinating. I am about to show you that your brain actually likes to make things up, that it is not 100 percent faithful to what the eyes broadcast to it.
如果我告诉你你现在正在产生幻觉，你可能会问我是不是喝多了。但这是真的。就在此刻，当你阅读这段文字时，你感知到的某些内容并不存在。也就是说，我的朋友，你正在产生幻觉。接下来，我要向你证明，你的大脑其实喜欢编造一些东西，它并非百分之百忠实于眼睛所接收到的信息。
Blind spots
盲点
There is a region in the eye where retinal neurons, carrying visual information, gather together to begin their journey into deep brain tissue. That gathering place is called the optic disk. It’s a strange region, because there are no cells that can perceive sight in the optic disk. It is blind in that region—and you are, too. It is called the blind spot, and each eye has one. Do you ever see two black holes in your field of view that won’t go away? That’s what you should see. But your brain plays a trick on you. As the signals are sent to your visual cortex, the brain detects the presence of the holes, examines the visual information 360 degrees around the spot, and calculates what is most likely to be there. Then, like a paint program on a computer, it fills in the spot. The process is called “filling in,” but it could be called “faking it.” Some scientists believe that the brain simply ignores the lack of visual information, rather than calculating what’s missing. Either way, you’re not getting a 100 percent accurate representation.
眼睛里有一个区域，视网膜神经元在这里聚集，它们携带视觉信息，然后开始向大脑深层组织传递信息。这个聚集点叫做视盘。这是一个很奇特的区域，因为视盘上没有任何细胞能够感知视觉。这个区域是盲区——你也是。它被称为盲点，每只眼睛都有一个。你是否曾经在视野中看到两个挥之不去的黑洞？你应该看到的就是这两个黑洞。但你的大脑会欺骗你。当信号传递到视觉皮层时，大脑会检测到盲点的存在，检查盲点周围360度的视觉信息，并计算出最有可能存在的信息。然后，就像电脑上的绘图程序一样，大脑会把盲点填满。这个过程被称为“填充”，但也可以称之为“假装”。一些科学家认为，大脑只是忽略了视觉信息的缺失，而不是计算缺失的信息。无论如何，你看到的都不是百分之百准确的视觉信息。
Dreams during the night—or day
夜间或白天的梦
It should not surprise you that the brain possesses an imaging system with a mind of its own. Proof is as close as your most recent dream. (There’s a hallucination for you.) Actually, the visual system is even more of a loose cannon than that. Millions of people suffer from a phenomenon known as the Charles Bonnet Syndrome. Most who have it keep their mouth shut, however, and perhaps with good reason. People with Charles Bonnet Syndrome see things that aren’t there.
大脑拥有一个仿佛拥有独立意识的成像系统，这应该不会让你感到惊讶。你最近的梦境就是最好的证明。（没错，这就是幻觉。）事实上，视觉系统比这还要难以捉摸。数以百万计的人患有一种被称为查尔斯·邦内综合征的疾病。然而，大多数患者都对此保持沉默，或许这也不无道理。查尔斯·邦内综合征患者会看到一些并不存在的事物。
Everyday household objects suddenly pop into view. Or unfamiliar people unexpectedly appear next to them at dinner. Neurologist Vilayanur Ramachandran describes the case of a woman who suddenly—and delightfully—observed two tiny policemen scurrying across the floor, guiding an even smaller criminal to a matchbox-size van. Other patients have reported angels, goats in overcoats, clowns, Roman chariots, and elves. The illusions often occur in the evening and are usually quite benign. Charles Bonnet Syndrome is common among the elderly, especially among those who previously suffered damage somewhere along their visual pathway. Interestingly, almost all of the patients know that the hallucinations aren’t real.
日常家居物品会突然出现在眼前。或者，在晚餐时，陌生人会出乎意料地出现在身边。神经学家维拉亚努尔·拉马钱德兰描述了一个案例：一位女士突然——而且欣喜地——看到两个小警察在地板上奔跑，押着一个更小的罪犯走向一辆火柴盒大小的货车。其他患者也报告过看到天使、穿着大衣的山羊、小丑、罗马战车和精灵。这些幻觉通常发生在晚上，而且通常无害。查尔斯·邦内综合征在老年人中很常见，尤其是在那些视觉通路曾受过损伤的老年人中。有趣的是，几乎所有患者都知道这些幻觉并非真实存在。
A camel in each eye
每只眼睛里都有一只骆驼
Besides filling in our blind spots and creating bizarre dreams, the brain has another way of participating in our visual experience. We have two eyes, each taking in a full scene, yet the brain creates a single visual perception. Since ancient times, people have wondered why. If there is a camel in your left eye and a camel in your right eye, why don’t you perceive two camels? Here’s an experiment to try that illustrates the issue nicely .
除了填补视觉盲点和创造奇特的梦境之外，大脑还有另一种参与我们视觉体验的方式。我们有两只眼睛，每只眼睛都能看到完整的场景，但大脑最终只会形成一个单一的视觉感知。自古以来，人们就一直在思考这是为什么。如果你的左眼看到一头骆驼，右眼也看到一头骆驼，为什么你不会看到两头骆驼呢？这里有一个实验可以很好地说明这个问题。
1) Point your left index finger to the sky. Touch your nose and then stretch your left arm out.
1）伸出左手食指指向天空。摸摸鼻子，然后伸直左臂。
2) Point your right index finger to the sky. Touch your nose and then move your finger about six inches away from your face.
2）伸出你的右手食指指向天空。用手指触摸你的鼻子，然后将手指移离脸部约六英寸。
3) Both fingers should be in line with each other, directly in front of your nose.
3）两根手指应并拢，位于鼻子的正前方。
