4) Now speedily wink your left eye and then your right one. Do this several times, back and forth. Your right finger will jump to the other side of your left finger and back again. When you open both eyes, the jumping will stop.
4）现在快速眨一下左眼，再快速眨一下右眼。来回重复几次。你的右手手指会跳到左手手指的另一侧，然后再跳回来。当你睁开双眼时，这种跳动就会停止。
This little experiment shows that the two images appearing on each retina always differ. It also shows that both eyes working together give the brain enough information to create one stable picture. One camel. Two non-jumping fingers. How?
这个小实验表明，出现在每只视网膜上的两个图像总是不同的。它还表明，双眼协同工作可以为大脑提供足够的信息，从而形成一幅稳定的图像。一只骆驼。两根不动的手指。这是怎么做到的？
The brain interpolates the information coming from both eyes. Just to make things more complicated, each eye has its own visual field, and they project their images upside down and backward. The brain makes about a gazillion calculations, then provides you its best guess. And it is a guess. You can actually show that the brain doesn’t really know where things are. Rather, it hypothesizes the probability of what the current event should look like and then, taking a leap of faith, approximates a viewable image. What you experience is not the image. What you experience is the leap of faith.
大脑会综合考虑来自双眼的信息。更复杂的是，每只眼睛都有各自的视野，而且它们投射的图像是上下颠倒、左右反转的。大脑会进行无数次计算，然后给出它认为最合适的估计。而这仅仅是估计。实际上，你可以证明大脑并不真正知道物体在哪里。它只是假设当前事件可能呈现的概率，然后凭借一种“信念飞跃”，近似地呈现出一个可见的图像。你所体验到的并非图像本身，而是这种“信念飞跃”。
The brain does this because it needs to solve a problem: The world is three-dimensional, but light falls on the retina in a two-dimensional fashion. The brain must deal with this disparity if it is going to portray the world with any accuracy. To make sense of it all, the brain is forced to start guessing. Upon what does the brain base its guesses, at least in part? Experience with past events. After inserting numerous assumptions about the visual information (some of these assumptions may be inborn), the brain then offers up its findings for your perusal. Now you see one camel when there really is only one camel—and you see its proper depth and shape and size and even hints about whether it will bite you.
大脑之所以这样做，是因为它需要解决一个问题：世界是三维的，但光线以二维的方式照射到视网膜上。如果大脑想要准确地描绘世界，就必须处理这种差异。为了理解这一切，大脑不得不开始猜测。那么，大脑的猜测至少部分基于什么呢？是过去的经验。在对视觉信息做出诸多假设（其中一些假设可能是与生俱来的）之后，大脑会将结果呈现给你。现在，你看到一头骆驼，而实际上也只有一头骆驼——你能看到它应有的深度、形状、大小，甚至还能感受到它是否会咬你的暗示。
Far from being a camera, the brain is actively deconstructing the information given to it by the eyes, pushing it through a series of filters, and then reconstructing what it thinks it sees. Or what it thinks you should see. All of this happens in about the time it takes to blink your eyes. Indeed, it is happening right now. If you think the brain has to devote to vision a lot of its precious thinking resources, you are right on the money. Visual processing takes up about half of everything your brain does, in fact. This helps explain why professional wine tasters toss aside their taste buds so quickly in the thrall of visual stimuli. And why vision affects other senses, too.
大脑远非一台相机，它一直在积极地解构眼睛接收到的信息，将其通过一系列过滤，然后重构它认为自己看到的东西，或者说是它认为你应该看到的东西。这一切都发生在眨眼的瞬间。事实上，它此刻正在发生。如果你认为大脑必须将大量宝贵的思维资源用于视觉处理，那么你的想法完全正确。事实上，视觉处理占据了大脑所有活动大约一半的时间。这有助于解释为什么专业的品酒师会在视觉刺激的驱动下迅速忽略味蕾的感受，以及为什么视觉也会影响其他感官。
Vision trumps touch, not just smell and taste
视觉胜过触觉，而不仅仅是嗅觉和味觉。
Amputees sometimes continue to experience the presence of their limb, even though the limb no longer exists. In some cases, the limb is perceived as frozen into a fixed position. Sometimes the person feels pain in the limb. Studies of people with phantom limbs demonstrate the powerful influence vision has on our other senses.
截肢患者有时即使肢体已不复存在，仍然会感觉到肢体的存在。在某些情况下，肢体会被感觉冻结在某个固定位置。有时，患者还会感到肢体疼痛。对幻肢患者的研究表明，视觉对其他感官有着强大的影响。
In one experiment, an amputee with a “frozen” phantom arm was seated at a table upon which had been placed a lidless box divided in half. The box had two portals in the front, one for the arm and one for the stump. The divider was a mirror on both sides. So the amputee could view a reflection of either his functioning hand or his stump. When the man looked down into the box, he could see his right arm present and his left arm missing. But when he looked at the reflection of his right arm in the mirror, he saw what looked like another arm. Suddenly, the phantom limb on the other side of the box “woke up.” If he moved his normal hand while gazing at its reflection, he could feel his phantom move, too. And when he stopped moving his right arm, he felt his missing left arm stop also. The addition of visual information began convincing his brain of a miraculous rebirth of the absent limb .
在一项实验中，一位截肢患者坐在桌旁，桌上放着一个没有盖子的盒子，盒子被分成两半。盒子正面有两个开口，一个用来放置手臂，另一个用来放置残肢。隔板两侧都是镜子。因此，截肢患者可以看到自己健全的手或残肢的倒影。当他低头看向盒子时，他可以看到自己的右臂还在，而左臂缺失。但是，当他看向镜子中右臂的倒影时，他看到了另一只手臂。突然，盒子另一侧的幻肢“苏醒”了。如果他一边看着镜子里的倒影一边移动健全的手，他就能感觉到幻肢也在动。当他停止移动右臂时，他也能感觉到缺失的左臂也停止了动。视觉信息的加入开始让他的大脑相信缺失的肢体奇迹般地重生了。
A picture really is worth a thousand words
一张图胜过千言万语
One way we can measure the dominance of vision is to look at its effect on learning. Researchers study this using two types of memory.
衡量视觉主导地位的一种方法是观察它对学习的影响。研究人员使用两种类型的记忆来研究这一点。
The first is called recognition memory, which underlies the concept of familiarity. We often deploy recognition memory when looking at old family photographs. Maybe you see a photo of an aunt not remembered for years. You don’t necessarily recall her name, or the photo, but you still recognize her as your aunt. With recognition memory, you may not recall certain details surrounding whatever you see, but as soon as you see it, you know that you have seen it before.
第一种叫做识别记忆，它是熟悉感的基础。我们经常在翻看老照片时运用识别记忆。也许你看到一张多年未见的姑姑的照片。你未必记得她的名字，也未必记得这张照片，但你仍然认出她是你的姑姑。有了识别记忆，你可能记不起所见事物的某些细节，但你一看到它，就知道你以前见过它。
The second involves working memory. Explained in greater detail in the Memory chapter, working memory is that collection of temporary storage buffers with fixed capacities and frustratingly short life spans. Visual short-term memory is the slice of that buffer dedicated to storing visual information. Most of us can hold the memory of about four objects at a time in that buffer, so it’s a pretty small space. And it appears to be getting smaller. As the complexity of objects in our world increases, we are capable of remembering fewer objects over our lifetimes. Evidence also suggests that the number of objects and complexity of objects are engaged by different systems in the brain—turning the whole notion of short-term capacity, if you will forgive me, on its head. These limitations make it all the more remarkable that vision is probably the best single tool we have for learning anything.
第二点涉及工作记忆。在“记忆”章节中有更详细的解释，工作记忆是一系列容量固定、寿命短暂的临时存储缓冲区。视觉短期记忆是专门用于存储视觉信息的部分。我们大多数人一次只能在这个缓冲区中记住大约四个物体，所以空间非常有限。而且，这个空间似乎还在不断缩小。随着我们所处世界物体的复杂性增加，我们一生中能够记住的物体数量也越来越少。有证据表明，物体的数量和复杂性是由大脑中不同的系统处理的——恕我直言，这彻底颠覆了我们对短期记忆容量的传统认知。正是由于这些限制，视觉或许是我们学习任何事物的最佳工具，这一点才显得更加令人惊叹。
When it comes to both recognition memory and working memory, pictures and text follow very different rules. Put simply, the more visual the input becomes, the more likely it is to be recognized—and recalled. It’s called the pictorial superiority effect. Researchers have known about it for more than 100 years. (This is why we created a series of videos and animations of the Brain Rules at www.brainrules.net , making this book just one part of a multimedia project. )
无论是识别记忆还是工作记忆，图片和文字遵循着截然不同的规则。简而言之，输入的信息越是视觉化，就越容易被识别和回忆起来。这被称为图像优势效应。研究人员对此现象已经了解超过100年。（正因如此，我们在www.brainrules.net网站上制作了一系列关于大脑规则的视频和动画，本书只是这个多媒体项目的一部分。）
The pictorial superiority effect is truly Olympian. Tests performed years ago showed that people could remember more than 2,500 pictures with at least 90 percent accuracy several days later, even though subjects saw each picture for about 10 seconds. (This is recognition memory, not working memory, at work.) Accuracy rates a year later still hovered around 63 percent. In one paper, picture recognition information was reliably retrieved several decades later. Sprinkled throughout these experiments were comparisons with text or oral presentations. The usual result was “picture demolishes them both.” It still does. Text and oral presentations are not just less efficient than pictures for retaining certain types of information; they are far less efficient. If information is presented orally, people remember about 10 percent, tested 72 hours after exposure. That figure goes up to 65 percent if you add a picture.
图片优势效应堪称卓越。多年前的测试表明，即使受试者每张图片只观看约10秒，几天后人们仍能以至少90%的准确率记住超过2500张图片。（这是识别记忆而非工作记忆在起作用。）一年后，准确率仍然徘徊在63%左右。在一篇论文中，人们甚至在几十年后仍能可靠地回忆起图片识别信息。这些实验中穿插着与文本或口头陈述的比较。通常的结果是“图片完胜两者”。时至今日，情况依然如此。文本和口头陈述在记忆某些类型的信息方面不仅不如图片有效，而且效率远低于图片。如果信息以口头形式呈现，人们在接触72小时后测试时，只能记住约10%。但如果加上图片，这个数字会上升到65%。
Why is text less efficient than pictures? Because, it turns out, the brain sees words as lots of tiny pictures. A word is unreadable unless the brain can separately identify simple features in the letters. Instead of words, we see complex little art-museum masterpieces, with hundreds of features embedded in hundreds of letters. Like an art junkie, our brains linger at each feature, rigorously and independently verifying it before moving to the next. So reading creates a bottleneck in comprehension. To our cortex, surprisingly, there is no such thing as words.
为什么文字的效率不如图片？原来，大脑把文字看作是许多微小的图像。除非大脑能够分别识别字母中的简单特征，否则文字就无法被理解。我们看到的不是文字，而是复杂的小型艺术博物馆杰作，数百个字母中嵌入了数百个特征。就像艺术爱好者一样，我们的大脑会在每个特征上停留片刻，严格且独立地验证它，然后再处理下一个特征。因此，阅读会造成理解的瓶颈。令人惊讶的是，在我们的大脑皮层看来，文字并不存在。
That’s not necessarily obvious. After all, the brain is as adaptive as Silly Putty. Given your years of reading books, writing email, and sending text messages, you might think your visual system could be trained to recognize common words without slogging through tedious additional steps of letter-feature recognition. But that is not what happens. No matter how experienced a reader you become, your brain will still stop and ponder the individual features of each letter you read—and do so until you can’t read anymore.
这一点并非显而易见。毕竟，大脑的适应能力就像橡皮泥一样有限。鉴于你多年来阅读书籍、撰写电子邮件和发送短信，你可能会认为你的视觉系统可以训练成无需经历繁琐的字母特征识别步骤就能识别常用词汇。但事实并非如此。无论你的阅读经验多么丰富，你的大脑仍然会停下来思考你所阅读的每个字母的特征——直到你无法再阅读为止。
By now, you can probably guess why this might be. Our evolutionary history was never dominated by books or email or text messages. It was dominated by trees and saber-toothed tigers. Vision means so much to us because most of the major threats to our lives in the savannah were apprehended visually. Ditto with most of our food supplies. Ditto with our perceptions of reproductive opportunity.
现在，你大概能猜到原因了。我们的进化史从来都不是被书籍、电子邮件或短信所主导的，而是被树木和剑齿虎所主导的。视觉对我们至关重要，因为在稀树草原上，我们生存面临的大多数重大威胁都是通过视觉感知的。我们的大部分食物来源也是如此。我们对繁殖机会的感知也是如此。
The tendency is so pervasive that, even when we read, most of us try to visualize what the text is telling us. “Words are only postage stamps delivering the object for you to unwrap,” George Bernard Shaw was fond of saying. A lot of brain science now backs him up.
这种倾向如此普遍，以至于即使在阅读时，我们大多数人也会试图将文本内容形象化。“文字只不过是邮票，把包裹送到你手中，等着你去拆开，”萧伯纳曾这样说过。如今，许多脑科学研究也支持他的观点。
Vision is king from Day One
从第一天起，愿景就至关重要。
Babies come with a variety of preloaded software devoted to visual processing. We can determine what babies are paying attention to simply by watching them stare at their world. The importance of a baby’s gazing behavior cannot be underestimated.
婴儿天生就拥有各种用于视觉处理的预装软件。我们只需观察婴儿注视周围的世界，就能判断他们关注的焦点。婴儿的注视行为的重要性不容低估。
You can see this for yourself (if you have a baby nearby). Tie a ribbon around the baby’s leg. Tie the other end to a mobile. At first she seems to be randomly moving her limbs. Soon, however, the infant learns that if she moves one leg, the mobile turns. She begins happily—and preferentially—moving that leg. Bring back the same mobile the next week, and the baby will move the same leg. Show the baby a different mobile, and she won’t move the leg. That’s what scientists found when they did this experiment. The baby is paying the most attention to the visual aspects of the mobiles. Since the mobiles don’t look the same, there’s not much reason to assume they would act the same. Babies use these visual cues even though nobody taught them to do so. This illustrates the importance of visual processing to our species.
如果你身边有宝宝，你可以自己观察一下。用丝带绑住宝宝的腿，另一端系在婴儿床挂饰上。起初，宝宝似乎只是随意地挥动四肢。但很快，宝宝就会发现，如果她动一条腿，挂饰就会转动。于是，她开始兴高采烈地——而且是特别喜欢地——动那条腿。下周再拿出同样的挂饰，宝宝依然会动同一条腿。换个挂饰，宝宝就不会动腿了。科学家们在做这个实验时也发现了同样的现象。宝宝最关注的是挂饰的视觉特征。由于挂饰的外观各不相同，我们没有理由认为它们的作用方式会相同。宝宝会利用这些视觉线索，尽管没有人教过他们这样做。这说明视觉处理对我们人类来说至关重要。
Other evidence points to the same fact. Babies display a preference for patterns with high contrast. They seem to understand the principle of common fate: Objects that move together are perceived as part of the same object, such as stripes on a zebra. They can discriminate human faces from nonhuman equivalents and seem to prefer the human faces. They possess an understanding of size related to distance—that if an object is getting closer (and therefore getting bigger), it is still the same object. Babies can even categorize visual objects by common physical characteristics. The dominance of vision begins in the tiny world of infants.
其他证据也指向同样的事实。婴儿偏爱高对比度的图案。他们似乎理解“共同命运”原则：一起移动的物体会被感知为同一个物体的一部分，例如斑马身上的条纹。他们能够区分人脸和非人脸，并且似乎更喜欢人脸。他们理解物体大小与距离的关系——如果一个物体越来越近（因此也越来越大），它仍然是同一个物体。婴儿甚至可以根据共同的物理特征对视觉物体进行分类。视觉优势在婴儿的微小世界里就已经确立了。
It also shows up in the even tinier world of DNA. Our sense of smell and color vision are fighting each other for evolutionary control, for the right to be consulted first whenever something on the outside happens. And vision is winning. In fact, about 60 percent of our smell-related genes have been permanently damaged in this neural arbitrage, and they are marching toward obsolescence at a rate fourfold faster than any other species sampled. The reason for this decommissioning is simple: The visual cortex and the olfactory cortex take up a lot of neural real estate. In the crowded zero-sum world of the sub-scalp, something has to give. Does this mean that we’ll permanently lose our sense of smell or that our heads are no longer getting bigger? Check back in several hundred thousand years. The evolutionary forces that actively selected against smell are not still in full force today. But what forces are replacing them is an active area of debate.
这种现象甚至在更小的DNA世界中也有所体现。我们的嗅觉和色觉正在争夺进化控制权，争夺在外部世界发生任何变化时首先被感知的权利。而视觉正在胜出。事实上，在这场神经博弈中，我们大约60%的嗅觉相关基因已经永久性受损，它们正以比其他任何物种快四倍的速度走向淘汰。这种淘汰的原因很简单：视觉皮层和嗅觉皮层占据了大量的神经空间。在拥挤的皮层下零和博弈世界中，总要有所取舍。这是否意味着我们将永久失去嗅觉，或者我们的头部不再增大？几十万年后再来看看。曾经积极选择淘汰嗅觉的进化力量如今已不再完全有效。但究竟是什么力量正在取而代之，目前仍是一个活跃的争论领域。
Whether looking at behavior, cells, or genes, we can observe how important the visual sense is to the human experience. Striding across our brain like an out-of-control superpower, giant swaths of biological resources are consumed by it. In return, our visual system creates movies, generates hallucinations, and consults with previous information before allowing us to see the outside. It happily bends the information from other senses to do its bidding and, at least in the case of smell, seems to be caught in the act of taking over.
无论从行为、细胞还是基因的角度来看，我们都能观察到视觉对人类体验的重要性。它如同失控的超能力般横扫我们的大脑，消耗着大量的生物资源。作为回报，我们的视觉系统创造影像、产生幻觉，并在让我们看到外部世界之前参考先前的信息。它乐于扭曲其他感官的信息来为己所用，而且，至少在嗅觉方面，它似乎正在试图接管我们的感官。
When it comes to applying this knowledge in your own daily life, is there any point in trying to ignore the vision juggernaut? You don’t have to look any further than the wine experts of Bordeaux for the answer.
当要将这些知识运用到日常生活中时，试图忽视这种视觉冲击力巨大的趋势还有意义吗？答案就在波尔多葡萄酒专家的身上。
More ideas
更多想法
The best visuals for learning
最佳学习视觉效果
What kind of pictures best grab attention and thus transfer information? We pay lots of attention to color. We pay lots of attention to orientation. We pay lots of attention to size. And we pay special attention if the object is in motion. Indeed, most of the things that threatened us in the Serengeti moved , and the brain has evolved unbelievably sophisticated trip wires to detect motion. We even have specialized regions to distinguish when our eyes are moving versus when our world is moving. These regions routinely shut down perceptions of eye movement in favor of the environmental movement.
什么样的图片最能吸引注意力，从而传递信息？我们非常关注色彩，非常关注方向，非常关注大小。如果物体在运动，我们会格外关注。事实上，在塞伦盖蒂草原上，大多数威胁我们的事物都在移动，而我们的大脑也进化出了极其精密的机制来检测运动。我们甚至有专门的区域来区分眼球运动和周围环境的运动。这些区域会优先感知环境运动，而忽略眼球运动。
That said, we need more research into practical applications. The pictorial superiority effect is a well-established fact for certain types of classroom material, but not for all material. Data are sparse. Do pictures communicate conceptual ideas such as “freedom” and “amount” better than, say, a narrative? Are language arts better represented in picture form or using other media? It’s unclear.
尽管如此，我们仍需对实际应用进行更多研究。图像优势效应对于某些类型的课堂材料而言已得到证实，但并非所有材料都如此。相关数据十分匮乏。例如，图像是否比叙述更能有效地传达“自由”和“数量”等概念？语言艺术的呈现方式是更适合用图像还是其他媒介？目前尚不明确。
Include video or animation
包含视频或动画
I owe my career choice to Donald Duck. I am not joking. I even remember the moment he convinced me. I was 8 years old at the time, and my mother trundled the family off to a showing of an amazing 27-minute animated short called Donald in Mathmagic Land . Using visual imagery, a wicked sense of humor, and the wide-eyed wonder of an infant, Donald Duck introduced me to math. Got me excited about it. From geometry to football to playing billiards, the power and beauty of mathematics were made so real for this nerd-in-training, I asked if I could see it a second time. My mother obliged, and the effect was so memorable, it eventually influenced my career choice. I now have a copy of those valuable 27 minutes in my own home and regularly inflict it upon my poor children. Donald in Mathmagic Land won an Academy Award for best animated short of 1959. It also should have gotten a Teacher of the Year award. The film illustrates—literally—the power of the moving image in communicating complex information to students.
我的职业选择要归功于唐老鸭。我可不是开玩笑。我甚至还记得他是如何说服我的。那时我才8岁，妈妈带着全家去看了一部精彩绝伦的27分钟动画短片，叫做《唐老鸭的数学奇幻世界》。唐老鸭用生动的画面、幽默诙谐的风格，以及孩童般充满好奇的眼神，让我接触到了数学，并深深地爱上了它。从几何到足球再到台球，这部影片让数学的力量和美感如此真实地展现在我这个“准书呆子”面前，我忍不住要求再看一遍。妈妈答应了，而这部影片给我留下了深刻的印象，最终影响了我的职业选择。现在，我家里还珍藏着这部27分钟的动画短片，并且经常把它“折磨”给我的孩子们看。《唐老鸭的数学奇幻世界》荣获了1959年奥斯卡最佳动画短片奖。它甚至应该获得年度最佳教师奖。这部电影生动地展现了动态影像在向学生传达复杂信息方面的力量。
Animating presentations is another way to capture the importance not only of color and placement but also of motion. The basics are not hard to learn. With today’s software, anybody who knows how to draw a square and a circle can create simple animations. Simple two-dimensional pictures are quite adequate; studies show that if the drawings are too complex or lifelike, they can distract from the transfer of information.
制作动画演示文稿是另一种展现色彩、布局和动态效果重要性的方法。动画制作的基础知识并不难学。如今，只要会画正方形和圆形，任何人都能用现代软件制作简单的动画。简单的二维图像就足够了；研究表明，如果图像过于复杂或逼真，反而会分散观众对信息的注意力。
Communicate with pictures more than words
用图片而非语言进行交流
“Less text, more pictures” were almost fighting words in 1982. They were used derisively to greet the arrival of USA Today, a brand-new type of newspaper with, as you know, less text, more pictures. Some predicted the style would never work. Others predicted that if it did, the style would spell the end of Western civilization as the newspaper-reading public knows it. The jury may be out on the latter prediction, but the former has a powerful and embarrassing verdict. Within four years, USA Today had the second-highest readership of any newspaper in the country, and within 10 years, it was number one. It still is.
“少文字，多图片”在1982年几乎是一句带有挑衅意味的口号。当时，人们用这句话来嘲讽《今日美国》的创刊，这是一种全新的报纸形式，正如你所知，它以少文字、多图片为特色。有人预言这种风格永远不会成功。也有人预言，如果这种风格成功了，它将终结西方文明——就报纸读者而言。对于后一种预言，或许还有待商榷，但前一种预言却已得出令人震惊且尴尬的结论。《今日美国》在短短四年内就成为全美读者人数第二高的报纸，十年之内更是跃居榜首。时至今日，它依然保持着这一地位。
What happened? Pictorial information may be initially more attractive to consumers, in part because it takes less effort to comprehend. Because it is also a more efficient way to glue information to a neuron, there may be strong reasons for entire marketing departments to think seriously about making pictorial presentations their primary way of transferring information.
发生了什么？图像信息最初可能对消费者更具吸引力，部分原因是它更容易理解。由于图像信息能更有效地将信息传递到神经元，因此整个营销部门或许有充分的理由认真考虑将图像展示作为其主要的信息传递方式。
The initial effect of pictures on attention has been tested. Using infrared eye-tracking technology, 3,600 consumers were tested on 1,363 print advertisements. The conclusion? Pictorial information was superior in capturing attention—independent of its size. Even if the picture was small and crowded with lots of other nonpictorial elements close to it, the eye went to the visual.
图片对注意力的初步影响已得到验证。研究人员利用红外眼动追踪技术，对3600名消费者进行了测试，测试对象为1363份平面广告。结论是：无论图片大小，图像信息都能更有效地吸引注意力。即使图片很小，周围环绕着大量其他非图像元素，人们的目光仍然会被图像所吸引。
Toss your PowerPoint presentations
扔掉你的PPT演示文稿吧
The presentation software called PowerPoint has become ubiquitous, from work meetings to college classrooms to conferences. What’s wrong with that? They’re mostly text, even though they don’t have to be. A typical PowerPoint business presentation has nearly 40 words per slide . Please, do two things: (1) Burn your current PowerPoint presentations. (2) Make new ones. Then see which one works better.
从工作会议到大学课堂再到各种研讨会，名为 PowerPoint 的演示软件已经无处不在。这有什么问题呢？它们大多是文字，尽管并非必须如此。一份典型的 PowerPoint 商务演示文稿每张幻灯片就接近 40 个字。请做两件事：（1）销毁你现有的 PowerPoint 演示文稿。（2）制作新的演示文稿。然后看看哪种效果更好。
Brain Rule #9
大脑法则#9
Vision trumps all other senses.
视觉凌驾于其他所有感官之上。
• Vision is by far our most dominant sense, taking up half of our brain’s resources.
•视觉是我们最主要的感官，占据了我们大脑一半的资源。
• What we see is only what our brain tells us we see, and it’s not 100 percent accurate.
•我们所看到的只是我们的大脑告诉我们所看到的，它并不百分之百准确。
• The visual analysis we do has many steps. The retina assembles photons into movie-like streams of information. The visual cortex processes these streams: some areas registering motion, others registering color, etc. Finally, we recombine that information so that we can see.
•我们进行的视觉分析包含许多步骤。视网膜将光子组装成类似电影画面的信息流。视觉皮层处理这些信息流：一些区域记录运动，另一些区域记录颜色等等。最后，我们将这些信息重新组合，从而使我们能够看到东西。
• We learn and remember best through pictures, not through written or spoken words.
•我们通过图片学习和记忆的效果最好，而不是通过文字或口头语言。

music
音乐
Brain Rule #10
大脑法则第10条
Study or listen to boost cognition.
通过学习或聆听来提升认知能力。
# ↩
HENRY DRYER IS A 92-year-old dementia patient living in an assisted living center. Henry sits alone in a wheelchair in the middle of a room, eyes downcast, face empty. His body seems vacant too. In the documentary film featuring him, Henry is described by famed neurologist Oliver Sacks as “inert, maybe depressed, unresponsive, and almost unalive.” Henry has barely spoken to anyone in the decade he’s lived at the center. This is not how he used to be, his daughter relates. Henry was outgoing for most of his life, blessed with a passionate love affair for the Bible and for dancing and singing. It was not unusual for him to spontaneously burst out into song in public.
亨利·德莱尔是一位92岁的痴呆症患者，住在一家辅助生活中心。他独自坐在房间中央的轮椅上，双眼低垂，面无表情。他的身体似乎也空洞无物。在一部关于他的纪录片中，著名神经学家奥利弗·萨克斯形容亨利“麻木、或许有些抑郁、反应迟钝，几乎如同行尸走肉”。自从十年前住进这家中心以来，亨利几乎没跟任何人说过话。他的女儿说，这和他以前的样子截然不同。亨利一生大部分时间都性格外向，热爱《圣经》，也喜欢跳舞唱歌。他经常会在公共场合突然放声歌唱。
On this day, Henry is part of a project helping elderly people reconnect by listening to music they love. Henry is given an iPod loaded with music. As soon as Henry hears the music, Henry starts making a noise like a horn. Suddenly, Henry’s eyes grow wide. His face instantly lights up, a bit contorted. Henry grabs his wrists and starts swaying, smiling, and singing. Henry becomes alive .
这一天，亨利参与了一个帮助老年人通过聆听他们喜爱的音乐来重拾联系的项目。亨利拿到了一台装满音乐的iPod。音乐一响起，亨利就发出类似喇叭的声音。突然，亨利的眼睛睁得老大，脸上瞬间绽放出光彩，表情也有些扭曲。他抓住自己的手腕，开始摇摆，脸上带着笑容，唱起了歌。亨利仿佛活了过来。
When the iPod is turned off, Henry doesn’t slink back into silence. He becomes articulate, funny and very enthusiastic. “Do you like music?” someone asks off-camera. Henry answers, “I’m CRAZY about music. You play beautiful music. Beautiful sounds!” “What was your favorite music when you were young?” Cab Calloway, Henry responds, then starts scatting. He sings, “I’ll Be Home for Christmas” with accurate pitch, wonderful emotion, and occasionally correct lyrics.
iPod关掉后，亨利并没有立刻安静下来。他变得健谈、风趣，而且热情洋溢。“你喜欢音乐吗？”镜头外有人问道。亨利回答说：“我超级喜欢音乐！你放的音乐太美了！美妙的旋律！”“你小时候最喜欢的音乐是什么？”亨利回答说是卡布·卡洛威，然后开始即兴演唱。他用精准的音准、饱含深情的嗓音，偶尔还能唱对歌词，唱出了《我会回家过圣诞节》。
He is asked “What does music do to you?” Face still animated, arms now gesticulating with purpose, Henry responds: “It gives me the feeling of love. Romance! I figure right now the world needs to come into music, singing, you’ve got beautiful music here. Beautiful. Lovely. I feel a band of love!”
他被问到“音乐对你有什么影响？”亨利脸上依然洋溢着喜悦，手臂也随之有意识地挥舞着，他回答说：“它让我感受到爱。浪漫！我觉得现在全世界都需要音乐，需要歌唱，你们这里就有美妙的音乐。美妙极了。动听极了。我感受到了爱的氛围！”
Dr. Sacks is delighted. “In some sense Henry is restored to himself,” he enthuses. “He has remembered who he is, and he’s reacquired his identity for a while through the power of music.” I barely heard Dr. Sacks, because I started tearing up. It’s one of the most moving videos I’ve ever seen.
萨克斯博士欣喜若狂。“从某种意义上说，亨利找回了自己，”他激动地说，“他记起了自己是谁，并通过音乐的力量暂时重拾了自我。”我几乎没听清萨克斯博士在说什么，因为我开始热泪盈眶。这是我见过的最感人的视频之一。
How does music light up the brain, as it clearly did for Henry? What effects does it have on young and old? What does listening to music do to the brain, compared with being trained in music? Scientists have intensively investigated these questions. In asking whether exposure to music produces benefits in nonmusical cognitive domains, scientists have looked at academic areas, like reading and math. They’ve looked at general intelligence. They’ve studied the effects of music on speech, physical development, and mood. And now we think we have an understanding of at least some of the effects of music on cognition.
音乐是如何点亮大脑的？就像它对亨利那样。它对年轻人和老年人分别有什么影响？与接受音乐训练相比，聆听音乐对大脑有何作用？科学家们对这些问题进行了深入研究。为了探究接触音乐是否能对非音乐认知领域产生益处，科学家们研究了阅读和数学等学术领域，也研究了音乐对一般智力的影响。他们还研究了音乐对语言、身体发育和情绪的影响。现在，我们认为至少对音乐对认知的影响有了一些了解。
Why “think” instead of “know”? Music research is complicated—starting with the fact that not everyone agrees what music is, or why it exists .
为什么是“思考”而不是“知道”？音乐研究很复杂——首先，并非每个人都认同音乐是什么，或者它为什么存在。
How would you define music?
你如何定义音乐？
Scientists aren’t sure how the brain defines music, in part because there is no universal agreement about exactly what music is. What may be annoying, unorganized, environmental noise to a person raised in culture A at time point A might be rapturous, organized, beautiful music to a person raised in culture B at time point B. For example, in 1971, George Harrison of The Beatles organized a benefit concert, called The Concert for Bangladesh, with sitar master Ravi Shankar. Shankar tuned his instrument before performing, an event heard over the loudspeakers by the mostly Western audience. The crowd clapped and cheered with wild enthusiasm. As they began to settle, Ravi addressed them: “Thank you. If you like our tuning so much, I hope you will enjoy the playing more.” Rap is another example. It is clearly speech and also clearly—what? Music? Generations don’t agree. Neither do composers. Neither do sociologists. One professor of music and science at Cambridge defines music this way: “Musics (yes, the author said musics) can be defined as those temporally patterned activities, individual and social, that involve the production and perception of sound and have no evident and immediate efficacy or fixed consensual reference.” That’s not exactly the way everyone would describe music. The definition of music has been so tough to determine that neuroscientist Seth Horowitz, in his book The Universal Sense , titled a chapter “Ten Dollars to the First Person who Can Define ‘Music’ (and Get a Musician, a Psychologist, a Composer, a Neuroscientist and Someone Listening to an iPod to Agree . . .).”
科学家们并不确定大脑是如何定义音乐的，部分原因是人们对音乐的确切定义并没有统一的共识。对于在A文化背景下成长的人来说，在A时期可能只是令人烦恼、杂乱无章的环境噪音，而对于在B文化背景下成长的人来说，在B时期则可能是令人陶醉、结构严谨、优美动听的音乐。例如，1971年，披头士乐队的乔治·哈里森组织了一场名为“孟加拉国音乐会”的慈善演出，邀请了西塔琴大师拉维·香卡。演出前，香卡为他的乐器调音，这一过程通过扬声器传到了现场，观众大多来自西方国家。人群热情地鼓掌欢呼。演出结束后，香卡对他们说：“谢谢大家。如果你们这么喜欢我们的调音，我希望你们会更加喜欢接下来的演奏。”说唱是另一个例子。它显然是语言，但同时又显然是——什么？音乐？不同世代对此看法不一。作曲家们也意见不一。社会学家们也同样如此。剑桥大学一位音乐与科学教授这样定义音乐：“音乐（没错，作者用的是‘音乐们’）可以定义为那些具有时间模式的活动，包括个人活动和社会活动，它们涉及声音的产生和感知，并且没有明显的、直接的功效或固定的共识性参照。”但这并非所有人都认同这种对音乐的描述。音乐的定义一直难以确定，以至于神经科学家塞思·霍洛维茨在他的著作《普遍感觉》中，专门用一章的标题写道：“谁能定义‘音乐’（并让一位音乐家、一位心理学家、一位作曲家、一位神经科学家和一位正在听iPod的人达成一致……），谁就奖励十美元。”
And yet, at some level, we all know what music is, as did our ancestors. Music has tempo, changes in frequency, and something we call timbre (the quality that separates the “sound” of a sitar from the “sound” of a violin, for example). It is often associated with movement, such as dancing. It is a real phenomenon, even if it is elusive to define .
然而，在某种程度上，我们都明白音乐是什么，就像我们的祖先一样。音乐有节奏、频率变化，以及我们称之为音色的东西（例如，西塔琴的“声音”与小提琴的“声音”之间的区别）。它常常与动作联系在一起，例如舞蹈。它是一种真实存在的现象，即使它难以定义。
Some scientists think we are born musical. You can certainly watch babies respond to music, swaying and responding with glee to specific intervals. They even love it when parents talk to them in musical speech called “parentese,” which is rhythmic and high-pitched, with long, drawn-out vowels. Music has been a part of the cultural expression of virtually every culture ever studied. It may even extend into prehistoric times. A 35,000-year-old flute made from bird bone has been discovered, to cite just one example. If every culture has some form of musical expression, and if babies so readily respond to it, some scientists say, music must serve some evolutionary function. We must be hardwired for music, with regions in the brain specifically devoted to music.
一些科学家认为我们天生具有音乐天赋。的确，你可以观察到婴儿对音乐的反应，他们会随着特定的音程摇摆，并欣喜地做出回应。他们甚至喜欢父母用一种被称为“父母语”的音乐语言与他们交谈，这种语言节奏感强，音调高，元音拖长。音乐几乎是所有被研究过的文化表达方式的一部分。它甚至可以追溯到史前时代。例如，人们发现了一支用鸟骨制成的、距今35000年的笛子。一些科学家认为，如果每种文化都有某种形式的音乐表达，而且婴儿如此容易对音乐做出反应，那么音乐必然具有某种进化功能。我们大脑中一定存在专门负责音乐的区域，这或许表明我们天生就对音乐感兴趣。
Harvard professor Steven Pinker begs to differ. “I suspect that music is auditory cheesecake, an exquisite confection crafted to tickle the sensitive spots of at least six of our mental faculties,” he writes in How the Mind Works . Like music, people love cheesecake, and they have for a very long time (a recipe for cheesecake was found around 5th century BCE). But that doesn’t mean the brain has a region specifically dedicated to cheesecake. We are hardwired to respond not to cheesecake specifically, Pinker says, but to fats and sugars. These major energy boosters were somewhat rare in the lean world of the Serengeti. Because of their scarcity, our brains became sensitized—dedicated, you might say—to detecting the presence of fats and sugars. Because of their value, our brains rewarded their consumption with a powerful jolt of pleasure. Pinker makes a similar argument for music. He thinks music stimulates specific regions in the brain that are actually hardwired to process nonmusical inputs. There is no reason to go after evolutionary arguments that explain dedicated musical modules in the brain, Pinker posits, for a very practical reason: there are none.
哈佛大学教授史蒂芬·平克对此持不同意见。他在《心智运作原理》一书中写道：“我怀疑音乐就像听觉上的芝士蛋糕，一种精心制作的美味甜点，旨在刺激我们至少六种心智能力的敏感点。” 就像音乐一样，人们喜爱芝士蛋糕，而且这种喜爱由来已久（早在公元前5世纪就发现了芝士蛋糕的配方）。但这并不意味着大脑中有一个专门负责芝士蛋糕的区域。平克说，我们大脑的运作机制并非针对芝士蛋糕本身，而是针对脂肪和糖。在食物匮乏的塞伦盖蒂草原上，这些重要的能量来源相当稀少。正因为如此，我们的大脑变得异常敏感——或者说，专门负责——感知脂肪和糖的存在。由于它们的价值，我们的大脑会在摄入它们时给予强烈的愉悦感作为奖励。平克对音乐也提出了类似的观点。他认为，音乐会刺激大脑中原本负责处理非音乐信息的特定区域。平克认为，没有理由去探究解释大脑中专门的音乐模块的进化论证，原因非常实际：根本没有这样的论证。
So the matter is unsettled on why music exists, and scientists don’t agree on how to even define music. Still, researchers forge ahead with studies on cognition and social skills. They’ve discovered fascinating ways that music may benefit the brain. The benefits just aren’t the ones that the average person thinks they are.
所以，音乐存在的意义至今仍未有定论，科学家们甚至对音乐的定义也莫衷一是。尽管如此，研究人员仍在继续推进音乐对认知和社会技能的研究。他们发现音乐可能以多种令人着迷的方式有益于大脑。只不过，这些益处并非普通人所认为的那样。
What music training does for the brain
音乐训练对大脑的作用
Ray Vizcarra was an award-winning music and band teacher in a Los Angeles high school. He took kids who had no musical training, and he whipped them into shape with such skill, and such speed, that the kids were soon winning all-city contests. That’s saying something, given that Los Angeles is ground zero for musical contests. The LA City Council singled him out for a special honor in 2011. And then he lost his job. In a round of budget cuts and layoffs, he didn’t have enough seniority to stay. The story was written up in the Los Angeles Times.
雷·维兹卡拉曾是洛杉矶一所高中的获奖音乐和乐队老师。他招收一些毫无音乐基础的孩子，并以精湛的技艺和惊人的速度将他们训练得炉火纯青，孩子们很快就在全市比赛中屡获殊荣。考虑到洛杉矶是音乐比赛的中心，这的确令人瞩目。2011年，洛杉矶市议会授予他特别荣誉。然而，他却因此失去了工作。在一轮预算削减和裁员中，他的资历不足以让他继续留任。《洛杉矶时报》对此进行了报道。
Most of my wife’s friends are professional musicians, and they were outraged. They saw his layoff as one more sad example of music falling to the wayside now that schools emphasize standardized tests, which favor reading and math. Invariably, the conversation turned to questions about the value of keeping music in schools. Doesn’t music help improve test scores in reading and math? they ask me.
我妻子的大多数朋友都是职业音乐家，他们对此感到非常愤怒。他们认为，如今学校重视标准化考试（而标准化考试又偏重阅读和数学），音乐逐渐被边缘化，这又是一个令人惋惜的例子。不出所料，谈话很快就转向了在学校保留音乐课程的价值问题。“音乐难道不能帮助提高阅读和数学的考试成绩吗？”他们问我。
My response is not what they expect.
我的回答出乎他们的意料。
“It’s not a simple story,” I usually respond. Then I start listing the variables. When they say “music,” do they mean listening to music all the time? Or do they mean music training, like what the band teacher did with his students? Both involve exposure to music but are hardly the same thing. Does “help” mean changing an SAT score? How about cognitive processes not generally covered by standardized tests; do those count?
“这可不是件简单的事，”我通常会这样回答。然后我会开始列举各种变量。他们说的“音乐”，是指一直听音乐吗？还是指音乐训练，就像乐队老师教学生的那样？两者都涉及接触音乐，但本质上却截然不同。“帮助”是指提高SAT成绩吗？那些标准化考试通常不会涵盖的认知过程呢？这些算数吗？
Usually they’re talking about the effect of music lessons on reading ability, math scores, or intelligence in general. And in that case, I have bad news—made worse because I first need to spend a few minutes giving a statistics lesson. The lesson centers around something called an r value .
他们通常会讨论音乐课对阅读能力、数学成绩或整体智力的影响。如果是这样，那我得告诉你一个坏消息——更糟糕的是，我得先花几分钟时间讲讲统计学。这堂课的核心是一个叫做r值的东西。
An r value is a quantifiable linear association between two variables. It measures the tightness of their relationship. R values are assigned a number between -1 and 1. As an r value gets closer to 1, there is an increasingly positive relationship between the two variables. My wife, to give one example, loves chocolate. Every time she eats it, she breaks out into a big smile. The relationship between chocolate and smile is tight. We could easily assign it an r value of 1.
r 值是衡量两个变量之间线性关联的量化指标，它衡量的是它们之间关系的紧密程度。r 值的取值范围在 -1 到 1 之间。r 值越接近 1，两个变量之间的正相关性就越强。举个例子，我的妻子非常喜欢巧克力。每次她吃巧克力的时候，脸上都会绽放出灿烂的笑容。巧克力和笑容之间的关系非常紧密，我们可以很容易地给它们的 r 值赋值为 1。
In science, we use r values when reviewing multiple investigations done over a period of years to look for patterns—called a meta-analysis. That’s usually the kind of study done to analyze whether music is associated with a boost in academic or cognitive performance. Let’s look at the actual results in a few areas rumored to be true.
在科学领域，我们会使用r值来回顾多年来的多项研究，以寻找规律——这被称为元分析。这类研究通常用于分析音乐是否与学业或认知能力的提升有关。让我们来看看一些传闻属实的领域中，实际的研究结果。
Music training improves math scores. The best score in the literature gives the association an r value of 0.16. That’s not much.
音乐训练可以提高数学成绩。文献中最好的结果显示，这种关联性的r值为0.16。这并不算高。
Music training improves reading ability. This sports an r value of about 0.11. In more recent studies, researchers are beginning to detect improvement in reading skills of musicians compared to nonmusicians, but more research is needed.
音乐训练可以提高阅读能力，其相关系数r约为0.11。在最近的研究中，研究人员开始发现音乐家的阅读技能比非音乐家有所提高，但仍需更多研究。
Music training improves IQ. The answer again is no. Musicians are smarter, but the reason may be that smarter people take music lessons.
音乐训练能提高智商吗？答案仍然是否定的。音乐家的确更聪明，但原因可能是更聪明的人会去学习音乐。
Music training improves something useful for academics, right? Yes: spatiotemporal reasoning. That’s the kind of reasoning that allows you to, among other things, rotate three-dimensional images in your head. This is the kind of skill used by an architect or engineer. There’s an r value of 0.32 between the two if you take group instruction in piano, 0.48 if you take individual lessons.
音乐训练能提升一项对学习有用的能力，对吧？没错：时空推理能力。这种推理能力能让你在脑海中旋转三维图像等等。建筑师或工程师也需要用到这种技能。如果你参加钢琴小组课，那么音乐训练与学习能力之间的相关系数（r 值）为 0.32；如果你参加一对一课程，相关系数则为 0.48。
This is not an impressive track record, taken together.
综合来看，这并非一份令人印象深刻的成绩单。
Nonetheless, r values even lower than these can make headlines. One of my favorite examples is the so-called Mozart Effect. Listening to Mozart, the news stories claimed, will improve your ability to do math. An entire cottage industry grew up around this phenomenon, selling DVDs and CDs marinated in Mozart, then marketed to anxious parents worried about their child’s cognitive development. At one point, the governor of Georgia issued classical music CDs to the parents of every newborn in the state. The basis of all this enthusiasm was a tiny little paper that got a giant dollop of publicity because it was published in the prestigious journal Nature . The paper showed that when undergraduate students listened to 10 minutes of Mozart just before taking spatial tests, their scores improved. The boost was not strong, and the statistical analysis was even less so. The r value was a miserable 0.06. Nature issued a critique of the paper a month later, questioning the finding. Scientists who tried to replicate the results found that any pleasurable listening (or reading) experience had the same effect—one lasting about 15 minutes. But that not-so-shiny fact generated almost no publicity. The lead author of the original study has denounced the cottage industry, and years later reflected that the money Georgia’s governor appropriated for the music CDs might have been better spent on music education in the public schools.
然而，即使r值远低于此，也能成为新闻头条。我最喜欢的例子之一就是所谓的“莫扎特效应”。新闻报道称，听莫扎特的音乐可以提高数学能力。围绕这一现象，一个完整的产业应运而生，销售莫扎特音乐DVD和CD，并将其推销给那些焦虑不安、担心孩子认知发展的父母。佐治亚州州长甚至一度向该州所有新生儿的父母赠送古典音乐CD。这一切热潮的根源在于一篇发表在著名期刊《自然》上的小论文，该论文获得了巨大的关注。论文显示，大学生在进行空间测试前听10分钟莫扎特的音乐，他们的分数有所提高。但这种提升并不显著，统计分析的结果更是如此。r值只有可怜的0.06。《自然》杂志一个月后发表了一篇评论文章，对这篇论文的发现提出了质疑。试图重复实验结果的科学家发现，任何令人愉悦的聆听（或阅读）体验都能产生同样的效果——持续约15分钟。但这一并不引人注目的事实几乎没有引起任何关注。最初研究的主要作者谴责了这种小型产业，并在多年后反思，佐治亚州州长拨给音乐CD的资金或许更应该用于公立学校的音乐教育。
That study was published more than 20 years ago. But even when I lecture on brain science today, I encounter people who think classical music is good for your brain. Happily, music does do the brain some good. First we’ll look at the effects of taking music lessons, and then the effects of listening to music.
那项研究发表于20多年前。但即使今天我讲授脑科学时，仍然会遇到认为古典音乐对大脑有益的人。令人欣慰的是，音乐确实对大脑有一些好处。首先，我们将探讨学习音乐的效果，然后再探讨聆听音乐的效果。
Musicians are better listeners
音乐家更善于倾听。
Let’s say you are in a lab listening to some audio that is familiar and predictable. All of a sudden the scientist inserts some change into the sound you are hearing (a rhythmic pattern change, or a pitch change, for example). This alteration could be dramatic or subtle, but the scientist is interested in one question: Did you detect it? The more subtle the change you can detect, the higher your score is.
假设你在实验室里听一段熟悉且可预测的音频。突然，科学家对这段音频进行了一些改变（例如，节奏模式或音调的变化）。这种改变可能很显著，也可能很细微，但科学家只关心一个问题：你是否察觉到了？你能察觉到的变化越细微，你的得分就越高。
Musicians score better than nonmusicians on such tests. But here’s the interesting thing. They also score better when the audio being played is speech, not music. For example, musicians show more robust neurological stimulation than nonmusicians to the frequency changes of their native tongue. Musicians also are better able to pick out and pay attention to a specific sound in a roomful of distracting noises. (The fancy name for this is auditory stream segregation.)
音乐家在这类测试中的得分高于非音乐家。但有趣的是，当播放的音频是语音而非音乐时，他们的得分也更高。例如，音乐家对母语频率变化的神经反应比非音乐家更强烈。此外，音乐家也更能从充满干扰噪音的房间里分辨并专注于特定的声音。（这种能力的专业术语是听觉流分离。）
Music training boosts language skills
音乐训练可以提升语言技能
In one study, researchers gave children twice-weekly music lessons for a school year, using “a music curriculum designed to teach prereading and writing skills.” The children’s neuroarchitecture changed in a way that boosts both motor skills (writing) and auditory skills (word recognition)—direct improvements in language processing. Ten-year-olds who have been practicing a musical instrument for at least three years see a boost in both their vocabulary and nonverbal reasoning skills over children who don’t. Kids who start music lessons prior to first grade show superior sensory-motor integration when they are adults. These findings alone make a strong case for parents starting music lessons before age 7.
在一项研究中，研究人员让孩子们每周上两次音乐课，持续一个学年，课程采用的是“旨在教授阅读和写作预备技能的音乐课程”。孩子们的神经结构发生了改变，运动技能（写作）和听觉技能（单词识别）都得到了提升——这直接改善了他们的语言处理能力。与没有学习乐器的孩子相比，练习乐器至少三年的十岁儿童的词汇量和非语言推理能力都有所提高。一年级前就开始学习音乐的孩子，成年后表现出更强的感觉运动整合能力。仅凭这些发现，就足以有力地证明家长应该在孩子七岁前就开始让他们学习音乐。
Musical training provides direct improvements in working memory, not only in the phonological loop but also in the visuospatial sketch pad (see the Miguel Najdorf story in the Memory chapter for more on that). Working memory is a key constituent of executive function. Executive function predicts students’ future undergraduate performances better than their SAT scores, or even their IQs. Selecting and focusing on relevant stimuli from a host of choices is also a component of executive function. Any assistance music provides in this domain (and helping students pick out specific auditory streams in a room filled with irrelevant noise is one big example) is probably a good thing for kids.
音乐训练能直接提升工作记忆，不仅包括语音回路，还包括视觉空间框架（详见“记忆”章节中米格尔·纳伊多夫的故事）。工作记忆是执行功能的重要组成部分。执行功能比SAT成绩甚至智商更能预测学生未来的大学表现。从众多选择中筛选并专注于相关刺激也是执行功能的一部分。音乐在这方面提供的任何帮助（例如，帮助学生在充满无关噪音的房间里辨别特定的听觉信息流）对孩子来说都是一件好事。
Taken together, these studies make a case for supporting music education. In the journal Nature Reviews Neuroscience, researchers Nina Kraus and Bharath Chandrasekaran write of the studies on listening: “The beneficial effects of music training on sensory processing confer advantages beyond music processing itself. This argues for an improvement in the quality and quantity of music training in schools.”
综合来看，这些研究都为支持音乐教育提供了论据。在《自然神经科学评论》杂志上，研究人员尼娜·克劳斯和巴拉特·钱德拉塞卡兰在谈到有关聆听的研究时写道：“音乐训练对感觉处理的有益影响远不止于音乐处理本身。这表明学校应该提高音乐训练的质量和数量。”
Music to Ray Vizcarra’s ears, no doubt.
毫无疑问，这番话会让雷·维兹卡拉非常高兴。
The link between speech and music
语言与音乐之间的联系
Why would music training benefit speech? We know that music and speech are not processed identically in the human brain. But we also know they share many common features.
为什么音乐训练对语言能力有益？我们知道，音乐和语言在人脑中的处理方式并不完全相同。但我们也知道，它们有很多共同之处。
Take rhythm, for one. People can speak in a pulsed pattern, as when reading a Shakespearean play, or a poem, or a rap. As any drummer will tell you, rhythm is very much a part of the musical experience, too.
以节奏为例。人们说话时可以有节奏感，就像朗读莎士比亚戏剧、诗歌或说唱歌曲时一样。任何鼓手都会告诉你，节奏也是音乐体验中非常重要的一部分。
Take pitch, for another. When people are finished speaking a sentence, the pitch of their voice invariably lowers. When people ask a question, their voice invariably rises. Pitch variation is a key part of speech. It is also one of the signature hallmarks of music.
以音调为例。人们说完一句话后，音调通常会降低；而当人们提出问题时，音调则会升高。音调变化是语言表达的重要组成部分，也是音乐的标志性特征之一。
Music processing in the brain may, I believe, be conceptually likened to a Venn diagram, where two circles partially overlap to create a shared region. The brain has regions that are speech-specific. Call it the red domain. And the brain has regions that are music-specific. Call it the blue domain. But speech and music also share some regions in common—psychologically and physiologically. With apologies to Alice Walker, color it purple.
我认为，大脑对音乐的处理过程在概念上可以比作维恩图，其中两个圆圈部分重叠，形成一个共享区域。大脑中有一些区域专门处理语言，我们称之为红色区域；还有一些区域专门处理音乐，我们称之为蓝色区域。但是，语言和音乐在心理和生理层面上也有一些共同的区域。借用爱丽丝·沃克的话来说，我们可以用紫色来形容这些区域。
The brain keeps its separate regions quite separate, as we know from cases like Monica, a Canadian nurse who suffers from a condition called congenital amusia. Monica can’t carry a tune in a bucket. Neither can many members of her family. Her condition, however, is not just that she can’t match the pitch she hears in a song. Studies show that Monica cannot discriminate between notes. She literally can’t tell one note from the other, can’t determine if one is “sour” compared to another, can’t detect melodic patterns of any kind. With respect to music, she is completely tone-deaf. Monica does not enjoy listening to music. It appears to be a source of stress, as perhaps her schoolmates could attest: Monica was in her church choir and school band as a little girl.
大脑的各个区域彼此独立，这一点从莫妮卡（Monica）的案例中可见一斑。莫妮卡是一位加拿大护士，患有先天性失乐症。她五音不全，她的许多家人也一样。然而，她的病情不仅仅是无法辨别歌曲的音高。研究表明，莫妮卡无法区分音符。她根本无法分辨不同的音符，无法判断哪个音符“刺耳”，也无法识别任何旋律模式。就音乐而言，她完全是个音痴。莫妮卡不喜欢听音乐。音乐似乎成了她的压力来源，她的同学或许可以作证：莫妮卡小时候曾是教堂唱诗班和学校乐队的成员。
You would never know that Monica has pitch discrimination issues if you struck up a conversation with her, however. She speaks just like the rest of us. Her voice goes down when she finishes a declarative sentence (she’s no Valley Girl), and her voice goes up when she is finished with a question. Monica can detect these changes in pitch, in both her voice and the voice of anyone else.
如果你和莫妮卡搭讪，你绝对不会察觉到她有音调辨别障碍。她说话的方式和我们其他人一样。陈述句说完后，她的声音会降低（她可不是那种说话含糊不清的“山谷女孩”），疑问句说完后，她的声音会升高。莫妮卡能够分辨出自己和他人声音中的这些音调变化。
In another case of amusia, a child attempted piano lessons. His instructor soon found he could not discriminate between two pitches (and also could not keep time). When it came to speech, though, it was a different story. He fluently spoke three languages besides his native tongue.
在另一个失乐症的案例中，一个孩子尝试学习钢琴。他的老师很快发现他无法分辨两个音高（也无法掌握节奏）。然而，在语言方面，情况却截然不同。除了母语之外，他还能流利地说三种语言。
It seems odd that people can detect pitch changes when their brains decide they are listening to speech , but they become completely addled if their brains decide they are listening to music . When sound waves enter your ear, how does the brain determine whether you are listening to environmental noise, speech, or music? This question turns out to be important for a variety of reasons. As we shall see later, people who have lost speech abilities can often regain them through exposure to music. That doesn’t happen if all they hear is the spoken word. How does that work? What is the brain’s criteria for distinguishing music? Scientists don’t know. We just know that the brain at some point seems to separate music from speech.
人们能够分辨出音调变化，尤其是在大脑判断他们正在聆听语音时，但如果大脑判断他们正在聆听音乐，他们就会完全失去感知能力，这似乎很奇怪。当声波进入耳朵时，大脑是如何判断你听到的是环境噪音、语音还是音乐的呢？这个问题之所以重要，原因有很多。正如我们稍后将看到的，一些失去语言能力的人可以通过接触音乐来恢复语言能力。但如果他们听到的只有人声，这种情况就不会发生。这是怎么回事呢？大脑区分音乐的标准是什么？科学家们并不清楚。我们只知道，大脑似乎会在某个时刻将音乐与语音区分开来。
However, it’s the purple section of our Venn diagram—the area where the neurological processing domains for speech and music overlap—that is most interesting to the question at hand. This overlap is the reason that music training affects aspects of speech: if you improve one, you can also improve the other .
然而，维恩图中紫色部分——即语音和音乐神经处理领域重叠的区域——才是与我们当前问题最相关的部分。正是这种重叠使得音乐训练能够影响语音的某些方面：如果其中一项得到改善，另一项也会随之改善。
Music lessons improve social skills
音乐课可以提高社交技能
What else can music training do—besides, of course, make people better musicians? Watch the jazz band the Pat Metheny Group play “Have You Heard” live, and you may get an idea.
除了提升人们的音乐家水平之外，音乐训练还能带来什么？观看帕特·梅西尼爵士乐队现场演奏《你听说过吗》，你或许就能找到答案。
Pat Metheny is a bushy-haired American jazz guitarist and composer, winner of 19 Grammy Awards. He has been making records since the mid-1970s. I saw a video of him performing live in Japan in 1995, and the group’s improvisatory prowess was on full display. Besides the joyous virtuoso performance, the impression that strikes me most is the almost ridiculous cooperation of the band. There are five saxes, five trumpets, two vocalists, a string bass, keyboards, several rhythm sections, and probably a bunch of people I can’t see. There is plenty of room for error, yet that is exactly what you don’t hear. The musicians switch off performing solos throughout the song, tossing around melodies like Frisbees, and yet they play as one person. They don’t even have to look at each other—they can’t, in fact; the stage is mostly dark. The musicians signal to each other using the subtle nonverbal cues so legendary in jazz performance, creating musical dialogues only seasoned musicians can make intelligible. It is exhilarating, magical stuff.
帕特·梅西尼是一位一头蓬乱头发的美国爵士吉他手兼作曲家，曾荣获19项格莱美奖。他自20世纪70年代中期就开始录制唱片。我曾看过一段他1995年在日本的现场演出视频，乐队的即兴演奏能力展现得淋漓尽致。除了令人愉悦的精湛技艺之外，最让我印象深刻的是乐队成员之间近乎不可思议的默契配合。乐队成员包括五支萨克斯管、五支小号、两位歌手、一位低音提琴手、键盘手、几个节奏组，可能还有一些我看不见的乐手。这样的阵容容错率极高，但你却听不到任何瑕疵。乐手们在整首歌中轮流演奏独奏，如同抛掷飞盘般传递旋律，却又浑然一体。他们甚至无需彼此对视——事实上，他们也根本无法做到；舞台上几乎一片漆黑。乐手们运用爵士乐表演中闻名遐迩的微妙非语言信号相互交流，创造出只有经验丰富的音乐家才能理解的音乐对话。这令人兴奋，充满魔力。
How do they achieve such coordination? Is there something about performing in a musical group that trains people to look for subtle cues in others, in the service of coordinating a goal-oriented activity? Behavior done for the good of a group, or for the good of another individual, is termed “prosocial.” The action could be as exotic as allowing another musician solo space in a jazz concert so that he or she may shine, or it could be as mundane as making dinner when your spouse is sick. Prosocial skills, you can imagine, profoundly influence a person’s social abilities in all aspects of life.
他们是如何做到如此协调的呢？是不是在音乐团体中表演的经历，训练人们去观察他人细微的肢体语言，从而更好地协调合作，达成共同的目标？为了团队或个人的利益而做出的行为，被称为“亲社会行为”。这种行为可以像在爵士音乐会上给另一位乐手留出独奏空间，让他/她尽情展现才华那样意义非凡，也可以像在伴侣生病时主动做饭那样平凡无奇。可以想象，亲社会技能对一个人在生活各个方面的社交能力都有着深远的影响。
Does music training confer social, not just cognitive, benefits? You don’t have to be good enough to play in Mr. Metheny’s band to know that is exactly what one finds. The research we’ll look at next spans the age spectrum from adults to infants .
音乐训练是否不仅能带来认知方面的益处，还能带来社交方面的益处？你无需达到梅西尼先生乐队演奏的水平也能明白，答案的确如此。接下来我们将探讨的研究涵盖了从成人到婴儿的各个年龄段。
Musicians are better at detecting emotion
音乐家更善于察觉情绪。
If you’ve ever cried because you were yelled at, you know: words convey emotions. You can find out what somebody is feeling by detecting how they are saying something. We call such abilities “vocal affective discrimination skills.” Researchers asked: How good are trained musicians at these skills compared to nonmusicians?
如果你曾因被吼叫而哭泣，你就会明白：语言能够传递情感。你可以通过辨别说话者的语气来了解他们的感受。我们称这种能力为“语音情感辨别能力”。研究人员提出了这样一个问题：受过专业训练的音乐家与非音乐家相比，在这些技能方面表现如何？
In one study, English-speaking musicians and nonmusicians heard various emotions expressed in Tagalog, a Philippine language that was foreign to them. They were asked to identify any emotion they heard. How good were they at detecting the emotional information in what was being said, even though they could not understand the words? The results were dramatic. Trained musicians were champs, while nonmusicians were surprisingly bad at it. Musicians were especially good at discerning sadness and fear. They actually scored higher when listening to Tagalog than when listening to their native English! Studies like these laid the groundwork for demonstrating that music might improve social skills.
在一项研究中，以英语为母语的音乐家和非音乐家聆听了用菲律宾塔加洛语（一种他们不熟悉的语言）表达的各种情绪。研究人员要求他们识别听到的任何情绪。即使听不懂这些词语，他们识别其中情绪信息的能力如何？结果令人惊讶。受过专业训练的音乐家表现出色，而非音乐家的表现却出奇地差。音乐家尤其擅长辨别悲伤和恐惧。事实上，他们在聆听塔加洛语时的得分甚至高于聆听母语英语时的得分！诸如此类的研究为证明音乐可以提升社交技能奠定了基础。
Another research effort involved college-age students who had received musical training for 10-plus years. The researchers eavesdropped on the students’ brain activity using noninvasive imaging technologies while playing various auditory cues. They were specifically interested in the students’ brain stems—the primal, most evolutionarily ancient parts of our brains. What exactly were their brains doing as they listened to the audio cues, compared to the brains of nonmusicians?
另一项研究的对象是接受过十年以上音乐训练的大学生。研究人员利用非侵入性成像技术，在播放各种听觉提示时监测学生的大脑活动。他们尤其关注学生的脑干——我们大脑中最原始、进化上最古老的部分。与非音乐家相比，这些学生在聆听音频提示时，大脑究竟在做什么？
Consistent with previous findings, the researchers found that the musicians outpaced the nonmusicians in discriminating emotional information. These undergraduates were especially good at detecting subtle changes in the sound, timing, and pitch of a baby’s cry, for heaven’s sake. (Getting this right can be enormously difficult to do.) We call such talents fine-grained discrimination. Extending the previous findings, the researchers showed that musicians’ brain stems were more efficient at this neural-processing task. Specifically, their brains exhibited increased time-domain responses to complex emotional information. Their brains , not just their behaviors, were better.
与之前的研究结果一致，研究人员发现，音乐家在辨别情绪信息方面优于非音乐家。这些大学生尤其擅长察觉婴儿哭声中细微的声音、节奏和音调变化。（要做到这一点极其困难。）我们称这种能力为精细辨别能力。研究人员进一步拓展了之前的研究结果，表明音乐家的脑干在处理这类神经信息时效率更高。具体来说，他们的大脑对复杂的情绪信息表现出更强的时域反应。他们的大脑，而不仅仅是他们的行为，都表现得更好。
Much research remains to be done, however. It’s unclear whether music training directly improves this ability, or whether people who are naturally better at fine-grained discrimination have a tendency to like music and stick with music lessons.
然而，仍有许多研究需要进行。目前尚不清楚音乐训练是否能直接提高这种能力，还是说那些天生擅长精细辨别能力的人往往更喜欢音乐并坚持学习音乐。
Music lessons make kids more empathetic
音乐课能让孩子更有同理心
Researchers wanted to know whether music training could directly cause changes in social ability.
研究人员想知道音乐训练是否能直接导致社交能力的改变。
Fifty kids, ages 8 to 11, were randomly assigned to one of three groups. The first group took group music classes for an entire academic year. The delightful curriculum consisted of rhythmic improvisation, musical games, melodic repetition, and shared musical experiences. The second group played games that also involved imitating and interactive experiences—but verbal mostly, no music. The third group simply attended the regular school year. The question was: How good were the children’s social abilities at the end of the school year? Before the experiments commenced, researchers established baseline measures by testing the children’s social skills, such as empathy, including Theory of Mind abilities.
五十名年龄在8至11岁之间的儿童被随机分配到三个小组。第一组参加了一整个学年的集体音乐课程。这套趣味盎然的课程包括节奏即兴创作、音乐游戏、旋律重复以及共同的音乐体验。第二组玩的游戏也包含模仿和互动环节，但主要以语言为主，不涉及音乐。第三组则正常上课。问题是：学年结束时，孩子们的社交能力如何？在实验开始前，研究人员通过测试孩子们的社交技能（例如同理心，包括心智理论能力）建立了基线测量值。
The children in the music group had the most improved empathy scores. Like the adults, these kids had a stronger ability to decode the emotional information in their social surroundings, both verbally and nonverbally. They also were better at imitating facial expressions. The children who took the music class also had more empathetic responses to artificially posed situations, as measured by the Bryant’s Index of Empathy (an instrument used to measure pediatric empathy). The other two groups showed no such improvement.
音乐组的孩子在同理心得分方面进步最大。和成年人一样，这些孩子能够更有效地解读社交环境中的情感信息，包括语言和非语言信息。他们也更擅长模仿面部表情。参加音乐课的孩子在人为设计的场景中也表现出更强的同理心，这通过布莱恩特同理心指数（一种用于测量儿童同理心的工具）的评估得以证实。其他两组孩子则没有表现出类似的进步。
Said lead researcher Tal-Chen Rabinowitch, “Overall, the capacity for empathy in children that participated in our musical group interaction program significantly increased. ”
首席研究员塔尔-陈·拉比诺维奇表示：“总体而言，参与我们音乐小组互动项目的儿童的同理心能力显著提高。”
The experiment has since been replicated with 6-year-olds, by researchers in Canada.
此后，加拿大的研究人员对 6 岁儿童进行了重复实验。
Infants are more social, too
婴儿也更具社交性。
So far, we can detect the social benefits of music lessons in older adults, undergraduates, and elementary-school children. How far back can you push this? Can you detect social benefits if you give music lessons to infants ? You can’t go much earlier than that. Amazingly, the researchers found similar findings.
目前，我们已经发现音乐课对老年人、大学生和小学生都有社会益处。那么，这种益处还能追溯到多早呢？如果给婴儿上音乐课，我们能发现它的社会益处吗？恐怕很难追溯到更早的年龄段了。令人惊讶的是，研究人员发现了类似的结论。
Six-month-old babies took a parent-and-child music class for six months. The instruction was based roughly on Suzuki methodology, one that requires active group participation. Activities involved lots of singing, lots of banging on instruments, and learning songs in class, which parents were asked to repeat at home. Not surprisingly, this group was called the Active Group. A second group served as the control. These parents and tots instead listened to Baby Einstein music CDs while playing with toys together. Predictably, they were called the Passive Group.
六个月大的婴儿参加了为期六个月的亲子音乐课。教学大致基于铃木教学法，该方法强调积极的集体参与。活动包括大量的唱歌、敲击乐器以及在课堂上学习歌曲，家长则被要求在家重复练习。不出所料，这个小组被称为“积极组”。第二个小组作为对照组。这些家长和婴儿则一起听“小小爱因斯坦”音乐CD，同时一起玩玩具。不出所料，他们被称为“消极组”。
You can actually measure social competence in babies using a complex instrument called the Infant Behavior Questionnaire (IBQ), which assesses infants on 14 aspects of temperament. Researchers measured both groups to get a baseline. Then the experiment commenced. How did the babies do? If you are a music advocate, get ready for some spine-tingling data.
实际上，你可以使用一种名为“婴儿行为问卷”（IBQ）的复杂工具来测量婴儿的社交能力。该问卷从14个方面评估婴儿的气质。研究人员对两组婴儿进行了测量以获得基线数据，然后实验正式开始。婴儿们的表现如何呢？如果你热爱音乐，那就准备好迎接一些令人毛骨悚然的数据吧。
The Active Group outpaced the Passive Group socially in virtually every way you can measure it. They smiled more. They laughed more. They were much easier to calm down when they were stressed. In limitation assessments (a measure of how well you react to unexpected stimuli), they exhibited much less stress than their Passive counterparts. The infants’ gestures—such as waving goodbye and pointing—were improved, a companion paper showed. That may be important. Such prelinguistic communication leads to more positive social interactions between parent and child. And that improves infant cognition in virtually every way you can measure it.
在几乎所有可衡量的社交方面，主动组的表现都优于被动组。他们笑容更多，笑声更多，压力过大时也更容易平静下来。在限制性评估（衡量个体对意外刺激的反应能力）中，他们的压力水平远低于被动组。另一篇相关论文显示，婴儿的手势——例如挥手告别和指点——也有所改善。这一点可能非常重要。这种语言前期的交流能够促进父母与孩子之间更积极的社交互动，从而在几乎所有可衡量的方面提升婴儿的认知能力。
What’s going on here? We don’t know for sure. The Passive Group was exposed to the same amount of music as the Active Group, as well as the same amount of social interaction. Making music may simply provide an environment where one gets to exercise greater social cooperation and generally prosocial behaviors than when playing with toys. In this view, the secret sauce lies not with the music, but with the interaction. Or it could be the music itself, for both groups of children experienced sustained interaction with their parents. Either way, a method involving music has been found to make kids more empathetic, more relational.
这到底是怎么回事？我们并不确定。被动组和主动组接触到的音乐量以及社交互动量都相同。音乐或许只是提供了一个环境，让孩子们有机会进行更多的社交合作，并展现出比玩玩具时更多的亲社会行为。从这个角度来看，关键不在于音乐本身，而在于互动。当然，也可能是音乐本身起了作用，因为两组孩子都与父母进行了持续的互动。无论如何，研究发现，音乐确实能够增强孩子的同理心和人际关系能力。
Which is the point.
这就是关键所在。
Though these and several other experiments are interventions, showing whether music training directly caused the effects, the vast majority of studies are associative in nature. Still, taken together, these studies suggest—sometimes strongly—that music training boosts foundational speech-processing tasks, spatial skills, the detection of emotional cues, empathy, and baby-size social skills. Next, let’s look at the effects of simply listening to music.
尽管这些以及其他一些实验都是干预性研究，旨在证明音乐训练是否直接产生了这些效果，但绝大多数研究本质上是关联性的。不过，综合来看，这些研究表明——有时证据非常有力——音乐训练能够提升基础性的语言处理能力、空间技能、情绪线索识别能力、同理心以及婴儿时期的社交技能。接下来，我们来看看单纯聆听音乐的效果。
Music changes your mood
音乐能改变你的心情
“The word is breast !” my mother yelled from the kitchen. This brought my 13-year-old mind very quickly to attention. She clarified: “Music soothes the savage breast ! I believe it was from some old play …” her voice trailed off.
“是‘乳房’这个词！”妈妈从厨房喊道。这声音立刻吸引了我这个十三岁少年的注意力。她解释说：“音乐能抚慰躁动的乳房！我想这应该是出自某个老剧本……”她的声音渐渐低了下去。
I was in the TV room, watching a Bugs Bunny cartoon called Hurdy-Gurdy Hare , and my mother had overheard a line. The plot was standard Looney Tunes fare, with dollops of humor for both adults and children, involving an escaped gorilla now after Bugs. After a lot of antics, the gorilla traps Bugs Bunny in the back room of an apartment. Conveniently, and in the nick of time, Bugs finds a violin and begins playing. Immediately the gorilla calms down, then begins moving to the music. Bugs says snarkily says to the camera, “They say music calms the savage beast.” I did not see what happened next because of my mom’s comment. She was right, of course. According to scholars, the line is from the pen of 17th-century playwright William Congreve, and properly reads “Music hath charms to soothe the savage breast . ”
我当时在电视房里，正看着一部叫《手摇风琴兔》（Hurdy-Gurdy Hare）的兔八哥动画片，我妈无意中听到了一句台词。剧情是标准的乐一通（Looney Tunes）风格，老少咸宜，笑料十足。故事讲的是一只逃跑的大猩猩追着兔八哥跑。一番折腾之后，大猩猩把兔八哥困在了公寓的后屋里。就在这时，兔八哥及时找到了一把小提琴，开始拉了起来。大猩猩立刻安静了下来，还随着音乐动了起来。兔八哥对着镜头，带着几分嘲讽地说：“他们说音乐能安抚野兽。” 因为妈妈的话，我没看到接下来的剧情。当然，她说得没错。据学者考证，这句话出自17世纪剧作家威廉·康格里夫（William Congreve）之手，原句是“音乐有抚慰野蛮心灵的魔力”。
Either way, music’s ability to affect one’s mood and subsequent behavior is a common theme in literature. Researchers will tell you the reason is biochemical. It is a surprisingly well-established fact that music can induce hormonal changes. These changes result in alterations of mood. Well duh, say music fans around the world. Anybody who has ever listened to their favorite song could testify to that . It is not earth-shattering to find that music can induce pleasure. “Enjoyment arousal,” as it’s called, is sometimes accompanied by a temporary boost in certain skills. For that, we can thank three hormones: dopamine, cortisol, and oxytocin.
无论如何，音乐影响人的情绪和行为的能力是文学作品中常见的题材。研究人员会告诉你，这是生物化学层面的。音乐能够诱发激素变化，这已是一个广为人知的事实。这些变化会导致情绪的改变。世界各地的乐迷都会说，这还用说吗？任何听过自己喜欢的歌曲的人都能证明这一点。音乐能够带来愉悦感，这并非什么惊天发现。这种被称为“愉悦唤醒”的现象，有时会伴随着某些技能的暂时提升。为此，我们要感谢三种激素：多巴胺、皮质醇和催产素。
Dopamine
多巴胺
Noted Canadian researcher Robert Zatorre has studied people’s emotional reactions to music for a long time. He and his colleagues have found that when people hear their very favorite music (I mean spine-tingling, awe-inspiring, fly-me-to-the-moon music), their bodies dump dopamine into a specific part of their brain.
加拿大著名研究员罗伯特·扎托雷长期研究人们对音乐的情感反应。他和他的同事发现，当人们听到自己最喜欢的音乐（我是指那种令人毛骨悚然、敬畏不已、仿佛带我飞向月球的音乐）时，他们的身体会向大脑的特定区域释放多巴胺。
Dopamine is a neurotransmitter, involved in mediating processes from feeling pleasure to memory formation. It floods the striatal system, a curved structure in the middle of the brain that’s involved in many functions, including evaluating the significance you assign to a given stimulus. Zatorre found that when you hear music that gives you goose bumps (called “musical frisson”), the striatal system is activated via dopamine release. Music may soothe the savage human by exploiting this mechanism .
多巴胺是一种神经递质，参与调节从愉悦感到记忆形成等多种过程。它会涌入纹状体系统——大脑中部一个弯曲的结构，负责多种功能，包括评估你赋予特定刺激的意义。扎托雷发现，当你听到让你起鸡皮疙瘩的音乐（称为“音乐颤栗”）时，纹状体系统会通过释放多巴胺而被激活。音乐或许正是利用了这种机制来安抚人类的原始本能。
Cortisol
皮质醇
Surgery is not a pleasurable experience for most people. Some patients are genuinely freaked out, however, to the point of requiring medical intervention. Researchers asked, “Could music reduce the stress of people about to undergo surgery?” To answer the question, they divided 372 patients into two groups. The first group would listen to music before going under the knife. The second group would take an antistress pill (midazolam) prior to surgery.
对大多数人来说，手术并非愉快的经历。然而，有些患者确实极度恐惧，甚至需要医疗干预。研究人员提出了这样一个问题：“音乐能否减轻即将接受手术的人的压力？”为了解答这个问题，他们将372名患者分成两组。第一组在手术前听音乐，第二组在手术前服用抗焦虑药物（咪达唑仑）。
Who experienced the least amount of stress, as measured by respiration and heart rate, among other assays? The music group. They felt 13 percent less anxious than the stress-pill group before their surgeries. Listening to classical or meditation music had the greatest effect.
在呼吸频率、心率等指标的测量中，谁感受到的压力最小？答案是音乐组。他们在术前焦虑程度比服用抗压药组低13%。聆听古典音乐或冥想音乐的效果最为显著。
Oxytocin
催产素
Oxytocin plays a huge role in social bonding. This talented molecule stimulates temporary feelings of trust, orgasms, lactation, and even birth (pitocin, a drug that induces contractions, is a synthetic form of oxytocin). It even gets some mammals, like the prairie vole, to mate for life. Given this social track record, it is a big deal when the brain increases its production of oxytocin as a response to some external cue.
催产素在社会联结中扮演着至关重要的角色。这种神奇的分子能够激发短暂的信任感、性高潮、泌乳，甚至分娩（催产素是一种诱导宫缩的药物，是催产素的合成形式）。它甚至能促使一些哺乳动物，例如草原田鼠，终生保持伴侣关系。鉴于催产素在社会联结中的重要作用，当大脑因某些外部刺激而增加催产素的分泌时，这无疑是一件意义非凡的事情。
Researchers have discovered that when people sing as a group, as they would in a choir, oxytocin courses through their brains. An uptick in the hormone is a fairly reliable indicator of feelings of trust, love, and acceptance. This may explain why people in a choir often report feeling so close to each other.
研究人员发现，当人们像在合唱团一样集体歌唱时，大脑中会分泌大量的催产素。这种激素水平的升高是信任、爱和接纳等情感的可靠指标。这或许可以解释为什么合唱团成员常常感觉彼此非常亲近。
University of Montreal researcher Dan Levitin, in an interview with NPR, said the same of playing music together: “We now know that when people play music together, oxytocin is released. … This is the bonding hormone that’s released when people have an orgasm together. And so you have to ask yourself, that can’t be a coincidence; there had to be some evolutionary pressure there. Language doesn’t produce it, music does. …” This flies in the face of Pinker’s auditory cheesecake, as you may have noted.
蒙特利尔大学研究员丹·莱维廷在接受美国国家公共电台（NPR）采访时也表达了类似的观点，他认为共同演奏音乐会促进情感联结：“我们现在知道，当人们一起演奏音乐时，会释放催产素……这种激素与人们共同达到性高潮时释放的激素类似。所以你必须扪心自问，这绝非巧合；其中必然存在某种进化压力。语言不会产生这种激素，音乐才会……”正如你可能已经注意到的，这与平克的“听觉芝士蛋糕”理论截然相反。
These data suggest a mechanism whereby music makes people happy, calms them down, maybe even makes them feel close to each other. I can personally attest to these feelings.
这些数据表明，音乐能够使人感到快乐、平静，甚至可能拉近人与人之间的距离。我个人对此深有体会。
My wife is a classically trained pianist and a composer (she scores documentaries). In the past few years, she has really gotten into Irish, Scottish, and Celtic music. One gorgeous Gaelic song she regularly listens to speaks to me also. I’m hydrated with this glorious cocktail of haunting, calming, restful feelings, right from its opening bars. That turned out to be important on a day we had driven from Seattle to Vancouver, British Columbia. We were on vacation, and I was not having a restful time at all. It was downtown at rush hour—Vancouver at its worst—and I was in a slow burn trying to find our hotel, my tension increasing with every missed intersection. Stress hormones were boiling my blood, something my wife is good at detecting. She found the CD with that Gaelic song, slipped it into the car stereo, and played it full volume. From a distance I detected the calming feelings. I attempted to give in to them and immediately felt peace wash over me. We quickly found our lodgings. As I can attest, the calming ability of music can be very pleasurable … especially for the other people in the car.
我的妻子是一位受过古典音乐训练的钢琴家和作曲家（她为纪录片配乐）。近几年，她迷上了爱尔兰、苏格兰和凯尔特音乐。她经常听的一首优美的盖尔语歌曲也深深打动了我。从前奏开始，我就沉浸在这美妙的音乐中，它融合了萦绕心头的宁静、平和与放松，让我感到无比舒畅。在我们从西雅图开车前往加拿大不列颠哥伦比亚省温哥华的那天，这首歌显得尤为重要。我们当时正在度假，但我却一点也不放松。正值温哥华最拥堵的时段，市中心交通拥堵不堪，我焦躁不安地寻找着酒店，每错过一个路口，我的紧张感就增加一分。压力激素让我怒火中烧，而我的妻子对此却很敏感。她找到了那张盖尔语歌曲的CD，把它放进车载音响，音量开到最大。即使隔着一段距离，我也能感受到那份平静。我试着让自己沉浸其中，立刻感到一股平和之感涌上心头。我们很快就找到了住处。我可以作证，音乐的镇静作用令人非常愉悦……尤其对车里的其他人来说更是如此。
But more importantly, these hormones represent a powerful effort from researchers to transform anecdotal, ephemeral impressions about the power of music into the exacting physical world of cells and molecules. The findings may have medical implications.
但更重要的是，这些激素代表着研究人员的一项重要努力，他们试图将关于音乐力量的零散印象转化为细胞和分子层面的精确物理世界。这些发现可能具有医学意义。
The promise of music therapy
音乐疗法的前景
Using music as medicine for sick patients has a long history. The Greek physician Hippocrates prescribed it for mentally ill patients. During World War I, hospitals in the UK employed musicians to play for wounded soldiers in convalescence. It seemed not only to calm them down but also to reduce their pain. None of this was measured in any formal way at the time, but the observation was so persistent that the practice continued into World War II. Observations like these eventually led to the establishment of formal music-therapy associations.
用音乐疗愈病患由来已久。古希腊医生希波克拉底就曾用音乐治疗精神病患者。第一次世界大战期间，英国的医院聘请音乐家为康复中的伤兵演奏。音乐不仅能安抚他们的情绪，还能减轻他们的疼痛。当时并没有对这些效果进行正式的测量，但这种观察如此普遍，以至于这种做法一直延续到第二次世界大战。正是这些观察最终促成了正式的音乐治疗协会的成立。
Slowly but surely, these anecdotal observations attracted the notice of the research community, and clear findings have emerged. Music has been shown to aid speech recovery in head-trauma patients, for example. Gabrielle Giffords (the US representative who survived a gunshot to the head) regained regular speech in part by singing. Researchers think it works by forcing the brain to sign up unused regions of the brain for speech duty. Nobody knows why music does this. Dr. Oliver Sacks, interviewed about Giffords’s recovery in a documentary, said: “Nothing activates the brain so extensively as music. It has been possible to create a new language area in the right hemisphere. And that blew my mind.”
这些零星的观察逐渐引起了研究界的关注，并最终得出了明确的结论。例如，研究表明音乐有助于头部外伤患者的语言功能恢复。美国众议员加布里埃尔·吉福兹（头部中枪后幸存）的部分恢复能力就来自于唱歌。研究人员认为，音乐的作用机制在于它能促使大脑激活原本不常用的语言区域。至于音乐为何能产生这种效果，目前尚无人知晓。奥利弗·萨克斯博士在一部纪录片中谈到吉福兹的康复时说道：“没有什么能像音乐那样广泛地激活大脑。它甚至有可能在右脑半球创造出一个新的语言区域。这真是让我大吃一惊。”
Music improves the recovery rates of specific cognitive abilities in stroke patients. In one study, patients who underwent six months of music therapy were compared to patients who got “talk therapy.” The results were extraordinary. In measurements of verbal memory, the talk therapy patients achieved a score of 7 (that’s not so good). The music group achieved a score of 23 (that’s really good). Measurements of focused attention showed a similar disparity: the talk-therapy group scored a 1, while the music-therapy group scored an 11. In overall language skills at the end of six months, the talk-therapy group scored a 5. The music-therapy group scored a 21.
音乐能够提高中风患者特定认知能力的恢复速度。一项研究将接受六个月音乐治疗的患者与接受“谈话疗法”的患者进行比较，结果令人瞩目。在语言记忆力测试中，谈话疗法组患者的得分为7分（表现不佳），而音乐治疗组患者的得分为23分（表现非常出色）。注意力集中度测试也显示出类似的差异：谈话疗法组患者的得分为1分，而音乐治疗组患者的得分为11分。六个月后，在整体语言能力方面，谈话疗法组患者的得分为5分，而音乐治疗组患者的得分为21分。
Among stroke patients with motor difficulties, including those with Parkinson’s and cerebral palsy, researchers find similar positive results. Music-therapy patients routinely outscore patients exposed to more traditional therapies in measurements of arm movements and of gait as they walk. Music seems to serve as a predictable metronome that helps people coordinate their movements .
研究人员在患有运动障碍的中风患者（包括帕金森病和脑瘫患者）中发现了类似的积极结果。接受音乐疗法的患者在手臂运动和步态测量方面的得分通常高于接受传统疗法的患者。音乐似乎起到了一种可预测的节拍器作用，帮助人们协调运动。
Most of these studies have been done on adults, often our oldest citizens. What about some of our youngest?
这些研究大多针对成年人，通常是年纪最大的公民。那么，我们最年轻的公民的情况又如何呢？
Prematurely born infants, living in a hospital’s Neonatal Intensive Care Unit (NICU), gained weight more rapidly when music was played. Music helped them learn how to suck at their mothers’ breasts more readily. It also reduced their overall stress levels, which may explain the other findings. One study found that female (though not male) infants’ stay in the unit would be decreased by 11 days if music were played, compared to no music. It is now standard for hospitals across the country to pipe calm, peaceful music into their NICUs.
早产儿在医院新生儿重症监护室（NICU）接受治疗时，播放音乐能加快他们的体重增长。音乐帮助他们更快地学会吸吮母亲的乳房。此外，音乐还能降低他们的整体压力水平，这或许可以解释其他研究结果。一项研究发现，与不播放音乐相比，播放音乐可使女婴（而非男婴）在NICU的住院时间缩短11天。如今，在全美各地的医院，播放舒缓平和的音乐已成为NICU的标配。
Why does music have these effects? Again, we don’t know for sure. One idea, the “arousal and mood hypothesis,” was published in 2001. It proposed that the three hormones explain why music speeds recovery. It’s still just a hypothesis, but it’s paving the way for some serious neuroscience. Stay tuned.
音乐为何会产生这些影响？我们目前尚无定论。一种名为“唤醒与情绪假说”的观点于2001年提出，认为三种激素可以解释音乐为何能加速恢复。这目前仍只是一个假说，但它为神经科学的深入研究铺平了道路。敬请期待。
More ideas
更多想法
Too many of these intriguing studies don’t prove cause, and they’re all done in a lab setting. I’d like to see a school district take up research on music programs and help determine the effects of music training in a real-world setting. As soon as kids enter first grade, schools would randomly assign a large number of them to one of two groups. The first group would take lessons on a musical instrument, with formal instruction and ensemble training. Lessons would be daily, consistent, and as mandatory as math class. The program would last at least 10 years, ending when the students are juniors in high school. The second group would receive no music training.
太多这类引人入胜的研究都无法证明因果关系，而且它们都是在实验室环境下进行的。我希望看到某个学区开展音乐课程研究，帮助确定音乐训练在真实环境中的效果。孩子们一年级入学后，学校会随机将他们分成两组。第一组学生将接受乐器课程，包括正规的乐器教学和合奏训练。课程每天进行，持续不断，并且像数学课一样是必修课。该项目至少持续十年，直到学生高中三年级结束。第二组学生则不接受任何音乐训练。
With this kind of large-scale, long-term research program, we could see whether students who get music training perform better on tests involving speech proficiency at the end of the 10-year period than those without the training. And language arts. And second languages. Since emotional regulation has such a powerful effect on academic performance (see the Stress chapter), additional questions are relevant as well. We could see if the kids with music training have better emotional regulation. If they get better grades. If they’re more cooperative in group settings not related to music. If music training reduces antisocial behavior, such as bullying, at school. Music training almost certainly teaches discipline, a form of impulse control (you continue practicing for 10 years, even if you’d rather not).
通过这种大规模、长期的研究项目，我们可以观察接受音乐训练的学生在十年后，在涉及语言能力的测试中是否比未接受训练的学生表现更好。语言艺术和第二语言方面也是如此。由于情绪调节对学业成绩有着显著的影响（参见“压力”章节），因此其他一些问题也同样重要。我们可以观察接受音乐训练的孩子是否拥有更好的情绪调节能力，他们的成绩是否更好，他们在与音乐无关的群体环境中是否更乐于合作，以及音乐训练是否能减少校园欺凌等反社会行为。音乐训练几乎肯定能培养自律能力，这是一种冲动控制方式（即使你并不想练习，你也会坚持练习十年）。
If the answer was affirmative to even one of these questions, we would end up with a truly interesting principle: One way to create a higher-functioning student is to hire back band teacher Ray Vizcarra. And if it comes time to cut the school budget, the last activity to go would be formal musical training.
如果这些问题中哪怕有一个的答案是肯定的，我们最终会得出一条非常有趣的原则：提高学生能力的一种方法就是重新聘请乐队老师雷·维兹卡拉。而且，如果到了削减学校预算的时候，最后被砍掉的肯定是正规的音乐培训。
Brain Rule #1 0
大脑法则第10条
Study or listen to boost cognition.
通过学习或聆听来提升认知能力。
• Formal musical training improves intellectual skills in several cognitive domains. Music boosts spatiotemporal skills, vocabulary, picking out sounds in a noisy environment, working memory, and sensory-motor skills.
•正规的音乐训练可以提高多个认知领域的智力技能。音乐可以增强时空感知能力、词汇量、在嘈杂环境中辨别声音的能力、工作记忆和感觉运动技能。
• Formal music training also aids social cognition. People with music training are better able to detect the emotional information in speech. Empathy skills and other prosocial behaviors improve.
正规的音乐训练也有助于社交认知。接受过音乐训练的人能够更好地识别言语中的情感信息，同理心和其他亲社会行为也会得到提升。
• Variations on these effects have been shown in adults, college students, schoolchildren, even infants.
•这些效应的不同表现形式已在成人、大学生、小学生甚至婴儿身上得到证实。
# ↩
gender
性别
Brain Rule #11
大脑法则第11条
Male and female brains are different.
男性和女性的大脑是不同的。
# ↩
THE MAN WAS A HOT DOG . The woman was a bitch.
那男人是个万人迷。那女人是个泼妇。
The results of the experiment could be summarized in those two sentences. Researchers had asked people to rate a fictional person’s job performance—an assistant vice president of an aircraft company. People were divided into four groups, each group with an equal number of men and women, for the experiment. The groups were given the vice president’s brief job description. But the first group also was told that the vice president was a man. Asked to rate both the competence and the likability of the candidate, this group gave a very flattering review, rating the man “very competent” and “likable.” The second group was told that the vice president was a woman. She was rated “likable” but “not very competent.” All other factors were equal. Only the perceived gender had changed.
实验结果可以用这两句话概括。研究人员要求参与者评价一位虚构人物的工作表现——一位飞机公司的助理副总裁。参与者被分成四组，每组男女人数相等。各组都获得了这位副总裁的简要职位描述。但第一组被告知这位副总裁是男性。当被要求评价候选人的能力和人缘时，该组给出了非常高的评价，认为这位男性“非常能干”且“人缘好”。第二组被告知这位副总裁是女性。她被评价为“人缘好”，但“能力一般”。所有其他因素都相同，只有感知到的性别不同。
The third group was told that the vice president was a male superstar, a stellar performer on the fast track at the company. The fourth group was told that the vice president was a female superstar, also on the express lane to the executive washroom. As before, the third group rated the man “very competent” and “likable.” The woman superstar also was rated “very competent.” But she was not rated “likable.” In fact, the group’s descriptions included words such as “hostile.” As I said, the man was a hot dog. The woman was a bitch.
第三组被告知，副总裁是一位男性超级明星，公司里业绩斐然、晋升迅速。第四组被告知，副总裁是一位女性超级明星，同样是高管晋升的捷径。和之前一样，第三组评价这位男性“非常能干”且“讨人喜欢”。这位女性超级明星也被评价为“非常能干”，但她却不被评价为“讨人喜欢”。事实上，该组对她的描述中甚至出现了“敌对”这样的字眼。正如我所说，这位男性超级明星魅力四射，而这位女性超级明星则令人厌恶。
The point is, gender biases hurt real people in real-world situations. As we hurtle headlong into the controversial world of gender differences, keeping these social effects in mind is excruciatingly important. There is a great deal of confusion regarding the way men and women relate to each other, and even more confusion about why they relate to each other differently. Terms are often confused as well, blurring the line between the concepts of “sex” and “gender.” In this chapter, sex will generally refer to biology and anatomy. Gender will refer mostly to social expectations. Sex is set into the concrete of DNA. Gender is not.
关键在于，性别偏见会在现实生活中伤害到真实的人。当我们一头扎进充满争议的性别差异领域时，牢记这些社会影响至关重要。人们对男女之间的关系存在诸多困惑，而对于他们为何会以不同的方式相处，人们更是百思不得其解。术语也常常被混淆，模糊了“生理性别”和“社会性别”之间的界限。在本章中，“生理性别”通常指的是生物学和解剖学意义上的生理性别，“社会性别”则主要指社会期望。生理性别由DNA决定，而社会性别则并非如此。
Differences between men’s and women’s brains can be viewed from several lenses: genetic, neuroanatomical, and behavioral. Scientists usually spend their whole careers exploring only one. So our tour of all three will be necessarily brief.
男女大脑的差异可以从多个角度来观察：遗传学、神经解剖学和行为学。科学家通常毕生只专注于其中一个方面进行研究。因此，我们对这三个方面的探讨必然是简短的。
How we become male or female
我们如何成为男性或女性
The differences between men’s and women’s brains start with genes, which determine whether we become male or female in the first place. The road to sex assignment starts out with all the enthusiasm sex usually stimulates. Four hundred million sperm fall all over themselves attempting to find one egg during intercourse. The task is not all that difficult. In the microscopic world of human fertilization, the egg is the size of the Death Star, and the sperm are the size of X-wing starfighters.
男女大脑的差异始于基因，基因决定了我们是男性还是女性。性别决定的过程始于性爱通常带来的激情。在性交过程中，四亿个精子争先恐后地寻找卵子。这项任务并不难。在人类受精的微观世界里，卵子如同死星般巨大，而精子则如同X翼星际战斗机般庞大。
X is the name of that very important chromosome that half of all sperm and all eggs carry. You recall chromosomes from biology class. They’re those writhing strings of DNA packed into the cell nucleus that contain the information necessary to make you. You can think of chromosomes as volumes in an encyclopedia. Creating you takes 46 of them. Twenty-three come from Mom, and 23 come from Dad. Two are sex chromosomes, either X or Y. At least one of your sex chromosomes has to be an X chromosome, or you will die. If you get two X chromosomes, you go into the ladies locker room all your life; an X and Y puts you forever in the men’s. The Y can be donated only by sperm—the egg never carries one—so sex assignment is controlled by the man. (Henry VIII’s wives wish that he had known that. He executed one of them, Anne Boleyn, for being unable to produce a son as heir to the throne, but it would have made more sense to execute himself.)
X是那条非常重要的染色体的名称，一半的精子和所有卵子都携带它。你还记得生物课上学过的染色体吗？它们是缠绕在细胞核内的DNA链，包含了构成你身体所需的全部信息。你可以把染色体想象成百科全书里的各个卷册。构成你身体需要46条染色体。其中23条来自母亲，23条来自父亲。两条是性染色体，分别是X染色体和Y染色体。你的性染色体中至少要有一条是X染色体，否则你会死亡。如果你拥有两条X染色体，你这辈子只能在女更衣室里活动；一条X染色体和一条Y染色体则让你永远只能在男更衣室里活动。Y染色体只能由精子提供——卵子本身不携带Y染色体——所以性别由男性决定。 （亨利八世的妻子们希望他早知道这一点。他处死了其中一位妻子安妮·博林，因为她无法生下儿子继承王位，但如果他处死自己，岂不更明智？）
What the X and Y chromosomes do
X染色体和Y染色体的作用
One of the most interesting facts about the Y chromosome is that you don’t need most of it to make a male. All it takes to kick-start the male developmental program is a small snippet near the middle, carrying a gene called SRY.
关于Y染色体，最有趣的事实之一是，构成男性并不需要它的大部分。启动男性发育程序只需要位于中间附近的一小段Y染色体，这段染色体携带一个名为SRY的基因。
David C. Page is the researcher who isolated SRY. Though in his 50s, Page looks to be about 28 years old.
