As director of the Whitehead Institute and a professor at MIT, he is a man of considerable intellect. He also is charming, with a refreshingly wicked sense of humor. Page is the world’s first molecular sex therapist. Or, better, sex broker. He discovered that you can destroy the SRY gene in a male embryo and get a female, or add SRY to a female embryo and turn her into a male (SR stands for “sex reversal”).
大卫·C·佩奇是分离出SRY基因的研究员。虽然他已年过五十，但看起来只有二十八岁左右。作为怀特黑德研究所所长和麻省理工学院教授，他学识渊博。他本人也魅力十足，幽默风趣，令人耳目一新。佩奇是世界上第一位分子性治疗师。或者更确切地说，是性交易专家。他发现，破坏雄性胚胎中的SRY基因就能得到雌性胚胎，而将SRY基因添加到雌性胚胎中就能将其转化为雄性胚胎（SR代表“性别逆转”）。
Why can you do this? In a fact troubling to anybody who believes males are biologically hardwired to dominate the planet, researchers discovered that the basic default setting of the mammalian embryo is to become female. Yet the male program is enthusiastic. The CIA estimates (though not everyone agrees) that 107 male babies are born for every 100 females worldwide. Because males die sooner, though, the adult ratio of men to women is about one to one .
为什么会这样？对于那些认为男性天生就应该主宰地球的人来说，一个令人不安的事实是：研究人员发现，哺乳动物胚胎的默认发育目标是雌性。然而，雄性程序却异常活跃。据美国中央情报局估计（尽管并非所有人都认同），全球每出生100名女婴，就会有107名男婴出生。但由于男性寿命较短，成年男女的比例约为1:1。
There is terrible inequality between the two chromosomes. The X chromosome carries about 1,500 genes, which do most of the heavy lifting to develop an embryo. The little Y chromosome, by comparison, has been shedding its associated genes at a rate of about five every one million years. It’s now down to less than 100 genes.
两条染色体之间存在着巨大的不平等。X染色体携带约1500个基因，这些基因承担着胚胎发育的大部分工作。相比之下，Y染色体却以每百万年约5个基因的速度流失，如今只剩下不到100个基因。
With only a single X chromosome, males need every one of those 1,500 genes. With two X chromosomes, females have double the necessary amount. You can think of it like a cake recipe calling for only one cup of flour. If you decide to put in two, it will change the results in a most unpleasant fashion. The female embryo uses what may be the most time-honored weapon in the battle of the sexes to solve the problem of two Xs: She simply ignores one of them. This chromosomal silent treatment is known as X inactivation. One of the chromosomes is tagged with the molecular equivalent of a “Do Not Disturb” sign. Because males require all 1,500 X genes to survive, and they have only one X chromosome, X inactivation does not occur in guys. And because males must get their X from Mom, all men are literally, with respect to their X chromosome, Momma’s Boys—unisexed.
男性只有一条X染色体，却需要这1500个基因。女性有两条X染色体，基因数量是所需数量的两倍。你可以把它想象成一个蛋糕食谱，只需要一杯面粉。如果你放了两杯，结果就会变得非常糟糕。女性胚胎使用了一种可能是性别之战中最古老的武器来解决两条X染色体的问题：她直接忽略其中一条。这种染色体上的“沉默处理”被称为X染色体失活。其中一条染色体就像被贴上了“请勿打扰”的分子标签。由于男性需要全部1500个X基因才能生存，而他们只有一条X染色体，所以男性不会发生X染色体失活。而且，由于男性必须从母亲那里获得X染色体，所以就X染色体而言，所有男性实际上都是“妈宝男”——无性。
That’s very different from their sisters, who are more genetically complex. Since female embryos have two Xs from which to choose, Mom’s or Dad’s, researchers wanted to know who preferentially got the sign. The answer was completely unexpected: There were no preferences. Some cells in the developing little girl embryo hung their sign around Mom’s X. Neighboring cells hung their sign around Dad’s. At this point in research, there doesn’t appear to be any rhyme or reason, and it is considered a random event. This means that cells in the female embryo are a complex mosaic of both active and inactive mom-and-pop X genes. These bombshells describe our first truly genetic-based findings of potential differences between men’s and women’s brains.
这与基因更为复杂的女性胚胎截然不同。由于女性胚胎有两个X染色体可供选择，分别来自母亲或父亲，研究人员想知道哪个细胞会优先获得标记。答案完全出乎意料：没有偏好。发育中的女婴胚胎中，一些细胞将标记悬挂在母亲的X染色体周围，而相邻的细胞则将标记悬挂在父亲的X染色体周围。目前的研究尚未发现任何规律，这被认为是一种随机事件。这意味着女性胚胎中的细胞是由活跃和不活跃的父母双方X染色体基因组成的复杂嵌合体。这些惊人的发现首次揭示了男性和女性大脑之间潜在的差异，而这些差异实际上是基于基因层面的。
What do many of the X’s 1,500 genes do? They govern how we think. In 2005 the human genome was sequenced, and a large percentage of the X chromosome genes were found to create proteins involved in brain manufacture. Some of these genes may be involved in establishing higher cognitive functions, from verbal skills and social behavior to certain types of intelligence. Researchers call the X chromosome a cognitive “hot spot.”
X染色体上的1500个基因中，很多都做什么呢？它们控制着我们的思维方式。2005年，人类基因组测序完成，研究人员发现X染色体上很大一部分基因编码参与大脑构建的蛋白质。其中一些基因可能与高级认知功能的形成有关，包括语言能力、社交行为以及某些类型的智力。研究人员将X染色体称为认知“热点”。
The purpose of genes is to create molecules that mediate the functions of the cells in which they reside. Collections of these cells create the large brain structures we’ve been talking about, like the cortex, the hippocampus, the thalamus and the amygdala. These make up the neuroanatomy of the brain, which we turn to next.
基因的作用是产生分子，这些分子调节它们所在细胞的功能。这些细胞聚集在一起，构成了我们一直在讨论的大脑大型结构，例如大脑皮层、海马体、丘脑和杏仁核。这些结构构成了大脑的神经解剖结构，接下来我们将对此进行探讨。
Differences in brain structure
大脑结构差异
When it comes to neuroanatomy, the real challenge is finding areas that aren’t affected by sex chromosomes. You can see differences in the cortex, the amygdala, even the biochemicals that brain cells use to communicate with each other.
在神经解剖学领域，真正的挑战在于找到不受性染色体影响的区域。你可以观察到大脑皮层、杏仁核，甚至脑细胞之间相互交流所用的生化物质的差异。
The frontal and prefrontal cortex control much of our decision-making ability. Labs—headed by scientists of both sexes, I should perhaps point out—have found that certain parts of this cortex is fatter in women than in men.
额叶皮层和前额叶皮层控制着我们大部分的决策能力。值得一提的是，一些由男女科学家领导的实验室发现，女性额叶皮层的某些部分比男性更厚。
The limbic system, home to the amygdala, controls not only the generation of emotions but also the ability to remember them. Running counter to current social prejudice, this region is much larger in men than it is in women. At rest, female amygdalas tend to talk mostly to the left hemisphere, while male amygdalas do most of their chatting with the right hemisphere.
杏仁核所在的边缘系统不仅控制着情绪的产生，还控制着情绪的记忆。与当前的社会偏见相反，男性的这一区域比女性大得多。在静息状态下，女性的杏仁核主要与左脑半球进行交互，而男性的杏仁核则主要与右脑半球进行交互。
Biochemicals have not escaped sex differences, either. Serotonin, key in regulating emotion and mood, is a particularly dramatic example. Males can synthesize serotonin about 52 percent faster than females. (Prozac works by altering the regulation of this neurotransmitter.)
生物化学物质也存在性别差异。血清素是调节情绪的关键物质，就是一个特别显著的例子。男性合成血清素的速度比女性快约52%。（百忧解的作用机制就是改变这种神经递质的调节。）
What do these physical differences really mean? In animals, the size of structures is thought to reflect their relative importance to survival. Human examples at first blush seem to follow a similar pattern. We already have noticed that violinists have bigger areas of the brain devoted to controlling their left hand than their right. But neuroscientists nearly come to blows over how brain structure relates to function. We don’t yet know whether differences in the size of a brain region translate to anything substantial when it comes to behavior.
这些生理差异究竟意味着什么？在动物中，人们认为大脑结构的大小反映了其对生存的重要性。乍一看，人类似乎也遵循类似的模式。我们已经注意到，小提琴手大脑中控制左手的区域比控制右手的区域更大。但神经科学家们对于大脑结构与功能之间的关系几乎争论不休。我们目前尚不清楚大脑区域大小的差异是否会对行为产生任何实质性的影响。
Differences in behavior
行为差异
I didn’t really want to write about this. Characterizing gender-specific behaviors has a long and mostly troubled history. Institutions holding our best minds aren’t immune. Larry Summers was Harvard’s president, for Pete’s sake, when in 2005 he attributed girls’ lower math and science scores to behavioral genetics, comments that cost him his job. The battle of the sexes has existed for a very long time, illustrated by three quotes separated by centuries:
我其实并不想写这个话题。给性别行为贴标签由来已久，而且大多充满争议。就连汇聚顶尖人才的机构也未能幸免。想想看，拉里·萨默斯可是哈佛大学的校长啊！2005年，他竟然把女生数学和科学成绩较差归因于行为遗传学，这番言论最终让他丢了饭碗。性别之争由来已久，以下三段相隔几个世纪的引言便可佐证：
“The female is an impotent male, incapable of making semen because of the coldness of her nature. We therefore should look upon the female state as if it were a deformity, though one that occurs in the ordinary course of nature.”
“女性如同阳痿的男性，因其天性冷漠而无法产生精液。因此，我们应该将女性的状态视为一种畸形，尽管它是自然界正常现象。”
Aristotle (384–332 BC )
亚里士多德（公元前384-332年）
“Girls begin to talk and to stand on their feet sooner than boys because weeds always grow up more quickly than good crops.”
“女孩比男孩更早开始说话和站立，因为杂草总是比庄稼长得快。”
Martin Luther (1483–1546)
马丁·路德（1483–1546）
“If they can put a man on the moon … why can’t they put them all there?”
“既然他们能把一个人送上月球……为什么不能把所有人都送上去呢？”
Jill (graffiti I saw on a bathroom wall in 1985, in response to Luther’s quote scribbled there)
吉尔（1985年我在浴室墙上看到的涂鸦，是对那里潦草写下的路德名言的回应）
Almost 2,400 years of history separate Aristotle from Jill, yet we seem to have barely moved. Invoking planet metaphors like Venus and Mars, some purport to expand perceived differences into prescriptions for relationships. And this is the most scientifically progressive era in human history.
从亚里士多德到吉尔，相隔近2400年的历史，而我们似乎几乎没有任何进步。有些人援引金星和火星等行星的比喻，试图将人们感知到的差异转化为维系人际关系的准则。而这，恰恰是人类历史上科学进步最为显著的时代。
Mostly, I think, it comes down to statistics. When people hear about measurable differences, they often think scientists are talking about individuals, such as themselves. That’s a big mistake. When scientists look for behavioral trends, they do not look at individuals. They look at populations. Trends emerge, but the many variations and overlaps mean that statistics in these studies can never apply to individuals. There may very well be differences in the way men and women think about some things. But exactly how that relates to your behavior is a completely separate question.
我觉得，归根结底还是统计学的问题。人们一听到“可测量的差异”，往往以为科学家是在谈论个体，比如他们自己。这是个很大的误区。科学家研究行为趋势时，关注的不是个体，而是群体。趋势固然会显现，但由于个体之间存在诸多差异和重叠，这些研究中的统计数据永远无法直接应用于个体。男性和女性在某些问题上的思考方式或许确实存在差异，但这究竟与你的行为有何关联，则是完全不同的另一个问题。
Mental disorders
精神障碍
Brain pathologies represent one of the strongest pieces of evidence that sex chromosomes are involved in brain function and thus brain behavior. Mental retardation is more common in males than in females in the general population. Many of these pathologies are caused by mutations in any one of 24 genes in the X chromosome. As you know, males have no backup X. If their X gets damaged, they have to live with the consequences. If a female’s X is damaged, she can often ignore the consequences.
脑部病变是性染色体参与大脑功能乃至大脑行为的最有力证据之一。在普通人群中，男性智力低下比女性更为常见。许多此类病变是由X染色体上24个基因中任何一个基因的突变引起的。众所周知，男性没有备用X染色体。如果他们的X染色体受损，他们必须承受其后果。而如果女性的X染色体受损，她们通常可以忽略其后果。
Mental-health professionals have known for years about sex-based differences in the type and severity of psychiatric disorders. Males are more severely afflicted by schizophrenia than females, for example. By more than two to one, women are more likely to get depressed than men, a figure that shows up just after puberty and remains stable for the next 50 years. Males have a greater tendency to be antisocial. Females have more anxiety. Most alcoholics and drug addicts are male. Most anorexics are female. Says Thomas Insel, from the National Institute of Mental Health, “It’s pretty difficult to find any single factor that’s more predictive for some of these disorders than gender. ”
精神健康专家多年来一直了解精神疾病的类型和严重程度存在性别差异。例如，男性患精神分裂症的程度比女性更严重。女性患抑郁症的概率是男性的两倍多，这种比例在青春期后不久就会显现，并在接下来的50年里保持稳定。男性更容易出现反社会行为。女性更容易焦虑。大多数酗酒者和吸毒者是男性。大多数厌食症患者是女性。美国国家精神卫生研究所的托马斯·因塞尔表示：“很难找到比性别更能预测这些疾病的单一因素。”
Emotions and stress
情绪和压力
It’s a horrible slide show. In it, a little boy is run over by a car while walking with his parents. If you ever see that show, you will never forget it. But what if you could forget it? The brain’s amygdala aids in the creation of emotions and our ability to remember them. Suppose there was a magic elixir that could momentarily suppress it? Such an elixir does exist, and it was used to show that men and women process emotions differently.
那是一个令人毛骨悚然的幻灯片。幻灯片里，一个小男孩和父母一起散步时被车撞了。如果你看过这个幻灯片，你永远不会忘记。但如果你能忘记它呢？大脑的杏仁核参与情绪的产生和记忆。假设有一种神奇的灵药可以暂时抑制杏仁核呢？这种灵药确实存在，它被用来证明男性和女性处理情绪的方式不同。
You have probably heard the term left brain versus right brain. You may have heard that this underscores creative versus analytical people. That’s a folk tale, the equivalent of saying the left side of a luxury liner is responsible for keeping the ship afloat, and the right is responsible for making it move through the water. Both sides are involved in both processes. That doesn’t mean the hemispheres are equal, however. The right side of the brain tends to remember the gist of an experience, and the left brain tends to remember the details.
你可能听说过“左脑”和“右脑”的说法。你也可能听说过，这种说法强调了创造力强的人和分析能力强的人之间的区别。这是一种民间说法，就像说豪华邮轮的左侧负责保持船身漂浮，右侧负责让它在水中航行一样。实际上，两个半球都参与了这两个过程。但这并不意味着左右脑的功能是相等的。右脑倾向于记住经历的要点，而左脑则倾向于记住细节。
Researcher Larry Cahill eavesdropped on men’s and women’s brains under acute stress (he showed them slasher films), and what he found is this: Men handled the experience by firing up the amygdala in their brain’s right hemisphere. Their left was comparatively silent. Women handled the experience with the opposite hemisphere. Their left amygdala lit up, their right comparatively silent. If males are firing up the side in charge of gist, does that mean males remember more gist than detail of a given emotional experience related to stress? Conversely, do females remember more detail than gist? Cahill decided to find out.
研究员拉里·卡希尔（Larry Cahill）通过观察男性和女性在急性压力下的大脑活动（他给他们播放恐怖电影），发现：男性通过激活大脑右半球的杏仁核来应对这种体验，而左半球则相对平静。女性则相反，她们的左侧杏仁核活跃，右侧杏仁核则相对平静。如果男性激活的是负责记忆要点的大脑半球，这是否意味着男性更容易记住与压力相关的特定情绪体验的要点而非细节？反之，女性是否更容易记住细节而非要点？卡希尔决定探究这个问题。
That magic elixir of forgetting, a drug called propranolol, normally is used to regulate blood pressure. As a beta-blocker, it also inhibits the biochemistry that activates the amygdala during emotional experiences. The drug is being investigated as a potential treatment for combat-related disorders .
这种被称为“遗忘灵药”的药物，名为普萘洛尔，通常用于调节血压。作为一种β受体阻滞剂，它还能抑制情绪体验中激活杏仁核的生化反应。目前，该药物正被研究作为治疗战斗相关疾病的潜在疗法。
But Cahill gave it to his subjects before they watched a traumatic film. One week later, he tested their memories of it. Sure enough, the men lost the ability to recall the gist of the story, compared with men who didn’t take the drug. Women lost the ability to recall the details. One must be careful not to overinterpret these data. The results clearly define only emotional responses to stressful situations, not objective details and summaries. This is not a battle between the accountants and the visionaries.
但卡希尔在受试者观看一部令人痛苦的影片之前就给他们服用了这种药物。一周后，他测试了他们对影片的记忆。果然，与未服用药物的男性相比，服用药物的男性失去了回忆故事梗概的能力。女性则失去了回忆细节的能力。我们必须谨慎解读这些数据，切勿过度解读。结果清楚地表明，这些结果仅仅反映了人们对压力情境的情绪反应，而非客观的细节和概括。这并非会计师与梦想家之间的较量。
Cahill’s results come on the heels of similar findings around the world. Other labs have extended his work, finding that women recall more emotional autobiographical events, more rapidly and with greater intensity, than men do. Women consistently report more vivid memories for emotionally important events such as a recent argument, a first date, or a vacation. Other studies show that, under stress, women tend to focus on nurturing their offspring, while men tend to withdraw. This tendency in females has sometimes been called “tend and befriend.” Is this caused by nature or nurture? As Stephen Jay Gould says, “It is logically, mathematically, and philosophically impossible to pull them apart.”
卡希尔的研究结果与世界各地类似的发现相呼应。其他实验室拓展了他的研究，发现女性比男性更容易、更迅速、更强烈地回忆起情感丰富的自传式事件。女性对诸如最近的争吵、第一次约会或假期等具有重要情感意义的事件，往往能留下更生动的记忆。其他研究表明，在压力下，女性倾向于专注于养育子女，而男性则倾向于退缩。女性的这种倾向有时被称为“照顾与结交”。这究竟是先天因素还是后天因素造成的呢？正如斯蒂芬·杰伊·古尔德所说：“从逻辑、数学和哲学的角度来看，将二者分开是不可能的。”
Verbal communication
口头交流
Over the past several decades, behaviorist Deborah Tannen and others have done some fascinating work on how men and women communicate verbally. The CliffsNotes version of their findings: Women are better at it.
过去几十年里，行为学家黛博拉·坦南等人对男女的语言沟通方式进行了一些引人入胜的研究。简而言之，他们的研究结果是：女性更擅长语言沟通。
Women tend to use both hemispheres when speaking and processing verbal information. Men primarily use one. Women tend to have thick cables connecting their two hemispheres. Men’s are thinner. It’s as though females have a backup system that males don’t. Researchers think these neuroanatomical differences may explain why language and reading disorders occur approximately twice as often in little boys as in little girls. Women also recover from stroke-induced verbal impairment better than men .
女性在说话和处理语言信息时往往同时使用大脑两个半球，而男性主要使用一个半球。女性连接大脑两个半球的神经纤维通常较粗，而男性的则较细。这就像女性拥有男性所没有的备用系统。研究人员认为，这些神经解剖学上的差异或许可以解释为什么男孩患语言和阅读障碍的概率大约是女孩的两倍。此外，女性从中风引起的语言障碍中恢复得也比男性好。
Girls seem verbally more sophisticated than little boys as they go through the school system. They are better at verbal memory tasks, verbal fluency tasks, and speed of articulation. When these little girls grow up, they are still champions at processing verbal information. Real as these data seem, however, almost none of them can be divorced from a social context. That’s why Gould’s comment is so helpful.
女孩在求学阶段的语言能力似乎比男孩更胜一筹。她们在语言记忆、语言流畅性和表达速度方面都表现更出色。即使长大成人，这些女孩在处理语言信息方面依然是佼佼者。然而，尽管这些数据看似真实，但几乎都无法脱离社会背景而独立存在。正因如此，古尔德的评论才显得尤为重要。
Tannen spent years observing and videotaping how little girls and little boys interact, especially when talking to their best friends. If any detectable patterns emerged in children, she wanted to know if they also showed up in college students. The patterns she found were both predictable and stable. The conversational styles we develop as adults come directly from the same-sex interactions we solidified as children. Tannen’s findings center on how boys and girls cement relationships and negotiate status within same-sex groups, and then how these entrenched styles clash as men and women try to communicate with one another as adults.
坦南花费数年时间观察并拍摄小男孩和小女孩的互动方式，尤其是他们与好朋友交谈时的互动。她想知道，如果在儿童身上发现了任何可察觉的模式，这些模式是否也会出现在大学生身上。她发现的模式既可预测又稳定。我们成年后形成的谈话风格直接来源于我们童年时期形成的同性互动模式。坦南的研究重点在于男孩和女孩如何在同性群体中巩固关系和协商地位，以及这些根深蒂固的模式如何在成年男女之间沟通时产生冲突。
Cementing relationships
巩固关系
When girl best friends communicate with each other, they lean in, maintain eye contact, and do a lot of talking. They use their sophisticated verbal talents to cement their relationships. Boys never do this. They rarely face each other directly, preferring either parallel or oblique angles. They make little eye contact, their gaze always casting about the room. They do not use verbal information to cement their relationships. Instead, commotion seems to be the central currency of a little boy’s social economy. Doing things physically together is the glue that cements their relationships.
女孩闺蜜之间交流时，会身体前倾，保持眼神交流，并且滔滔不绝。她们运用娴熟的语言技巧来巩固彼此的友谊。男孩则截然不同。他们很少正面对视，而是更喜欢侧身或斜对着对方。他们很少进行眼神交流，目光总是四处游移。他们不用语言来维系关系。相反，喧闹似乎成了小男孩社交圈的核心。一起做一些事情才是维系他们友谊的纽带。
My sons, Josh and Noah, have been playing a one-upmanship game since they were toddlers. A typical version might involve ball throwing. Josh would say, “I can throw this up to the ceiling,” and would promptly try. Then they would laugh. Noah would respond by grabbing and throwing the ball, saying, “Oh yeah? I can throw this up to the sky.” This ratcheting, with laughter, would continue until they reached the “galaxy” or the big prize, “God.”
我的两个儿子，乔什和诺亚，从蹒跚学步起就开始玩一种较劲的游戏。一个典型的版本是扔球。乔什会说：“我可以把球扔到天花板上！”然后立刻尝试。接着他们俩就哈哈大笑。诺亚会抢过球扔出去，说：“哦，是吗？我可以把球扔到天上！”就这样，他们你追我赶，笑声不断，直到他们喊出“银河系”或者最终的“上帝”为止。
Tannen consistently saw this style everywhere she looked—except when observing little girls. The female version goes something like this. One sister says, “I can take this ball and throw it to the ceiling,” and she does. Both laugh. The other sister grabs the ball, throws it up to the ceiling, and says, “I can, too!” Then they talk about how cool it is that they can both throw the ball. This style persists into adulthood for both sexes. Tannen’s data, unfortunately, have been misinterpreted as “Boys always compete, and girls always cooperate.” As this example shows, however, boys are being extremely cooperative. They are simply doing it through competition, deploying their favorite strategy of physical activity.
坦南发现，这种风格在她观察的任何地方都普遍存在——唯独在观察小女孩时例外。女孩版的“合作”大概是这样的：一个妹妹说：“我可以把球扔到天花板上，”然后她真的这么做了。两人都笑了。另一个妹妹也拿起球，扔到天花板上，说：“我也可以！”接着她们讨论起自己都能扔球这件事有多酷。这种风格在男孩女孩中都会延续到成年。不幸的是，坦南的数据被误解为“男孩总是竞争，女孩总是合作”。然而，正如这个例子所示，男孩们其实也非常合作。他们只是通过竞争的方式来表达合作，运用了他们最喜欢的体育活动策略。
Negotiating status
谈判状态
By elementary school, boys finally start using their verbal skills for something: to negotiate their status in a large group. Tannen found that high-status males give orders to the rest of the group, verbally or even physically pushing the low-status boys around. The “leaders” maintain their fiefdoms not only by issuing orders but also by making sure the orders are carried out. Other strong members try to challenge them, so the guys at the top learn quickly to deflect challenges. Hierarchy is very evident with boys. It can be hard on them, too: The life of a low-status male is often miserable.
到了小学，男孩们终于开始运用他们的语言能力：在群体中确立自己的地位。坦南发现，地位高的男孩会向群体中的其他成员发号施令，他们甚至会用言语或肢体压制地位低的男孩。这些“领导者”不仅通过发布命令来维护自己的领地，还会确保命令得到执行。其他强势成员会试图挑战他们，因此处于顶端的男孩很快就学会了如何化解挑战。男孩之间的等级制度非常明显。这对他们来说也很艰难：地位低的男孩往往过得很痛苦。
Tannen found that little girls have hierarchies of status, too. But they used strikingly different strategies to generate and maintain them. Verbal communication is so important that the type of talk determines the status of the relationship. Your “best friend” is the one to whom you tell secrets. The more secrets revealed, the more likely the girls are to identify each other as close. Girls tend to deemphasize the status between them in these situations. Using their sophisticated verbal ability, the girls tend not to give top-down imperial orders. If one of the girls tries issuing commands, the style is usually rejected: The girl is tagged as “bossy” and isolated socially. Not that decisions aren’t made. Various members of the group give suggestions, discuss alternatives, and come to a consensus.
坦南发现，小女孩之间也存在等级制度。但她们建立和维持这种等级制度的策略截然不同。语言交流对她们来说至关重要，以至于谈话的内容决定了彼此关系的等级。“最好的朋友”就是你会倾诉秘密的人。透露的秘密越多，女孩们就越有可能将彼此视为亲密的朋友。在这种情况下，女孩们往往会淡化彼此之间的等级关系。凭借她们娴熟的语言表达能力，女孩们通常不会自上而下地发号施令。如果某个女孩试图发号施令，这种做法通常会遭到拒绝：这个女孩会被贴上“专横跋扈”的标签，并在社交上被孤立。但这并不意味着她们不做决定。群体中的不同成员会提出建议，讨论各种方案，最终达成共识。
The difference between girls’ and boys’ communication could be described as the addition of a single powerful word. Boys might say, “Do this.” Girls would say, “ Let’s do this.”
女孩和男孩沟通方式的差异可以用一个强有力的词来概括。男孩可能会说“做这件事”，而女孩会说“我们一起做这件事”。
Styles persist, then clash
风格持续存在，然后发生冲突
Tannen found that, over time, these ways of using language become increasingly reinforced. By college age, most of these styles are deeply entrenched. And that’s when the problems between men and women become most noticeable.
坦南发现，随着时间的推移，这些语言使用方式会不断强化。到了大学阶段，这些语言风格大多已经根深蒂固。而这正是男女之间问题最为突出的时候。
Tannen tells the story of a woman driving with her husband. “Would you like to stop for a drink?” the wife asked. The husband wasn’t thirsty. “No,” he replied. The woman was annoyed because she had wanted to stop; the man was annoyed because she wasn’t direct. In her book You Just Don’t Understand , Tannen explains: “From her point of view, she had shown concern for her husband’s wishes, but he had shown no concern for hers.” How would this conversation likely go between two women? The thirsty woman would ask, “Are you thirsty?” With lifelong experience at verbal negotiation, her friend would know what she wanted and respond, “I don’t know. Are you thirsty?” Then a small discussion would ensue about whether they were both thirsty enough to stop the car and get water.
坦南讲述了一个女人和丈夫开车的故事。“你想停下来喝点东西吗？”妻子问道。丈夫并不渴。“不用了。”他回答道。妻子很生气，因为她本来就想停车喝水；丈夫则生气，因为她说话不够直接。在她的著作《你就是不明白》中，坦南解释道：“从妻子的角度来看，她已经顾及了丈夫的意愿，但他却丝毫没有顾及她的感受。”如果换成两个女人，她们之间的对话会如何发展呢？口渴的女人会问：“你渴吗？”她的朋友凭借多年的口头协商经验，会明白妻子的意图，并回答：“我不知道。你渴吗？”然后，她们会就两人是否都渴到需要停车喝水展开一番讨论。
These differences in social sensitivity play out in the workforce just as easily as in marriage. At work, women who exert “male” leadership styles are in danger of being perceived as bossy and aggressive. Men who do the same thing are often praised as decisive and assertive. Tannen’s great contribution was to show that these stereotypes form very early in our social development, perhaps assisted by asymmetric verbal development. They transcend geography, age, and even time. Tannen, who was an English literature major, sees these tendencies in manuscripts that go back centuries .
这些社会敏感性的差异在职场中与在婚姻中一样显而易见。在工作中，女性如果展现出“男性化”的领导风格，就容易被视为专横跋扈、咄咄逼人。而男性如果采取同样的做法，往往会被赞扬为果断自信。坦南的伟大贡献在于，他指出这些刻板印象在我们社会发展的早期阶段就已经形成，或许与语言发展的不对称性有关。它们超越了地域、年龄，甚至时间的限制。坦南主修英国文学，他发现早在几个世纪前的手稿中就存在这些倾向。
Nature or nurture?
先天因素还是后天因素？
Tannen’s findings are statistical patterns, not an all-or-none phenomenon. Many factors affect our language patterns, she found. Regional background, individual personality, profession, social class, age, ethnicity, and birth order all affect how we use language to negotiate our social ecologies. Boys and girls are treated differently socially the moment they are born, and they are often reared in societies filled with centuries of entrenched prejudice. It would be a miracle if we somehow transcended our experience and behaved in an egalitarian fashion.
坦南的研究结果是统计模式，而非非此即彼的现象。她发现，许多因素都会影响我们的语言模式。地域背景、个人性格、职业、社会阶层、年龄、种族和出生顺序都会影响我们如何运用语言来应对社会环境。男孩和女孩从出生起就受到不同的社会对待，他们往往在充满根深蒂固的偏见的社会中长大。如果我们能够超越自身的经历，以平等的方式行事，那将是一个奇迹。
Given the influence of culture on behavior, it is overly simplistic to invoke a purely biological explanation for Tannen’s observations. Given the great influence of brain biology on behavior, it is also simplistic to invoke a purely social explanation. The real answer to the nature-or-nurture question is “We don’t know.” That can be frustrating to hear. As scientists explore how genes and cells and behaviors connect, their findings give us not completed bridges but boards and nails. It’s dangerous to assume the bridges are complete. Just ask Larry Summers.
鉴于文化对行为的影响，仅仅用生物学解释坦南的观察结果未免过于简单。同样，鉴于大脑生物学对行为的巨大影响，仅仅用社会因素解释也过于简单。关于先天与后天之争的真正答案是“我们不知道”。听到这个答案可能会令人沮丧。科学家们探索基因、细胞和行为之间的联系时，他们的发现并非完整的桥梁，而只是木板和钉子。想当然地认为桥梁已经完工是危险的。不妨问问拉里·萨默斯就知道了。
More ideas
更多想法
Get the facts straight on emotions
弄清情绪的真相
Dealing with the emotional lives of men and women is a big part of the job for teachers and managers. They need to know:
处理男女学生的情感问题是教师和管理者工作的重要组成部分。他们需要了解：
1) Emotions are useful. They make the brain pay attention.
1）情绪是有用的。它们能使大脑集中注意力。
2) Men and women process certain emotions differently.
2）男性和女性处理某些情绪的方式不同。
3) The differences are a product of complex interactions between nature and nurture .
3）这些差异是先天因素和后天因素之间复杂相互作用的结果。
Experiment with same-sex classrooms
尝试开设同性课堂
My son’s third-grade teacher began seeing a stereotype that worsened as the year progressed. The girls were excelling in the language arts, and the boys were pulling ahead in math and science. This was only the third grade ! The language-arts differences made some sense to her. But she knew there was no statistical support for the contention that men have a better aptitude for math and science than women. Why, for heaven’s sake, was she presiding over a stereotype? The teacher guessed that part of the answer lay in the students’ social participation during class. When the teacher asked a question of the class, who answered first turned out to be unbelievably important. In the language arts, the girls invariably answered first. Other girls reacted with that participatory “me too” instinct. The reaction on the part of the boys was hierarchical. The girls usually knew the answers, the boys usually did not, and the males responded by doing what low-status males tend to do: They withdrew. A performance gap quickly emerged.
我儿子三年级的老师开始注意到一种刻板印象，而且随着学年的推进愈演愈烈。女生在语文方面表现出色，而男生则在数学和科学方面遥遥领先。这才三年级啊！语文方面的差异在她看来情有可原。但她知道，没有任何统计数据支持“男性比女性更有数学和科学天赋”这种说法。天哪，她为什么要让这种刻板印象影响到自己呢？老师猜测，部分原因在于学生在课堂上的社交参与度。当老师提问时，谁先回答竟然至关重要。在语文课上，女生总是第一个回答。其他女生也出于那种“我也是”的本能而积极参与。而男生的反应则带有等级观念。女生通常知道答案，男生通常不知道，于是男生就做了那些地位低下的男生通常会做的事：他们选择退缩。很快，男女之间的成绩差距就显现出来了。
In math and science, boys and girls were equally likely to answer a question first. But the boys used their familiar “top each other” conversational styles when they participated, attempting to establish a hierarchy based on who knew more. This included drubbing anyone who didn’t make the top, including the girls. Bewildered, the girls began withdrawing from participating in the subjects. Once again, a performance gap emerged.
在数学和科学考试中，男孩和女孩回答问题的概率大致相同。但男孩们在回答问题时会采用他们惯常的“互相攀比”的交流方式，试图建立一个基于知识水平的等级制度。这其中就包括贬低任何未能胜出的人，包括女孩。女孩们感到困惑，开始逐渐退出这些科目的学习。成绩差距再次显现。
The teacher called a meeting of the girls and verified her observations. Then she asked for a consensus about what they should do. The girls decided that they wanted to learn math and science separately from the boys. Previously a strong advocate for mixed-sex classes, the teacher wondered aloud if that made any sense. Yet if the girls started losing the math-and-science battle in the third grade, the teacher reasoned, they were not likely to excel in the coming years. She obliged. It took only two weeks to close the performance gap .
老师召集女生开会，核实了自己的观察结果。然后，她征求大家的意见，决定下一步该怎么做。女生们决定要和男生分开学习数学和科学。这位老师之前一直大力支持男女混合班，但她不禁质疑这种做法是否合理。然而，老师转念一想，如果女生们在三年级就开始在数学和科学方面落后于男生，那么她们在未来的几年里就很难取得优异的成绩。于是，她同意了女生们的提议。仅仅两周时间，女生们的成绩差距就缩小了。
Can the teacher’s result be applied to classrooms all over the world? One classroom in a single school year does not make for a valid experiment. We need to test hundreds of classrooms and thousands of students from all walks of life, over a period of years.
这位老师的研究结果能否推广到世界各地的课堂？仅仅一个班级、一个学年的研究不足以构成有效的实验。我们需要在数年时间内，对数百个班级、数千名来自各行各业的学生进行测试。
Pair men and women in workplace teams
在工作场所团队中安排男女搭档
One day, I spoke about gender with a group of executives-in-training at the Boeing Leadership Center in St. Louis. After showing some of Larry Cahill’s data about gist and detail, I said, “Sometimes women are accused of being more emotional than men, from the home to the workplace. I think that women might not be any more emotional than anyone else.” I explained that because women perceive their emotional landscape with more data points (that’s the detail) and see it in greater resolution, women may simply have more information to which they are capable of reacting. If men perceived the same number of data points, they might have the same reactions. Two women in the back began crying softly. After the lecture, I asked them about it, fearing I may have offended them. What they said instead blew me away. “It was the first time in my professional life,” one of them said, “that I didn’t feel like I had to apologize for who I was.”
有一天，我在圣路易斯波音领导力中心给一群正在接受培训的高管讲授性别议题。在展示了拉里·卡希尔关于要点和细节的一些数据后，我说：“人们有时会指责女性比男性更情绪化，无论是在家庭还是职场。我认为女性的情绪化程度可能并不比其他人更高。”我解释说，因为女性感知自身情绪时会掌握更多的数据点（这就是细节），并且能够更清晰地看到这些数据，所以她们可能只是能够对更多信息做出反应。如果男性感知到的数据点数量相同，他们的反应也可能相同。后排的两位女士开始低声啜泣。讲座结束后，我担心自己可能冒犯了她们，便询问她们的感受。但她们的回答却让我震惊。“这是我职业生涯中第一次，”其中一位女士说，“我感觉自己不需要为自己的所作所为道歉。”
And that got me to thinking. In our evolutionary history, having a team that could understand both the gist and details of a given stressful situation helped us conquer the world. Why would the world of business be exempted from that advantage? Having an executive team or work group capable of simultaneously understanding both the emotional forests and the trees of a stressful project, such as a merger, might be a marriage made in business heaven. It could even affect the bottom line.
这让我开始思考。在人类进化史上，拥有一支能够把握特定压力情境的要点和细节的团队，曾帮助我们征服世界。商业世界为何不能拥有这种优势呢？如果一支高管团队或工作小组能够同时理解诸如并购这类压力项目的全局和细节，那简直就是天作之合。这甚至可能影响企业的最终盈利。
Companies often train managers by setting up simulations of various situations. They could take a mixed-sex team and a unisex team and have each work on the same project. Give another two teams the same project, but first teach them what we know about brain differences between the sexes. Would the mixed teams do better than the unisex teams? Would the groups prepped on how the brain works do better than the unprepped groups? You might find that management teams with a gist/detail balance create the best chance for productivity. At the very least, it means both men and women have an equal right to be at the decision-making table.
公司通常会通过模拟各种情境来培训管理者。例如，他们可以组建一个男女混合团队和一个男女同工团队，让两组团队分别负责同一个项目。然后再给另外两组团队布置同样的项目，但事先向他们讲解男女大脑差异的相关知识。男女混合团队的表现会优于男女同工团队吗？事先了解大脑运作原理的团队的表现会优于未接受过相关培训的团队吗？你可能会发现，能够兼顾要点和细节的管理团队更有可能提高工作效率。至少，这意味着男性和女性都拥有平等的决策权。
Imagine environments where gender differences are both noted and celebrated, as opposed to ignored and marginalized. We might have more women in science and engineering. We might shatter the archetypal glass ceiling. We might create better businesses. We might even create better marriages.
想象一下，如果性别差异被重视和尊重，而不是被忽视和边缘化，那会是怎样一番景象？我们或许会看到更多女性投身科学和工程领域。我们或许能够打破职场中根深蒂固的“玻璃天花板”。我们或许能够创造出更优秀的企业。我们甚至或许能够缔造更美满的婚姻。
Brain Rule #1 1
大脑法则第11条
Male and female brains are different.
男性和女性的大脑是不同的。
• The X chromosome that males have one of and females have two of—though one acts as a backup—is a cognitive “hot spot,” carrying an unusually large percentage of genes involved in brain manufacture.
•男性拥有一条 X 染色体，女性拥有两条 X 染色体（其中一条作为备用），X 染色体是认知“热点”，携带了异常大比例的与大脑制造相关的基因。
• Women are genetically more complex, because the active X chromosomes in their cells are a mix of Mom’s and Dad’s. Men’s X chromosomes all come from Mom, and their Y chromosome carries less than 100 genes, compared with about 1,500 for the X chromosome.
•女性的基因结构更为复杂，因为她们细胞中活跃的X染色体是父母双方基因的混合体。男性的X染色体全部来自母亲，他们的Y染色体携带的基因不到100个，而X染色体则携带约1500个基因。
• Men’s and women’s brains are different structurally and biochemically—men have a bigger amygdala and produce serotonin faster, for example—but we don’t know if those differences have significance.
•男性和女性的大脑在结构和生化方面有所不同——例如，男性的杏仁核更大，血清素的产生速度更快——但我们不知道这些差异是否具有意义。
• Men and women respond differently to acute stress: Women activate the left hemisphere’s amygdala and remember the emotional details. Men activate the right hemisphere’s amygdala and get the gist.
•男性和女性对急性压力的反应不同：女性会激活左脑杏仁核，记住情绪细节；男性会激活右脑杏仁核，把握大局。
# ↩
exploration
勘探
Brain Rule #12
大脑法则第12条
We are powerful and natural explorers.
我们是强大而天生的探险家。
# ↩
MY DEAR SON JOSH got a painful beesting at the tender age of 2, and he almost deserved it.
我亲爱的儿子乔什在两岁时遭受了严重的马虱叮咬，这几乎是他咎由自取。
It was a warm, sunny afternoon. We were playing the “pointing game,” a simple exercise where he would point at something, and I would look. Then we’d both laugh. Josh had been told not to touch bumblebees because they could sting him; we used the word “danger” whenever he approached one. There, in a patch of clover, he spotted a big, furry, buzzing temptress. As he reached for it, I calmly said, “Danger,” and he obediently withdrew his hand. He pointed at a distant bush, continuing our game.
那是一个温暖晴朗的下午。我们正在玩“指点游戏”，一个简单的游戏，他指着什么东西，我去看。然后我们俩都会笑。乔什被告知不要碰大黄蜂，因为它们会蜇人；每当他靠近大黄蜂时，我们都会说“危险”。就在这时，在一片三叶草丛里，他发现了一只毛茸茸的、嗡嗡叫的“小妖精”。他伸手去抓它时，我平静地说：“危险”，他乖乖地把手缩了回去。他指着远处的一丛灌木，继续我们的游戏。
As I looked toward the bush, I suddenly heard a 110-decibel yelp. While I was looking away, Josh reached for the bee, which promptly stung him. Josh had used the pointing game as a diversion, and I was outwitted by a 2-year-old.
我朝灌木丛方向望去，突然听到一声110分贝的尖叫。我刚把目光移开，乔什就伸手去抓那只蜜蜂，结果被蛰了一下。乔什用指认蜜蜂的游戏转移了我的注意力，我竟然被一个两岁小孩耍了。
“DANGER!” he sobbed as I held him close.
“危险！”我紧紧抱着他，他抽泣着说。
“Danger,” I repeated sadly, hugging him, getting some ice, and wondering what puberty would be like in 10 years or so .
“危险，”我悲伤地重复道，一边拥抱他，一边拿来一些冰块，一边想着大约 10 年后青春期会是什么样子。
This incident was Dad’s inauguration into a behavioral suite often called the terrible twos. It was a rough baptism for me and the little guy. Yet it also made me smile. The mental faculties kids use to distract their dads are the same they will use as grown-ups to discover the composition of distant suns or the next alternative energy. We are natural explorers, even if the habit sometimes stings us. The tendency is so strong, it is capable of turning us into lifelong learners. But you can see it best in our youngest citizens, often when they seem at their worst.
这件事标志着爸爸正式踏入了所谓的“可怕的两岁”行为模式。对我和小家伙来说，这都是一次艰难的洗礼。然而，它也让我不禁莞尔。孩子们用来分散爸爸注意力的那些思维能力，与他们长大后用来探索遥远恒星的组成或下一代替代能源的能力如出一辙。我们天生就是探索者，即使这种习惯有时会让我们感到痛苦。这种倾向如此强烈，足以让我们成为终身学习者。但你往往能在孩子们最年幼的时候，尤其是在他们看起来最糟糕的时候，最能感受到这一点。
Babies give researchers a clear view, unobstructed by years of contaminating experiences, of how humans naturally acquire information. Preloaded with lots of information-processing software, infants acquire information using surprisingly specific strategies, many of which are preserved into adulthood. In part, understanding how humans learn at this age means understanding how humans learn at any age.
婴儿为研究人员提供了一个清晰的视角，让他们得以观察人类如何自然地获取信息，而无需受到多年经验的干扰。婴儿天生就具备丰富的信息处理能力，他们运用一些出人意料的特定策略来获取信息，其中许多策略会一直保留到成年。从某种程度上说，了解人类在这个年龄段的学习方式，就意味着了解人类在任何年龄段的学习方式。
We didn’t always think that way. If you had said something about preset brain wiring to researchers 40 years ago, their response would have been an indignant, “What are you smoking?” or, less politely, “Get out of my laboratory.” This is because researchers for decades thought that babies were a blank slate—a tabula rasa. They thought that everything a baby knew was learned by interactions with its environments, primarily with adults. This perspective undoubtedly was formulated by overworked scientists who never had any children. We know better now. Amazing strides have been made in understanding the cognitive world of the infant. Indeed, the research world now looks to babies to show how humans, including adults, think about practically everything.
我们并非一直都这么想。如果你在40年前跟研究人员提起大脑预设连接的概念，他们的反应很可能是愤慨地问：“你在胡说八道什么？”或者更不客气地说：“滚出我的实验室！”这是因为几十年来，研究人员一直认为婴儿就像一张白纸——一张空白的画布。他们认为婴儿所知道的一切都是通过与环境（主要是与成人）的互动习得的。毫无疑问，这种观点是由那些从未生育过孩子的、工作过度的科学家们提出的。现在我们有了更深刻的认识。在理解婴儿的认知世界方面，我们已经取得了惊人的进步。事实上，如今的研究界正着眼于婴儿，以揭示人类（包括成人）是如何思考几乎所有事情的。
Babies test everything—including you
婴儿会试探一切——包括你。
Babies are born with a deep desire to understand the world around them and an incessant curiosity that compels them to aggressively explore it. This need for explanation is so powerfully stitched into their experience that some scientists describe it as a drive, just as hunger and thirst and sex are drives.
婴儿天生就渴望了解周围的世界，他们拥有永无止境的好奇心，驱使他们积极地探索世界。这种寻求解释的需求深深根植于他们的经验之中，以至于一些科学家将其描述为一种本能，就像饥饿、口渴和性欲一样。
All babies gather information by actively testing their environment, much as a scientist would. They make a sensory observation, form a hypothesis about what is going on, design an experiment capable of testing the hypothesis, and then draw conclusions from the findings. They use a series of increasingly self-corrected ideas to figure out how the world works.
所有婴儿都像科学家一样，通过积极探索周围环境来获取信息。他们进行感官观察，对正在发生的事情形成假设，设计能够验证假设的实验，然后根据实验结果得出结论。他们运用一系列不断自我修正的想法来理解世界的运作方式。
42 minutes old: Newborns can imitate
出生42分钟：新生儿就能模仿
In 1979, Andy Meltzoff rocked the world of infant psychology by sticking out his tongue at a newborn and being polite enough to wait for a reply. What he found astonished him. The baby stuck her tongue back out at him! He reliably measured this imitative behavior with infants only 42 minutes old. The baby had never seen a tongue before, not Meltzoff’s and not her own, yet the baby knew she had a tongue, knew Meltzoff had a tongue, and somehow intuited the idea of mirroring. Further, the baby’s brain knew that if it stimulated a series of nerves in a certain sequence, she could also stick her tongue out. That’s definitely not consistent with the notion of tabula rasa.
1979年，安迪·梅尔佐夫（Andy Meltzoff）的一项实验震惊了婴儿心理学界。他向一个新生儿吐舌头，并礼貌地等待回应。结果令他震惊：婴儿竟然也向他吐了舌头！他可靠地测量了仅42分钟大的婴儿的这种模仿行为。这个婴儿之前从未见过舌头，无论是梅尔佐夫的还是自己的，但她知道自己有舌头，知道梅尔佐夫有舌头，并且不知何故领悟到了镜像模仿的概念。此外，婴儿的大脑知道，如果按特定顺序刺激一系列神经，她也可以吐舌头。这显然与“白板说”相悖。
I tried this with my son Noah. He and I started our relationship in life by sticking our tongues out at each other. In his first 30 minutes of life, we had struck up an imitative conversation. By the end of his first week, we were well entrenched in dialogue: Every time I came into his crib room, we greeted each other with tongue protrusions. It was purely delightful on my part and purely adaptive on his. If I had not stuck my tongue out initially, he would not be doing so with such predictability every time he saw me.
我和儿子诺亚试过这种方法。我们俩的“亲密互动”是从互相吐舌头开始的。在他出生后的前30分钟，我们就开始模仿着对方说话。到他出生后的第一个星期结束时，我们的“对话”已经非常熟练了：每次我走进他的婴儿房，我们都会互相吐舌头打招呼。对我来说，这纯粹是件乐事；对他来说，这纯粹是适应环境的结果。如果我一开始没有吐舌头，他就不会每次见到我都如此有规律地吐舌头了。
Three months later, my wife picked me up after a lecture at a medical school, Noah in tow. I was still fielding questions, but I scooped up Noah and held him close while answering. Out of the corner of my eye, I noticed Noah gazing at me expectantly, flicking his tongue out about every five seconds. I smiled and stuck my tongue out at Noah mid-question. Immediately he squealed and started sticking his tongue out with abandon, every half second or so. I knew exactly what he was doing. Noah made an observation (Dad and I stick our tongues out at each other), formed a hypothesis (I bet if I stick my tongue out at Dad, he will stick his tongue back out at me), created and executed his experiment (I will stick my tongue out at Dad), and changed his behavior as a result of the evaluation of his research (sticking his tongue out more frequently).
三个月后，我妻子带着诺亚来医学院接我下课。我还在回答问题，但还是把诺亚抱起来搂在怀里。我眼角的余光瞥见诺亚正满怀期待地看着我，大约每隔五秒钟就吐一次舌头。我笑着，在提问的过程中也朝诺亚吐了吐舌头。他立刻尖叫起来，开始肆无忌惮地吐舌头，大约每半秒钟就吐一次。我完全明白他在做什么。诺亚观察到（我和爸爸会互相吐舌头），提出了一个假设（我打赌，如果我朝爸爸吐舌头，他也会朝我吐舌头），设计并执行了他的实验（我要朝爸爸吐舌头），并根据实验结果改变了自己的行为（更频繁地吐舌头）。
Nobody taught Noah, or any other baby, how to do this. And it is a lifelong strategy. You probably did it this morning when you couldn’t find your glasses, hypothesized they were in the bathroom, and went to look. From a brain science perspective, we don’t even have a good metaphor to describe how you know to do that. It is so automatic, you probably had no idea you were looking at the results of a successful experiment when you found your glasses lying on a towel.
没人教过诺亚，或者其他任何婴儿如何做到这一点。而且这是一种终身策略。你今天早上可能就这么做了：找不到眼镜，你猜想它们在浴室里，然后就去寻找。从脑科学的角度来看，我们甚至找不到合适的比喻来解释你为什么会这样做。这太自动化了，以至于当你发现眼镜躺在毛巾上时，你可能根本没意识到自己正在经历一次成功的实验。
Noah’s story is just one example of how babies use their precious preloaded information-gathering strategies to gain knowledge they didn’t have at birth. We also can see it in broken stuff, disappearing cups and temper tantrums.
诺亚的故事只是一个例子，说明婴儿如何利用他们与生俱来的宝贵信息收集策略来获取出生时并不具备的知识。我们也能在打碎的物品、消失的杯子和发脾气中看到这一点。
12 months old: Infants analyze how objects act
12个月大的婴儿：分析物体的运动方式
Babies younger than a year old will systematically analyze an object with every sensory weapon at their disposal. They will feel it, kick it, try to tear it apart, stick it in their ear, stick it in their mouth, give it to you so that you can stick it in your mouth. They appear to be intensely gathering information about the properties of the object. Babies methodically do experiments on the objects to see what else they will do. In our household, this usually meant breaking stuff.
不到一岁的婴儿会运用所有感官系统地分析物体。他们会触摸它、踢它、试图撕碎它、把它塞进耳朵里、塞进嘴里，甚至递给你让你也塞进嘴里。他们似乎在竭尽全力地收集关于物体特性的信息。婴儿会系统地对物体进行各种实验，看看还能做些什么。在我们家，这通常意味着他们会把东西弄坏。
These object-oriented research projects grow increasingly sophisticated. In one set of experiments, babies were given a rake, and a toy was placed nearby. The babies quickly learned to use the rake to get the toy. This is not exactly a groundbreaking discovery, as every parent knows. After a few successful attempts, the babies lost interest in the toy. But not in the experiment. Again and again, they would take the toy and move it to a different place, then use the rake to grab it. You can almost hear them exclaiming, “Wow! How does this happen?”
这些面向对象的实验项目日趋复杂。在一组实验中，研究人员给婴儿一把耙子，并在旁边放了一个玩具。婴儿很快就学会了用耙子拿到玩具。这并非什么惊天发现，每个家长都知道。几次成功之后，婴儿对玩具失去了兴趣。但他们对实验本身却兴致盎然。他们一次又一次地拿起玩具，把它挪到另一个地方，然后再用耙子把它捞出来。你仿佛能听到他们惊叹：“哇！这是怎么做到的？”
18 months old: Objects still exist if you can’t see them
18个月大：即使看不见，物体仍然存在
Little Emily, before 18 months of age, still believes that if an object is hidden from view, that object has disappeared. She does not have what is known as “object permanence.” That is about to change. Emily has been playing with a washcloth and a cup. She covers the cup with the cloth, and then pauses for a second, a concerned look on her brow. Slowly she pulls the cloth away from the cup. The cup is still there! She glares for a moment, then quickly covers it back up. Thirty seconds go by before her hand tentatively reaches for the cloth. Repeating the experiment, she slowly removes the cloth. The cup is still there! She squeals with delight. Now things go quickly. She covers and uncovers the cup again and again, laughing loudly each time. It is dawning on Emily that the cup has object permanence: Even if removed from view, it has not disappeared. She will repeat this experiment for more than half an hour. If you have ever spent time with an 18-month-old, you know that getting one to concentrate on anything for 30 minutes is some kind of miracle. Yet it happens, and to babies at this age all over the world.
不到18个月大的小艾米丽仍然认为，如果一个物体被遮住，它就消失了。她还没有“物体恒存性”的概念。但这种情况即将改变。艾米丽一直在玩一块毛巾和一个杯子。她用毛巾盖住杯子，然后停顿了一下，眉头紧锁，一脸担忧。她慢慢地把毛巾从杯子上拿开。杯子还在那里！她瞪了一会儿，然后迅速地又盖了回去。过了三十秒，她的手才小心翼翼地伸向毛巾。她重复着这个实验，慢慢地把毛巾拿开。杯子还在那里！她高兴地尖叫起来。现在，她玩得很快。她一遍又一遍地盖住、揭开毛巾，每次都开怀大笑。艾米丽渐渐明白了杯子具有物体恒存性：即使被移开，它也没有消失。她会重复这个实验超过半个小时。如果你曾经和18个月大的孩子相处过，你就会知道，让他们集中注意力30分钟简直是个奇迹。然而，这并非不可能，而且全世界这个年龄段的婴儿都能做到。
Though this may sound like a delightful form of peekaboo, it is actually an experiment whose failure would have lethal evolutionary consequences. Object permanence is an important concept to have if you live in the savannah. Saber-toothed tigers still exist, for example, even if they suddenly duck down in the tall grass. Those who didn’t acquire this knowledge usually were on some predator’s menu .
这听起来像是玩捉迷藏一样有趣，但实际上却是一项实验，一旦失败，将会对进化造成致命的后果。对于生活在稀树草原的人来说，物体恒存性是一个至关重要的概念。例如，即使剑齿虎突然躲进高高的草丛中，它们依然存在。那些没有掌握这种知识的生物，通常都会成为捕食者的盘中餐。
18 months old: Your preferences aren’t the same as mine
18个月大的孩子：你的喜好和我的不一样。
The distance between 14 months of age and 18 months of age is extraordinary. Around 14 months, toddlers think that because they like something, the whole world likes the same thing—as summed up in the “Toddler’s Creed”:
14个月到18个月之间的差距非常显著。大约14个月大的幼儿会认为，如果他们喜欢某样东西，那么全世界都喜欢同样的东西——正如“幼儿信条”所概括的那样：
If I want it, it is mine.
如果我想要，它就是我的。
If I give it to you and change my mind later, it is mine.
如果我把它给你，之后又改变主意，那它就是我的了。
If I can take it away from you, it is mine.
如果我能把它从你身边夺走，它就是我的了。
If we are building something together, all of the pieces are mine.
如果我们一起建造什么东西，所有的部件都属于我。
If it looks just like mine, it is mine.
如果它看起来和我的一模一样，那就是我的。
If it is mine, it will never belong to anybody else, no matter what.
如果是我的，无论如何，它永远不会属于其他人。
If it is yours, it is mine.
如果它是你的，那就是我的。
Around 18 months, it dawns on babies that this viewpoint may not always be accurate. They begin to learn that adage that most newlyweds have to relearn in spades: “What is obvious to you is obvious to you.”
大约18个月大的时候，婴儿们开始意识到这种观点可能并不总是正确的。他们开始明白那句大多数新婚夫妇都必须重新学习的格言：“对你来说显而易见的事情，对你来说就是显而易见的。”
How do babies react to such new information? By testing it, as usual. Before the age of 2, babies do plenty of things parents would rather them not do. But after the age of 2, small children will do things because their parents don’t want them to. The compliant little darlings seem to transform into rebellious little tyrants. Many parents think their children are actively defying them at this stage. (The thought certainly crossed my mind as I nursed Joshua’s unfortunate beesting.) That would be a mistake, however. This stage is simply the natural extension of a sophisticated research program begun at birth. You push the boundaries of people’s preferences, then stand back and see how they react. Then you repeat the experiment, pushing them to their limits over and over again to see how stable the findings are, as if you were playing peekaboo. Slowly you begin to perceive the length and height and breadth of people’s desires, and how they differ from yours. Then, just to be sure the boundaries are still in place, you occasionally do the whole experiment over again.
婴儿对这种新信息会作何反应？和往常一样，他们会通过试探来检验。两岁之前，婴儿会做很多父母不希望他们做的事情。但两岁之后，小孩子反而会去做一些父母不希望他们做的事情。那些乖巧听话的小宝贝似乎变成了叛逆的小暴君。许多父母认为，在这个阶段，他们的孩子是在故意违抗他们。（当我给被蜜蜂蜇伤的约书亚喂奶时，我也曾有过这样的想法。）然而，这种想法是错误的。这个阶段仅仅是从出生就开始的一项复杂研究计划的自然延伸。你不断挑战人们的喜好界限，然后退后一步，观察他们的反应。接着，你重复这个实验，一次又一次地将他们推向极限，以检验研究结果的稳定性，就像玩捉迷藏一样。慢慢地，你开始感知人们欲望的广度、深度和深度，以及它们与你自身欲望的差异。然后，为了确保界限依然存在，你偶尔会把整个实验再做一遍。
Babies may not have a whole lot of understanding about their world, but they know a whole lot about how to get it. It reminds me of the old proverb, “Catch me a fish and I eat for a day; teach me to fish and I eat for a lifetime.”
婴儿可能对周围的世界了解不多，但他们却非常懂得如何获取信息。这让我想起一句古老的谚语：“授人以鱼不如授人以渔。”
Babies reveal more of the brain’s secrets each year
婴儿每年都会揭示大脑更多的秘密。
Why does a baby stick its tongue back out at you? The beginnings of a neural road map have been drawn in the past few years, at least for some of the “simpler” thinking behaviors, such as imitation. Three investigators at the University of Parma were studying the macaque, assessing brain activity as it reached for different objects in the laboratory. The researchers recorded the pattern of neural firing when the monkey picked up a raisin. One day, researcher Leonardo Fogassi walked into the laboratory and casually plucked a raisin from a bowl. Suddenly, the monkey’s brain began to fire excitedly. The recordings were in the raisin-specific pattern, as if the animal had just picked up the raisin . But the monkey had not picked up the raisin. It simply saw Fogassi do it.
为什么婴儿会朝你吐舌头？过去几年里，人们已经初步绘制出一些神经活动图谱，至少对于一些“比较简单”的思维行为，例如模仿，来说是如此。帕尔马大学的三位研究人员正在研究猕猴，评估它们在实验室里伸手抓取不同物体时的大脑活动。研究人员记录了猴子拿起一颗葡萄干时的神经元放电模式。一天，研究员莱昂纳多·福加西走进实验室，随意地从碗里拿了一颗葡萄干。突然，猴子的大脑开始兴奋地放电。记录显示，这种放电模式与葡萄干的放电模式完全一致，就好像猴子刚刚拿起了葡萄干一样。但实际上，猴子并没有拿起葡萄干，它只是看到了福加西这样做。
The astonished researchers quickly replicated and extended their findings, and then published them in a series of landmark papers describing the existence of “mirror neurons.” Mirror neurons are cells whose activity reflect their surroundings. Cues that could elicit mirror neural responses were found to be remarkably subtle. If a primate simply heard the sound of someone doing something it had previously experienced—say, tearing a piece of paper—these neurons could fire as if the monkey were experiencing the full stimulus. It wasn’t long before researchers identified human mirror neurons. These neurons are scattered across the brain, and a subset is involved in action recognition—that classic imitative behavior such as babies sticking out their tongues. Other neurons mirror a variety of motor behaviors .
震惊的研究人员迅速重复并扩展了他们的发现，随后发表了一系列里程碑式的论文，描述了“镜像神经元”的存在。镜像神经元是活动反映周围环境的细胞。能够引发镜像神经元反应的线索极其微妙。如果一只灵长类动物仅仅听到有人做它以前经历过的事情的声音——比如撕纸——这些神经元就会像猴子亲身经历了完整的刺激一样活跃起来。不久之后，研究人员就发现了人类的镜像神经元。这些神经元遍布大脑，其中一部分参与动作识别——例如婴儿吐舌头等经典的模仿行为。其他神经元则反映各种运动行为。
We also are beginning to understand which regions of the brain are involved in our ability to learn from a series of increasingly self-corrected ideas. We use our right prefrontal cortex to predict error and to retrospectively evaluate input for errors. The anterior cingulate cortex, just south of the prefrontal cortex, signals us when perceived unfavorable circumstances call for a change in behavior. Every year, the brain reveals more and more of its secrets, with babies leading the way.
我们也开始了解大脑的哪些区域参与了我们从一系列不断自我纠正的想法中学习的能力。我们利用右侧前额叶皮层来预测错误，并回顾性地评估输入信息中的错误。位于前额叶皮层南部的扣带回前部，会在我们感知到不利情况需要改变行为时发出信号。每年，大脑都在揭示越来越多的秘密，而婴儿则引领着这一进程。
We never outgrow the desire to know
我们永远不会失去求知的渴望。
We can remain lifelong learners. No question. This fact was brought home to me as a postdoctoral scholar at the University of Washington. In 1992, Edmond Fischer and Edwin Krebs shared the Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine. I had the good fortune to be familiar with both their work and their offices. They were just down the hall from mine. By the time I arrived at the university, Fischer and Krebs were already in their mid-70s. The first thing I noticed upon meeting them was that they were not retired. Not physically and not mentally. Long after they had earned the right to be lounging on some tropical island, both had powerful, productive laboratories in full swing. Every day I would see them walking down the hall, oblivious to others, chatting about some new finding, swapping each other’s journals, and listening intently to each other’s ideas. Sometimes they would have someone else along, grilling them and in turn being grilled about some experimental result. They were as creative as artists, wise as Solomon, lively as children. They had lost nothing . Their intellectual engines were still revving, and curiosity remained the fuel. They taught me that our learning abilities don’t have to change as we age.
我们可以终身学习，这一点毋庸置疑。我在华盛顿大学做博士后研究员时，对此有了更深刻的体会。1992年，埃德蒙·费舍尔和埃德温·克雷布斯共同荣获诺贝尔生理学或医学奖。我有幸熟悉他们的工作，也经常去他们的办公室。他们的办公室就在我隔壁。我到大学时，费舍尔和克雷布斯都已年过七旬。见到他们的第一印象就是他们并没有退休。无论身体还是精神，他们都还很年轻。尽管他们早已有资格在某个热带岛屿上享受悠闲时光，但他们的实验室依然运转良好，硕果累累。我每天都能看到他们沿着走廊走来走去，仿佛对周围的人视而不见，热烈地讨论着新的发现，交换着彼此的期刊，认真地倾听着对方的想法。有时，他们还会带上其他人，就一些实验结果向对方提出问题，反之亦然。他们像艺术家一样富有创造力，像所罗门王一样智慧，像孩子一样活泼。他们一无所有。他们的求知欲依然旺盛，好奇心依然是他们前进的动力。他们让我明白，随着年龄的增长，我们的学习能力并不会改变。
The brain remains malleable
大脑仍具有可塑性。
Research shows that the brain is wired to keep learning as we age. Some regions of the adult brain stay as malleable as a baby’s brain, so we can grow new connections, strengthen existing connections, and even create new neurons, allowing all of us to be lifelong learners. We didn’t always think that. Until five or six years ago, the prevailing notion was that we were born with all of the brain cells we were ever going to get, and they steadily eroded in a depressing journey through adulthood to old age. We do lose synaptic connections with age. Some estimates of neural loss alone are close to 30,000 neurons per day. But the adult brain also continues creating neurons within the regions normally involved in learning. These new neurons show the same plasticity as those of newborns.
研究表明，大脑天生就具备随着年龄增长而持续学习的能力。成年人大脑的某些区域仍然像婴儿的大脑一样具有可塑性，因此我们可以建立新的连接、加强现有的连接，甚至产生新的神经元，从而使我们所有人都能终身学习。我们并非一直都这么认为。直到五六年前，人们普遍认为我们出生时就拥有了我们所能获得的全部脑细胞，它们会在从成年到老年的令人沮丧的旅程中逐渐减少。随着年龄的增长，我们的突触连接确实会减少。据估计，仅神经元的损失就接近每天3万个。但成年人的大脑也会在通常参与学习的区域内继续产生神经元。这些新生的神经元与新生儿的神经元一样具有可塑性。
Throughout life, your brain retains the ability to change its structure and function in response to your experiences.
在人的一生中，大脑始终保持着根据自身经历改变其结构和功能的能力。
Why? Evolutionary pressure, as usual. Problem solving was greatly favored in the unstable environment of the Serengeti. But not just any kind of problem solving. When we came down from the trees to the savannah, we did not say to ourselves, “Good Lord, give me a book and a lecture and a board of directors so that I can spend 10 years learning how to survive in this place.” Our survival did not depend upon exposure to organized, preplanned packets of information. Our survival depended upon chaotic, reactive information-gathering experiences. That’s why one of our best attributes is the ability to learn through a series of increasingly self-corrected ideas. “The red snake with the white stripe bit me yesterday, and I almost died,” is an observation we readily made. Then we went a step further: “I hypothesize that if I encounter the same snake, the same thing will happen!” It is a scientific learning style we have exploited literally for millions of years. It is not possible to outgrow it in the whisper-short seven to eight decades we spend on the planet.
为什么？一如既往，是进化压力。在塞伦盖蒂动荡的环境中，解决问题的能力至关重要。但并非任何一种解决问题的能力都适用。当我们从树上来到稀树草原时，我们不会对自己说：“上帝啊，请赐予我一本书、一场讲座和一个董事会，让我花十年时间学习如何在这个地方生存。”我们的生存并不依赖于接触有组织、预先计划好的信息包。我们的生存依赖于混乱的、被动的信息收集经验。这就是为什么我们最强大的能力之一就是通过一系列不断自我修正的想法来学习。“昨天那条带白条纹的红蛇咬了我，我差点就死了。”这是我们很容易就能做出的观察。然后我们更进一步：“我假设如果我遇到同一条蛇，同样的事情还会发生！”这是一种我们已经运用了数百万年的科学学习方式。在地球上短暂的七八十年里，我们不可能摆脱它。
So it’s possible for us to continue exploring our world as we age. Of course, we don’t always find ourselves in environments that encourage such curiosity as we grow older. I’ve been fortunate to have a career that allowed me the freedom to pick my own projects. Before that, I was lucky to have my mother .
所以，随着年龄增长，我们依然可以继续探索世界。当然，随着年龄增长，我们并非总能身处鼓励这种好奇心的环境。我很幸运，我的职业让我可以自由选择自己感兴趣的项目。在此之前，我很幸运拥有我的母亲。
Encouraging curiosity with a passion
以热情鼓励好奇心
I remember, when I was 3 years old, obtaining a sudden interest in dinosaurs. I had no idea that my mother had been waiting for it. That very day, the house began its transformation into all things Jurassic. And Triassic. And Cretaceous. Pictures of dinosaurs would go up on the wall. I would begin to find books about dinosaurs strewn on the floor and sofas. Mom would even call dinner “dinosaur food,” and we would spend hours laughing our heads off trying to make dinosaur sounds. And then, suddenly, I would lose interest in dinosaurs, because some friend at school acquired an interest in spaceships and rockets and galaxies. Extraordinarily, my mother was waiting. Just as quickly as my whim changed, the house would begin its transformation from big dinosaurs to Big Bang. The reptilian posters came down, and in their places, planets would begin to hang from the walls. I would find little pictures of satellites in the bathroom. Mom even got “space coins” from bags of potato chips, and I eventually gathered all of them into a collector’s book.
我记得三岁那年，我突然对恐龙产生了浓厚的兴趣。我当时完全不知道，妈妈其实一直在等着我。就在那天，家里开始变成侏罗纪、三叠纪、白垩纪的世界。墙上贴满了恐龙的图片。地板和沙发上到处散落着恐龙书。妈妈甚至把晚餐叫做“恐龙食物”，我们俩会花好几个小时，一边模仿恐龙的叫声一边开怀大笑。然后，突然之间，我对恐龙的兴趣就消失了，因为学校里某个朋友迷上了宇宙飞船、火箭和星系。神奇的是，妈妈早就预料到了。我的兴致一变，家里就立刻从恐龙主题变成了宇宙大爆炸主题。恐龙海报被取了下来，取而代之的是行星的图案挂在墙上。我甚至会在浴室里发现卫星的小图片。妈妈甚至从薯片包装袋里收集到了“太空硬币”，我最终把它们全部收集到了一本收藏册里。
This happened over and over again in my childhood. I got an interest in Greek mythology, and she transformed the house into Mount Olympus. My interests careened into geometry, and the house became Euclidean, then cubist. Rocks, airplanes. By the time I was 8 or 9, I was creating my own house transformations.
这样的事在我童年时期反复发生。我对希腊神话产生了兴趣，她就把房子改造成了奥林匹斯山。后来我的兴趣转向了几何学，房子变成了欧几里得几何风格，然后又变成了立体主义风格。岩石、飞机……到了八九岁，我就开始自己改造房子了。
One day, around age 14, I declared to my mother that I was an atheist. She was a devoutly religious person, and I thought this announcement would crush her. Instead, she said something like “That’s nice, dear,” as if I had just declared I no longer liked nachos. The next day, she sat me down by the kitchen table, a wrapped package in her lap. She said calmly, “So I hear you are now an atheist. Is that true?” I nodded yes, and she smiled. She placed the package in my hands. “The man’s name is Friedrich Nietzsche, and the book is called Twilight of the Idols ,” she said. “If you are going to be an atheist, be the best one out there. Bon appetit! ”
大约14岁的时候，有一天我向母亲宣布我是个无神论者。她是个虔诚的信徒，我以为这番话会让她崩溃。没想到，她只是淡淡地说了句“真好，亲爱的”，就好像我只是宣布自己不再喜欢吃玉米片一样。第二天，她让我坐在厨房的桌子旁，腿上放着一个包装好的包裹。她平静地问：“听说你现在是无神论者了，是真的吗？”我点点头，她笑了。她把包裹放在我手里。“这个人名叫弗里德里希·尼采，书名叫《偶像的黄昏》。”她说，“如果你要做个无神论者，那就做到最好。祝你胃口好！”
I was stunned. But I understood a powerful message: Curiosity itself was the most important thing. And what I was interested in mattered . I have never been able to turn off this fire hose of curiosity.
我当时震惊了。但我领悟到一个重要的信息：好奇心本身才是最重要的。而我感兴趣的事物也至关重要。我永远也无法关闭这股源源不断的好奇心。
Most developmental psychologists believe that a child’s need to know is a drive as pure as a diamond and as distracting as chocolate. Even though there is no agreed-upon definition of curiosity in cognitive neuroscience, I couldn’t agree more. I firmly believe that if children are allowed to remain curious, they will continue to deploy their natural tendencies to discover and explore until they are 101. This is something my mother seemed to know instinctively.
大多数发展心理学家认为，孩子的求知欲纯粹如钻石，却也像巧克力一样令人难以抗拒。尽管认知神经科学界对好奇心尚未达成共识，但我对此深表赞同。我坚信，如果允许孩子保持好奇心，他们就会一直运用这种与生俱来的探索和发现的本能，直到101岁高龄。我的母亲似乎对此有着与生俱来的领悟。
For little ones, discovery brings joy. Like an addictive drug, exploration creates the need for more discovery so that more joy can be experienced. It is a straight-up reward system that, if allowed to flourish, will continue into the school years. As children get older, they find that learning brings them not only joy but also mastery. Expertise in specific subjects breeds the confidence to take intellectual risks. If these kids don’t end up in the emergency room, they may end up with a Nobel Prize.
对孩子们来说，探索带来快乐。就像上瘾的毒品一样，探索会激发他们渴望发现更多，从而体验更多快乐。这是一种直接的奖励机制，如果任其发展，这种机制会一直延续到学龄阶段。随着孩子年龄的增长，他们会发现学习不仅带来快乐，还能带来成就感。对特定学科的精通会培养他们敢于尝试新事物的自信。如果这些孩子最终没有进急诊室，他们或许会获得诺贝尔奖。
I believe it is possible to break this cycle, anesthetizing both the process and the child. By first grade, for example, children learn that education means an A. They begin to understand that they can acquire knowledge not because it is interesting, but because it can get them something. Fascination can become secondary to “What do I need to know to get the grade?” But I also believe the curiosity instinct is so powerful that some people overcome society’s message to go to sleep intellectually, and they flourish anyway.
我相信打破这种恶性循环是可能的，即通过麻痹学习过程和孩子本身。例如，到了一年级，孩子们就明白学习意味着拿A。他们开始明白，获取知识不是因为有趣，而是因为知识能给他们带来好处。兴趣爱好变得次要，取而代之的是“我需要知道什么才能拿到好成绩？”但我相信，好奇心是如此强大，以至于有些人能够克服社会灌输的“停止思考”的观念，最终依然能够茁壮成长。
My grandfather was one of those people. He was born in 1892 and lived to be 101 years old. He spoke eight languages, went through several fortunes, and remained in his own house (mowing his own lawn) until the age of 100. He was lively as a firecracker to the end. At a party celebrating his centenary, he took me aside. “You know, Juanito ,” he said, clearing his throat, “sixty-six years separate the Wright brothers’ airplane from Neil Armstrong and the moon.” He shook his head, marveling. “I was born with the horse and buggy. I die with the space shuttle. What kind of thing is that?” His eyes twinkled. “I live the good life!”
我的祖父就是这样的人。他生于1892年，活到了101岁。他会说八种语言，几度发家致富，直到100岁高龄都一直住在自己的房子里（自己修剪草坪）。他直到生命的尽头都像个活生生的鞭炮。在他百岁生日的庆祝会上，他把我拉到一边。“你知道吗，胡安尼托，”他清了清嗓子说，“从莱特兄弟发明飞机到尼尔·阿姆斯特朗登月，这中间相隔了66年。”他摇了摇头，惊叹道：“我出生的时候马车还很古老，去世的时候航天飞机已经发射了。这算什么？”他的眼睛闪闪发光。“我过着多么美好的生活啊！”
He died a year later.
一年后他去世了。
I think of him a lot when I think of exploration. I think of my mother and her magically transforming rooms. I think of my youngest son experimenting with his tongue, and my oldest son’s overwhelming urge to take on a beesting. And I think that we must do a better job of encouraging lifelong curiosity, in our workplaces, our homes, and especially in our schools.
每当我想到探索，我就会想起他。我会想起我的母亲和她那神奇的、能把房间变成各种奇景的房间。我会想起我最小的儿子用舌头做各种尝试，以及我大儿子对蜜蜂叮咬的强烈渴望。我认为，我们必须在工作场所、家庭，尤其是在学校里，更好地鼓励终身好奇心。
More ideas
更多想法
On a personal level, what this tells us is to follow our passions. But I would also like to see change on a broader scale so that our environments truly support our individual efforts to remain curious.
就个人而言，这告诉我们应该追随自己的热情。但我同时也希望看到更广泛的改变，使我们所处的环境真正支持我们保持好奇心的个人努力。
Free time at work
工作中的空闲时间
Smart companies take to heart the power of exploration. For example, companies such as 3M, Genentech, and Google allowed employees to use 15 or 20 percent of their workweek to go where their mind asks them to go. The proof is in the bottom line: At Google, fully 50 percent of new products—including Gmail, Google News, and AdSense—came from “20 percent time.” Facebook, LinkedIn, and other tech companies hold “hackathons”: marathon programming sessions where coders can earn prizes for creating something interesting.
聪明的公司深谙探索的力量。例如，3M、基因泰克和谷歌等公司允许员工每周利用15%到20%的工作时间去探索他们脑海中浮现的任何想法。最终的成果证明了这一点：在谷歌，高达50%的新产品——包括Gmail、谷歌新闻和AdSense——都源于“20%的自由时间”。Facebook、LinkedIn和其他科技公司会举办“黑客马拉松”：马拉松式的编程活动，程序员可以通过创造出有趣的东西来赢取奖品。
Schools where you learn on the job
在职学习学校
If you could step back in time to one of the first Western-style universities, say, the University of Bologna, and visit its biology labs, you would laugh out loud. I would join you. By today’s standards, biological science in the 11th century was a joke, a mix of astrological influences, religious forces, dead animals, and rude-smelling chemical concoctions. But if you went down the hall and peered inside Bologna’s standard lecture room, you wouldn’t feel as if you were in a museum. You would feel at home. There is a lectern for the teacher to hold forth, surrounded by chairs for the students to absorb whatever is being held forth—much like today’s classrooms. Could it be time for a change?
如果你能穿越时空，回到最早的西式大学之一，比如博洛尼亚大学，参观一下它的生物实验室，你一定会捧腹大笑。我也会和你一样。以今天的标准来看，11世纪的生物科学简直是个笑话，它混杂着占星术、宗教信仰、动物标本和气味难闻的化学制剂。但如果你走进博洛尼亚大学标准的阶梯教室，你不会感觉像置身博物馆，反而会感到宾至如归。教室里有讲台供老师讲课，周围摆放着椅子供学生聆听——和今天的教室很像。或许是时候做出改变了？
Some people have tried to harness our natural exploratory tendencies by using “problem-based” or “discovery-based” learning models. What’s missing are empirical results that show the long-term effects of these styles. To this end, I would like to see more degree programs modeled after medical schools. The best medical-school model has three components: a teaching hospital; faculty who work in the field as well as teach; and research laboratories. It is a surprisingly successful way of transferring complex information from one brain to another. Students get consistent exposure to the real world, by the third year spending half of their time in class and half learning on the job. They are taught by people who actually do what they teach as their “day job.” And they get to participate in practical research programs.
有些人尝试利用“问题导向”或“发现导向”的学习模式来激发我们天生的探索倾向。然而，目前缺乏实证研究来证明这些学习方式的长期效果。为此，我希望看到更多学位课程效仿医学院的模式。最佳的医学院模式包含三个要素：教学医院；既从事临床实践又兼任教学的教师；以及科研实验室。这种模式能够有效地将复杂的知识从一个人的大脑传递给另一个人。学生们能够持续接触真实世界，到第三年时，他们一半的时间用于课堂学习，一半的时间用于在职学习。他们的老师本身就是从事相关工作的专业人士。此外，他们还有机会参与实践性的研究项目。
Here’s a typical experience in medical school: The clinician-professor is lecturing in a traditional classroom setting and brings in a patient to illustrate some of his points. The professor announces: “Here is the patient. Notice that he has disease X with symptoms A, B, C, and D.” He then begins to lecture on the biology of disease X. While everybody is taking notes, a smart medical student raises her hand and says, “I see symptoms A, B, C, and D. What about symptoms E, F, and G?” The professor looks a bit chagrined (or excited) and responds, “We don’t know about symptoms E, F, and G.” You can hear a pin drop at those moments, and the impatient voices whispering inside the students’ heads are almost audible: “Well, let’s find out!” These are the opening words of most of the great research ideas in human medicine.
以下是医学院里一个典型的场景：临床教授在传统的课堂上讲课，并带进一位病人来阐释一些观点。教授宣布：“这位病人就是病人。请注意，他患有X疾病，症状有A、B、C和D。”然后，他开始讲解X疾病的生物学原理。大家都在记笔记的时候，一位聪明的医学生举手问道：“我看到了症状A、B、C和D。那么症状E、F和G呢？”教授看起来有些尴尬（或者兴奋），回答说：“我们对症状E、F和G并不了解。”那一刻，教室里鸦雀无声，学生们心中焦急的声音几乎清晰可闻：“那我们就来研究一下！”这往往是人类医学中大多数伟大研究理念的开篇之语。
That’s true exploratory magic. The tendency is so strong that you have to deliberately cut off the discussions to keep the ideas from forming. Rather than cutting off such discussions, most American medical schools possess powerful research wings. By simple juxtaposition of real-world needs with traditional book learning, a research program is born.
这才是真正的探索魔法。这种倾向如此强烈，以至于你必须刻意阻止讨论，以免想法形成。然而，大多数美国医学院并没有阻止此类讨论，而是拥有强大的研究部门。通过将现实世界的需求与传统的书本知识相结合，研究项目便应运而生。
I envision a college of education where the program is all about brain development. Like a medical school, it is divided into three parts. It has traditional classrooms. It is a community school staffed and run by three types of faculty: traditional education faculty who teach the college students, certified teachers who teach the little ones attending the community school, and brain scientists who run the research labs devoted to a single purpose: investigating how the human brain learns in teaching environments, then actively testing hypothesized ideas in real-world classroom situations.
我设想建立一所教育学院，其课程全部围绕大脑发育展开。它像医学院一样，分为三个部分：传统的教室；一所社区学校，由三种类型的教师组成：教授大学学生的传统教育教师；教授社区学校低年级学生的持证教师；以及负责研究实验室的脑科学家。这些实验室致力于一个共同的目标：研究人类大脑在教学环境中的学习方式，并将假设应用于真实的课堂情境中进行验证。
Students would get a bachelor of science in education. Future educators are infused with deep knowledge about how the human brain acquires information. After their first year of study, students would start actively participating in the on-site school.
学生将获得教育学理学士学位。未来的教育工作者将深入了解人脑如何获取信息。完成第一年的学习后，学生将开始积极参与校内教学活动。
This model honors our evolutionary need to explore. It creates teachers who know about brain development. And it’s a place to do the real-world research so sorely needed to figure out how, exactly, the rules of the brain should be applied to our lives. The model could apply to other academic subjects as well. A business school teaching how to run a small business might actually run one, for example.
这种模式尊重我们与生俱来的探索欲。它培养出了解大脑发育的教师。它也为开展亟需的现实世界研究提供了场所，帮助我们弄清楚大脑的运行规律究竟应该如何应用于我们的生活。这种模式也可以应用于其他学科。例如，一所教授如何经营小型企业的商学院，其学生或许真的会去经营一家小型企业。
A student could create a version of this learning experience on her own, by seeking out internship opportunities while in school.
学生可以通过在校期间寻找实习机会，自行创造类似的学习体验。
A sense of wonder
一种惊奇感
My 2-year-old son Noah and I were walking down the street on our way to preschool when he suddenly noticed a shiny pebble embedded in the concrete. Stopping midstride, the little guy considered it for a second, found it thoroughly delightful, and let out a laugh. He spied a small plant an inch farther, a weed valiantly struggling through a crack in the asphalt. He touched it gently, then laughed again. Noah noticed beyond it a platoon of ants marching in single file, which he bent down to examine closely. They were carrying a dead bug, and Noah clapped his hands in wonder. There were dust particles, a rusted screw, a shiny spot of oil. Fifteen minutes had passed, and we had gone only 20 feet. I tried to get him to move along, having the audacity to act like an adult with a schedule. He was having none of it. And I stopped, watching my little teacher, wondering how long it had been since I had taken 15 minutes to walk 20 feet.
我和两岁的儿子诺亚正走在去幼儿园的路上，突然他注意到水泥地上嵌着一颗闪闪发光的小石子。他停下脚步，仔细端详了一会儿，觉得这小东西可爱极了，哈哈大笑起来。他又看到一小株植物，一株杂草顽强地从沥青路面的缝隙里挣扎着生长。他轻轻地摸了摸，又笑了起来。诺亚注意到植物后面有一队蚂蚁排成一列行进，他弯下腰仔细观察。蚂蚁们正抬着一只死虫子，诺亚惊奇地拍起了手。地上还有灰尘、生锈的螺丝钉和一小块闪亮的油渍。十五分钟过去了，我们才走了二十英尺。我试图催他快点走，还自作聪明地像个有时间安排的大人。他根本不听。我停下脚步，看着我的小老师，心想自己上次走二十英尺要花十五分钟是什么时候了。
The greatest Brain Rule of all is something I cannot prove or characterize, but I believe in it with all my heart. As my son was trying to tell me, it is the importance of curiosity. For his sake and ours, I wish classrooms and companies were designed with the brain in mind. If we started over, curiosity would be the most vital part of both demolition crew and reconstruction crew. As I hope to have related here, I am very much in favor of both.
大脑最重要的法则我无法证明或描述，但我真心相信它。正如我儿子试图告诉我的那样，那就是好奇心的重要性。为了他，也为了我们自己，我希望教室和公司在设计时都能以大脑为中心。如果一切可以重来，好奇心将是拆迁队和重建队最重要的组成部分。正如我在此所表达的，我非常支持这两种做法。
I will never forget the moment my little professor taught his daddy about what it meant to be a student. I was thankful and a little embarrassed. After 47 years, I was finally learning how to walk down the street.
我永远不会忘记我的小教授教他爸爸什么是学生的那一刻。我既感激又有点不好意思。47年后，我终于学会了如何走在街上。
Brain Rule #12
大脑法则第12条
We are powerful and natural explorers.
我们是强大而天生的探险家。
• Babies are the model of how we learn—not by passive reaction to the environment but by active testing through observation, hypothesis, experiment, and conclusion.
•婴儿是我们学习方式的典范——不是被动地对环境做出反应，而是通过观察、假设、实验和得出结论来进行主动测试。
• Specific parts of the brain allow this scientific approach. The right prefrontal cortex looks for errors in our hypothesis (“The saber-toothed tiger is not harmless”), and an adjoining region tells us to change behavior (“Run!”).
•大脑的特定区域使我们能够进行这种科学思考。右侧前额叶皮层会寻找我们假设中的错误（“剑齿虎并非无害”），而邻近区域则会告诉我们改变行为（“快跑！”）。
• We can recognize and imitate behavior because of “mirror neurons” scattered across the brain.
•由于大脑中散布着“镜像神经元”，我们能够识别和模仿他人的行为。
• Some parts of our adult brains stay as malleable as a baby’s so that we can create neurons and learn new things throughout our lives.
•我们成年人的大脑某些部分仍然像婴儿的大脑一样具有可塑性，以便我们能够在一生中不断产生神经元并学习新事物。

The human brain evolved, too.
人类大脑也随之进化。

运动能增强脑力。

睡好觉，才能头脑清醒。

压力过大的大脑学习方式与正常大脑不同。

Acknowledgments
致谢
IN A LIST OF just about anything, items at the beginning and end are the easiest for the brain to retrieve. It’s called serial position effect, and I mention it because I am about to list some of the many people who helped bring this project to fruition. There obviously will be a first person and a last person and lots of people in between. This is not because I see these folks in a hierarchy of values; it is simply because written languages are necessarily, cursedly linear. Please pay attention, dear reader, to the folks in the middle as well as to those at the end points. As I have often mentioned to graduate students, there is great value in the middle of most U-shaped curves.
在任何清单中，开头和结尾的项目最容易被大脑提取。这被称为序列位置效应，我之所以提到它，是因为我即将列出一些为这个项目的成功做出贡献的人。显然，名单上会有第一位和最后一位，以及中间的许多人。这并非因为我把这些人放在价值等级的位置上；而是因为书面语言必然是线性的，尽管这种线性令人头疼。亲爱的读者，请您不仅关注两端的人，也关注中间的人。正如我经常跟研究生们提到的，大多数U型曲线的中间部分都蕴藏着巨大的价值。
First, I thank my publisher at Pear Press, Mark Pearson, the guiding hand of this project and easily the wisest, oldest young man with whom I have ever had the joy to work. It was a pleasure to work with editor Tracy Cutchlow, who with patience, laughter, and extraordinary thoughtfulness, taught me how to write.
首先，我要感谢梨出版社的马克·皮尔森，他是这个项目的指导者，也是我合作过的最睿智、最有经验的年轻人。与编辑特蕾西·卡奇洛的合作也十分愉快，她以耐心、幽默和非凡的细致，教会了我如何写作。
Special thanks to Dan Storm and Eric Chudler for providing invaluable scientific comments and expertise .
特别感谢 Dan Storm 和 Eric Chudler 提供宝贵的科学意见和专业知识。
I am grateful to friends on this journey with me: Lee Huntsman, for hours of patient listening and friendship for almost 20 years. Dennis Weibling, for believing in me and giving me such freedom to sow seeds. Paul Lange, whose curiosity and insights are still so vibrant after all these years (not bad for a “plumber”!). Bruce Hosford, for deep friendship, one of the most can-do people I have ever met.
我衷心感谢一路陪伴我的朋友们：李·亨茨曼，感谢他近二十年来耐心倾听我的心声，以及给予我的友谊；丹尼斯·韦布林，感谢他对我的信任，并给予我充分的自由去播撒梦想的种子；保罗·兰格，多年来他依然保持着旺盛的好奇心和敏锐的洞察力（对于一个“水管工”来说，这可真了不起！）；布鲁斯·霍斯福德，感谢他给予我的深厚友谊，他是我见过的最有干劲的人之一。
Thanks to Paul Yager, and my friends in the department of bioengineering at the University of Washington School of Medicine, for giving me opportunity. I’m also grateful to my colleagues at Seattle Pacific University: Frank Kline, Rick Eigenbrod, and Bill Rowley, for a spirit of adventure and for tolerance. Don Nielsen, who knew without a doubt that education really was about brain development. Julia Calhoun, who reigns as the premier example of emotional greatness. Alden Jones, amazing as you are, without whom none of my professional life would work.
感谢保罗·亚格尔，以及华盛顿大学医学院生物工程系的各位朋友，是他们给了我这个机会。我也要感谢西雅图太平洋大学的同事们：弗兰克·克莱恩、里克·艾根布罗德和比尔·罗利，感谢他们勇于探索的精神和宽容的胸怀。感谢唐·尼尔森，他坚信教育的真谛在于大脑发育。感谢朱莉娅·卡尔霍恩，她是情感卓越的典范。感谢奥尔登·琼斯，你如此出色，没有你，我的职业生涯将寸步难行。
And my deepest thanks to my beloved wife, Kari, who continually reminds me that love is the thing that makes you smile, even when you are tired. You, dear, are one in a million.
我最深的谢意要献给我挚爱的妻子卡莉，她总是提醒我，爱能让你微笑，即使在你疲惫的时候。亲爱的，你是万里挑一的。

About the author
关于作者
DR. JOHN J. MEDINA is a developmental molecular biologist focused on the genes involved in human brain development and the genetics of psychiatric disorders. He has spent most of his professional life as a private research consultant, working primarily in the biotechnology and pharmaceutical industries on research related to mental health. Medina holds an affiliate faculty appointment at the University of Washington School of Medicine, in its Department of Bioengineering.
约翰·J·梅迪纳博士是一位发育分子生物学家，专注于人类大脑发育相关基因和精神疾病遗传学的研究。他职业生涯的大部分时间都担任私人研究顾问，主要服务于生物技术和制药行业，从事与精神健康相关的研究。梅迪纳博士目前在华盛顿大学医学院生物工程系担任兼职教授。
Medina was the founding director of two brain research institutes: the Brain Center for Applied Learning Research, at Seattle Pacific University, and the Talaris Research Institute, a nonprofit organization originally focused on how infants encode and process information.
梅迪纳是两个脑科学研究所的创始主任：西雅图太平洋大学的脑科学应用学习研究中心和塔拉里斯研究所（一个非营利组织，最初专注于研究婴儿如何编码和处理信息）。
In 2004, Medina was appointed to the rank of affiliate scholar at the National Academy of Engineering. He has been named Outstanding Faculty of the Year at the College of Engineering at the University of Washington; the Merrill Dow/Continuing Medical Education National Teacher of the Year; and, twice, the Bioengineering Student Association Teacher of the Year. Medina has been a consultant to the Education Commission of the States and a regular speaker on the relationship between neurology and education.
2004年，梅迪纳被任命为美国国家工程院附属学者。他曾荣获华盛顿大学工程学院年度杰出教师奖、美林道/继续医学教育年度全国教师奖，并两次荣获生物工程学生协会年度教师奖。梅迪纳曾担任州教育委员会顾问，并经常就神经病学与教育的关系发表演讲。
Medina’s books include Brain Rules for Baby: How to Raise a Smart and Happy Child from Zero to Five ; The Genetic Inferno ; The Clock of Ages ; Depression: How It Happens, How It’s Healed; What You Need to Know About Alzheimer’s ; The Outer Limits of Life; Uncovering the Mystery of AIDS ; and Of Serotonin, Dopamine and Antipsychotic Medications .
梅迪纳的著作包括《婴儿大脑规则：如何从零到五岁培养聪明快乐的孩子》、《基因炼狱》、《年龄时钟》、《抑郁症：它的发生和治愈方法》、《关于阿尔茨海默病你需要知道的事》、《生命的极限》、《揭开艾滋病的秘密》以及《血清素、多巴胺和抗精神病药物》。
Medina has a lifelong fascination in how the mind reacts to and organizes information. As a husband and as a father of two boys, he has an interest in how the brain sciences might influence the way we teach our children. In addition to his research, consulting, and teaching, Medina speaks often to public officials, business and medical professionals, school boards, and nonprofit leaders.
梅迪纳毕生致力于研究大脑如何对信息做出反应并进行组织。作为一位丈夫和两个男孩的父亲，他关注脑科学如何影响我们教育孩子的方式。除了研究、咨询和教学之外，梅迪纳还经常为政府官员、商业和医疗专业人士、学校董事会成员以及非营利组织领导人发表演讲。
